items.ex: Under the Articles (in force March 1, 1781), each state kept its sovereignty, and Congress had no way to force states to obey its acts or national treaties. The Supremacy Clause, written in 1787, made national law supreme and bound state judges to follow it.
w: the Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause in Article IV makes states honor each other's records and judgments; it does not place national law above state law.
the Establishment Clause
The Establishment Clause, ratified in 1791, concerns religion, not national-state conflicts.
the Guarantee Clause
The Guarantee Clause promises each state a republican government; it does not settle conflicts of law.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article II of the Articles of Confederation (in force 1781), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Each state retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence…”
Source: Articles of Confederation, Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Why did the framers believe in 1787 that a supremacy clause was needed?
alt.a: States had ignored national laws and treaties
alt.ex: Under the Articles of Confederation (1781–1789), Congress had no national court system or separate executive to enforce its decisions, and states disregarded requisitions and the 1783 Treaty of Paris. The 1787 Supremacy Clause made national law binding on the states.
w: Congress had vetoed too many state laws
Congress under the Articles had no veto over state laws; the weakness was the opposite.
The President had overruled state governors
There was no President under the Articles of Confederation.
Federal courts had overturned too many state laws
The Articles created no general federal court system to overturn anything.

alt.q: Which sequence is in the correct order?
alt.a: Articles take effect → Treaty of Paris → Supremacy Clause written
alt.ex: The Articles took effect in 1781, the Treaty of Paris ended the Revolutionary War in 1783, and the Supremacy Clause was written in 1787. States' violations of the 1783 treaty under the weak Articles were one reason for the clause.
w: Treaty of Paris → Supremacy Clause written → Articles take effect
The Articles took effect in 1781, before both the 1783 treaty and the 1787 clause.
Supremacy Clause written → Articles take effect → Treaty of Paris
The Supremacy Clause (1787) came last, after the Articles (1781) and the treaty (1783).
Articles take effect → Supremacy Clause written → Treaty of Paris
The Treaty of Paris (1783) came before the Supremacy Clause (1787).

items.q: In July 1787, Convention delegates rejected James Madison's plan to let Congress veto state laws. What did they adopt instead?
items.a: a rule binding state judges to federal law
items.ex: On July 17, 1787, the congressional veto (the “negative”) failed 3–7, and the delegates then adopted, without dissent, a resolution making national laws and treaties supreme and binding on state judges. Most delegates thought courts were a simpler way to void conflicting state laws.
w: a rule letting governors veto federal laws
The Convention moved toward national supremacy; it gave governors no veto over federal law.
a plan for Congress to appoint state judges
State judges are chosen under state law; no such plan was adopted.
a council of states to review federal laws
No council of states was created; conflicts were left to the courts.

alt.q: Why did most Convention delegates vote in July 1787 against giving Congress a veto over all state laws?
alt.a: Courts could void conflicting state laws instead
alt.ex: On July 17, 1787, delegates such as Roger Sherman and Gouverneur Morris argued that a congressional veto was unnecessary and clumsy because courts would refuse to apply state laws that conflicted with national law. The veto failed 3–7, and the supremacy resolution passed the same day.
w: States had no laws that needed review
States passed many laws that conflicted with national interests; that was the problem being addressed.
The President already had that power
No President existed yet, and no executive was ever given a veto over state laws.
The Articles already gave Congress that same power
The Articles gave Congress no veto over state laws, which is why Madison proposed one.

alt.q: Whose motion in July 1787 became the starting point for the Supremacy Clause?
alt.a: Luther Martin of Maryland
alt.ex: On July 17, 1787, after the congressional veto on state laws was defeated, Luther Martin moved that national laws and treaties be the supreme law of the states, binding state judges; it passed without dissent. Martin wanted courts, not Congress, to handle conflicts.
w: James Madison of Virginia
Madison proposed the congressional veto over state laws, which was voted down that same day.
Roger Sherman of Connecticut
Sherman opposed the veto and is best known for the Great Compromise, not the supremacy motion.
Gouverneur Morris of Pennsylvania
Morris opposed the veto and later polished the Constitution's wording, but he did not make this motion.

items.q: Madison wrote this passage in 1788 to defend which part of the proposed Constitution?
items.a: the Supremacy Clause
items.ex: In Federalist No. 44 (1788), Madison argued that without the Supremacy Clause the national government would be subordinate to the states, a “monster” with the head directed by its members. He defended the clause to win ratification.
w: the Commerce Clause
The passage is about whole-versus-parts authority, the problem the Supremacy Clause solves, not trade.
the Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns states honoring one another's records, not national authority over states.
the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment did not exist in 1788; it was ratified in 1791.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from The Federalist No. 44 (1788) by James Madison, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…it would have seen the authority of the whole society every where subordinate to the authority of the parts; it would have seen a monster, in which the head was under the direction of the members.”
Source: The Federalist No. 44

alt.q: Based on this 1788 passage, what did Madison warn would happen without the Supremacy Clause?
alt.a: The states would control the national government
alt.ex: Madison wrote in 1788 that without supremacy, the authority of the whole society would be subordinate to “the parts,” meaning the states. He supported the clause so the national government could act for the whole nation.
w: The President would gain control over Congress
The passage is about the states (“the parts”) and the nation (“the whole”), not the branches.
The national government would abolish the states
Madison feared the opposite: the parts (states) ruling the whole (nation).
The federal courts would gain control of the President
The passage does not discuss courts or the President.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from The Federalist No. 44 (1788) by James Madison, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…it would have seen the authority of the whole society every where subordinate to the authority of the parts; it would have seen a monster, in which the head was under the direction of the members.”
Source: The Federalist No. 44

alt.q: In which year did Madison publish this defense of national supremacy during the fight over ratification?
alt.ex: Federalist No. 44 appeared in January 1788, while the states were debating ratification of the 1787 Constitution. Madison wrote it to answer Anti-Federalist fears that the Supremacy Clause would swallow the states.
w: In 1776 the colonies declared independence; there was no Constitution to defend.
In 1781 the Articles of Confederation took effect; the Federalist essays came seven years later.
In 1798 Madison wrote the Virginia Resolutions, which took a states'-rights position, not this essay.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from The Federalist No. 44 (1788) by James Madison, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…it would have seen the authority of the whole society every where subordinate to the authority of the parts; it would have seen a monster, in which the head was under the direction of the members.”
Source: The Federalist No. 44

items.q: In Ware v. Hylton (1796), why did the Supreme Court strike down a Virginia law about debts owed to British creditors?
items.a: It conflicted with the 1783 Treaty of Paris
items.ex: In 1796 the Court held that the Treaty of Paris, which promised British creditors no lawful impediment to collecting pre-war debts, overrode a 1777 Virginia law letting debtors pay into a state loan office. Under Article VI, a treaty is supreme over state law.
w: It violated the First Amendment
The case was about a treaty and debts, not speech, press, or religion.
It taxed the Bank of the United States
That describes Maryland's law in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
It clashed with a federal steamboat license
That describes New York's monopoly in Gibbons v. Ogden (1824).

alt.q: Which case, decided in 1796, applied the Supremacy Clause to place a treaty above a state law?
alt.a: Ware v. Hylton
alt.ex: In Ware v. Hylton (1796), the Court ruled that the 1783 Treaty of Paris overrode a Virginia law on British debts. It showed that the new Constitution, unlike the Articles of Confederation, could force states to honor national treaties.
w: Marbury v. Madison
Marbury (1803) established judicial review over a federal law, not treaty supremacy over a state.
Missouri v. Holland
Missouri v. Holland upheld a treaty-based federal law over state claims, but in 1920, not 1796.
McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch (1819) involved a state tax on a federal bank, not a treaty.

alt.q: Under Article VI of the Constitution, which outcome is most likely?
alt.a: The treaty controls, and the debt is still owed
alt.ex: Article VI (1787) makes treaties supreme over state law. In Ware v. Hylton (1796), the Court applied this to the 1783 Treaty of Paris, so British creditors could still collect despite Virginia's law.
w: The state law controls, since debts are a local matter
A valid treaty overrides conflicting state law, even on a subject states normally handle.
The treaty applies only after Congress repeals the law
Congress does not repeal state laws; the treaty overrides them automatically.
The debt is canceled because the war ended it
The treaty expressly protected pre-war debts, so the war did not cancel them.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: After the Revolutionary War, a state passes a law letting residents who owe money to British merchants pay the debt into a state loan office instead. A peace treaty signed by the United States says creditors shall meet no lawful impediment to collecting such debts. A British creditor sues to collect.

items.q: Based on this 1819 passage, why could Maryland not tax the Second Bank of the United States?
items.a: A state tax could destroy a valid federal institution
items.ex: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Chief Justice Marshall reasoned that if states could tax federal institutions, they could destroy them. Because the bank was a valid exercise of federal power, the Supremacy Clause barred Maryland's tax.
w: The bank was not named in the Constitution
Maryland argued this to claim the bank was invalid; the Court rejected it and upheld the bank.
Maryland voters had not approved the tax
The ruling did not depend on voter approval; any state tax on the bank was barred.
Only Congress may tax any bank that operates inside a state
States may tax their own banks; they may not tax federal institutions.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That the power to tax involves the power to destroy; that the power to destroy may defeat and render useless the power to create…”
Source: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)

alt.q: In what year did the Supreme Court decide McCulloch v. Maryland, ruling that a state could not tax a federal bank?
alt.ex: McCulloch v. Maryland was decided March 6, 1819. The unanimous Court upheld the Second Bank of the United States under implied powers and struck down Maryland's tax because federal law is supreme over state law.
w: 1803 is the year of Marbury v. Madison, which established judicial review.
1824 is the year of Gibbons v. Ogden, about steamboats and interstate commerce.
In 1832 South Carolina tried to nullify federal tariffs, and Jackson vetoed the bank's recharter.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case most directly supports striking down this tax?
alt.a: McCulloch v. Maryland
alt.ex: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court held that states may not tax or otherwise burden the operations of a valid federal institution, because federal law is supreme. A state tax aimed at the U.S. Postal Service's operations would fail for the same reason.
w: Gibbons v. Ogden
Gibbons (1824) struck down a state steamboat monopoly; it was not about state taxes on federal operations.
Marbury v. Madison
Marbury (1803) concerned judicial review of a federal law, not a state tax.
Dartmouth College v. Woodward
Dartmouth College (1819) protected a private college charter under the Contract Clause; it did not involve taxes.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state passes a special tax on every package the U.S. Postal Service handles inside the state, to raise money for state roads. The Postal Service refuses to pay, and the state sues.

items.q: Based on this passage from 1787, which officials must swear or affirm to support the U.S. Constitution?
items.a: both federal and state officials
items.ex: Article VI, Clause 3 (1787) requires members of Congress, state legislators, and all executive and judicial officers of both the United States and the states to swear or affirm support for the Constitution. The oath ties state officers to the national Constitution, reinforcing the Supremacy Clause.
w: only officials of the federal government
The passage also names state legislators and state executive and judicial officers.
only members of Congress
Congress is included, but so are state and executive and judicial officers.
only state court judges
State judges are included, but so are many other federal and state officials.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article VI of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Senators and Representatives before mentioned, and the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution; but no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: The first law passed by the new Congress, signed June 1, 1789, carried out which part of Article VI?
alt.a: the oath to support the Constitution
alt.ex: The first act of Congress, signed by President Washington on June 1, 1789, set the time and manner of administering the Article VI oath to support the Constitution. It put into practice the 1787 rule that federal and state officers be bound by oath.
w: the ban on religious tests for office
The religious-test ban is also in Article VI, but the 1789 act dealt with administering oaths.
the promise to pay earlier national debts
Article VI, Clause 1 kept Confederation debts valid; the first act was about oaths.
the rule making treaties supreme law
Treaties are supreme under Clause 2 automatically; the first act concerned oaths.

alt.q: In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), why did the Court point to the oath that state officials take under Article VI?
alt.a: The oath commits them to obey the Constitution
alt.ex: In 1958 the Court said every state legislator, executive, and judicial officer is bound by the Article VI, Clause 3 oath to support the Constitution, so Arkansas officials could not defy Brown v. Board of Education. The oath turns national supremacy into a personal duty.
w: The oath lets them reject federal court rulings
The Court said the oath means the opposite: officials cannot war against the Constitution.
The oath applies only to federal judges
Article VI, Clause 3 names state legislators and state executive and judicial officers too.
The oath requires a belief in God
Article VI bans religious tests for federal office; the oath has no religious requirement.

items.q: Based on this 1824 passage, why did New York's steamboat monopoly law fail?
items.a: It conflicted with a federal license law
items.ex: In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), Chief Justice Marshall held that New York's monopoly clashed with Gibbons's license under the federal coasting act of 1793. When a valid act of Congress and a state law conflict, the state law must yield under the Supremacy Clause.
w: It took private property without payment
The Takings Clause was not the basis; the ruling rested on a conflict with an act of Congress.
It taxed a federally chartered bank
That was the issue in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
It lacked the New York governor's signature
The ruling did not concern how New York enacted the law; it concerned the conflict with federal law.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“In every such case, the act of Congress or the treaty is supreme, and the law of the State, though enacted in the exercise of powers not controverted, must yield to it.”
Source: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)

alt.q: Which case, decided in 1824, struck down a state steamboat monopoly because it clashed with an act of Congress?
alt.a: Gibbons v. Ogden
alt.ex: In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), the Court ruled that New York's monopoly on steamboats conflicted with a federal license granted under a 1793 act. Because federal law is supreme, the monopoly could not stop licensed boats from operating between states.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch (1819) struck down a state tax on a federal bank, not a steamboat monopoly.
Fletcher v. Peck
Fletcher (1810) struck down a state law under the Contract Clause; it had nothing to do with steamboats.
Dartmouth College v. Woodward
Dartmouth College (1819) protected a college charter under the Contract Clause.

alt.q: What was the most significant effect of Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)?
alt.a: It widened federal power over interstate commerce
alt.ex: Gibbons (1824) read the Commerce Clause broadly to include navigation and held that a conflicting state monopoly must yield to federal law. This opened waterways to competition and strengthened national authority over trade between states.
w: It let the states alone license all interstate shipping
The ruling did the reverse: a federal license overrode New York's control.
It ended the Second Bank of the United States
The bank's charter expired in 1836 after Jackson's 1832 veto, not because of Gibbons.
It upheld state monopolies on major rivers
The Court struck down New York's monopoly as conflicting with federal law.

items.q: Which federal laws was this 1798 resolution written to protest?
items.a: the Alien and Sedition Acts
items.ex: Virginia adopted these resolutions in December 1798 to protest the Alien and Sedition Acts, passed by a Federalist Congress earlier that year. Critics said the acts exceeded federal power and violated freedom of speech and the press.
w: the Tariff of 1828
The 1828 tariff led to South Carolina's nullification in 1832, decades after these resolutions.
the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
This law sparked northern resistance, such as Wisconsin's in Ableman v. Booth (1859).
the Judiciary Act of 1789
The 1789 act created the federal courts; it was not the target of the 1798 resolutions.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Virginia Resolutions (1798), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…in case of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of other powers, not granted by the said compact, the states who are parties thereto, have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil…”
Source: Virginia Resolutions, Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Based on this passage, what right did Virginia claim in 1798?
alt.a: a right to resist unconstitutional federal laws
alt.ex: The 1798 Virginia Resolutions claimed that states could “interpose” against federal laws they judged to exceed the Constitution, here the Alien and Sedition Acts. This states'-rights theory clashes with the Supremacy Clause and with federal courts' final say.
w: a right to leave the Union at any time it wished
The resolutions did not claim a right to secede; they claimed a right to interpose.
a right to make its own treaties with foreign nations
Article I, Section 10 forbids states to make treaties, and the passage does not claim it.
a right to elect the judges of the federal courts
Federal judges are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Virginia Resolutions (1798), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…in case of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of other powers, not granted by the said compact, the states who are parties thereto, have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil…”
Source: Virginia Resolutions, Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Which pair of founders secretly wrote the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798?
alt.a: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison
alt.ex: In 1798 Vice President Jefferson secretly drafted the Kentucky Resolutions and Madison the Virginia Resolutions. They wanted to rally opposition to the Alien and Sedition Acts, which they believed exceeded federal power and attacked free speech.
w: John Adams and Alexander Hamilton
Adams signed the Alien and Sedition Acts, and Hamilton was a leading Federalist; they did not oppose them.
John Marshall and John Jay
Marshall and Jay were Federalists who favored national power, not these protests.
Andrew Jackson and John C. Calhoun
Calhoun built on the resolutions in 1828–32, and Jackson opposed nullification; neither wrote them.

items.q: Which later event put the idea in this 1799 passage into action?
items.a: South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification
items.ex: Kentucky's 1799 resolution called nullification of unauthorized federal acts “the rightful remedy.” In November 1832, South Carolina acted on that theory by declaring the federal tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void within the state.
w: the Missouri Compromise passed by Congress in 1820
The Missouri Compromise balanced free and slave states; no state nullified a federal law.
the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848
Seneca Falls was a women's rights meeting, not a state's attempt to void federal law.
the Compromise of 1850
The Compromise of 1850 was passed by Congress; it was not a state nullifying federal law.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Kentucky Resolutions of 1799, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…a nullification, by those sovereignties, of all unauthorized acts done under colour of that instrument, is the rightful remedy…”
Source: Kentucky Resolutions, Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Why does the doctrine described in this 1799 passage contradict Article VI of the Constitution?
alt.a: Article VI makes valid federal law supreme over state law
alt.ex: Article VI (1787) makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties supreme and binds state judges to them. Nullification, as Kentucky described it in 1799, would let each state void federal laws on its own, which the Supremacy Clause does not allow.
w: Article VI lets each state void federal laws it dislikes
This describes nullification itself; Article VI says the opposite.
Article VI gives Congress a veto over all state laws
The Convention rejected a congressional veto in 1787; courts resolve conflicts instead.
Article VI applies only to treaties made with other nations
Article VI covers the Constitution and federal laws as well as treaties.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Kentucky Resolutions of 1799, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…a nullification, by those sovereignties, of all unauthorized acts done under colour of that instrument, is the rightful remedy…”
Source: Kentucky Resolutions, Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Which of these happened first?
alt.a: Kentucky calls nullification a remedy
alt.ex: Kentucky's resolution came in 1799. South Carolina nullified the tariffs in 1832, Wisconsin's court freed Sherman Booth in 1854, and Arkansas resisted integration at Little Rock in 1957. Each challenged the supremacy of federal authority.
w: South Carolina nullifies two federal tariffs
South Carolina's ordinance came in November 1832, after Kentucky's 1799 resolution.
Wisconsin's top court frees Sherman Booth
Wisconsin's court freed Booth in 1854, leading to Ableman v. Booth (1859).
Arkansas blocks integration at Little Rock
The Little Rock crisis happened in 1957, long after 1799.

items.q: Why did South Carolina adopt its Ordinance of Nullification in November 1832?
items.a: to block federal tariffs it called unfair
items.ex: In November 1832, a South Carolina convention declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void in the state. Leaders like John C. Calhoun argued the high tariffs hurt the South's export economy and that a state could nullify unconstitutional federal laws.
w: to block a branch of the national bank
Maryland's 1818 tax on a bank branch led to McCulloch v. Maryland, not to nullification in 1832.
to protest the Alien and Sedition Acts
Those 1798 laws prompted the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, not the 1832 ordinance.
to resist federal school integration orders
Resistance to school integration came in the 1950s, as at Little Rock in 1957.

alt.q: The Nullification Crisis of 1832–33 began when South Carolina declared which federal laws void?
alt.a: the tariffs of 1828 and 1832
alt.ex: South Carolina's November 1832 ordinance declared the tariffs of 1828 (the “Tariff of Abominations”) and 1832 void. The state argued protective tariffs favored northern manufacturers over southern planters, testing the Supremacy Clause.
w: the Alien and Sedition Acts
These 1798 laws were protested by Virginia and Kentucky, not nullified by South Carolina in 1832.
the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
This law was passed in 1850, nearly twenty years after the crisis.
the Embargo Act of 1807
New England protested the Embargo Act, but it was repealed in 1809, long before 1832.

alt.q: This scenario most closely resembles which historical event?
alt.a: the Nullification Crisis of 1832–33
alt.ex: In 1832 a South Carolina convention declared federal tariff laws void in the state and barred their collection, and President Jackson replied that no state could annul a federal law. The crisis ended in 1833 with a compromise tariff and the Force Bill.
w: the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 in Pennsylvania
The Whiskey Rebellion was an armed revolt by farmers, not a state convention declaring a law void.
the Hartford Convention of 1814–15
The Hartford Convention proposed amendments; it did not declare any federal law void.
the Little Rock crisis of 1957
Little Rock concerned school integration orders, not federal tax laws.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state convention declares two federal tax laws void inside the state and forbids federal officers to collect the taxes there. The President answers that no single state may cancel a federal law and asks Congress for power to use force if needed.

items.q: Which constitutional principle best supports the argument in this 1832 passage?
items.a: national supremacy
items.ex: President Andrew Jackson issued this proclamation on December 10, 1832, after South Carolina nullified federal tariffs. He argued that the Constitution, which makes federal law supreme, forbids one state to annul a federal law.
w: state sovereignty
State sovereignty was South Carolina's argument; the passage rejects it.
separation of powers
The passage concerns the states and the nation, not the branches of government.
limited government
The passage defends federal authority over a state, not limits on government.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a presidential proclamation of December 1832, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“I consider, then, the power to annul a law of the United States, assumed by one State, incompatible with the existence of the Union, contradicted expressly by the letter of the Constitution, unauthorized by its spirit, inconsistent with every principle on which it was founded, and destructive of the great object for which it was formed.”
Source: Proclamation Regarding Nullification, December 10, 1832

alt.q: How did the Nullification Crisis end in March 1833?
alt.a: Congress passed a compromise tariff and the Force Bill
alt.ex: In March 1833, Congress passed Henry Clay's Compromise Tariff, which lowered rates over time, and the Force Bill, which let the President use the military to collect duties. South Carolina then withdrew its nullification of the tariffs, avoiding armed conflict.
w: South Carolina left the Union for two years
South Carolina did not secede until December 1860.
The Supreme Court struck down every federal tariff then in force
No Supreme Court ruling ended the crisis; Congress and the President did.
Federal troops occupied Charleston for a decade
No such occupation occurred; the crisis ended with a compromise.

alt.q: Which President issued this proclamation, and why?
alt.a: Andrew Jackson, to oppose South Carolina's nullification
alt.ex: Andrew Jackson issued this proclamation on December 10, 1832, after South Carolina's convention declared federal tariffs void. Jackson argued that no state could annul a federal law, defending national supremacy.
w: John Quincy Adams, to defend the Tariff of Abominations of 1828
Adams signed the 1828 tariff but left office in March 1829, before this 1832 proclamation.
Thomas Jefferson, to oppose the Sedition Act
Jefferson opposed the Sedition Act in 1798, and he died in 1826.
Abraham Lincoln, to answer southern secession
Lincoln took office in 1861; this proclamation dates from 1832.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a presidential proclamation of December 1832, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“I consider, then, the power to annul a law of the United States, assumed by one State, incompatible with the existence of the Union, contradicted expressly by the letter of the Constitution, unauthorized by its spirit, inconsistent with every principle on which it was founded, and destructive of the great object for which it was formed.”
Source: Proclamation Regarding Nullification, December 10, 1832

items.q: Which sequence of challenges to federal supremacy is in the correct order?
items.a: Virginia Resolutions → Nullification Crisis → Ableman v. Booth → Little Rock crisis
items.ex: The Virginia Resolutions came in 1798, the Nullification Crisis in 1832–33, Ableman v. Booth in 1859, and the Little Rock crisis in 1957. In each, a state challenged federal authority, and no state's claimed power to override federal law was ever accepted.
w: Nullification Crisis → Virginia Resolutions → Little Rock crisis → Ableman v. Booth
The Virginia Resolutions (1798) came before nullification (1832), and Ableman (1859) came before Little Rock (1957).
Virginia Resolutions → Ableman v. Booth → Nullification Crisis → Little Rock crisis
The Nullification Crisis (1832) came before Ableman v. Booth (1859).
Ableman v. Booth → Virginia Resolutions → Nullification Crisis → Little Rock crisis
Ableman v. Booth (1859) came after both the 1798 resolutions and the 1832 crisis.

alt.q: Which of these challenges to federal authority happened most recently?
alt.a: Arkansas's governor blocks Black students
alt.ex: Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to block nine Black students from Little Rock Central High in September 1957. The others came earlier: Kentucky's protest in 1798, South Carolina's nullification in 1832, and Wisconsin's freeing of Sherman Booth in 1854.
w: Wisconsin's court frees a federal prisoner
Wisconsin's court freed Sherman Booth in 1854, and the Supreme Court reversed in 1859.
South Carolina nullifies a federal tariff
South Carolina's nullification came in 1832.
Kentucky protests the Sedition Act
Kentucky's resolutions against the Alien and Sedition Acts came in 1798.

alt.q: What did the Virginia Resolutions (1798), the Nullification Crisis (1832), and the Little Rock crisis (1957) have in common?
alt.a: A state resisted federal authority it opposed
alt.ex: In 1798 Virginia protested the Alien and Sedition Acts, in 1832 South Carolina nullified tariffs, and in 1957 Arkansas defied court-ordered integration. Each time a state challenged federal supremacy, and each time the state's claimed power to override federal law was rejected.
w: A state asked Congress for more federal power
Each state sought to resist federal power, not expand it.
The Supreme Court ruled for the state
The Court did not side with these states; in 1958 it ruled against Arkansas in Cooper v. Aaron.
A President refused to enforce federal law
Jackson in 1832 and Eisenhower in 1957 both acted to enforce federal law.

items.q: Which 1859 case held that a state court could not free a prisoner held under federal law?
items.a: Ableman v. Booth
items.ex: In Ableman v. Booth (1859), Chief Justice Taney ruled that Wisconsin's courts could not use habeas corpus to free Sherman Booth, who had been convicted in federal court. Under the Supremacy Clause, state courts cannot override federal courts on federal law.
w: Dred Scott v. Sandford
Dred Scott (1857) denied citizenship to Black Americans; it did not involve a state court freeing a federal prisoner.
Prigg v. Pennsylvania
Prigg (1842) struck down a Pennsylvania law on returning fugitives, but it did not involve a state court freeing a federal prisoner.
Cooper v. Aaron
Cooper (1958) required Arkansas officials to obey desegregation rulings.

alt.q: Based on the 1859 precedent of Ableman v. Booth, how would the U.S. Supreme Court most likely rule?
alt.a: The state court had no power to free him
alt.ex: In Ableman v. Booth (1859), the Court held that a state court cannot release a person held under federal authority or override the U.S. Supreme Court on federal law. Article VI binds state judges to federal law, and federal courts have the final say on it.
w: The state court's ruling on federal law is final
The U.S. Supreme Court, not a state court, has the final word on federal law.
The man must be retried in a state court
Federal crimes are tried in federal court; the state court had no role.
The governor must decide whether to free him
Governors have no power to release federal prisoners.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state supreme court declares a federal law unconstitutional and orders the release of a man convicted in federal court for violating it. The state court also tells its clerk to ignore orders from the U.S. Supreme Court. The federal government appeals.

alt.q: Why did Wisconsin's Supreme Court try to free Sherman Booth in the 1850s?
alt.a: It judged the Fugitive Slave Act unconstitutional
alt.ex: Booth was charged in 1854 with helping a man escape slavery, in violation of the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850. Wisconsin's court called the act unconstitutional and freed him, but in 1859 the Supreme Court reversed, holding that state courts cannot override federal authority.
w: It judged the federal tariff laws unconstitutional
Tariffs were the issue in South Carolina's 1832 nullification, not Booth's case.
It judged the Kansas-Nebraska Act unconstitutional
Booth was charged under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, not the 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act.
It judged the Sedition Act unconstitutional
The Sedition Act of 1798 had expired in 1801, long before Booth's case.

items.q: In Missouri v. Holland (1920), why did the Court uphold a federal law protecting migratory birds?
items.a: It carried out a valid treaty, which is supreme law
items.ex: In 1920 Justice Holmes upheld the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918, which carried out a 1916 treaty with Great Britain (for Canada). Because Article VI makes valid treaties supreme, Missouri's Tenth Amendment claim to control wild birds failed.
w: Birds are named in the Commerce Clause
The Commerce Clause does not mention birds; the ruling rested on the treaty power.
The Tenth Amendment gives control of wildlife to Congress
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to states; Missouri relied on it and lost.
Missouri had agreed to the law in advance
Missouri sued to stop the law; it never agreed to it.

alt.q: The federal law upheld in Missouri v. Holland (1920) carried out a 1916 treaty with which country?
alt.a: Great Britain, on behalf of Canada
alt.ex: The 1916 Migratory Bird Treaty was made with Great Britain, which then handled Canada's foreign affairs. Congress carried it out with a 1918 act, and in 1920 the Court held that the treaty and act were supreme over Missouri's claims.
w: Mexico, its neighbor on the southern border
A U.S.–Mexico bird treaty came in 1936, years after this case.
France, as a wartime ally
France was a World War I ally, but it was not party to the 1916 bird treaty.
Russia, across the Bering Sea
Russia was not a party to the 1916 Migratory Bird Treaty.

alt.q: Based on the 1920 precedent of Missouri v. Holland, how would the Court most likely rule?
alt.a: The federal law stands as part of supreme law
alt.ex: In Missouri v. Holland (1920), the Court held that a valid treaty and a federal law carrying it out are supreme under Article VI, even on subjects like wildlife that states usually regulate. The Tenth Amendment does not override a valid treaty.
w: The state wins, since wildlife is a reserved power
The Court rejected this Tenth Amendment argument in 1920.
The treaty is void unless the state approves it
States have no veto over treaties; only the Senate must approve them.
The law stands only if the House approved the treaty
Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate, not House approval.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state claims that wild animals within its borders belong to the state alone. To carry out a treaty approved by the Senate, Congress passes a law limiting the hunting of certain migrating animals. The state sues, citing the Tenth Amendment.

items.q: Under the 1947 ruling in Testa v. Katt, what must the state court do?
items.a: hear the case and apply the federal law
items.ex: In Testa v. Katt (1947), the Court unanimously held that Rhode Island's courts could not refuse to enforce a valid federal price-control law. Article VI binds “the Judges in every State,” so state courts cannot reject federal claims because of state policy.
w: send the case to Congress for review
Congress does not decide lawsuits; courts do.
apply state law instead of federal law
Under Article VI, valid federal law prevails over conflicting state policy.
dismiss it unless the governor consents
Governors have no power to block state courts from applying federal law.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A man sues a car dealer in state court under a valid federal law that lets buyers recover damages for being overcharged. The state court refuses to hear the case, saying the federal law's penalties go against the state's own policy.

alt.q: Which words of Article VI (1787) did the Court rely on in Testa v. Katt (1947) to require state courts to enforce federal law?
alt.a: the Judges in every State shall be bound
alt.ex: Article VI, Clause 2 (1787) says “the Judges in every State shall be bound” by federal law. In 1947 the Court used this to hold that state courts must hear valid federal claims, even if the state dislikes the federal policy.
w: no religious Test shall ever be required
This Article VI, Clause 3 phrase bans religious tests for office; it does not concern court duties.
Full Faith and Credit shall be given
This Article IV phrase concerns states honoring each other's records, not federal law.
the powers not delegated are reserved
This is from the Tenth Amendment (1791), which reserves powers to the states.

alt.q: Why did the framers in 1787 bind state judges, and not only federal judges, to follow federal law?
alt.a: State courts would hear many federal cases
alt.ex: In 1787 the framers created only the Supreme Court and left lower federal courts up to Congress, so state courts would often decide cases involving federal law. Binding “the Judges in every State” made sure federal law would be applied across the nation.
w: The Constitution created no federal courts
Article III created the Supreme Court; only lower federal courts were left to Congress.
State judges were appointed by Congress
State judges are chosen under state law, not by Congress.
State judges could veto federal laws
State judges have no veto; Article VI requires them to follow federal law.

items.q: Why did President Eisenhower send federal troops to Little Rock, Arkansas, in September 1957?
items.a: to enforce a court order to desegregate a school
items.ex: In September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Central High School. Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne and federalized the Guard so that the federal court's desegregation order, based on Brown v. Board of Education (1954), would be obeyed.
w: to stop a state from blocking federal tax collection
Federal tax collection was the issue in South Carolina's 1832 nullification, not Little Rock.
to protect voters registering under a 1965 law
The Voting Rights Act passed in 1965, eight years after Little Rock.
to end a strike at a federal military base
The troops escorted students into a high school; no labor strike was involved.

alt.q: Which Arkansas governor used the state National Guard in 1957 to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock Central High School?
alt.a: Orval Faubus
alt.ex: In September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to block the Little Rock Nine, defying federal desegregation orders. President Eisenhower responded by sending federal troops, enforcing the supremacy of federal law.
w: George Wallace
Wallace was governor of Alabama and stood in a University of Alabama doorway in 1963.
Ross Barnett
Barnett was governor of Mississippi and resisted James Meredith's admission in 1962.
Lester Maddox
Maddox was a Georgia segregationist who became governor in 1967.

alt.q: Which sequence is in the correct order?
alt.a: Brown v. Board → Little Rock crisis → Cooper v. Aaron
alt.ex: Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954, the Little Rock crisis began in September 1957, and Cooper v. Aaron followed in 1958. Brown required desegregation, Arkansas resisted, and Cooper held that state officials must obey the Court's ruling.
w: Little Rock crisis → Brown v. Board → Cooper v. Aaron
Brown (1954) came before the Little Rock crisis (1957); the crisis was resistance to Brown.
Cooper v. Aaron → Brown v. Board → Little Rock crisis
Cooper (1958) came after both Brown (1954) and the Little Rock crisis (1957).
Brown v. Board → Cooper v. Aaron → Little Rock crisis
The Little Rock crisis (1957) led to Cooper v. Aaron (1958), not the reverse.

items.q: Which constitutional requirement is the Court referring to in this 1958 passage?
items.a: the oath to support the Constitution
items.ex: In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), the Court said state officials are bound by the oath required by Article VI, Clause 3 to support the Constitution. Defying Brown v. Board of Education would break that oath, so Arkansas officials had to comply.
w: the ban on religious tests for office
That ban is also in Article VI, but the passage is about officials' “undertaking to support” the Constitution.
the guarantee of a republican government
The Guarantee Clause in Article IV is not about officials' duty to obey the Constitution.
the right to a speedy public trial
The Sixth Amendment trial right is unrelated to state officials resisting the Constitution.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1958 Supreme Court opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“No state legislator or executive or judicial officer can war against the Constitution without violating his undertaking to support it.”
Source: Cooper v. Aaron (1958)

alt.q: In what year did the Supreme Court decide Cooper v. Aaron, rejecting Arkansas's attempt to delay school integration?
alt.ex: The Court decided Cooper v. Aaron in September 1958, a year after the Little Rock crisis of 1957. It held that state officials could not nullify Brown v. Board of Education (1954), because Article VI makes the Constitution, as the Court interprets it, binding on the states.
w: 1954 is the year of Brown v. Board of Education, the ruling Arkansas resisted.
1957 is the year of the Little Rock crisis itself; the Court's ruling came the next year.
1964 is the year of the Civil Rights Act, not of Cooper v. Aaron.

alt.q: In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), why did the Court refuse the Little Rock school board's request to delay integration?
alt.a: Officials' own resistance could not justify delay
alt.ex: In 1958 the school board asked to postpone integration because of the turmoil of 1957. The Court refused, ruling that constitutional rights cannot be sacrificed to violence and disorder caused by state officials' own resistance to Brown v. Board of Education.
w: Brown v. Board of Education did not apply to Arkansas
Brown (1954) applied to every state; the Court said Arkansas was bound by it.
The school board lacked money for new schools
Funding was not the issue; the Court rejected delay based on official resistance.
Congress had already banned all delays by law
No federal law was the basis; the ruling rested on the Constitution and Article VI.

items.q: In this 1958 passage, the Court traced this principle to which earlier case?
items.a: Marbury v. Madison
items.ex: In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), the Court cited Marbury v. Madison (1803) for the principle that the federal judiciary has the final word on what the Constitution means. Combined with Article VI, this meant Arkansas had to obey Brown v. Board of Education.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch (1819) addressed implied powers and state taxation, not the courts' final say on the Constitution.
Gibbons v. Ogden
Gibbons (1824) addressed interstate commerce and a state monopoly.
Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld segregation and was rejected by Brown in 1954.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1958 Supreme Court opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“This decision declared the basic principle that the federal judiciary is supreme in the exposition of the law of the Constitution…”
Source: Cooper v. Aaron (1958)

alt.q: What did Cooper v. Aaron (1958) say about the Court's ruling in Brown v. Board of Education (1954)?
alt.a: It is the supreme law of the land, binding on states
alt.ex: In 1958 the Court held that Brown's interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment is the supreme law of the land and that Article VI makes it binding on the states. This rejected Arkansas's claim that it was not bound by Brown.
w: It applied only to the schools in Kansas
Brown applied nationwide; Cooper confirmed Arkansas was bound.
It bound states only after Congress agreed
The Court said Article VI made Brown binding without any act of Congress.
It was only advisory until each state chose to accept it
The Court said states could not choose; Brown was binding supreme law.

alt.q: Which 1958 precedent most directly rejects the governor's position?
alt.a: Cooper v. Aaron
alt.ex: In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), the Court held that state officials are bound by the Court's interpretation of the Constitution under Article VI and their oaths. It rejected Arkansas's attempt to ignore Brown v. Board of Education.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld “separate but equal”; it did not address state defiance of the Court.
Brown v. Board of Education
Brown (1954) was the ruling Arkansas defied; Cooper (1958) addressed that defiance.
Baker v. Carr
Baker (1962) let federal courts hear redistricting cases; it is not about defying rulings.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A governor announces that a recent Supreme Court ruling on the Constitution is wrong and that state officials need not follow it. State agencies then begin ignoring the ruling, and affected citizens go to federal court.

items.q: When Congress writes a clause into a federal law saying states may not adopt their own rules on that subject, which kind of preemption is this?
items.a: express preemption
items.ex: Preemption comes from the Supremacy Clause of 1787. When Congress states in the statute itself that state law is displaced, it is express preemption; the Court summarized this category in Arizona v. United States (2012).
w: field preemption
Field preemption is implied from a federal scheme so complete that it leaves no room for states.
conflict preemption
Conflict preemption is implied when a state law clashes with federal law or blocks its goals.
state nullification
Nullification is a state claim to void federal law, rejected in 1832–33 and by the Constitution.

alt.q: Which statement best describes implied preemption, as the Court explained it in Arizona v. United States (2012)?
alt.a: Congress's intent to displace state law is inferred
alt.ex: In 2012 the Court explained that, even without an express clause, state law is preempted when Congress has occupied a whole field or when state law conflicts with federal law. This implied preemption rests on the Supremacy Clause.
w: Congress writes into the law that states are barred
That is express preemption, not implied preemption.
States choose to repeal laws Congress dislikes
Preemption works automatically; states need not repeal anything.
The President orders states to drop a law
Preemption comes from federal law and the Supremacy Clause, not presidential orders.

alt.q: Why can a valid federal law preempt a conflicting state law?
alt.a: The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme
alt.ex: Article VI (1787) makes valid federal laws the supreme law of the land, notwithstanding contrary state law. In Murphy v. NCAA (2018), the Court confirmed that preemption rests on the Supremacy Clause.
w: The Tenth Amendment grants Congress unlimited power
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to the states and people; it does not grant Congress power.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause requires it
That clause concerns states honoring each other's acts, not federal-state conflicts.
The Bill of Rights bans most state laws
The Bill of Rights protects individual rights; it is not the source of preemption.

items.q: In Arizona v. United States (2012), why did the Court block most of Arizona's 2010 immigration law, S.B. 1070?
items.a: Federal immigration law preempted it
items.ex: In 2012 the Court held that three of the four challenged parts of S.B. 1070 were preempted, because immigration is governed by a detailed federal system. Under the Supremacy Clause, state laws that intrude on that system are invalid.
w: It violated the Second Amendment right to bear arms
The case was about immigration enforcement, not gun rights.
It taxed federal border agents
The law created state immigration crimes and arrest powers; it did not tax anyone.
Arizona lacked any police power
States do have police powers; the issue was conflict with federal immigration law.

alt.q: Which part of S.B. 1070 did the Court allow to go forward, at least for the time being, in 2012?
alt.a: status checks by officers during lawful stops
alt.ex: In Arizona v. United States (2012), the Court let Section 2B, requiring officers to check the immigration status of some people they lawfully stop, take effect because it had not yet been shown to conflict with federal law. It struck down three other parts as preempted.
w: a crime for not carrying registration papers
The Court held this part field-preempted, since Congress occupies alien registration.
a crime for unauthorized immigrants seeking work
The Court held this part conflicted with Congress's choice not to punish such workers.
warrantless arrests of suspected deportable people
The Court held this part preempted for giving officers more arrest power than federal law allows.

alt.q: In what year did the Supreme Court decide Arizona v. United States, a major case on federal preemption of state immigration laws?
alt.ex: The Court decided Arizona v. United States on June 25, 2012, two years after Arizona passed S.B. 1070. It held most of the law preempted because immigration is mainly a federal responsibility under the Supremacy Clause.
w: 2005 is the year of Gonzales v. Raich, on federal drug law and state medical marijuana.
Arizona passed S.B. 1070 in 2010; the Court ruled on it two years later.
2018 is the year of Murphy v. NCAA, on anti-commandeering and sports betting.

items.q: Under the reasoning of Arizona v. United States (2012), why is this state law invalid?
items.a: Congress has occupied the whole field
items.ex: In 2012 the Court held that Congress has created a complete federal system for alien registration, leaving no room for states, even with matching rules. This is field preemption, an implied form of preemption under the Supremacy Clause.
w: It violates the Fourth Amendment
The ruling rested on preemption, not on search-and-seizure rights.
The state failed to hold a referendum
Nothing requires a referendum; the problem is conflict with federal law.
The Tenth Amendment bars all state crimes
States may create crimes under their police powers; this one intruded on a federal field.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state makes it a state crime for an immigrant to fail to carry federal registration papers. Congress has already created a complete federal system for registering immigrants and punishing violations.

alt.q: In 2012, why did the Court say this state law was preempted?
alt.a: It blocked the system Congress chose
alt.ex: In Arizona v. United States (2012), the Court held that Arizona's crime for unauthorized workers stood as an obstacle to Congress's decision in 1986 to penalize employers rather than workers. This is conflict (obstacle) preemption under the Supremacy Clause.
w: It repeated a valid federal law word for word
No federal law made seeking work a crime for workers; the state law went beyond federal law.
It was passed without Congress's consent
States do not need Congress's consent to pass laws; the problem was conflict.
It applied only to residents of other states
The law applied within Arizona; the issue was its clash with federal law.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state makes it a crime for an unauthorized immigrant to seek or hold a job. In federal law, Congress chose to punish employers who hire unauthorized workers, but not the workers themselves.

alt.q: Which kind of preemption did the Court apply in 2012 to Arizona's crime of failing to carry federal registration papers?
alt.a: field preemption
alt.ex: In Arizona v. United States (2012), the Court held that federal law occupies the entire field of alien registration, so even a state law that mirrors federal rules is invalid. This field preemption flows from the Supremacy Clause.
w: express preemption
No federal clause expressly barred this state law; the Court found preemption from the federal scheme.
conflict preemption
The Court used conflict preemption for two other provisions, not the registration crime.
reverse preemption
Reverse preemption, where federal law yields to state law in areas like insurance, is not what the Court applied here.

items.q: Based on this 2005 passage, could California's 1996 medical marijuana law protect users from federal prosecution?
items.a: No, because federal law prevails in a conflict
items.ex: In Gonzales v. Raich (2005), the Court held that Congress could ban homegrown marijuana under the Controlled Substances Act of 1970, even when California's Compassionate Use Act of 1996 allowed it. Because federal law prevails over conflicting state law, the state law gave no protection from federal enforcement.
w: Yes, because states control all medical practice
States regulate medicine, but they cannot override a valid federal law.
Yes, because the users never sold any marijuana
The Court held that Congress could regulate homegrown marijuana as part of a national market.
No, because California never passed such a law
California voters approved the Compassionate Use Act in 1996.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 2005 Supreme Court opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Supremacy Clause unambiguously provides that if there is any conflict between federal and state law, federal law shall prevail.”
Source: Gonzales v. Raich (2005)

alt.q: In what year did the Supreme Court decide Gonzales v. Raich, allowing federal drug enforcement against state-approved medical marijuana users?
alt.ex: Gonzales v. Raich was decided June 6, 2005. The Court held 6–3 that the Commerce Clause let Congress reach homegrown marijuana, and California's law could not shield users because federal law is supreme.
w: 1995 is the year of United States v. Lopez, which limited the commerce power.
2000 is the year of United States v. Morrison, another limit on the commerce power.
2012 is the year of Arizona v. United States and the Affordable Care Act case.

alt.q: Which law did the federal government enforce in Gonzales v. Raich (2005), despite a conflicting state law?
alt.a: the Controlled Substances Act of 1970
alt.ex: In 2005 the Court upheld applying the Controlled Substances Act of 1970 to Californians who grew marijuana for medical use under state law. The federal act controlled because, under the Supremacy Clause, federal law prevails over conflicting state law.
w: the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906
This early law dealt with food and drug labeling and was not at issue in Raich.
the Compassionate Use Act of 1996
This was California's state law, which the Court held could not block federal enforcement.
the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act of 1993
The Brady Act concerned gun background checks and was at issue in Printz (1997).

items.q: Which statement best describes the legal situation?
items.a: Federal agents may still enforce federal law there
items.ex: Recreational marijuana remains illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act (1970). Under Gonzales v. Raich (2005) and the Supremacy Clause, a state law cannot shield anyone from federal enforcement, though anti-commandeering cases such as Murphy v. NCAA (2018) mean the state need not enforce the federal ban itself.
w: The state law cancels the federal law inside the state
State law cannot cancel federal law; the Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law supreme.
Congress may order the state to restore its own ban
Under Murphy v. NCAA (2018), Congress cannot order states to keep or pass particular laws.
Residents must follow whichever law was passed last
Supremacy depends on federal versus state law, not on which is newer.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 2026 a state legalizes recreational marijuana for adults under state law. Federal law still prohibits selling marijuana for recreational use. A store opens in the state and sells marijuana to adult customers.

alt.q: Why may a state stop arresting people for marijuana even though federal law still bans it?
alt.a: Congress cannot force states to enforce federal law
alt.ex: Under the anti-commandeering principle of Printz v. United States (1997) and Murphy v. NCAA (2018), Congress cannot make state officers enforce federal law or make states keep a ban. Federal agents can still enforce the federal ban, as Gonzales v. Raich (2005) confirmed.
w: The Supremacy Clause lets states pick which laws apply
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme; it does not let states choose.
Gonzales v. Raich legalized marijuana nationwide
Raich (2005) upheld federal power to ban marijuana, the opposite of legalizing it.
The Tenth Amendment voids all federal drug laws
Federal drug laws remain valid under the Commerce Clause, as Raich held in 2005.

alt.q: Which pair of rulings best explains why states may legalize marijuana under state law while federal law still bans it?
alt.a: Gonzales v. Raich and Murphy v. NCAA
alt.ex: Gonzales v. Raich (2005) held that the federal ban still applies inside states that allow marijuana. Murphy v. NCAA (2018) held that Congress cannot order states to keep their own bans, so state legalization and federal prohibition exist side by side.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden
These 1819 and 1824 cases expanded federal power but said nothing about marijuana or commandeering.
Plessy v. Ferguson and Brown v. Board
These cases concerned racial segregation, not drug laws or state legalization.
Marbury v. Madison and Cooper v. Aaron
These cases concern judicial review and obeying Court rulings, not state legalization.

items.q: Why did the Court in Printz v. United States (1997) strike down part of the 1993 Brady Act?
items.a: Congress cannot order state officers to run federal programs
items.ex: In 1997 the Court held 5–4 that the Brady Act's interim requirement that local sheriffs run background checks on handgun buyers unconstitutionally commandeered state officers. The Supremacy Clause covers only laws made in pursuance of the Constitution, so it could not save the requirement.
w: The Second Amendment forbids all gun background checks
The Court did not rule on the Second Amendment; federal background checks continue.
The act conflicted with an earlier treaty on firearms
No treaty was involved; the issue was federal orders to state officers.
Congress has no constitutional power at all to regulate gun sales
Congress can regulate gun sales; it just cannot draft state officers to do the work.

alt.q: Which sequence of anti-commandeering cases is in the correct order?
alt.a: New York v. United States → Printz v. United States → Murphy v. NCAA
alt.ex: New York v. United States (1992) barred Congress from ordering state legislatures to act, Printz (1997) barred it from commandeering state officers, and Murphy (2018) barred it from forbidding states to repeal their own laws. These cases mark limits on federal supremacy.
w: Printz v. United States → Murphy v. NCAA → New York v. United States
New York v. United States (1992) came first, before Printz (1997).
Murphy v. NCAA → New York v. United States → Printz v. United States
Murphy (2018) is the most recent of the three.
New York v. United States → Murphy v. NCAA → Printz v. United States
Printz (1997) came before Murphy (2018).

alt.q: Based on the 1997 precedent of Printz v. United States, this law would most likely be
alt.a: unconstitutional, since it commandeers local officers
alt.ex: In Printz v. United States (1997), the Court held that Congress may not command state or local officers to carry out a federal regulatory program. The Supremacy Clause does not save such a law, because it is not made in pursuance of the Constitution.
w: constitutional, because of the Supremacy Clause
The Supremacy Clause covers only constitutional laws, and commandeering is unconstitutional.
constitutional, if the President approves it
Presidential approval cannot cure a law that violates the Constitution.
unconstitutional, since it limits the sheriffs' free speech
The problem is commandeering state officers, not speech.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law requiring every county sheriff to inspect and certify each new car sold in the county, as part of a new federal safety program. Congress provides no funding, and the sheriffs object.

items.q: Why did the Court in Murphy v. NCAA (2018) strike down the 1992 federal ban on states authorizing sports betting?
items.a: It dictated which laws state legislatures could pass
items.ex: In 2018 the Court held that the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act of 1992 commandeered the states by forbidding them to authorize sports betting. Because it regulated states rather than private actors, it was not a valid preemption law under the Supremacy Clause.
w: It violated bettors' freedom of speech
The case turned on anti-commandeering, not the First Amendment.
It conflicted with an earlier international gambling treaty
No treaty was involved; the issue was federal orders to state legislatures.
It imposed a tax Congress could not collect
The law was not a tax; it barred states from authorizing sports betting.

alt.q: Based on this 2018 passage, which federal action would be constitutional?
alt.a: a federal law banning sports betting by private companies
alt.ex: In Murphy v. NCAA (2018), the Court said Congress may regulate sports gambling directly, and such a law would preempt state law under the Supremacy Clause. What Congress may not do, as the 1992 law did, is order states what laws to keep.
w: a federal law ordering states to keep betting bans
This would commandeer state legislatures, which Murphy forbids.
a federal law forbidding states to repeal betting bans
This is what the 1992 law did, and the Court struck it down in 2018.
a federal order directing state police to raid betting shops
Under Printz (1997), Congress cannot command state officers to enforce federal policy.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 2018 Supreme Court opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Congress can regulate sports gambling directly, but if it elects not to do so, each State is free to act on its own.”
Source: Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association (2018)

alt.q: What was the most significant effect of Murphy v. NCAA (2018)?
alt.a: States became free to legalize sports betting
alt.ex: By striking down the 1992 federal law in 2018, the Court allowed each state to decide whether to legalize sports betting, and many states quickly did. The ruling reinforced that the Supremacy Clause does not let Congress simply command state legislatures.
w: Congress gained power to run state lotteries
The ruling limited federal power over states; it gave Congress no lottery power.
The Court banned sports betting nationwide
The Court struck down a ban on state authorization; it banned nothing.
States lost all of their power to regulate gambling
The ruling left states free to legalize, regulate, or ban sports betting.

items.q: The first ten amendments, ratified on December 15, 1791, were added mainly to answer which concern raised during the ratification debates?
items.a: that the Constitution lacked guarantees of individual rights
items.ex: Anti-Federalists objected that the Constitution signed in 1787 had no bill of rights, and several states ratified in 1788 expecting amendments. Congress proposed twelve amendments in 1789, and ten were ratified on December 15, 1791, as the Bill of Rights.
w: that the Articles of Confederation gave Congress too little power
That concern produced the Constitutional Convention of 1787, not the Bill of Rights of 1791.
that small states lacked equal representation in Congress
The Great Compromise of 1787 settled representation by giving each state two senators.
that the President would be chosen directly by the voters
The Constitution created the Electoral College in 1787; direct election was never the issue behind the 1791 amendments.

alt.q: Congress sent twelve proposed amendments to the states in 1789. In what year had enough states approved ten of them for the Bill of Rights to take effect?
alt.ex: Ratification by three-fourths of the states was completed on December 15, 1791. The ten amendments answered Anti-Federalist demands for written protections of individual rights against the new national government.
w: 1789 is when the First Congress proposed the amendments (September 25), not when the states finished ratifying them.
1788 is when New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the Constitution itself.
1795 is when the Eleventh Amendment was ratified, after Chisholm v. Georgia.

alt.q: Which development most directly resulted from actions like this?
alt.a: the ratification of the Bill of Rights in 1791
alt.ex: Several state conventions ratified the Constitution in 1788 while recommending amendments to protect individual rights. James Madison turned these ideas into proposals in 1789, and ten were ratified in 1791 as the Bill of Rights.
w: the ratification of the Eleventh Amendment in 1795
The Eleventh Amendment (1795) limited lawsuits against states after Chisholm v. Georgia (1793); it did not protect these rights.
the adoption of the Articles of Confederation in 1781
The Articles took effect in 1781, years before this 1788 convention.
the passage of the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798
The Sedition Act of 1798 restricted criticism of the government; it did not protect the press.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state convention in 1788 votes to ratify the new Constitution but attaches a list of recommended changes protecting freedom of religion, freedom of the press, and trial by jury. The delegates expect the new Congress to act on these proposals.

items.q: Which sequence lists these events in the correct chronological order?
items.a: Constitution signed; amendments proposed; Bill of Rights ratified; 11th ratified
items.ex: The Constitution was signed on September 17, 1787. The First Congress proposed twelve amendments on September 25, 1789, ten were ratified as the Bill of Rights on December 15, 1791, and the Eleventh followed in 1795 in response to Chisholm v. Georgia (1793).
w: amendments proposed; Constitution signed; Bill of Rights ratified; 11th ratified
Amendments could not be proposed before the Constitution existed; it was signed in 1787 and amendments came in 1789.
Constitution signed; Bill of Rights ratified; amendments proposed; 11th ratified
The amendments had to be proposed (1789) before they could be ratified (1791).
Constitution signed; amendments proposed; 11th ratified; Bill of Rights ratified
The Bill of Rights (1791) came before the Eleventh Amendment (1795).

alt.q: Which of these was added to the Constitution first?
alt.a: the Bill of Rights
alt.ex: The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791 to satisfy demands for protections of individual liberty. Later came the Eleventh Amendment (1795), the Twelfth (1804), and finally the Twenty-seventh (1992), even though the Twenty-seventh had been proposed in 1789.
w: the Eleventh Amendment
The Eleventh Amendment was ratified in 1795, four years after the Bill of Rights.
the Twelfth Amendment
The Twelfth Amendment was ratified in 1804, after the election of 1800 tie.
the Twenty-seventh Amendment
The Twenty-seventh was proposed in 1789 with the Bill of Rights but not ratified until 1992.

alt.q: About how much time passed between the signing of the Constitution and the ratification of the Bill of Rights?
alt.a: about four years, 1787 to 1791
alt.ex: The Constitution was signed in 1787 without a bill of rights. The new Congress first met in 1789 and proposed amendments, and three-fourths of the states had ratified ten of them by December 15, 1791.
w: about one year, 1787 to 1788
1788 is when the ninth state ratified the Constitution; the Bill of Rights was still years away.
about two years, 1787 to 1789
In 1789 Congress only proposed the amendments; ratification took until 1791.
about eight years, 1787 to 1795
1795 is the year of the Eleventh Amendment, not the Bill of Rights.

items.q: Which Supreme Court decision led Congress and the states to adopt the Eleventh Amendment, ratified in 1795?
items.a: Chisholm v. Georgia (1793)
items.ex: In Chisholm v. Georgia (1793), the Court allowed a citizen of another state to sue Georgia in federal court over a Revolutionary War debt. Alarmed states responded quickly: Congress proposed the Eleventh Amendment in 1794, and it was ratified on February 7, 1795.
w: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
Marbury (1803) established judicial review and came eight years after the Eleventh Amendment.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
McCulloch (1819) upheld the national bank and implied powers, long after 1795.
Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Gibbons (1824) concerned interstate commerce and came long after 1795.

alt.q: Why was this amendment added to the Constitution in 1795?
alt.a: to undo a ruling that let an out-of-state citizen sue a state
alt.ex: In Chisholm v. Georgia (1793), the Supreme Court let a citizen of another state sue Georgia in federal court. The Eleventh Amendment, ratified in 1795, reversed that result by barring such suits.
w: to stop federal courts from reviewing acts of Congress
Judicial review was confirmed later in Marbury v. Madison (1803); the Eleventh Amendment does not limit it.
to end the practice of states suing one another in federal court
The amendment covers suits by citizens of other states or foreign countries, not suits between states.
to let states sue the national government over federal taxes
The amendment limits suits against states; it says nothing about states suing the national government.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Eleventh Amendment, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Judicial power of the United States shall not be construed to extend to any suit in law or equity, commenced or prosecuted against one of the United States by Citizens of another State, or by Citizens or Subjects of any Foreign State.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: The Eleventh Amendment was the first amendment ratified after the Bill of Rights. In what year was it ratified?
alt.ex: The Eleventh Amendment was ratified on February 7, 1795, in response to Chisholm v. Georgia (1793), which had allowed a citizen of another state to sue Georgia in federal court.
w: 1791 is when the Bill of Rights was ratified.
1793 is when Chisholm v. Georgia was decided, the ruling that prompted the amendment.
1804 is when the Twelfth Amendment was ratified after the election of 1800.

items.q: Which event most directly led to the Twelfth Amendment, ratified in 1804?
items.a: the Jefferson–Burr electoral tie of 1800
items.ex: Under the original Article II, each elector cast two votes for President without naming a vice-presidential choice. In 1800 Thomas Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr each received 73 electoral votes, and the House needed 36 ballots to choose Jefferson. The Twelfth Amendment (1804) requires separate votes for President and Vice President.
w: the disputed Hayes–Tilden election of 1876
The 1876 dispute came 72 years after the Twelfth Amendment was ratified.
Washington's unanimous election in 1789
Washington's unanimous election caused no tie or crisis that needed fixing.
the House's choice of John Quincy Adams in 1824
The 1824 election was decided under the Twelfth Amendment, twenty years after it was ratified.

alt.q: Which U.S. amendment, ratified in 1804, changed rules like these after a similar crisis?
alt.a: the Twelfth Amendment
alt.ex: In the election of 1800, Jefferson and Burr tied with 73 electoral votes each because electors could not distinguish between President and Vice President. The Twelfth Amendment (1804) made electors cast separate ballots for each office.
w: the Eleventh Amendment
The Eleventh Amendment (1795) limited lawsuits against states, not electoral voting.
the Twentieth Amendment
The Twentieth Amendment (1933) changed the dates terms begin, not how electors vote.
the Twenty-second Amendment
The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limited presidents to two elected terms.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Under a nation's election rules, each elector casts two votes for president, and the runner-up becomes vice president. A party's candidate for president and its candidate for vice president receive exactly the same number of electoral votes, and the legislature must break the tie.

alt.q: What was the most significant change made by the Twelfth Amendment in 1804?
alt.a: Electors cast separate ballots for President and Vice President.
alt.ex: The tie between Jefferson and Burr in 1800 showed the danger of electors casting two undifferentiated votes. Since the Twelfth Amendment (1804), electors vote separately for President and for Vice President.
w: Voters, not electors, now choose the President directly.
The Electoral College remains; the Twelfth Amendment only changed how electors vote.
A tie for President is now decided by the Senate, not the House.
The House still chooses the President when no one has a majority; the Senate chooses the Vice President.
Presidents are now limited to two elected terms in office.
The two-term limit came from the Twenty-second Amendment in 1951.

items.q: Why did Congress propose this amendment in 1865 even though the Emancipation Proclamation had been issued in 1863?
items.a: The Proclamation freed only people in areas in rebellion.
items.ex: The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) was a wartime order that applied only to areas in rebellion and could be challenged after the war. The Thirteenth Amendment, passed by Congress in January 1865 and ratified on December 6, 1865, ended slavery everywhere in the United States permanently.
w: The Proclamation had been struck down by the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court never struck down the Emancipation Proclamation.
The Proclamation applied only to the loyal border states.
The reverse is true: the Proclamation exempted the border states and covered only areas in rebellion.
The Proclamation ended slavery but not the slave trade.
Congress had already banned the international slave trade in 1808; that was not the reason for the amendment.

sc.title: Use the excerpt below, from the Thirteenth Amendment, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: In what year was the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery, ratified?
alt.ex: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified on December 6, 1865, months after the Civil War ended. It made abolition permanent and nationwide, going beyond the wartime Emancipation Proclamation of 1863.
w: 1863 is when Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which covered only Confederate-held areas.
1868 is when the Fourteenth Amendment, on citizenship and equal protection, was ratified.
1857 is when the Dred Scott decision was handed down, before the Civil War.

alt.q: What was the most significant impact of the Thirteenth Amendment (1865)?
alt.a: It made the end of slavery permanent and nationwide.
alt.ex: Ratified in 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude (except as punishment for a crime) everywhere in the United States, securing what the 1863 Emancipation Proclamation had begun as a war measure.
w: It granted citizenship to everyone born in the United States.
Birthright citizenship came from the Fourteenth Amendment in 1868.
It guaranteed Black men the right to vote in every state.
Protection against racial voting bans came from the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870.
It freed enslaved people only in the Confederate states.
That describes the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863, which the amendment went beyond.
