The clause gives no role to state legislatures; it names only rebellion or invasion.
advance approval by the Supreme Court
The clause does not require court approval; it limits suspension to rebellion or invasion.
a declaration of war on a foreign nation
The clause names rebellion or invasion, not a declaration of war, as the grounds.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article I, Section 9 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Privilege of the Writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion the public Safety may require it.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

items.q: During the 1780s, several state legislatures printed paper money and passed laws letting debtors escape their contracts. How did the Constitution of 1787 respond?
items.a: It barred states from impairing contracts
items.ex: Article I, Section 10 (1787) forbids states to emit bills of credit or pass any law impairing the obligation of contracts. The framers wanted to protect creditors and give the nation a stable economy after the troubles of the 1780s.
w: It let Congress cancel all private debts nationwide
The Constitution gives Congress no power to cancel private debts; bankruptcy laws are different and must be uniform.
It required states to print more money
The Constitution did the opposite, barring states from issuing paper money.
It gave states power to coin gold money
Article I, Section 10 forbids states to coin money of any kind.

alt.q: Which of these does Article I, Section 10 of the 1787 Constitution forbid to the states but NOT to Congress?
alt.a: coining money
alt.ex: Article I, Section 10 (1787) forbids states to coin money, while Article I, Section 8 gives that power to Congress, creating one national currency. Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and titles of nobility are denied to both levels.
w: passing ex post facto laws
Ex post facto laws are forbidden to Congress (Section 9) and to the states (Section 10).
granting titles of nobility
Titles of nobility are forbidden to both the national government and the states.
passing bills of attainder
Bills of attainder are forbidden to both Congress and the states.

alt.q: Under Article I, Section 10 of the 1787 Constitution, the state's tax is
alt.a: invalid without the consent of Congress
alt.ex: Article I, Section 10 (1787) bars states from laying duties on imports or exports, except what is needed for inspection laws, without Congress's consent. Under the Articles (1781), states taxed one another's trade; the Constitution put foreign trade under Congress.
w: valid as a reserved power of the state
The Tenth Amendment reserves only powers not prohibited; import duties are restricted by Section 10.
valid as a concurrent power of both levels
Taxing is generally concurrent, but import duties are an exception limited by Section 10.
invalid only if the president vetoes it
The president cannot veto state laws; the limit comes from the Constitution itself.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state wants to raise money by placing a tax on every shipment of oranges imported from foreign countries. It does not ask Congress for permission.

items.q: Which part of the 1787 Constitution settles a conflict between a valid federal law and a state law, a problem the Articles of Confederation (1781) had no way to resolve?
items.a: Article VI's Supremacy Clause
items.ex: Article VI (1787) makes the Constitution, federal laws made under it, and treaties “the supreme Law of the Land,” binding state judges. Under the Articles (1781), states could ignore national measures with no penalty.
w: Article IV's Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause makes states honor each other's records and rulings; it does not rank federal over state law.
the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
The Tenth Amendment (1791) reserves undelegated powers; it does not resolve conflicts with valid federal law.
Article I's Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause lets Congress carry out its powers; it does not rank laws.

alt.q: How would a court most likely resolve the conflict, and on what basis?
alt.a: The federal rule wins under Article VI
alt.ex: Under the Supremacy Clause of Article VI (1787), a valid federal law overrides a conflicting state law. The framers included it so national law would be uniform and could not be ignored state by state.
w: The state law wins under the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment (1791) does not let states override valid federal law.
Both stand until the state's voters decide
No referendum can override valid federal law; the Constitution settles the conflict.
The governor decides the issue under Article IV
Article IV concerns relations among states, not conflicts between federal and state law.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state law allows farmers to use a pesticide that a valid federal regulation bans nationwide. A farmer who uses the pesticide argues that the state law protects him.

alt.q: Which statement best explains why the framers in 1787 made valid federal law supreme over conflicting state law?
alt.a: so states could not defy national laws
alt.ex: Under the Articles of Confederation (1781), states often ignored Congress's requests and treaties. The Supremacy Clause in Article VI (1787) made the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties binding on every state.
w: so state judges could ignore the Constitution
Article VI does the opposite; it binds state judges to follow the Constitution.
so Congress could abolish the state governments
The Constitution preserves the states; Congress cannot abolish them.
so the president could veto state laws
The president has no veto over state laws.

items.q: The Full Faith and Credit Clause appears in Article IV of the 1787 Constitution. Which earlier document, in force from 1781, already contained a similar clause?
items.a: the Articles of Confederation
items.ex: Article IV of the Articles of Confederation (in force 1781) required full faith and credit for other states' records, acts, and judicial proceedings. The framers kept the idea in 1787 to bind the states together as one union.
w: the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration (1776) declared independence and set up no rules for relations among states.
the Northwest Ordinance
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) governed western territories, not relations among existing states.
the Virginia Declaration of Rights
Virginia's 1776 declaration listed individual rights for one state, not duties among states.

alt.q: Which provision of the 1787 Constitution most directly requires Ohio to accept the record, and why does it exist?
alt.a: Full Faith and Credit, to unite states as one nation
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 1 (1787) requires each state to give full faith and credit to the public acts, records, and court proceedings of every other state. It keeps the states from treating one another like foreign countries.
w: Privileges and Immunities, to protect travelers' rights
That clause bars unfair discrimination against out-of-state citizens; it does not cover honoring records.
Supremacy Clause, to make state law yield to federal
No federal law is in conflict here; the issue is one state honoring another state's record.
Tenth Amendment, to reserve record-keeping to states
The Tenth Amendment (1791) does not require states to honor each other's records.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A man born in Florida moves to Ohio. An Ohio state office refuses to accept his official Florida birth certificate as proof of his age, saying that only Ohio records count.

alt.q: Which problem was this clause, written in 1787, mainly meant to prevent?
alt.a: dodging court rulings by moving states
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 1 (1787) requires states to honor other states' public acts, records, and court proceedings. Without it, a person could escape a judgment simply by crossing a state line.
w: states taxing goods shipped from other states
That problem was addressed by the Commerce Clause in Article I, Section 8.
states printing their own paper money
That problem was addressed by Article I, Section 10.
Congress overriding state court rulings
The clause concerns states honoring each other, not Congress and the courts.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article IV, Section 1 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

items.q: In Puerto Rico v. Branstad (1987), the Supreme Court overruled Kentucky v. Dennison (1861). What was the impact on extradition?
items.a: Federal courts can order governors to return fugitives
items.ex: Branstad (1987) unanimously held that the Extradition Clause of Article IV, Section 2 creates a duty federal courts can enforce. It reversed Dennison (1861), which had said courts could not force a governor to return a fugitive.
w: Governors may refuse to return any fugitive they choose
That was closer to the effect of Dennison (1861), which Branstad overruled.
States may ignore other states' arrest warrants
Branstad strengthened, not weakened, the duty to return people charged in other states.
Only Congress may decide extradition requests
Requests are made by state governors and enforced by courts, not decided by Congress.

alt.q: This clause of the 1787 Constitution, carried over from the Articles of Confederation (1781), is known as
alt.a: the Extradition Clause
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 2 (1787) requires a state to return a person charged with a crime who flees there, when the state they fled from demands it. Like the similar rule in the Articles (1781), it keeps fugitives from finding a safe haven across state lines.
w: the Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause (Article IV, Section 1) concerns honoring other states' records and rulings.
the Privileges and Immunities Clause
That clause protects visiting citizens from unfair discrimination.
the Fugitive Slave Clause
That separate clause concerned escaped enslaved people and was made obsolete by the Thirteenth Amendment (1865).

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article IV, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“A Person charged in any State with Treason, Felony, or other Crime, who shall flee from Justice, and be found in another State, shall on Demand of the executive Authority of the State from which he fled, be delivered up, to be removed to the State having Jurisdiction of the Crime.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: In Kentucky v. Dennison (1861), what did the Supreme Court decide?
alt.a: The governor had a duty but courts could not force him
alt.ex: In 1861 the Court said Article IV, Section 2 creates a duty to return fugitives, but that federal courts could not compel a governor to carry it out. States could thus defy extradition requests until Puerto Rico v. Branstad overruled Dennison in 1987.
w: The governor had no duty at all to return any fugitive
The Court said a duty existed; it only held that courts could not enforce it.
Federal courts could order the governor to return him
That became the rule only in 1987, when Puerto Rico v. Branstad overruled Dennison.
Kentucky could send its militia into Ohio to seize him
Nothing in the ruling allowed one state to use force inside another state.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1859, Willis Lago, a free Black man, was charged in Kentucky with helping an enslaved woman escape, and he was found in Ohio. In 1860, Ohio's governor, William Dennison, refused Kentucky's demand to return him.

items.q: In 1798, the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, secretly written by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, protested which federal laws?
items.a: the Alien and Sedition Acts
items.ex: Kentucky (November 1798, Jefferson) and Virginia (December 1798, Madison) called the Alien and Sedition Acts unconstitutional, partly because the Sedition Act punished criticism of the government. They argued states could judge federal laws, an early form of the nullification theory.
w: the Tariffs of 1828 and 1832
These tariffs prompted South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification in 1832.
the Fugitive Slave Act
The Fugitive Slave Act was passed in 1850, decades after 1798.
the Kansas-Nebraska Act
The Kansas-Nebraska Act was passed in 1854.

alt.q: President Andrew Jackson issued this statement in response to which action?
alt.a: South Carolina voiding federal tariffs
alt.ex: On November 24, 1832, South Carolina declared the Tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null and void. Jackson's proclamation of December 10, 1832 rejected nullification as incompatible with the Union, and the crisis ended in 1833 with the Force Bill and a compromise tariff.
w: Kentucky protesting the Sedition Act
Kentucky's protest came in 1798, when Jackson was not president.
Georgia's removal of the Cherokee Nation
Georgia defied the Supreme Court over the Cherokee, but Jackson sided with Georgia; this proclamation answered South Carolina's tariff nullification.
Virginia's secession from the Union
Virginia seceded in 1861, long after Jackson's presidency ended in 1837.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a presidential proclamation, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“I consider, then, the power to annul a law of the United States, assumed by one State, incompatible with the existence of the Union . . .”
Source: Andrew Jackson, Proclamation to the People of South Carolina, December 10, 1832, Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Which sequence of challenges to federal authority is in the correct order?
alt.a: Kentucky Resolutions; Ordinance of Nullification; secession
alt.ex: The Kentucky Resolutions came in 1798, South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification in 1832, and South Carolina's secession in December 1860. Each claimed states could resist federal authority, a claim that conflicts with the Supremacy Clause and was settled by the Civil War.
w: Ordinance of Nullification; Kentucky Resolutions; secession
The Kentucky Resolutions (1798) came before the Ordinance of Nullification (1832).
Kentucky Resolutions; secession; Ordinance of Nullification
Secession (1860) came after the Ordinance of Nullification (1832).
secession; Kentucky Resolutions; Ordinance of Nullification
Secession (1860) was the last of these events, not the first.

items.q: In Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918), the Supreme Court struck down a federal child labor law, ruling that manufacturing was a local matter for the states. Which theory of federalism did this decision reflect?
items.a: dual federalism
items.ex: Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918) struck down the Keating-Owen Act of 1916, treating national and state powers as separate spheres, which is dual federalism, the “layer cake” model. It was overruled by United States v. Darby (1941) as the New Deal changed federalism.
w: cooperative federalism
Cooperative federalism, which grew in the 1930s, blends national and state roles instead of separating them.
New Federalism
New Federalism refers to efforts in the 1970s and 1980s to return power to states, mostly through grants.
creative federalism
Creative federalism refers to the 1960s Great Society, when Washington expanded direct aid programs.

alt.q: Which statement best describes dual federalism, the dominant view of national-state relations from the 1800s until the New Deal of the 1930s?
alt.a: Each level works in its own separate sphere
alt.ex: Dual federalism, often called “layer cake” federalism, held that national and state governments have separate, distinct areas of power. It gave way in the 1930s, when the New Deal mixed national and state roles.
w: Both levels share and blend most programs
That describes cooperative, or “marble cake,” federalism that grew in the 1930s.
States run programs paid for by federal grants
That describes later cooperative and grant-based federalism, not dual federalism.
The national government controls all policy
That describes a unitary system, not any form of American federalism.

alt.q: Which later case overruled Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918) by upholding federal limits on child labor and wages?
alt.a: United States v. Darby (1941)
alt.ex: In 1941, United States v. Darby upheld the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 and overruled Hammer v. Dagenhart. The decision ended the dual-federalism view that manufacturing was beyond Congress's commerce power.
w: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Gibbons came nearly a century before Hammer and could not overrule it.
United States v. Lopez (1995)
Lopez (1995) limited, rather than expanded, the commerce power.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
McCulloch (1819) concerned a national bank and came long before Hammer.

items.q: During the Great Depression of the 1930s, the New Deal shifted American federalism toward which model?
items.a: cooperative federalism
items.ex: New Deal laws of the 1930s, such as the Social Security Act of 1935, had national and state governments share programs and funding. This cooperative, or “marble cake,” federalism replaced the sharper separation of dual federalism.
w: layer-cake dual federalism
Dual federalism, with separate spheres, was the older model the New Deal moved away from.
the New Federalism model
New Federalism came in the 1970s and 1980s and sought to return power to the states.
a confederal system of states
A confederation, like the Articles of 1781, has a weak center; the New Deal strengthened the national role.

alt.q: This arrangement, created during the New Deal, best illustrates
alt.a: cooperative federalism
alt.ex: The Social Security Act of 1935 set up federal-state unemployment insurance: Washington set standards and provided funds while states ran the programs. Such shared responsibility is cooperative federalism.
w: layer-cake dual federalism
Dual federalism keeps each level in a separate sphere; here they share one program.
state nullification of laws
Nullification is a state's claim to void federal law, as South Carolina tried in 1832.
a unitary system of government
In a unitary system the central government controls everything; here states run their own offices.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Under a 1935 law, the national government sets basic standards and provides money, while each state runs its own unemployment insurance office and sets benefit levels within those standards.

alt.q: Why did the national government take on a much larger role alongside the states in the 1930s?
alt.a: The Depression overwhelmed state budgets
alt.ex: By 1933, about one in four workers was unemployed, and states and cities could not pay for relief on their own. New Deal programs like the Social Security Act of 1935 brought national money and shared programs, creating cooperative federalism.
w: The Supreme Court ended all state powers
The Court never ended state powers; the states kept their reserved powers.
The states voted to dissolve their legislatures
No state dissolved its legislature; states took part in New Deal programs.
The Articles of Confederation were restored
The Articles were replaced in 1789 and never restored.

items.q: In 1972, President Richard Nixon signed general revenue sharing into law, sending federal tax money to states and cities with few strings attached. What was the main goal of this New Federalism?
items.a: to return power and choices to the states
items.ex: The State and Local Fiscal Assistance Act of 1972 shared federal revenue with states and localities to spend largely as they chose. Nixon's New Federalism, continued by Reagan in the 1980s, aimed to shift decisions back to state and local governments.
w: to end all federal aid to state governments
Revenue sharing gave states more federal money, not less.
to place states under direct federal control
It did the opposite, loosening federal control over how money was spent.
to replace the states with regional agencies
New Federalism sought to strengthen states, not replace them.

alt.q: Which president, in 1981, pushed Congress to merge dozens of narrow categorical grants into broader block grants as part of his New Federalism?
alt.a: Ronald Reagan
alt.ex: In 1981 Reagan persuaded Congress to fold dozens of categorical grant programs into a few block grants, with less total funding. His goal was to give states more flexibility and shrink the federal role.
w: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Roosevelt's New Deal in the 1930s expanded the federal role through cooperative federalism.
Lyndon B. Johnson
Johnson's Great Society in the 1960s created many new categorical grants.
Jimmy Carter
Carter served 1977–1981 and did not lead the 1981 block-grant consolidation.

alt.q: Which sequence correctly orders these eras of American federalism?
alt.a: dual federalism; cooperative federalism; New Federalism
alt.ex: Dual federalism dominated from the 1800s until the 1930s, cooperative federalism grew with the New Deal of the 1930s, and New Federalism came in the 1970s and 1980s under Nixon and Reagan.
w: cooperative federalism; dual federalism; New Federalism
Dual federalism came first; cooperative federalism began with the New Deal in the 1930s.
dual federalism; New Federalism; cooperative federalism
New Federalism (1970s–1980s) came after cooperative federalism (1930s).
New Federalism; dual federalism; cooperative federalism
New Federalism was the most recent of the three, not the first.

items.q: In 1996, Congress replaced a welfare program with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), a fixed sum that states may spend on broad goals with wide discretion. TANF is best classified as
items.a: a block grant
items.ex: The 1996 welfare reform replaced Aid to Families with Dependent Children with the TANF block grant. Block grants give states a fixed amount for broad purposes, allowing states to design their own programs.
w: a categorical grant
Categorical grants have narrow purposes and strict rules, the opposite of TANF's broad discretion.
an unfunded mandate
An unfunded mandate imposes requirements without money; TANF provides money.
general revenue sharing
General revenue sharing (1972–1986) gave money with almost no stated purpose and had ended a decade earlier.

alt.q: Which statement best distinguishes a categorical grant from a block grant, the type favored by New Federalism in the 1970s and 1980s?
alt.a: Categorical grants have narrow purposes and strict rules
alt.ex: Categorical grants fund specific purposes under detailed federal rules, while block grants fund broad areas with more state choice. New Federalism in the 1970s and 1980s favored block grants to give states flexibility.
w: Categorical grants let states spend money on anything
That is closer to general revenue sharing; categorical grants are the most restricted kind.
Categorical grants flow from the states to the national government
Grants-in-aid flow from the national government to states and localities.
Categorical grants are required by the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment (1791) does not mention grants; they come from Congress's spending power.

alt.q: Which type of federal aid does this early program most closely resemble?
alt.a: a categorical grant-in-aid
alt.ex: The Morrill Act of 1862 gave states federal land, but only for a specific purpose: colleges teaching agriculture and the mechanic arts. Aid for a narrow purpose with conditions is a categorical grant, and the act helped create land-grant universities.
w: an unfunded federal mandate
An unfunded mandate imposes duties without aid; this program gave states land.
general revenue sharing
Revenue sharing (1972) gave money with few strings; this aid was tied to one purpose.
a broad block grant-in-aid
Block grants cover broad areas with wide discretion; this aid had a narrow, specific purpose.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Under the Morrill Act of 1862, Congress gave each state federal land to sell, but only if the state used the proceeds to support colleges teaching agriculture and the mechanic arts.

items.q: In 1984, instead of passing a national drinking age directly, Congress threatened to withhold part of federal highway funds from states that let people under 21 buy alcohol. Why did the Supreme Court uphold this approach in South Dakota v. Dole (1987)?
items.a: The condition was mild and tied to highway safety
items.ex: In June 1987 the Court ruled 7–2 that Congress may attach conditions to federal spending if they relate to the program's purpose and are not coercive. Losing 5 percent of highway funds was mild pressure tied to safe interstate travel.
w: The Tenth Amendment requires states to obey grant rules
The Tenth Amendment (1791) protects states; it does not require them to accept federal conditions.
States may never refuse federal highway money
States may refuse federal grants; that freedom is why conditions are not commands.
Congress may order states to pass any law it wants
Congress cannot command state legislatures or officers, as New York v. United States (1992) and Printz (1997) later held.

alt.q: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), why did the Supreme Court limit the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion?
alt.a: Threatening all existing Medicaid funds was coercive
alt.ex: In June 2012, seven justices held that threatening states with the loss of all existing Medicaid money unless they expanded the program was unconstitutionally coercive. States may now decline the expansion without losing existing funds, unlike the mild 5 percent condition upheld in Dole (1987).
w: Medicaid is a reserved power that Congress cannot fund
Congress may fund Medicaid under its spending power; the problem was the coercive condition.
The expansion was an unconstitutional tax on states
The tax ruling concerned the individual mandate, which was upheld; the Medicaid ruling concerned coercion.
States cannot accept any federal health grants
States may accept federal health grants; they could not be forced by losing all existing funds.

alt.q: Which statement correctly compares South Dakota v. Dole (1987) and NFIB v. Sebelius (2012)?
alt.a: Dole upheld a funding condition; NFIB found one coercive
alt.ex: Dole (1987) upheld withholding 5 percent of highway funds as mild encouragement, while NFIB (2012) held that threatening all existing Medicaid funds crossed the line into coercion. Together they show Congress may use, but not abuse, conditional grants.
w: Dole found a funding condition coercive; NFIB upheld one
This reverses the rulings; Dole upheld the highway condition and NFIB struck the Medicaid threat.
Both cases banned all conditions on federal grants
Neither case banned conditions; Dole expressly upheld one.
Both cases involved federal highway money
Only Dole involved highway funds; NFIB involved Medicaid.

items.q: Which law, passed in 1995, responded to state and local complaints about costly federal requirements by making Congress weigh their costs before voting?
items.a: the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
items.ex: The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 requires the Congressional Budget Office to estimate costs that bills impose on state and local governments and lets members object to costly unfunded mandates. It answered complaints that Washington ordered programs without paying for them.
w: the Civil Rights Act
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination; it was not a response to mandate costs.
the Americans with Disabilities Act
The ADA (1990) was itself cited as a costly mandate; it did not limit mandates.
the Social Security Act
The Social Security Act (1935) created New Deal programs, not limits on mandates.

alt.q: Which statement best describes an unfunded mandate, the problem targeted by a 1995 federal law?
alt.a: a federal requirement without money to pay for it
alt.ex: An unfunded mandate is a federal order that states or localities must follow without federal money to cover the cost. The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 made such mandates harder for Congress to pass.
w: a federal grant that states may spend on almost anything
That describes general revenue sharing or a broad block grant, which provide money.
a federal grant offered only if states accept conditions
That is a conditional grant, like the highway funds in South Dakota v. Dole (1987).
a state law that conflicts with federal law
That is a preemption problem resolved by the Supremacy Clause.

alt.q: What was the main effect of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995?
alt.a: It made mandates harder to pass, not illegal
alt.ex: The 1995 act requires cost estimates for mandates on state, local, and tribal governments and lets members raise a point of order against costly unfunded mandates. It added procedural hurdles but did not ban unfunded mandates.
w: It banned all unfunded federal mandates on states
The act did not ban mandates; Congress can still pass them.
It required Congress to fully fund all mandates
No full-funding requirement exists; the act relies on cost estimates and points of order.
It let states nullify any unfunded mandate
States cannot nullify federal law; the Supremacy Clause still applies.

items.q: In Wickard v. Filburn (1942), the Supreme Court ruled that Congress could limit wheat a farmer grew for use on his own farm. What was the most significant effect of this ruling?
items.a: It greatly widened Congress's commerce power
items.ex: In November 1942 the Court unanimously upheld the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938, reasoning that many farmers' home-grown wheat, added together, substantially affected interstate commerce. The aggregate-effects idea expanded federal reach for decades, until Lopez (1995).
w: It reserved farming to the state governments
The Court ruled for the federal government, not the states.
It struck down the New Deal farm program
The Court upheld the 1938 farm program.
It barred states from regulating local farms
The case let Congress regulate; it did not stop states from regulating farms too.

alt.q: Why did the Supreme Court in Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964) accept Congress's use of its commerce power here?
alt.a: Discrimination burdened interstate travel
alt.ex: In December 1964 the Court unanimously upheld Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 under the Commerce Clause. Refusing service to Black travelers discouraged travel between states, so Congress could ban it.
w: The motel was owned by the national government
The motel was privately owned; that is why the commerce power was needed.
Georgia had asked Congress to regulate the motel
No state request was involved; the power came from the Commerce Clause.
The motel had violated a treaty with other nations
No treaty was involved; the case turned on interstate commerce.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A 216-room motel in Atlanta, near two interstate highways, refuses to rent rooms to Black travelers. About three-fourths of its guests come from other states. The owner says Congress cannot regulate his private business.

alt.q: Which sequence of Commerce Clause cases is in the correct order?
alt.a: Gibbons v. Ogden; Wickard v. Filburn; Heart of Atlanta Motel
alt.ex: Gibbons v. Ogden was decided in 1824, Wickard v. Filburn in 1942, and Heart of Atlanta Motel in 1964. Each widened Congress's power over commerce: navigation, local farming, and civil rights in public accommodations.
w: Wickard v. Filburn; Gibbons v. Ogden; Heart of Atlanta Motel
Gibbons (1824) came more than a century before Wickard (1942).
Gibbons v. Ogden; Heart of Atlanta Motel; Wickard v. Filburn
Wickard (1942) came before Heart of Atlanta (1964).
Heart of Atlanta Motel; Wickard v. Filburn; Gibbons v. Ogden
This reverses the order; Gibbons (1824) was first.

items.q: Five years after United States v. Lopez (1995), the Supreme Court again limited the commerce power in which case, involving part of the Violence Against Women Act?
items.a: United States v. Morrison
items.ex: In May 2000, Morrison struck down the Violence Against Women Act's civil remedy, ruling that gender-motivated violence is not economic activity Congress may regulate. Like Lopez (1995), it kept a general police power with the states.
w: Printz v. United States
Printz (1997) struck down part of the Brady Act on anti-commandeering grounds, not the Violence Against Women Act.
Gonzales v. Raich
Raich (2005) upheld federal power to regulate home-grown marijuana.
National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius
NFIB (2012) concerned the Affordable Care Act, not the Violence Against Women Act.

alt.q: Based on United States v. Lopez (1995) and United States v. Morrison (2000), how would the Supreme Court most likely rule?
alt.a: Struck down, since vandalism is not economic activity
alt.ex: Lopez (1995) and Morrison (2000) held that Congress may not regulate noneconomic local crime just by adding up its effects on the national economy. Such crimes fall under the states' police powers.
w: Upheld, since all crimes affect the national economy
Lopez and Morrison rejected this reasoning for noneconomic crimes.
Struck down, since parks are protected by the First Amendment
The First Amendment protects expression, not parks; the issue is the commerce power.
Upheld, since the Supremacy Clause covers all crimes
The Supremacy Clause applies only to valid federal laws; it does not create power.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law making it a federal crime to vandalize any local public park. Congress argues that vandalism, added up nationwide, hurts tourism and the national economy.

alt.q: How did United States v. Lopez (1995) change the trend set by Wickard v. Filburn (1942)?
alt.a: It set limits after decades of commerce expansion
alt.ex: After Wickard (1942), the Court upheld nearly every use of the commerce power for more than 50 years. Lopez (1995) struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act, ruling that gun possession near a school is not economic activity.
w: It expanded commerce power even beyond Wickard
Lopez narrowed, not expanded, the commerce power.
It overruled Wickard and returned farming to states
Lopez did not overrule Wickard, which was later relied on in Gonzales v. Raich (2005).
It ended the Court's power of judicial review
Lopez used judicial review to strike down a federal law.

items.q: In Printz v. United States (1997), the Supreme Court struck down part of the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act of 1993. What was the Court's main reason?
items.a: Congress cannot command state officers
items.ex: In June 1997 the Court ruled 5–4 that requiring local sheriffs to run background checks commandeered state officers in violation of the Tenth Amendment's protection of state sovereignty. It extended New York v. United States (1992) from state legislatures to state executive officials.
w: Gun background checks violate the Second Amendment
Printz rested on state sovereignty, not the Second Amendment.
Gun sales are not interstate commerce
The Court did not rule on the commerce power; the problem was ordering state officers.
The president alone regulates gun sales
Congress, not the president alone, makes gun laws; the issue was commandeering.

alt.q: This principle, applied in 1997 to strike down a federal order to local sheriffs, is known as
alt.a: the anti-commandeering doctrine
alt.ex: Printz v. United States (1997), building on New York v. United States (1992), held that Congress may not force states or their officers to carry out federal programs. The doctrine protects state sovereignty under the Tenth Amendment.
w: the dual sovereignty doctrine
Dual sovereignty lets both the state and the nation prosecute the same act, as in Gamble (2019).
the doctrine of nullification
Nullification, claimed in 1798 and 1832, says states may void federal law; the Court has rejected it.
the separate but equal doctrine
Separate but equal came from Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) and concerned segregation.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Federal Government may not compel the States to enact or administer a federal regulatory program.”
Source: Printz v. United States (1997), quoting New York v. United States (1992), United States Reports

alt.q: Which sequence of Supreme Court decisions limiting federal power over the states is in the correct order?
alt.a: Lopez; Printz; NFIB v. Sebelius
alt.ex: United States v. Lopez (1995) limited the commerce power, Printz v. United States (1997) barred commandeering of state officers, and NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) barred coercive grant conditions. Together they marked a revival of limits on national power.
w: Printz; Lopez; NFIB v. Sebelius
Lopez (1995) came before Printz (1997).
Lopez; NFIB v. Sebelius; Printz
Printz (1997) came well before NFIB (2012).
NFIB v. Sebelius; Printz; Lopez
This reverses the order; NFIB (2012) was the most recent.

items.q: Which feature of the U.S. Constitution, signed in 1787, most directly reflects the idea in this passage?
items.a: separate federal courts in Article III
items.ex: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) warned that liberty is lost if judging is joined to lawmaking or enforcing. In 1787 the framers acted on this by placing the judicial power in a separate branch under Article III, with judges who hold office during good behaviour.
w: a two-house legislature in Article I
Bicameralism (1787) came from the Great Compromise between large and small states, not from separating judges from lawmakers.
the Electoral College set up in Article II
The Electoral College (1787) is a method for choosing the President; it does not separate judging from other powers.
the amendment process in Article V
Article V (1787) sets out how to change the Constitution; it does not divide judicial power from the other branches.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from The Spirit of the Laws (1748) by Baron de Montesquieu, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Again, there is no liberty, if the judiciary power be not separated from the legislative and executive. Were it joined with the legislative, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary control; for the judge would be then the legislator.”
Source: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws, Book XI, Chapter 6 (Thomas Nugent translation)

alt.q: Which Enlightenment work, published in 1748, most influenced the framers' decision to divide the national government into three separate branches?
alt.a: The Spirit of the Laws
alt.ex: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) argued that lawmaking, enforcing and judging must be held by different bodies to protect liberty. The framers followed this in 1787 by creating Articles I, II and III.
w: Two Treatises of Government
John Locke's work (1689) is known for natural rights and government by consent, not the three-branch model.
The Social Contract
Jean-Jacques Rousseau's work (1762) stressed the general will, not separating three branches.
Common Sense
Thomas Paine's pamphlet (1776) urged independence from Britain; it did not design three branches.

alt.q: Based on the passage, why did the framers of the 1787 Constitution follow Montesquieu's 1748 idea of separating powers?
alt.a: to keep all power from resting in one group
alt.ex: In The Federalist No. 47 (1788), Madison called the joining of all three powers in the same hands the very definition of tyranny, and he cited Montesquieu (1748) as the leading authority. Dividing power among three branches was meant to prevent that.
w: to let the states appoint national judges
Madison's point is about concentrated power, not state control of judges; federal judges are nominated by the President.
to help the government pass laws faster
Separating powers often slows government down; speed was not Madison's reason.
to give the President control of Congress
Giving one branch control of another would concentrate power, the very thing the passage condemns.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from The Federalist No. 47 (1788) by James Madison, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands … may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.”
Source: The Federalist No. 47

items.q: Which article of the Constitution, signed in 1787, vests “the executive Power” in a President?
items.a: Article II
items.ex: Article II (1787) begins, “The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America.” The framers created a single executive because the Articles of Confederation (in force 1781) had none, leaving no one to enforce national laws.
w: Article I
Article I (1787) creates Congress, the legislative branch.
Article III
Article III (1787) creates the judicial branch.
Article IV
Article IV (1787) covers relations among the states and admission of new states.

alt.q: Under the Articles of Confederation, in force from 1781, the national government had no separate executive or national court system. How did the Constitution of 1787 fix this weakness?
alt.a: by creating two new branches in Articles II and III
alt.ex: The 1787 Constitution kept a Congress (Article I) but added a President (Article II) to enforce laws and a Supreme Court (Article III) to decide cases, because the Confederation Congress alone could not carry out or interpret national laws.
w: by letting Congress appoint every state's governor
The Constitution never gave Congress power to choose governors; states choose their own.
by sending all national cases to the state courts
This describes the old problem; Article III created federal judicial power instead.
by placing a bill of rights inside Article VII
Article VII covers ratification; the Bill of Rights came as amendments ratified in 1791.

alt.q: In the Constitution signed in 1787, which branch did the framers describe first, in Article I, reflecting their view that lawmaking by elected representatives was central to a republic?
alt.a: the legislative branch
alt.ex: Article I (1787) creates Congress and lists its powers in the greatest detail. The framers put the people's representatives first because, after the colonial experience under a king, they saw elected lawmakers as the heart of republican government.
w: the executive branch
The executive branch is created second, in Article II (1787).
the judicial branch
The judicial branch is created third, in Article III (1787).
the state governments
States are addressed later, mainly in Article IV (1787); they are not a branch of the national government.

items.q: Why did Congress pass the Reapportionment Act of 1929, which kept the House of Representatives at 435 members?
items.a: Congress had not reapportioned seats after the 1920 census
items.ex: After the 1920 census Congress never agreed on a new apportionment, leaving districts badly unequal. The act signed June 18, 1929, kept the House at 435 (its size since 1913) and created an automatic process for dividing seats after each census, starting in 1930.
w: The Seventeenth Amendment had just added new House seats
The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) changed how senators are chosen; it added no House seats.
The Supreme Court had ordered the House reduced to 435
No court ordered this; Congress sets House size by statute.
Several new states had joined the Union during the 1920s
No state was admitted between 1912 (Arizona, New Mexico) and 1959 (Alaska, Hawaii).

alt.q: Which law explains why the total stayed the same?
alt.a: the Reapportionment Act of 1929
alt.ex: The Reapportionment Act of 1929 fixed the House at 435 seats and set up automatic reapportionment after each census, beginning in 1930. It was passed because Congress had failed to reapportion after the 1920 census, so today states trade seats but the total does not change.
w: the Judiciary Act of 1789
The Judiciary Act of 1789 set up the federal courts, not the size of the House.
the Presidential Succession Act of 1947
The 1947 act sets the line of succession to the presidency.
the Voting Rights Act of 1965
The 1965 act bans racial discrimination in voting; it does not set House size.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: After the 2020 census, Florida gained one seat in the U.S. House of Representatives while some other states lost seats. Even so, the total number of voting House members stayed at 435.

alt.q: The House of Representatives has had 435 seats since 1913, except for a few years after 1959. Why did the House briefly have 437 members?
alt.a: Alaska and Hawaii became states in 1959
alt.ex: Congress temporarily added two seats when Alaska and Hawaii were admitted in 1959, so the new states would be represented. The House returned to 435 after the reapportionment based on the 1960 census, as the 1929 act requires.
w: D.C. gained two voting members in 1961
The Twenty-third Amendment (1961) gave D.C. electors for President, not voting House members.
Puerto Rico and Guam won voting seats
U.S. territories have only non-voting delegates in the House.
the 1960 census showed rapid growth
Population growth changes how seats are divided, not the total, under the 1929 act.

items.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1913, changed how U.S. senators are chosen?
items.a: the Seventeenth Amendment
items.ex: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified April 8, 1913, requires senators to be elected directly by the people of each state for six-year terms. Before it, Article I (1787) let state legislatures choose senators.
w: the Sixteenth Amendment
The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) let Congress tax incomes; it did not change Senate elections.
the Nineteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) barred denying the vote on account of sex.
the Twelfth Amendment
The Twelfth Amendment (1804) changed how electors vote for President and Vice President.

alt.q: Which reform, ratified in 1913, was meant to end problems like these?
alt.a: direct election of senators by the voters
alt.ex: Under the original 1787 system, state legislatures chose senators and sometimes deadlocked for months or were accused of bribery. Progressive Era reformers won the Seventeenth Amendment (1913) so that the people of each state would elect their senators directly.
w: a limit of two terms for each senator
Senators have never had term limits; the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limits only Presidents.
a federal tax on personal incomes
The income tax came from the Sixteenth Amendment (1913), which did not change how senators are chosen.
a ban on poll taxes in federal elections
Poll taxes in federal elections were banned by the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964).

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In the early 1900s, a state legislature argues for months without agreeing on whom to send to the U.S. Senate, leaving the seat empty. Newspapers in another state report that a wealthy candidate won his Senate seat by paying state legislators for their votes.

alt.q: Which sequence lists these changes to Congress in the correct order?
alt.a: Constitution signed, senators elected by voters, House fixed at 435
alt.ex: The Constitution was signed in 1787; the Seventeenth Amendment (1913) made senators popularly elected to curb corruption; and the Reapportionment Act of 1929 permanently fixed the House at 435 after Congress failed to reapportion following the 1920 census.
w: House fixed at 435, Constitution signed, senators elected by voters
The 1929 act came long after the 1787 Constitution.
Senators elected by voters, House fixed at 435, Constitution signed
The Constitution (1787) came first; the other two are from 1913 and 1929.
Constitution signed, House fixed at 435, senators elected by voters
Direct election of senators (1913) came before the 1929 act.

mt.q: Match each amendment to what it did.
pairs: No poll taxes in federal elections
mt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.

items.q: For which federal office does she meet every qualification set by the Constitution of 1787?
items.a: U.S. Representative
items.ex: Article I (1787) requires a Representative to be 25, a citizen for 7 years and an inhabitant of the state, which she meets. A Senator must be a citizen for 9 years, and a President must be a natural born citizen, so she does not yet qualify for those offices.
w: U.S. Senator
A Senator must have been a citizen for 9 years (Article I, 1787); she has only 8.
President of the United States
Article II (1787) requires a natural born citizen; she was naturalized.
Vice President
The Twelfth Amendment (1804) applies the President's qualifications to the Vice President, so she is not eligible.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A 32-year-old woman was born abroad and became a U.S. citizen 8 years ago. She has lived in Florida for 20 years and wants to run for federal office from Florida in the 2026 election.

alt.q: The Constitution of 1787 requires senators to have been citizens for nine years, two more than representatives. What reason did the framers give for this longer requirement?
alt.a: Senators would share in treaties and foreign affairs
alt.ex: In The Federalist No. 62 (1788), Madison explained that senators need longer citizenship because the Senate takes part in dealings with foreign nations, such as consenting to treaties. The 1787 Constitution therefore set 9 years for senators versus 7 for representatives.
w: Senators would choose the President after a tie
The House, not the Senate, chooses the President when no one wins a majority (1787; Twelfth Amendment, 1804).
Senators would write every bill that raises taxes
Revenue bills must start in the House under Article I, Section 7 (1787).
Senators would also serve as federal trial judges
Senators never serve as judges; Article III (1787) gives judicial power to the courts.

alt.q: Which requirement for the presidency, written into Article II in 1787, was meant mainly to guard against foreign influence over the nation's highest office?
alt.a: being a natural born citizen
alt.ex: Article II (1787) limits the presidency to natural born citizens (or citizens at the time of adoption). John Jay urged this in a 1787 letter to Washington, fearing a foreign-born commander in chief, and the framers adopted it to keep foreign powers from gaining control.
w: being at least 35 years old
The age requirement (1787) was meant to ensure maturity and experience, not to block foreign influence.
having first served in Congress
The Constitution has never required prior service in Congress.
owning land in one of the states
The Constitution of 1787 set no property requirement for the presidency.

items.q: Under Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution (1787), what may the Vice President do?
items.a: cast a vote to break the tie
items.ex: Article I, Section 3 (1787) makes the Vice President President of the Senate, with no vote unless the Senate is equally divided. The framers gave the Vice President this role so that ties in a Senate with an even number of members could be resolved.
w: veto the bill for the President
Only the President may veto a bill (Article I, Section 7, 1787).
send the bill to the House Speaker
The Vice President has no power to redirect bills to the Speaker.
ask the Supreme Court to decide it
Courts decide cases, not Senate ties; asking them would break separation of powers.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 2026, the U.S. Senate votes 50–50 on a bill. The Vice President is present in the chamber.

alt.q: Which officer does Article I (1787) allow the Senate to choose to preside in this situation?
alt.a: the president pro tempore
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3 (1787) lets the Senate choose “a President pro tempore, in the Absence of the Vice President.” The framers provided this so the Senate could keep working when the Vice President was away or serving as President.
w: the Speaker of the House
The Speaker leads the House, not the Senate (Article I, Section 2, 1787).
the Chief Justice
The Chief Justice presides in the Senate only during a President's impeachment trial (Article I, Section 3, 1787).
the Secretary of State
The Secretary of State is an executive officer and has no role in leading the Senate.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: The Vice President is traveling overseas on a diplomatic trip while the Senate is in session. The Senate still needs an officer to preside over its business.

alt.q: Which leader is chosen by the members of the House under Article I (1787) and, since the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, stands next in line after the Vice President?
alt.a: the Speaker of the House
alt.ex: Article I, Section 2 (1787) lets the House “chuse their Speaker.” The Presidential Succession Act of 1947 placed the Speaker right after the Vice President because President Truman wanted an elected official next in line.
w: the president pro tempore
The president pro tempore is chosen by the Senate and is third in line under the 1947 act.
the Senate majority leader
The majority leader is a party post, not mentioned in the Constitution or the 1947 line.
the House majority leader
The House majority leader is a party post and is not in the line of succession.

items.q: In 1791, Congress chartered the First Bank of the United States, even though Article I, Section 8 never mentions a bank. Which part of the Constitution did supporters such as Alexander Hamilton rely on?
items.a: the Necessary and Proper Clause
items.ex: The last clause of Article I, Section 8 (1787) lets Congress make laws “necessary and proper” to carry out its listed powers. Hamilton argued in 1791 that a bank helped Congress tax, borrow and manage money; the Supreme Court agreed about the Second Bank in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
w: the Supremacy Clause
The Supremacy Clause (Article VI, 1787) settles conflicts between federal and state law; it does not grant Congress new powers.
the Take Care Clause
The Take Care Clause (Article II, 1787) directs the President to enforce laws, not Congress to create banks.
the Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause (Article IV, 1787) makes states honor each other's records and court rulings.

alt.q: Why did Roosevelt need Congress to act?
alt.a: Article I gives Congress the power to declare war.
alt.ex: Article I, Section 8 (1787) gives Congress the power “To declare War,” while the President is Commander in Chief. The framers gave the decision to the people's representatives because European kings had often led nations into war on their own; Congress used this power on December 8, 1941.
w: Article II makes Congress head of the military.
Article II (1787) makes the President, not Congress, Commander in Chief.
Article III requires the courts to approve wars.
Courts play no role in declaring war under the 1787 Constitution.
Article IV lets Congress defend only the states.
Article IV (1787) protects states against invasion, but the war power is in Article I.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: On December 8, 1941, the day after the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt went before Congress and asked it to declare war on Japan. Congress voted for the declaration that same day.

alt.q: Which source of power did Congress use when it passed this law?
alt.a: Article I's power to coin money
alt.ex: Article I, Section 8 (1787) gives Congress the power “To coin Money” and regulate its value. Congress used it in the Coinage Act of 1792 so the nation would have one uniform currency instead of a confusing mix of coins.
w: Article II's power to grant pardons
The pardon power (Article II, 1787) belongs to the President and concerns crimes, not money.
Article III's power over federal cases
Article III (1787) gives courts power to decide cases, not to create money.
Article IV's power over territories
Article IV (1787) lets Congress govern territories; it is not the source of the money power.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1792, Congress passed a law creating a national mint in Philadelphia to make U.S. coins. Before then, Americans used a confusing mix of foreign coins and different kinds of paper money.

items.q: On September 8, 1974, President Gerald Ford pardoned former President Richard Nixon for any federal crimes he may have committed in office. Which part of the Constitution gave Ford this power?
items.a: Article II, Section 2
items.ex: Article II, Section 2 (1787) gives the President power to grant pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment. Ford used it in 1974, saying he wanted to end the national division over Watergate.
w: Article I, Section 8
Article I, Section 8 (1787) lists the powers of Congress, which cannot grant pardons.
Article III, Section 2
Article III, Section 2 (1787) sets the reach of the judicial power.
the Twenty-fifth Amendment
The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) covers vacancies and disability; it let Ford become Vice President in 1973 but gives no pardon power.

alt.q: Why did President Ford say he granted his September 1974 pardon to Richard Nixon?
alt.a: to spare the nation more division over Watergate
alt.ex: Ford said the 1974 pardon, issued under Article II, Section 2 (1787), was meant to end the bitter national division over the Watergate scandal rather than prolong it through a trial of a former President.
w: to cancel Nixon's conviction in his Senate trial
Nixon was never impeached or tried; he resigned on August 9, 1974.
to allow Nixon to run for President once again
Nixon had been elected twice, so the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) barred another run; Ford gave no such reason.
to end an ongoing Senate impeachment trial
No Senate trial ever began; Nixon resigned before the House voted.

alt.q: Which presidential action is based on Article II, Section 3 rather than Section 2?
alt.a: giving a State of the Union report
alt.ex: Article II, Section 3 (1787) directs the President to give Congress information on the State of the Union and recommend measures. Washington gave the first annual message in January 1790; the duty keeps Congress informed and lets the President propose laws.
w: nominating a judge to a federal court
Nominating judges is in Article II, Section 2 (1787).
granting a pardon for a federal crime
The pardon power is in Article II, Section 2 (1787).
commanding the nation's armed forces
The Commander in Chief role is in Article II, Section 2 (1787).

items.q: Why did this case begin in the U.S. Supreme Court instead of a lower court?
items.a: Article III gives it original jurisdiction when a state is a party
items.ex: Article III, Section 2 (1787) gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases in which a state is a party. The framers wanted a neutral national court, not one state's courts, to settle disputes between states, as in Florida v. Georgia (2021).
w: Congress voted to send this water dispute straight to the Court
Congress did not vote on this case; the Constitution itself gives original jurisdiction.
State courts are barred from hearing any case about water
State courts hear many water cases; the issue is that two states were the parties.
The Judiciary Act of 1789 requires all appeals to start there
Appeals by definition begin in lower courts; this case began in the Supreme Court as a trial.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Florida sued Georgia, claiming that Georgia used too much water from a river system the two states share, harming Florida's oyster industry. The case started in the U.S. Supreme Court rather than in a lower court, and the Court decided it in 2021.

alt.q: Under Article III, Section 2 (1787), federal judicial power extends to cases arising under the Constitution, federal laws and treaties. Why did the framers give these cases to federal courts?
alt.a: so federal law would be applied the same way nationwide
alt.ex: Article III (1787) lets federal courts hear cases arising under the Constitution, federal laws and treaties because, under the Articles of Confederation (1781), there were no national courts and federal law could be read differently in each state.
w: so state courts could veto federal laws they disliked
Federal jurisdiction was meant to prevent states from undermining national law, not to let them veto it.
so Congress could overturn court rulings by majority vote
Congress cannot overturn court decisions by simple vote; that would violate separation of powers.
so the President could choose which cases judges hear
Courts, not the President, decide cases; the framers kept the judiciary independent.

alt.q: Which article of the Constitution, signed in 1787, gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases involving ambassadors and those in which a state is a party?
alt.a: Article III
alt.ex: Article III, Section 2 (1787) gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases affecting ambassadors and those in which a state is a party. These sensitive cases go straight to the highest court to protect foreign relations and keep peace among the states.
w: Article I
Article I (1787) sets out the powers of Congress, not the jurisdiction of courts.
Article II
Article II (1787) sets out the President's powers, including receiving ambassadors.
Article VI
Article VI (1787) contains the Supremacy Clause and the oath requirement.

items.q: What happens to the bill?
items.a: It becomes law without a signature.
items.ex: Article I, Section 7 (1787) says that a bill not returned within ten days (Sundays excepted) becomes law as if signed, unless Congress has adjourned. The framers did this so a President could not kill a bill simply by ignoring it while Congress is in session.
w: It dies by means of a pocket veto.
A pocket veto happens only when Congress's adjournment prevents the bill's return (Article I, Section 7, 1787).
It goes back to a committee for changes.
Nothing in the Constitution sends an unsigned bill back to committee.
It goes to the Supreme Court for review.
The Supreme Court does not review bills before they become law.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a bill and presents it to the President on June 1, 2026. Congress stays in session. The President neither signs nor vetoes the bill, and ten days (Sundays excepted) pass.

alt.q: Under Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution (1787), what must happen for a bill to become law over the President's veto?
alt.a: two-thirds of each house votes to override
alt.ex: Article I, Section 7 (1787) requires two-thirds of both the House and the Senate to override a veto. The framers rejected an absolute veto but set a high bar so the President's objections would carry real weight.
w: three-fourths of the states vote to approve it
State approval by three-fourths is needed to ratify amendments (Article V, 1787), not to pass bills.
the Supreme Court upholds the bill
Courts do not take part in passing laws; they review them only after enactment in real cases.
a majority of each house votes again
A simple majority is not enough; the 1787 Constitution requires two-thirds.

alt.q: Which sequence best describes how a bill usually becomes law under the process set up in 1787?
alt.a: introduced, studied in committee, passed by both houses, signed
alt.ex: Under Article I, Section 7 (1787), a bill must pass both houses and be presented to the President. Committees, used since the First Congress in 1789, study bills first so the full chamber votes on worked-out proposals.
w: passed by both houses, introduced, studied in committee, signed
A bill must be introduced before anything else can happen to it.
introduced, signed, studied in committee, passed by both houses
The President signs only after both houses pass the bill (Article I, Section 7, 1787).
studied in committee, signed, introduced, passed by both houses
A bill cannot be studied or signed before it is introduced and passed.

items.q: In November 1973, Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over President Nixon's veto. Why did Congress pass this law?
items.a: to limit the President's war-making power
items.ex: Angered by the Vietnam War and the secret bombing of Cambodia, Congress overrode Nixon's veto on November 7, 1973. The law requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of sending forces into hostilities and limits such use to 60 days without approval.
w: to give the President the power to declare war
Only Congress may declare war (Article I, Section 8, 1787); the law limited the President.
to end the military draft for the Vietnam War
The draft ended separately in 1973; the War Powers Resolution concerns sending troops into combat.
to let the Senate command troops stationed overseas
The President remains Commander in Chief (Article II, 1787); Congress did not take command.

alt.q: Which constitutional check did Congress use to make the War Powers Resolution law on November 7, 1973?
alt.a: overriding a veto by a two-thirds vote
alt.ex: Nixon vetoed the War Powers Resolution in October 1973, and two-thirds of both houses overrode the veto on November 7, 1973, as Article I, Section 7 (1787) allows. Congress wanted to reassert its war powers after Vietnam.
w: impeaching the President in the House
No impeachment was involved; Nixon resigned in 1974 before a House vote.
refusing to confirm an appointment
Confirmation (Article II, 1787) concerns nominees, not passing laws.
rejecting a treaty in the Senate
Treaty rejection (Article II, 1787) concerns agreements with other nations, not passing laws.

alt.q: Under the War Powers Resolution of 1973, what must the President do?
alt.a: report to Congress within 48 hours
alt.ex: The War Powers Resolution (1973) requires the President to report to Congress within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities, and to end the use of force within 60 days unless Congress approves. Congress passed it after Vietnam to protect its power to declare war.
w: get Supreme Court approval first
Courts do not approve military actions in advance; the law involves Congress, not the Court.
win a two-thirds Senate vote first
The law requires notice to Congress, not prior Senate approval by two-thirds.
pull all troops out within 10 days
The law allows 60 days (plus up to 30 for withdrawal), not 10.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A President orders U.S. troops into combat in another country to protect American citizens there. Congress has not declared war or passed any law authorizing the action.

items.q: In Clinton v. City of New York (1998), the Supreme Court struck down the Line Item Veto Act of 1996. What was the Court's main reason?
items.a: A President must accept or veto a bill as a whole.
items.ex: On June 25, 1998, the Court ruled 6–3 that letting the President cancel parts of signed laws violated the Presentment Clause of Article I, Section 7 (1787). Laws may be changed only through passage by both houses and presentment to the President.
w: Only governors may use a line-item veto.
Many governors have this power under state constitutions, but that was not the Court's reasoning.
Congress may not pass spending bills at all.
Congress clearly has spending power under Article I, Section 8 (1787).
The Senate must approve every presidential veto.
No such rule exists; vetoes go back to Congress for a possible override.

alt.q: Which 1998 Supreme Court decision held that the President may not cancel individual spending items from a law he has signed?
alt.a: Clinton v. City of New York
alt.ex: Clinton v. City of New York (June 25, 1998) struck down the Line Item Veto Act of 1996 because the Presentment Clause (Article I, Section 7, 1787) gives the President only the choice to sign or veto an entire bill.
w: Clinton v. Jones
Clinton v. Jones (1997) held that a sitting President may be sued over private conduct before taking office.
Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
Youngstown (1952) held that President Truman could not seize steel mills without authority from Congress.
INS v. Chadha
INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down a one-house legislative veto, not a line-item veto.

alt.q: Based on the Supreme Court's 1998 ruling in Clinton v. City of New York, this law would most likely be
alt.a: unconstitutional, since it bypasses the lawmaking process
alt.ex: In 1998 the Court held that cancelling parts of a signed law amends it without the votes of both houses and presentment required by Article I, Section 7 (1787). The framers designed that process so no single official could rewrite laws alone.
w: constitutional, since Congress agreed to give up the power
The Court ruled that Congress cannot hand away the Constitution's lawmaking procedure.
constitutional, since many governors have this same power
State constitutions do not control the federal Presentment Clause.
unconstitutional, since only the Senate may control spending
Both houses share spending power; spending bills begin in the House.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law allowing the President, after signing a budget bill, to strike out any single spending item he or she dislikes, while the rest of the law stays in force.

items.q: Why does the Constitution of 1787 require the Chief Justice, rather than the Vice President, to preside when a President is tried in the Senate?
items.a: The Vice President would gain from a conviction
items.ex: Article I, Section 3 (1787) has the Chief Justice preside over a President's trial because the Vice President, who normally presides over the Senate, would become President if the President were removed. Chief Justice Salmon P. Chase first did so at Andrew Johnson's trial in 1868.
w: The Vice President may not attend the Senate
The Vice President is President of the Senate under Article I, Section 3 (1787).
The Chief Justice alone decides the verdict
Senators vote on the verdict; two-thirds of those present are needed to convict.
The House chooses the judge for each trial
The Constitution, not the House, names the Chief Justice for presidential trials.

alt.q: In 1804, the Senate convicted federal judge John Pickering and removed him from office. What vote did the Constitution require for this conviction?
alt.a: two-thirds of the senators present
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3 (1787) says no one may be convicted without two-thirds of the members present. Pickering, removed on March 12, 1804, was the first judge removed this way; the framers set a high bar so removals would not be merely partisan.
w: a simple majority of the full Senate
A simple majority is enough to confirm nominees, but conviction requires two-thirds.
three-fourths of the senators present
Three-fourths is the share of states needed to ratify amendments (Article V, 1787).
a majority of both the House and Senate
The House impeaches by majority; only the Senate votes on conviction.

alt.q: What is the result of the Senate vote?
alt.a: The secretary stays because 67 votes were needed.
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3 (1787) requires two-thirds of senators present, here 67 of 100, to convict. The framers set this high bar so officials would not be removed by a bare partisan majority.
w: The secretary is removed because most voted guilty.
A majority is not enough; conviction requires two-thirds.
The secretary is removed because the House impeached.
Impeachment is only a formal charge; removal requires Senate conviction.
The Supreme Court must now make the final decision.
The Senate has “the sole Power to try all Impeachments” (1787); courts do not review the verdict.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: The House votes to impeach a cabinet secretary. At the Senate trial, all 100 senators vote: 55 vote guilty and 45 vote not guilty.

items.q: Why did the House impeach President Andrew Johnson in 1868?
items.a: He removed his Secretary of War in defiance of a law.
items.ex: On February 24, 1868, the House impeached Johnson mainly for removing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in violation of the Tenure of Office Act (1867), amid a bitter fight with Congress over Reconstruction. The Senate acquitted him by one vote in May 1868.
w: He lied under oath to a federal grand jury.
This was a charge against Bill Clinton in 1998.
He pressured a foreign leader to aid his campaign.
This describes the 2019 charges against Donald Trump.
He ordered the cover-up of a political burglary.
This describes Richard Nixon and Watergate (1972–74); Nixon resigned before a House vote.

alt.q: What was the outcome of President Andrew Johnson's 1868 impeachment trial in the Senate?
alt.a: He was acquitted by a single vote.
alt.ex: In May 1868 the Senate voted 35–19 to convict Johnson, one vote short of the two-thirds required by Article I, Section 3 (1787). The high bar protected the President from removal over what many saw as a political dispute about Reconstruction.
w: He was convicted and removed from office.
No President has ever been convicted and removed by the Senate.
He resigned before the Senate could vote.
Richard Nixon, not Johnson, resigned (1974) before facing a vote.
The House dropped the charges before trial.
The House impeached Johnson on February 24, 1868, and the Senate held a full trial.

alt.q: Which of these presidential impeachments happened first?
alt.a: Andrew Johnson's impeachment
alt.ex: Andrew Johnson was impeached in 1868 over his clash with Congress about Reconstruction and his removal of Secretary of War Stanton. Bill Clinton was impeached in 1998, and Donald Trump in 2019 and again in 2021; all were acquitted by the Senate.
w: Bill Clinton's impeachment
Clinton was impeached in December 1998, 130 years after Johnson.
Donald Trump's first impeachment
Trump was first impeached in December 2019.
Donald Trump's second impeachment
Trump was impeached a second time in January 2021.

items.q: In December 1998, the House impeached President Bill Clinton. What were the charges?
items.a: perjury and obstruction of justice
items.ex: On December 19, 1998, the House impeached Clinton for perjury and obstruction of justice related to statements about his conduct with a White House intern. The Senate acquitted him on February 12, 1999, because neither article got the two-thirds vote needed.
w: abuse of power and obstruction of Congress
These were the charges against Donald Trump in December 2019.
incitement of insurrection
This was the charge against Donald Trump in January 2021.
violating the Tenure of Office Act
This was the main charge against Andrew Johnson in 1868.

alt.q: In January 2021, the House impeached President Donald Trump for a second time. On what charge?
alt.a: incitement of insurrection
alt.ex: On January 13, 2021, a week after the January 6 attack on the Capitol, the House impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection. The Senate voted 57–43 to convict on February 13, 2021, short of the 67 votes needed, so he was acquitted.
w: perjury and obstruction of justice
These were the charges against Bill Clinton in 1998.
abuse of power and obstruction of Congress
These were the charges in Trump's first impeachment, in December 2019.
violating the Tenure of Office Act
This was the main charge against Andrew Johnson in 1868.

alt.q: In February 2021, 57 senators voted to convict former President Donald Trump, yet he was acquitted. Why?
alt.a: Conviction needs 67 votes, two-thirds of 100.
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3 (1787) requires two-thirds of senators present to convict. In the February 13, 2021, vote, 57 of 100 voted guilty, ten short of 67. The framers set this high bar so removal would need broad, not merely partisan, support.
w: The House had already removed him from office.
The House can only impeach (charge); it cannot remove anyone.
The Chief Justice ruled the trial was invalid.
No such ruling occurred; the trial ended with the Senate's vote.
A majority of senators voted to acquit him.
Only 43 senators voted to acquit; 57 was a majority for conviction.

items.q: In July 1974, the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment against President Richard Nixon, but the full House never voted on them. Why?
items.a: Nixon resigned in August 1974 before a House vote.
items.ex: After the Supreme Court ordered him to release the Watergate tapes in July 1974, Nixon lost support in Congress and resigned on August 9, 1974, the only President to resign. The threat of impeachment under Article I (1787) pushed him out before a vote.
w: The Senate had already acquitted Nixon of the charges.
The Senate cannot try a President until the House impeaches; it never held a trial.
The Supreme Court blocked the House from voting.
The Court ruled against Nixon on the tapes; it did not stop impeachment.
Vice President Ford pardoned Nixon before a vote.
Ford's pardon came on September 8, 1974, after Nixon resigned, and pardons cannot stop impeachment.

alt.q: What does President Nixon's resignation in August 1974 show about impeachment as a check on the executive branch?
alt.a: The threat of removal can push officials to resign.
alt.ex: Facing almost certain impeachment by the House and likely conviction by the Senate, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974. The case shows that the impeachment power the framers gave Congress in 1787 can hold a President accountable even without a vote.
w: Presidents can be removed only by the Supreme Court.
Removal comes through Senate conviction (Article I, 1787), not the Court.
The House alone can remove a President from office.
The House only impeaches; the Senate must convict to remove.
A President can stop impeachment by firing prosecutors.
Nixon's firing of the special prosecutor in 1973 increased, not stopped, the push for impeachment.

alt.q: Which sequence of events from 1974 is in the correct order?
alt.a: Court orders tapes released, Nixon resigns, Ford pardons Nixon
alt.ex: In United States v. Nixon (July 24, 1974), the Court ordered the tapes released; Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974; and Ford pardoned him on September 8, 1974, saying he wanted to end national division over Watergate.
w: Nixon resigns, Court orders tapes released, Ford pardons Nixon
The Court's ruling (July 24) came before the resignation (August 9).
Ford pardons Nixon, Nixon resigns, Court orders tapes released
Ford could pardon Nixon only after becoming President on August 9.
Court orders tapes released, Ford pardons Nixon, Nixon resigns
The pardon (September 8) came after the resignation (August 9).

items.q: In November 1919, the Senate voted against the Treaty of Versailles, which President Wilson strongly supported. Which constitutional rule allowed opponents to block the treaty?
items.a: Treaties need two-thirds of the senators present.
items.ex: Article II, Section 2 (1787) lets the President make treaties only if two-thirds of the senators present concur. The framers required a supermajority so that binding agreements with foreign nations would have broad support; the treaty failed in 1919 and again in March 1920.
w: Treaties need approval by three-fourths of the states.
States do not vote on treaties; three-fourths of states ratify amendments (Article V).
Treaties need a majority vote of the House.
