The House has no formal vote on treaties under Article II (1787).
Treaties need approval from the Supreme Court.
The Court does not approve treaties before they take effect.

alt.q: Why did many senators, led by Henry Cabot Lodge, oppose the Treaty of Versailles in 1919–1920?
alt.a: They feared the League could pull the U.S. into wars.
alt.ex: Lodge and his allies objected that the League of Nations covenant could commit the U.S. to defend other nations without a vote of Congress, which holds the power to declare war under Article I (1787). Without two-thirds support, the treaty failed in 1919 and 1920.
w: They objected that the House had not voted on it.
The Constitution (1787) gives treaty consent to the Senate alone, so this was not an objection.
They wanted the U.S. to annex Germany's colonies.
The U.S. did not seek German colonies; the fight centered on the League.
They wanted Germany to pay large war costs to the U.S.
The U.S. sought no reparations for itself; the fight centered on the League of Nations and Congress's war power.

alt.q: When senators voted down the Treaty of Versailles in November 1919, which power were they checking?
alt.a: the President's power to make treaties
alt.ex: Under Article II, Section 2 (1787), the President negotiates treaties but needs two-thirds of the Senate to agree. The Senate's 1919 vote checked President Wilson's treaty-making power, showing how the framers split foreign-policy power between branches.
w: the courts' power to review laws
Judicial review comes from Marbury v. Madison (1803) and was not involved.
the House's power to start tax bills
Revenue bills (Article I, Section 7, 1787) had nothing to do with the treaty.
the states' power to regulate trade
States may not make treaties (Article I, Section 10, 1787); this was a national question.

items.q: On October 23, 1987, the Senate voted 58–42 against confirming Robert Bork, President Reagan's Supreme Court nominee. Which power did the Senate use?
items.a: its advice and consent on appointments
items.ex: Article II, Section 2 (1787) says the President nominates and, with the Senate's advice and consent, appoints Supreme Court justices. The framers added this check so a President could not fill the courts with unfit choices; Bork's 1987 defeat is a famous example.
w: its sole power to try all impeachments
Impeachment trials (Article I, Section 3, 1787) remove officials already in office.
its power to override vetoes
Veto overrides (Article I, Section 7, 1787) apply to bills, not nominees.
its power to start revenue bills
Revenue bills must begin in the House, not the Senate (Article I, Section 7, 1787).

alt.q: Which statement correctly compares the Senate votes needed under Article II of the Constitution (1787)?
alt.a: Majority to confirm a nominee; two-thirds for a treaty
alt.ex: Article II, Section 2 (1787) requires two-thirds of senators present for treaties, but appointments, such as Supreme Court justices, are confirmed by a simple majority. The framers set a higher bar for treaties because they bind the whole nation in foreign affairs.
w: Two-thirds to confirm a nominee; majority for a treaty
This reverses the rule: treaties, not nominees, need two-thirds.
Three-fifths to confirm a nominee; two-thirds for a treaty
The Constitution sets no three-fifths rule; that number comes from a Senate debate rule (cloture).
A simple majority for both nominees and treaties
Treaties require two-thirds of senators present, not a simple majority.

alt.q: What is the result of the Senate vote?
alt.a: The nominee cannot take office.
alt.ex: Under Article II, Section 2 (1787), the President's nominee takes office only with the Senate's consent, given by majority vote. The Senate rejected John Tower as Secretary of Defense 47–53 in 1989, showing this check on the executive.
w: The nominee takes office anyway.
Without Senate consent, the President cannot appoint the nominee (Article II, 1787).
The House holds a second vote.
The House has no role in confirming nominees.
The Supreme Court decides it.
Courts do not review the Senate's confirmation votes.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A President nominates a person to be Secretary of Defense. During confirmation hearings, senators question the nominee's fitness for the job. The full Senate then votes 47 in favor and 53 against.

items.q: Why was the Twelfth Amendment, ratified in 1804, added to the Constitution?
items.a: Running mates tied in the 1800 election.
items.ex: In 1800, Thomas Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr each received 73 electoral votes because electors cast two votes without naming which was for President. After the House needed 36 ballots to choose Jefferson in 1801, the Twelfth Amendment (1804) required separate votes for President and Vice President.
w: The 1824 election was decided by the House.
The 1824 election came 20 years after the amendment and was decided under it.
Senators had been chosen by state legislatures.
This problem led to the Seventeenth Amendment (1913).
Washington's two-term tradition was broken.
This led to the Twenty-second Amendment (1951).

alt.q: Which change made by the Twelfth Amendment (1804) was meant to prevent a repeat of this problem?
alt.a: separate electoral votes for President and Vice President
alt.ex: The Twelfth Amendment (1804) requires electors to cast distinct ballots for President and Vice President. It was adopted after the 1800 election, when Jefferson and Burr tied with 73 votes each and the House needed 36 ballots in February 1801 to choose Jefferson.
w: direct election of the President by a national popular vote
The Twelfth Amendment kept the Electoral College created in 1787.
selection of every Vice President by the House of Representatives
The House chooses only when no candidate wins a majority, and the Senate picks the Vice President in that case.
a limit of two terms for any President
Term limits came from the Twenty-second Amendment (1951).

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In the election of 1800, each Democratic-Republican elector cast one vote for Thomas Jefferson and one for Aaron Burr, without saying which vote was for President. Both men finished with 73 electoral votes, and the House of Representatives needed 36 ballots to choose Jefferson.

alt.q: Which constitutional provision governed how the House made this choice?
alt.a: the Twelfth Amendment
alt.ex: Under the Twelfth Amendment (1804), if no one wins a majority of electoral votes, the House chooses among the top three, with each state delegation casting one vote. The House used this rule in February 1825 to choose John Quincy Adams.
w: the Seventeenth Amendment
The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) provides for direct election of senators.
the Twenty-second Amendment
The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limits presidential terms.
the Twenty-fifth Amendment
The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) covers presidential vacancy and disability.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In the election of 1824, Andrew Jackson won the most electoral votes, but no candidate won a majority. In February 1825, the House of Representatives, voting by state delegation, chose John Quincy Adams as President.

items.q: Today the Electoral College has 538 electors. Which combination produces this total?
items.a: 435 House seats, 100 senators and 3 for D.C.
items.ex: Article II (1787) gives each state electors equal to its House and Senate seats (435 + 100), and the Twenty-third Amendment (1961) gave the District of Columbia 3 electors, so D.C. residents could vote for President. A candidate needs 270 to win.
w: 435 House seats, 100 senators and 3 for territories
U.S. territories such as Puerto Rico have no electoral votes.
435 House seats and 103 senators from all states
There are exactly 100 senators, two per state (Article I, 1787).
538 House districts with one elector for each
There are 435 House districts; the total also counts senators and D.C.

alt.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1961, gave residents of the District of Columbia electoral votes for President?
alt.a: the Twenty-third Amendment
alt.ex: The Twenty-third Amendment (1961) gave D.C. electors equal to the least populous state, now 3, because residents of the nation's capital had no voice in choosing the President.
w: the Twenty-fourth Amendment
The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections.
the Twenty-sixth Amendment
The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971) set the voting age at 18.
the Twenty-second Amendment
The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limits presidents to two elected terms.

alt.q: Why did the framers in 1787 create the Electoral College instead of having Congress choose the President?
alt.a: to keep the President independent of Congress
alt.ex: At the Convention of 1787, delegates worried that a President chosen by Congress would depend on it, weakening separation of powers. Article II instead had electors chosen in each state, a compromise between a vote by Congress and a direct national vote.
w: to let the Supreme Court approve the winner
The Supreme Court has no role in approving the winner under Article II (1787).
to give every state the same number of votes
Electors are based on House plus Senate seats, so larger states get more.
to make the House the judge of every election
The House chooses only when no one wins a majority, not in every election.

items.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected President twice?
items.a: the Twenty-second Amendment
items.ex: The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) says no one may be elected President more than twice. Congress proposed it in 1947 after Franklin Roosevelt won four elections, breaking the two-term tradition begun by George Washington.
w: the Twentieth Amendment
The Twentieth Amendment (1933) moved inauguration to January 20 and shortened lame-duck periods.
the Twenty-fifth Amendment
The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) covers vacancies and presidential disability.
the Twelfth Amendment
The Twelfth Amendment (1804) requires separate electoral votes for President and Vice President.

alt.q: Which earlier tradition did this 1951 amendment turn into constitutional law?
alt.a: Washington's practice of serving only two terms
alt.ex: George Washington retired in 1797 after two terms, and Presidents followed his example until Franklin Roosevelt won in 1940 and 1944. The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) made the two-term limit part of the Constitution to prevent long presidential rule.
w: the custom that Vice Presidents run for President
No such custom existed, and the amendment says nothing about Vice Presidents running.
the practice of the House choosing Presidents
The House chooses only when no one wins a majority (Twelfth Amendment, 1804).
Jefferson's practice of serving only one term
Jefferson served two terms (1801–1809), following Washington's example.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Twenty-second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution (1951), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice …”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Under the Twenty-second Amendment (1951), how many times may this person be elected President?
alt.a: once
alt.ex: The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) says a person who has held the office for more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected only once. It was added after Franklin Roosevelt's four elections to limit how long one person could hold power.
w: twice
Two elections are allowed only if the person served two years or less of someone else's term.
three times
No one may be elected more than twice under the 1951 amendment.
never
The amendment allows one election in this case, for a maximum of about ten years in office.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A President dies in office with three years left in the term. The Vice President becomes President and serves out those three years.

items.q: Why was the Twenty-fifth Amendment, ratified in 1967, added to the Constitution?
items.a: to set clear rules for vacancies and disability
items.ex: After President Kennedy's assassination in 1963 left the vice presidency empty for over a year, Congress proposed the Twenty-fifth Amendment in 1965. Ratified in 1967, it explains how to fill a vice-presidential vacancy and what happens when a President is unable to serve.
w: to limit Presidents to two elected terms
Term limits come from the Twenty-second Amendment (1951).
to let voters directly elect senators
Direct election of senators comes from the Seventeenth Amendment (1913).
to require separate votes for Vice President
Separate electoral votes come from the Twelfth Amendment (1804).

alt.q: Which provision was being used?
alt.a: Section 2 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment
alt.ex: Section 2 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) lets the President nominate a Vice President, who takes office after majority votes of both houses. It was used for Ford in 1973 and Rockefeller in 1974, so the vice presidency would not stay empty.
w: Section 1 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment
Section 1 (1967) makes the Vice President become President when the President dies, resigns or is removed.
the Twelfth Amendment
The Twelfth Amendment (1804) covers electoral votes, not filling vacancies.
the Presidential Succession Act of 1947
The 1947 act sets who acts as President after the Vice President; it does not fill a vice-presidential vacancy.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In August 1974, Gerald Ford became President, leaving the vice presidency empty. Ford nominated Nelson Rockefeller, and in December 1974 both houses of Congress confirmed him as Vice President.

alt.q: Which event most directly led Congress to propose the Twenty-fifth Amendment in 1965?
alt.a: the assassination of President Kennedy
alt.ex: When President Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963, Lyndon Johnson became President and the vice presidency stayed empty until January 1965. Congress proposed the Twenty-fifth Amendment in 1965 to fill such vacancies; it was ratified in 1967.
w: the resignation of Vice President Agnew
Agnew resigned in 1973, after the amendment was ratified; Section 2 was then used to replace him.
the Watergate scandal
Watergate (1972–1974) came after ratification in 1967.
the impeachment of Andrew Johnson
Johnson's impeachment (1868) did not lead to the 1965 proposal.

items.q: Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, who is next in line for the presidency after the Vice President?
items.a: the Speaker of the House
items.ex: The Presidential Succession Act, signed by President Truman on July 18, 1947, places the Speaker of the House after the Vice President, followed by the president pro tempore and then cabinet officers. Truman wanted an elected official next in line.
w: the president pro tempore
The president pro tempore comes after the Speaker under the 1947 act.
the Secretary of State
The Secretary of State was first after the Vice President under the 1886 act, but now follows the two congressional leaders.
the Chief Justice
The Chief Justice is not in the line of succession.

alt.q: Why did Truman push for the Presidential Succession Act of 1947?
alt.a: to put elected leaders ahead of appointed officials
alt.ex: After becoming President in 1945 with no Vice President, Truman argued that the Speaker, an elected representative, should be next in line rather than appointed cabinet members. The 1947 act restored the Speaker and president pro tempore ahead of the cabinet.
w: to give the Chief Justice a place in the line
The 1947 act did not add the Chief Justice; judges are kept out of the line.
to end the Vice President's role in the Senate
The Vice President's Senate role comes from Article I (1787) and was not changed.
to let voters hold a special presidential election
The 1947 act provides for succession, not special elections.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Harry Truman became President in April 1945 when Franklin Roosevelt died, leaving the vice presidency empty. Under the succession law of 1886, the next person in line was the Secretary of State, an appointed rather than elected official.

alt.q: Which sequence lists these laws and amendments affecting the presidency in the correct order?
alt.a: Succession Act, Twenty-second Amendment, Twenty-fifth Amendment
alt.ex: The Presidential Succession Act was signed in 1947 to put elected leaders next in line; the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) set a two-term limit after FDR's four elections; and the Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) addressed vacancies after Kennedy's assassination.
w: Twenty-second Amendment, Succession Act, Twenty-fifth Amendment
The Succession Act (1947) came before the Twenty-second Amendment (1951).
Twenty-fifth Amendment, Twenty-second Amendment, Succession Act
This is reversed; the 1947 act came first and the 1967 amendment last.
Succession Act, Twenty-fifth Amendment, Twenty-second Amendment
The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) came before the Twenty-fifth (1967).

items.q: Article III (1787) created only one Supreme Court and left lower courts to Congress. Which law, signed by President Washington in September 1789, first set up the lower federal courts?
items.a: the Judiciary Act of 1789
items.ex: The Judiciary Act of 1789, signed September 24, 1789, created federal district and circuit courts, set the Supreme Court at six justices and created the office of Attorney General. Congress acted because Article III left the design of lower courts to it.
w: the Northwest Ordinance of 1787
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) organized western territories; it did not create federal courts for the states.
the Judiciary Act of 1869
The 1869 act set the Supreme Court at nine justices; lower courts already existed.
the Reapportionment Act of 1929
The 1929 act fixed the House at 435 members.

alt.q: How many justices did the Judiciary Act of 1789 provide for the first Supreme Court?
alt.a: six
alt.ex: The Judiciary Act of 1789 set the Court at six justices: a Chief Justice and five associate justices. Article III (1787) did not fix a number, so Congress has changed it by law; it has been nine since 1869.
w: five
A 1801 law would have cut the Court to five, but it was repealed in 1802 before taking effect.
seven
Congress raised the Court to seven in 1807.
nine
The Court reached nine in 1837 and has been fixed at nine since 1869.

alt.q: Why did the Constitution leave it to Congress, through laws such as the Judiciary Act of 1789, to create the lower federal courts?
alt.a: Delegates in 1787 disagreed on whether they were needed
alt.ex: At the 1787 Convention, some delegates thought state courts could hear federal cases while others wanted national lower courts. They compromised by letting Congress decide, and Congress created lower federal courts in the Judiciary Act of 1789.
w: The Supreme Court had asked to design its own lower courts
The Supreme Court did not yet exist in 1787 and made no such request.
The President was meant to create courts by order
Article III (1787) gives this power to Congress, not the President.
Each state wanted to appoint the federal judges
Federal judges are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate (Article II, 1787).

items.q: Why has the U.S. Supreme Court had nine justices since 1869?
items.a: Congress set that number by law
items.ex: Article III (1787) does not fix the Court's size, so Congress sets it by statute. The number changed several times, from six in 1789 to as many as ten in 1863, before the Judiciary Act of April 10, 1869, set it at nine.
w: Article III fixes the number at nine
Article III (1787) creates “one supreme Court” but names no number of justices.
the Chief Justice chose the number
The Chief Justice has no power to set the Court's size.
a 1937 amendment set the size
No amendment sets the Court's size; FDR's 1937 plan to enlarge it failed.

alt.q: Why did President Franklin Roosevelt propose adding up to six justices to the Supreme Court in 1937?
alt.a: The Court had struck down key New Deal laws.
alt.ex: On February 5, 1937, Roosevelt proposed adding a justice for each one over 70, up to six, after the Court had struck down major New Deal programs. Critics saw it as a threat to judicial independence, and the plan failed in the Senate that summer.
w: Several justices had been impeached and removed.
No Supreme Court justice has ever been removed by impeachment.
The Constitution required a larger Supreme Court.
Article III (1787) sets no number, so nothing required more justices.
Congress had cut the Court down to seven justices.
Congress cut the Court to seven in 1866, but restored nine in 1869.

alt.q: What happened to President Franklin Roosevelt's 1937 plan to enlarge the Supreme Court?
alt.a: It failed in the Senate; the Court stayed at nine.
alt.ex: In June 1937 the Senate Judiciary Committee issued a negative report, and by July 1937 the Senate set the plan aside. Many senators saw it as an attack on the independence of the judicial branch, and the Court has remained at nine, as set in 1869.
w: Congress passed it, and the Court grew to fifteen.
The plan never passed; the Court has never had fifteen justices.
The Court struck it down as unconstitutional.
The plan never became law, so the Court never ruled on it.
It became an amendment ratified by the states.
It was proposed as a bill, not an amendment, and it was never adopted.

items.q: Which power, not directly stated in the Constitution, did the Supreme Court claim in Marbury v. Madison (1803)?
items.a: judicial review
items.ex: In Marbury v. Madison, decided February 24, 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall held that courts may strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution. The ruling made the judiciary a real check on Congress and the President.
w: executive privilege
Executive privilege is a presidential claim, addressed in United States v. Nixon (1974).
original jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction is stated directly in Article III, Section 2 (1787).
the power to declare war
Declaring war belongs to Congress under Article I, Section 8 (1787).

alt.q: Why did the Supreme Court refuse in 1803 to order delivery of Marbury's commission?
alt.a: The law granting that power conflicted with Article III.
alt.ex: In 1803 the Court held that Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 tried to add to the original jurisdiction set by Article III (1787). Because a law cannot change the Constitution, the Court refused to use that power, establishing judicial review.
w: Marbury had never been nominated by the President.
President John Adams nominated Marbury, and the Senate confirmed him.
The Senate had voted to reject Marbury's appointment.
The Senate confirmed Marbury before his commission went undelivered.
Congress had already abolished Marbury's office.
The Court decided the case on the jurisdiction question, not on any abolition of his office.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1801, outgoing President John Adams appointed William Marbury a justice of the peace, but Marbury's commission was never delivered. Marbury asked the Supreme Court directly to order the new Secretary of State, James Madison, to deliver it, relying on a power granted in the Judiciary Act of 1789.

alt.q: Which sequence lists these events in the correct order?
alt.a: Constitution signed, Judiciary Act passed, Marbury decided
alt.ex: The Constitution was signed in 1787; Congress passed the Judiciary Act in 1789 to set up federal courts; and in Marbury v. Madison (1803) the Court struck down part of that act, establishing judicial review.
w: Judiciary Act passed, Constitution signed, Marbury decided
Congress could not pass the Judiciary Act until the Constitution created it.
Constitution signed, Marbury decided, Judiciary Act passed
Marbury (1803) struck down part of the 1789 act, so the act came first.
Marbury decided, Judiciary Act passed, Constitution signed
This order is fully reversed; the Constitution came first in 1787.

items.q: Which action would the framers of this 1787 provision most likely want to prevent?
items.a: Congress cutting a judge's pay to punish a ruling
items.ex: Article III (1787) gives federal judges tenure during good behaviour and bars cutting their pay while in office. The framers wanted judges free to rule against Congress or the President without fear of losing their jobs or salaries.
w: a judge serving on the bench for thirty years
Long service is exactly what “during good Behaviour” allows.
a President nominating a judge from another state
Nothing in Article III limits where nominees come from.
the Senate holding hearings on a judicial nominee
Hearings are part of the Senate's advice and consent role (Article II, 1787).

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article III of the U.S. Constitution (1787), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts, shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour, and shall, at stated Times, receive for their Services, a Compensation, which shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: A President serves a four-year term, but under Article III (1787) federal judges usually serve until they die, retire or are removed. Why did the framers make this difference?
alt.a: to free judges from political pressure in their rulings
alt.ex: The framers gave federal judges tenure during good behaviour in 1787, and Hamilton defended it in The Federalist No. 78 (1788), so judges could decide cases by law rather than to please voters or officials who could replace them.
w: to let judges run for reelection like other officials
Federal judges never run for election; they are appointed.
to let Congress fire judges after unpopular rulings
Congress can remove judges only by impeachment and conviction, not for unpopular rulings.
to make judges answer directly to the President
Life tenure was meant to make judges independent of the President.

alt.q: Since 1789, which is the only way to remove a federal judge from office against his or her will?
alt.a: impeachment and Senate conviction
alt.ex: Because Article III (1787) lets judges serve during good behaviour, they can be removed only by House impeachment and conviction by two-thirds of the Senate. Judge John Pickering was the first removed this way, in 1804; the high bar protects judicial independence.
w: a recall election held by the people
Federal judges are not elected, and the Constitution has no recall process.
an order from the President
The President appoints judges but cannot fire them under Article III.
a ruling by the Chief Justice
The Chief Justice has no power to remove other federal judges.

items.q: In 1789, Congress created the first executive departments to help President Washington carry out the laws. Which departments were they?
items.a: State, Treasury and War
items.ex: In 1789 Congress created the Departments of Foreign Affairs (soon renamed State), War and the Treasury, plus the office of Attorney General. Article II (1787) mentions executive departments but leaves their creation to Congress.
w: State, Justice and Homeland Security
The Justice Department was created in 1870 and Homeland Security in 2002.
Treasury, Interior and Commerce
Interior was created in 1849 and Commerce in 1903.
War, Navy and Education
The Navy Department was created in 1798 and Education in 1979.

alt.q: Which cabinet department was created in 2002, and why?
alt.a: Homeland Security, after the September 11 attacks
alt.ex: Congress passed the Homeland Security Act in November 2002 after the September 11, 2001, attacks, combining many agencies into one department to protect the nation. Like all departments, it was created by Congress, as Article II (1787) assumes.
w: Energy, after the oil crisis of the 1970s
The Department of Energy was created in 1977, not 2002.
Education, after national reports on failing schools
The Department of Education was created in 1979, not 2002.
Veterans Affairs, after the Persian Gulf War
Veterans Affairs became a department in 1989, before the Gulf War (1991).

alt.q: Which clause of Article II is the constitutional basis for this practice?
alt.a: the Opinion Clause, on advice from department heads
alt.ex: Article II, Section 2 (1787) says the President “may require the Opinion, in writing, of the principal Officer in each of the executive Departments.” Washington began meeting with his department heads as a group in the 1790s, creating the cabinet tradition to get expert advice.
w: the State of the Union Clause, on reports to Congress
This clause (Article II, Section 3, 1787) concerns informing Congress, not consulting department heads.
the Recess Appointments Clause, on filling vacancies
This clause lets the President fill vacancies while the Senate is in recess.
the Necessary and Proper Clause, on implied powers
This clause is in Article I, Section 8 (1787) and concerns Congress's powers.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: The word “cabinet” does not appear in the Constitution. Even so, every President since George Washington has regularly asked the heads of the executive departments for advice on major decisions.

items.q: Which document, forced on King John by rebel English barons in 1215, first established that the king himself was bound by the law?
items.a: Magna Carta
items.ex: In June 1215 at Runnymede, King John accepted Magna Carta to end a revolt by barons angry over heavy taxes and arbitrary punishments. It mattered because it put the monarch under the law, an early root of the rule of law.
w: the English Bill of Rights
The English Bill of Rights came much later, in 1689, after the Glorious Revolution, under William and Mary.
the Mayflower Compact
The Mayflower Compact (1620) was an agreement among colonists, not a limit forced on an English king.
the Petition of Right
The Petition of Right was sent by Parliament to King Charles I in 1628, not to King John.

alt.q: In what year did King John agree to Magna Carta, limiting the power of the English monarch?
alt.ex: Magna Carta was sealed in June 1215 after barons rebelled against King John's heavy taxes and arbitrary rule. It mattered because it set the precedent that even the king must obey the law.
w: 1066 is the year of the Norman Conquest of England, about 150 years before Magna Carta.
1295 is the year of Edward I's so-called Model Parliament, 80 years after Magna Carta.
1689 is the year of the English Bill of Rights, not Magna Carta.

alt.q: What was the main reason English barons forced King John to accept Magna Carta in 1215?
alt.a: to stop the king from ruling arbitrarily
alt.ex: The barons rebelled because King John imposed heavy taxes and punished people without lawful judgment. Magna Carta (1215) answered this by placing limits on the king, which made it an early foundation of the rule of law.
w: to give all English people the right to vote
Magna Carta did not create voting rights; most protections at first benefited the barons and free men.
to declare England's independence from Rome
England's break with the Roman Church came under Henry VIII in the 1530s, not in 1215.
to make Parliament the supreme lawmaker
Parliament did not yet exist in 1215; parliamentary supremacy was confirmed by the English Bill of Rights in 1689.

items.q: Which protection in the U.S. Constitution most directly descends from this promise made in 1215?
items.a: the Fifth Amendment's due process guarantee
items.ex: Clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215) promised that no free man would be punished except by lawful judgment of his peers or “the law of the land.” This idea became “due process of law” in the Fifth Amendment (1791), which limits government power over life, liberty, and property.
w: the First Amendment's free press guarantee
The First Amendment protects expression; clause 39 is about lawful procedure before punishment.
the Third Amendment's ban on quartering troops
The Third Amendment deals with housing soldiers, not lawful judgment before imprisonment.
the Second Amendment's right to bear arms
The Second Amendment concerns keeping arms, which clause 39 does not address.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any other way, nor will we proceed with force against him, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.”
Source: Magna Carta (1215), clause 39, English translation, Museum of Australian Democracy

alt.q: Based on the passage, which principle did this 1215 document establish?
alt.a: Government must use lawful procedures before punishing.
alt.ex: Clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215) required “lawful judgement” or “the law of the land” before a free man could be imprisoned or stripped of property. This is the root of due process and the rule of law, later written into the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.
w: The king may imprison nobles whenever peace is threatened.
The passage forbids imprisonment except by lawful judgment, so it limits the king rather than empowering him.
All people must share equally in the kingdom's property.
The passage protects a person's possessions from unlawful seizure; it does not redistribute property.
Barons must swear loyalty to the king before trial.
The passage says nothing about oaths of loyalty; it requires lawful judgment.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any other way, nor will we proceed with force against him, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.”
Source: Magna Carta (1215), clause 39, English translation, Museum of Australian Democracy

alt.q: A ruler orders a critic jailed and his land taken with no charge and no trial. Which document from 1215 first forbade such actions by an English king?
alt.a: Magna Carta
alt.ex: Magna Carta (1215) promised that no free man would be imprisoned or lose his possessions except by lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land. It mattered because it limited arbitrary royal power, the idea behind American due process.
w: the Mayflower Compact
The Mayflower Compact (1620) created a colonial government; it was not a limit on an English king.
the English Bill of Rights
The English Bill of Rights (1689) limited the Crown, but it came 474 years after the 1215 charter.
the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration (1776) listed grievances against George III; it was not written in 1215.

items.q: Which agreement, signed aboard ship in November 1620 before the settlers went ashore at Plymouth, created a government based on the consent of its members?
items.a: the Mayflower Compact
items.ex: On November 11, 1620, 41 male passengers signed the Mayflower Compact because they had landed outside the area of their Virginia patent and needed their own government. It mattered as an early American example of self-government by consent.
w: the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut
The Fundamental Orders were adopted in 1639 by Connecticut towns, not aboard the Mayflower.
the Virginia Declaration of Rights
The Virginia Declaration of Rights was adopted in June 1776, over 150 years later.
the Massachusetts Constitution
The Massachusetts Constitution was ratified in 1780, not in 1620.

alt.q: Why did the Pilgrims write and sign the Mayflower Compact in 1620?
alt.a: They landed outside their charter and had no government.
alt.ex: The Pilgrims' patent covered northern Virginia, but they reached Cape Cod in November 1620. With no legal government there, the men signed the Mayflower Compact (1620) to form a “civil Body Politick” and obey laws for the general good, an early act of self-government.
w: They wanted to declare independence from King James.
The signers called themselves loyal subjects of King James; independence came in 1776.
They needed to settle a border dispute with Virginia.
There was no border dispute; the problem was that no legal authority covered Plymouth.
They were ordered to write a constitution by Parliament.
Parliament did not order the compact; the settlers made it themselves.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which idea does this 1620 agreement best express?
alt.a: self-government by consent
alt.ex: In the Mayflower Compact (1620), the settlers themselves agreed to make just and equal laws for the colony's general good and to obey them. It mattered because it set a precedent for government created by the people's own agreement, later echoed in the Constitution.
w: the divine right of kings
The settlers created laws by their own agreement, not by claiming a ruler's divine authority.
separation of church and state
The compact says nothing about separating church and state.
judicial review of colonial laws
Judicial review is a much later idea associated with Marbury v. Madison (1803).

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Mayflower Compact (1620), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…do enact, constitute, and frame, such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions, and Officers, from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general Good of the Colony”
Source: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School

items.q: Which document, accepted by William and Mary in 1689 after the Glorious Revolution, limited the monarch's power and confirmed the rights of Parliament?
items.a: the English Bill of Rights
items.ex: The English Bill of Rights (1689) followed the overthrow of James II. It barred the Crown from suspending laws, levying money, or keeping a peacetime army without Parliament's consent, ideas that later shaped the U.S. Bill of Rights.
w: Magna Carta
Magna Carta was accepted by King John in 1215, not by William and Mary.
the Petition of Right
The Petition of Right was presented to Charles I in 1628, before the Glorious Revolution.
the Instrument of Government
The Instrument of Government (1653) set up Oliver Cromwell's rule as Lord Protector, decades before William and Mary.

alt.q: Why did Parliament require William and Mary to accept the English Bill of Rights in 1689?
alt.a: to prevent a monarch from ruling without Parliament
alt.ex: James II had suspended laws and kept a standing army without Parliament's consent. After the Glorious Revolution, the English Bill of Rights (1689) made such acts illegal, establishing limited monarchy and inspiring later American rights guarantees.
w: to give the American colonies seats in Parliament
The 1689 document did not address colonial representation.
to end the slave trade throughout the empire
Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807, not in 1689.
to replace the monarchy with a republic
The document kept the monarchy; William and Mary became joint monarchs.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which principle did this 1689 document support?
alt.a: The Crown needed Parliament's consent to raise money.
alt.ex: The English Bill of Rights (1689) declared it illegal for the Crown to levy money without a grant of Parliament. It mattered because it tied taxing power to an elected legislature, an idea behind the colonists' 1760s protest of “no taxation without representation.”
w: The Crown could collect taxes during any emergency.
The passage says levying money by prerogative is illegal, with no emergency exception.
Colonists were exempt from all royal taxes.
The passage concerns the Crown and Parliament; it says nothing about colonies being exempt.
Courts must approve every tax law before it is used.
The passage requires Parliament's grant, not court approval.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the English Bill of Rights (1689), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That levying money for or to the use of the Crown by pretence of prerogative, without grant of Parliament, for longer time, or in other manner than the same is or shall be granted, is illegal;”
Source: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School

items.q: Which part of the U.S. Bill of Rights repeats this 1689 language almost word for word?
items.a: the Eighth Amendment
items.ex: The English Bill of Rights (1689) banned excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments. The Eighth Amendment (ratified 1791) copied this language to protect people accused or convicted of crimes from abusive punishment.
w: the Fourth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment covers unreasonable searches and seizures, not bail or punishment.
the Sixth Amendment
The Sixth Amendment covers trial rights such as counsel and a speedy jury trial.
the Fifth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment covers self-incrimination, double jeopardy, and due process, not bail.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the English Bill of Rights (1689), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That excessive bail ought not to be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted;”
Source: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: The Eighth Amendment's ban on excessive bail and “cruel and unusual punishments” was taken almost word for word from which document of 1689?
alt.a: the English Bill of Rights
alt.ex: The English Bill of Rights (1689) declared that excessive bail and fines and cruel and unusual punishments should not be imposed. The Eighth Amendment (1791) adopted this language to limit government power over the accused.
w: Magna Carta
Magna Carta dates from 1215 and does not use the phrase “cruel and unusual punishments.”
the Mayflower Compact
The Mayflower Compact (1620) formed a government; it lists no limits on punishment.
the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut
The Fundamental Orders (1639) set up a colonial government; they did not limit bail or punishments.

alt.q: Which amendment is the lawyer relying on?
alt.a: the Eighth Amendment
alt.ex: The Eighth Amendment (1791) bars excessive bail, language taken from the English Bill of Rights (1689). It exists so that government cannot use huge bail or fines to punish people before or beyond what is fair.
w: the Seventh Amendment
The Seventh Amendment guarantees jury trials in civil cases, not limits on bail.
the Ninth Amendment
The Ninth Amendment protects unlisted rights; it does not mention bail.
the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to states or people; it does not address bail.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state court sets bail at $50 million for a person charged with shoplifting a $40 item. The defendant's lawyer argues that the amount violates a protection the Framers borrowed from England's 1689 Bill of Rights.

mt.q: Match each Bill of Rights amendment to what it protects (6th–10th).
pairs: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer
No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail
Rights not listed still belong to the people
Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people
mt.ex: Bill of Rights (1791): 6th Amendment: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer; 7th Amendment: Jury trial in civil cases; 8th Amendment: No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail; 9th Amendment: Rights not listed still belong to the people; 10th Amendment: Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people.

items.q: Which sequence lists these documents in the order they were written, from earliest to latest?
items.a: Magna Carta, Mayflower Compact, English Bill of Rights, Common Sense
items.ex: Magna Carta came in 1215, the Mayflower Compact in 1620, the English Bill of Rights in 1689, and Common Sense in January 1776. Together they trace the growing idea that rulers must be limited by law and by the people's consent.
w: Mayflower Compact, Magna Carta, Common Sense, English Bill of Rights
Magna Carta (1215) is centuries older than the Mayflower Compact (1620), and Common Sense (1776) came after 1689.
Magna Carta, English Bill of Rights, Mayflower Compact, Common Sense
The Mayflower Compact (1620) came before the English Bill of Rights (1689).
English Bill of Rights, Magna Carta, Mayflower Compact, Common Sense
The English Bill of Rights (1689) came after both Magna Carta (1215) and the Mayflower Compact (1620).

alt.q: Which of these documents was written first?
alt.a: the Mayflower Compact
alt.ex: The Mayflower Compact was signed in 1620, before the English Bill of Rights (1689), Common Sense (1776), and the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776). It mattered as the first written framework of self-government in the English colonies of New England.
w: the English Bill of Rights
The English Bill of Rights dates from 1689, 69 years after the Mayflower Compact.
the Virginia Declaration of Rights
The Virginia Declaration of Rights was adopted June 12, 1776.
Common Sense
Common Sense was published in January 1776.

alt.q: Which of these documents was written last?
alt.a: the English Bill of Rights
alt.ex: The English Bill of Rights came in 1689, after the Mayflower Compact (1620), the Petition of Right (1628), and the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639). It confirmed Parliament's power over the Crown after the Glorious Revolution.
w: the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut
The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut were adopted in 1639, before 1689.
the Mayflower Compact
The Mayflower Compact was signed in 1620, before 1689.
the Petition of Right
The Petition of Right was presented to Charles I in 1628, before 1689.

items.q: Which pamphlet, published by Thomas Paine in January 1776, persuaded many colonists that they should break away from Britain?
items.a: Common Sense
items.ex: Thomas Paine published Common Sense in Philadelphia on January 10, 1776. Written in plain language, it attacked monarchy and argued for independence, building public support in the months before the Declaration of Independence.
w: The Federalist
The Federalist essays were written in 1787–1788 to support the Constitution, not independence.
Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania
John Dickinson's Letters (1767–1768) protested the Townshend Acts but did not call for independence.
Brutus No. 1
Brutus No. 1 (October 1787) opposed the Constitution; it was not about independence.

alt.q: What was the most significant effect of Thomas Paine's Common Sense in 1776?
alt.a: It built popular support for declaring independence.
alt.ex: Common Sense (January 1776) sold widely and convinced many ordinary colonists that independence, not reconciliation with King George III, was the answer. Six months later, Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
w: It convinced states to ratify the Articles of Confederation.
The Articles were not sent to the states until 1777 and took effect in 1781.
It persuaded New York to ratify the Constitution.
That was the aim of the Federalist Papers in 1787–1788.
It ended the war by persuading Britain to negotiate.
The war ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783, not because of Paine's pamphlet.

alt.q: Which document was published closest to the adoption of the Declaration of Independence in July 1776?
alt.a: Common Sense
alt.ex: Common Sense appeared on January 10, 1776, just six months before July 4, 1776, and helped turn public opinion toward independence. The Mayflower Compact (1620), English Bill of Rights (1689), and Albany Plan (1754) were all much earlier.
w: the English Bill of Rights
The English Bill of Rights dates from 1689, almost a century earlier.
the Albany Plan of Union
Benjamin Franklin's Albany Plan was proposed in 1754, 22 years earlier.
the Mayflower Compact
The Mayflower Compact was signed in 1620.

items.q: Based on the passage, which action was the author urging in early 1776?
items.a: independence from Great Britain
items.ex: In Common Sense (January 1776), Thomas Paine argued it made no sense for a large continent to be ruled forever by a small island. His purpose was to persuade colonists to seek independence, which Congress declared that July.
w: repeal of the Stamp Act
The Stamp Act was repealed in 1766, ten years before Common Sense.
representation in Parliament
Paine rejected staying under British rule at all, rather than seeking seats in Parliament.
ratification of the Constitution
The Constitution was written in 1787, eleven years later.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“There is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.”
Source: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776), Project Gutenberg

alt.q: Who wrote these words in a pamphlet published in January 1776?
alt.a: Thomas Paine
alt.ex: Thomas Paine wrote Common Sense, published January 10, 1776. He argued that being governed by a distant island was absurd, a reason for independence that reached thousands of ordinary colonists.
w: Thomas Jefferson
Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence in June 1776; he did not write Common Sense.
John Adams
Adams wrote Thoughts on Government (1776) and the Massachusetts Constitution (1780), not Common Sense.
Samuel Adams
Samuel Adams organized protests in Boston but did not write Common Sense.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a pamphlet published in January 1776, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“There is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.”
Source: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776), Project Gutenberg

alt.q: Which argument is the author making in this 1776 pamphlet?
alt.a: Government is needed, but it should be kept limited.
alt.ex: In Common Sense (January 1776), Thomas Paine described government as a “necessary evil.” This reasoning supported his case for a limited, republican government chosen by the people instead of a hereditary king.
w: Government is the main source of goodness in society.
Paine says society is the blessing and government at best a necessary evil.
A strong king is the best guard of liberty.
Paine attacked monarchy and hereditary rule throughout Common Sense.
Society cannot exist unless a king rules it.
Paine separates society, which he calls a blessing, from government.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil”
Source: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776), Project Gutenberg

items.q: Which document, written mainly by George Mason and adopted on June 12, 1776, was the first American state declaration of rights?
items.a: the Virginia Declaration of Rights
items.ex: Virginia's convention adopted George Mason's Declaration of Rights on June 12, 1776. It listed natural rights and limits on government, and it influenced Jefferson's Declaration of Independence that July and Madison's Bill of Rights in 1789.
w: the Massachusetts Constitution
The Massachusetts Constitution was drafted mainly by John Adams and ratified in 1780.
the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration was drafted by Jefferson and adopted July 4, 1776, not June 12.
the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were drafted by the Continental Congress and agreed to in November 1777.

alt.q: Which of these documents was adopted first?
alt.a: the Virginia Declaration of Rights
alt.ex: The Virginia Declaration of Rights was adopted June 12, 1776, about three weeks before the Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776). Its statement of natural rights influenced Jefferson's wording.
w: the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration of Independence was adopted July 4, 1776, after Virginia's June 12 declaration.
the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were agreed to by Congress in November 1777.
the Massachusetts Constitution
The Massachusetts Constitution was ratified in 1780.

alt.q: What was a major long-term impact of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776)?
alt.a: It was a model for the U.S. Bill of Rights.
alt.ex: George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 12, 1776) protected freedoms such as a free press, religious exercise, and jury trial. James Madison drew on it when he proposed the amendments in 1789 that became the Bill of Rights (1791).
w: It created the first national government.
The first national framework was the Articles of Confederation, in force in 1781.
It ended slavery in the state of Virginia.
The Virginia Declaration did not end slavery; Virginia allowed slavery until the Civil War era.
It set the rules for admitting new states.
Admission of new states was set by the Northwest Ordinance (1787) and Article IV.

items.q: Which part of the U.S. Bill of Rights later protected the freedom described in this 1776 passage?
items.a: the First Amendment
items.ex: Section 12 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 12, 1776) called a free press a great bulwark of liberty. The First Amendment (1791) protected freedom of the press nationally so government could not silence criticism.
w: the Fourth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
the Sixth Amendment
The Sixth Amendment protects the rights of the accused at trial.
the Ninth Amendment
The Ninth Amendment protects unlisted rights; press freedom is expressly named in the First.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That the freedom of the press is one of the great bulwarks of liberty, and can never be restrained but by despotic governments.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Who was the main author of the 1776 document containing this passage?
alt.a: George Mason
alt.ex: George Mason wrote most of the Virginia Declaration of Rights, adopted June 12, 1776. He later refused to sign the U.S. Constitution in 1787 partly because it lacked a similar bill of rights.
w: James Madison
Madison later drafted the federal Bill of Rights (1789), but Mason was the main author of Virginia's 1776 declaration.
Patrick Henry
Henry was a leading Virginia patriot and Anti-Federalist but not the main author of this document.
Thomas Jefferson
Jefferson was in Philadelphia drafting the Declaration of Independence in June 1776.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a declaration adopted in Virginia in June 1776, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That the freedom of the press is one of the great bulwarks of liberty, and can never be restrained but by despotic governments.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which principle does this 1776 passage most directly express?
alt.a: popular sovereignty
alt.ex: Section 2 of George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 12, 1776) says all power comes from the people and officials are their servants. This idea of popular sovereignty opens the U.S. Constitution with “We the People.”
w: federalism
Federalism divides power between national and state governments; the passage is about the people as the source of power.
judicial review
Judicial review is a court's power to void unconstitutional laws, which the passage does not mention.
separation of powers
The passage is about where power comes from, not how it is divided among branches.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Section 2 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That all power is vested in, and consequently derived from, the people; that magistrates are their trustees and servants and at all times amenable to them.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

mt.q: Match each Bill of Rights amendment to what it protects (1st–5th).
pairs: Freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition
Right to keep and bear arms
No forced quartering of soldiers in homes
Due process; no self-incrimination or double jeopardy
mt.ex: Bill of Rights (1791): 1st Amendment: Freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition; 2nd Amendment: Right to keep and bear arms; 3rd Amendment: No forced quartering of soldiers in homes; 4th Amendment: No unreasonable searches and seizures; 5th Amendment: Due process; no self-incrimination or double jeopardy.

items.q: On July 2, 1776, the Second Continental Congress voted for independence by approving which measure?
items.a: the Lee Resolution
items.ex: Richard Henry Lee of Virginia introduced a resolution on June 7, 1776, that the colonies are and ought to be free and independent states. Congress approved it on July 2, 1776, and then adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4 to explain the decision.
w: the Olive Branch Petition
The Olive Branch Petition (July 1775) asked King George III for reconciliation, not independence.
the Albany Plan of Union
The Albany Plan (1754) proposed colonial cooperation during the French and Indian War.
the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were agreed to by Congress in November 1777.

alt.q: Why did Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, after already voting for independence on July 2?
alt.a: to explain the reasons for independence
alt.ex: Congress approved the Lee Resolution for independence on July 2, 1776. The Declaration, adopted July 4, stated the reasons, including natural rights and a list of grievances against King George III, to win support at home and abroad.
w: to set up the first national government
The Declaration created no government; the Articles of Confederation did that, in force in 1781.
to approve a peace treaty with Britain
Peace with Britain came with the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
to ratify the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were not ratified until March 1, 1781.

alt.q: Which sequence of events in 1776 is in the correct order?
alt.a: Lee Resolution proposed, independence vote, Declaration adopted
alt.ex: Richard Henry Lee proposed independence on June 7, 1776; Congress voted for it on July 2; and the Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4. The Declaration came last because its job was to explain the decision already made.
w: Declaration adopted, Lee Resolution proposed, independence vote
The Declaration (July 4) came after both the June 7 proposal and the July 2 vote.
Independence vote, Declaration adopted, Lee Resolution proposed
The Lee Resolution was proposed first, on June 7, 1776.
Lee Resolution proposed, Declaration adopted, independence vote
The independence vote (July 2) came before the Declaration was adopted (July 4).

items.q: Who was the principal author of the document adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776?
items.a: Thomas Jefferson
items.ex: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence for a committee of five that also included John Adams and Benjamin Franklin. Congress adopted it on July 4, 1776, to justify separation from Britain.
w: John Adams
Adams served on the drafting committee but Jefferson wrote the draft.
Benjamin Franklin
Franklin served on the committee and made edits, but Jefferson was the main author.
James Madison
Madison is the main author of the Constitution (1787), not the Declaration.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the main purpose of the Declaration of Independence, adopted July 4, 1776?
alt.a: to justify separation from Britain
alt.ex: The Declaration (July 4, 1776) argued that people have natural rights, that government rests on consent, and that King George III had violated those rights. Its purpose was to justify independence, not to set up a government.
w: to set up a national government
The Declaration created no government; the Articles of Confederation (in force 1781) did.
to list rights protected by courts
Enforceable rights came later in the Bill of Rights (1791).
to end slavery in all thirteen states
The Declaration did not end slavery; that came with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865.

alt.q: Which response best corrects the student?
alt.a: The Declaration explained independence; the Constitution is the plan.
alt.ex: The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) stated the reasons for separating from Britain. The plan of government came later: first the Articles of Confederation (1781), then the U.S. Constitution, signed September 17, 1787, and in effect in 1789.
w: The Declaration created Congress, which later wrote the Bill of Rights.
The Continental Congress existed before the Declaration, which did not create any branch of government.
The Declaration is the plan, and the Constitution only added rights.
The Constitution is the plan of government; rights were added by the Bill of Rights in 1791.
The Declaration was the plan until the Bill of Rights replaced it.
The Bill of Rights (1791) amended the Constitution; it did not replace the Declaration.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: During a class discussion, a student claims that the Declaration of Independence is the plan of government that the United States still uses today, including its rules for Congress and the president.

items.q: Which amendment in the Bill of Rights was most directly a response to this 1776 complaint?
items.a: the Sixth Amendment
items.ex: The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) accused King George III of denying colonists jury trials. The Sixth Amendment (1791) guarantees accused persons a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury so that this abuse could not recur.
w: the Second Amendment
The Second Amendment protects the right to bear arms, not jury trials.
the Fourth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
the Eighth Amendment
The Eighth Amendment limits bail, fines, and punishments, not jury trials.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Declaration of Independence, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“For depriving us in many cases, of the benefits of Trial by Jury:”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which constitutional power was given to the elected Congress partly because of this grievance from 1776?
alt.a: the power to collect taxes
alt.ex: The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) protested taxes imposed without the colonists' consent. The Constitution (1787) gave the power to tax to Congress, the branch elected by the people, in Article I, Section 8.
w: the power to grant pardons
The pardon power belongs to the President under Article II and is unrelated to taxation.
the power to appoint judges
The President nominates judges and the Senate confirms them; this is not about taxes.
the power to make treaties
Treaties are made by the President with Senate consent; this is not about taxes.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Declaration of Independence, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“For imposing Taxes on us without our Consent:”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which constitutional provision was most directly inspired by this complaint against King George III?
alt.a: the First Amendment's right to petition
alt.ex: The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) said the colonists' petitions for redress had been answered “only by repeated injury.” The First Amendment (1791) protects the right to “petition the Government for a redress of grievances.”
w: the Third Amendment's limit on quartering
The Third Amendment answers a different grievance, about housing soldiers.
the Fifth Amendment's ban on double jeopardy
Double jeopardy is about being tried twice, not about petitioning.
the Seventh Amendment's civil jury right
The Seventh Amendment covers civil juries, not petitions to government.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Declaration of Independence, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“In every stage of these Oppressions We have Petitioned for Redress in the most humble terms: Our repeated Petitions have been answered only by repeated injury.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

mt.q: Match each Bill of Rights amendment to what it protects (6th–10th).
pairs: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer
No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail
Rights not listed still belong to the people
Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people
mt.ex: Bill of Rights (1791): 6th Amendment: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer; 7th Amendment: Jury trial in civil cases; 8th Amendment: No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail; 9th Amendment: Rights not listed still belong to the people; 10th Amendment: Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people.

items.q: Why did the Declaration of Independence (1776) include a long list of grievances against King George III?
items.a: to show the king had violated their rights
items.ex: The Declaration (July 4, 1776) argued that people may alter or abolish a government that destroys their rights. The grievances were the evidence that the king had done so, which justified independence.
w: to ask Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act
The Stamp Act had already been repealed in 1766; the Declaration sought independence, not repeal.
to propose a new plan of national government
The plan of government came later in the Articles of Confederation (1777, in force 1781).
to ask France to send troops to the colonies
The French alliance came in 1778; the grievances were addressed to the world and the king.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which conclusion did the authors of the Declaration reach in 1776?
alt.a: The king was unfit to rule a free people.
alt.ex: After listing grievances, the Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) concluded that a prince marked by acts of a tyrant is unfit to rule a free people. This conclusion justified breaking with Britain.
w: Parliament should replace the king as ruler.
The Declaration rejected the authority of both the king and Parliament over the colonies.
The colonies should seek seats in Parliament.
The Declaration called for independence, not representation in Parliament.
The king should be tried by a colonial court.
The Declaration proposed no trial; it declared independence.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Declaration of Independence, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“A Prince, whose character is thus marked by every act which may define a Tyrant, is unfit to be the ruler of a free people.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which grievance from the Declaration of Independence (1776) led most directly to the Third Amendment?
alt.a: keeping armed troops in colonists' homes
alt.ex: The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) condemned the king “For Quartering large bodies of armed troops among us.” The Third Amendment (1791) bars quartering soldiers in private homes in peacetime without the owner's consent.
w: cutting off colonial trade with the world
Trade complaints relate to Congress's commerce power, not the Third Amendment.
dissolving colonial representative houses
This grievance concerns legislatures and representation, not housing soldiers.
denying colonists the benefit of a jury
The jury grievance relates to the Sixth and Seventh Amendments.

items.q: The Articles of Confederation were agreed to by Congress in 1777. When did they finally take effect?
items.a: March 1, 1781
items.ex: Congress approved the Articles on November 15, 1777, but every state had to ratify. Maryland held out until other states gave up western land claims, so the Articles took effect on March 1, 1781.
w: July 4, 1776
July 4, 1776, is when the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
September 17, 1787
September 17, 1787, is when the Constitution was signed.
June 21, 1788, is when New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the Constitution.

alt.q: Why did it take until 1781 for the Articles of Confederation to go into effect after Congress approved them in 1777?
alt.a: All thirteen states had to ratify them.
alt.ex: The Articles required the consent of every state. Maryland refused to ratify until states such as Virginia gave up their western land claims, so the Articles did not take effect until March 1, 1781.
w: Nine states had to approve them in conventions.
Nine-state ratification was the rule for the Constitution (1787), not the Articles.
The king had to approve them first.
The states had declared independence in 1776 and did not seek the king's approval.
Congress had to wait until the war ended.
The war did not end until 1783, two years after the Articles took effect.

alt.q: Which sequence of events from the 1780s is in the correct order?
alt.a: Articles take effect, Shays' Rebellion, Constitution signed
alt.ex: The Articles took effect March 1, 1781; Shays' Rebellion broke out in 1786–1787; and the Constitution was signed September 17, 1787. The rebellion exposed the Articles' weakness and helped push leaders toward a new Constitution.
w: Shays' Rebellion, Articles take effect, Constitution signed
The Articles took effect in 1781, five years before Shays' Rebellion began in 1786.
Constitution signed, Articles take effect, Shays' Rebellion
The Constitution was signed in 1787, after both other events.
Articles take effect, Constitution signed, Shays' Rebellion
Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787) came before the Constitution was signed in September 1787.

items.q: Based on the passage, what was the main weakness of the national government under this document, in effect from 1781 to 1789?
items.a: The states kept most power, so Congress was weak.
items.ex: Article II of the Articles of Confederation (in force March 1, 1781) let each state keep its sovereignty and every power not expressly given to Congress. As a result, Congress could not tax or enforce its laws, which led to the Constitution of 1787.
w: The President held too much power over the states.
The Articles created no President or separate executive.
Federal courts could overturn state laws at will.
The Articles created no national court system with such power.
Congress could tax citizens directly without limit.
Congress under the Articles could only request money from the states.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article II of the Articles of Confederation, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Each state retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence, and every power, jurisdiction, and right, which is not by this Confederation expressly delegated to the United States, in Congress assembled.”
Source: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Under the Articles of Confederation (1781–1789), why did Congress struggle to pay its war debts?
alt.a: It had no power to tax, only to request money.
alt.ex: The Articles, in force from March 1, 1781, gave Congress no power to tax; it could only request funds from the states, which often refused. The Constitution (1787) fixed this by giving Congress power to lay and collect taxes.
w: It had to share all tax revenue with Britain.
After independence the United States paid no revenue to Britain.
The President vetoed every spending bill.
There was no President under the Articles.
The Supreme Court struck down its tax laws.
There was no Supreme Court under the Articles, and Congress had no tax laws.

alt.q: Based on the passage, why was the Articles of Confederation so hard to fix during the 1780s?
alt.a: Every state had to approve any change.
alt.ex: Article XIII of the Articles of Confederation (in force 1781) required changes to be confirmed by every state legislature. A single state could block reform, so in 1787 delegates wrote a new Constitution whose Article V needs only three-fourths of the states.
w: Only the President could propose changes.
There was no President under the Articles.
Changes required approval by the British Parliament.
The states were independent after 1776 and did not need Parliament's approval.
The Supreme Court had to review each change.
The Articles created no Supreme Court.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article XIII of the Articles of Confederation, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“unless such alteration be agreed to in a Congress of the United States, and be afterwards confirmed by the legislatures of every State.”
Source: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School

items.q: Which event of 1786–1787 most convinced American leaders that the Articles of Confederation needed to be replaced?
items.a: Shays' Rebellion
items.ex: In 1786–1787, indebted Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays closed courts to stop foreclosures, and Congress was too weak to help. The uprising alarmed leaders and boosted support for the Constitutional Convention that met in May 1787.
w: the Whiskey Rebellion
The Whiskey Rebellion took place in 1794, under the Constitution.
the Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party (1773) protested British tea taxes, before independence.
Bacon's Rebellion
Bacon's Rebellion took place in colonial Virginia in 1676.

alt.q: Which document was written mainly in response to the weaknesses exposed by Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787)?
alt.a: the U.S. Constitution
alt.ex: Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787) showed the national government under the Articles could not keep order. Delegates met in Philadelphia from May to September 1787 and wrote the Constitution, signed September 17, 1787, to create a stronger national government.
w: the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration (1776) came a decade before Shays' Rebellion.
the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were the system whose weakness the rebellion exposed.
the Massachusetts Constitution
The Massachusetts Constitution was ratified in 1780, before the rebellion.

alt.q: What was the most significant effect of Shays' Rebellion?
alt.a: It built support for a stronger national government.
alt.ex: Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787) showed that Congress under the Articles could not raise an army or keep order. Alarmed leaders backed the Philadelphia Convention of 1787, which produced a Constitution with a stronger national government.
w: It led directly to the adoption of the Bill of Rights.
The Bill of Rights (1791) came from Anti-Federalist demands during ratification.
It caused Massachusetts to leave the Union.
Massachusetts stayed in the Union and ratified the Constitution in 1788.
It ended the use of paper money in all states.
The rebellion did not end paper money; the Constitution later barred states from coining money.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1786, farmers in western Massachusetts, many of them Revolutionary War veterans deep in debt, closed courts to stop the seizure of their farms. Early in 1787 they marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield. Congress lacked the money and power to raise troops to respond.

items.q: Which state constitution, drafted mainly by John Adams and ratified in 1780, is still in effect today and is the oldest functioning written constitution in the United States?
items.a: the Massachusetts Constitution
items.ex: John Adams drafted the Massachusetts Constitution in 1779, and it was ratified on June 15, 1780. Its separate executive, two-house legislature, and independent judiciary served as a model for the U.S. Constitution of 1787.
w: the Virginia Constitution
Virginia's constitution of 1776 was replaced long ago; it was not drafted by John Adams.
the Pennsylvania Constitution
Pennsylvania's 1776 constitution had a one-house legislature and was replaced in 1790.
the New York Constitution
New York's first constitution (1777) was largely drafted by John Jay and has been replaced.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which principle did John Adams build into this 1780 constitution?
alt.a: the rule of law
alt.ex: Article XXX of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights (1780) separated the branches so the state would be “a government of laws and not of men.” This means rulers are governed by laws rather than personal will, an idea also basic to the U.S. Constitution (1787).
w: judicial review
The passage does not say courts may strike down laws.
popular sovereignty
The phrase stresses that laws, not persons, rule; it does not address where power comes from.
federalism
Federalism divides power between national and state levels; this passage concerns one state's government.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article XXX of the Massachusetts Constitution (1780), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“to the end it may be a government of laws and not of men.”
Source: Massachusetts Legislature (malegislature.gov)

alt.q: Based on the passage, which idea from this 1780 constitution was also found in the 1620 Mayflower Compact?
alt.a: Government is formed by the agreement of the people.
alt.ex: The Preamble of the Massachusetts Constitution (1780), drafted by John Adams, calls the body politic a “social compact” formed by voluntary association. Like the Mayflower Compact (1620), it grounds government in the people's consent.
w: Government power comes from God through the king.
The passage bases government on a voluntary association, not divine right.
Only property owners belong to the body politic.
The passage speaks of the whole people and each citizen, not just property owners.
A national government must outrank the states.
The passage concerns forming a state body politic, not national supremacy.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Preamble of the Massachusetts Constitution (1780), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The body politic is formed by a voluntary association of individuals: it is a social compact, by which the whole people covenants with each citizen, and each citizen with the whole people”
Source: Massachusetts Legislature (malegislature.gov)

items.q: Which law, passed by the Confederation Congress in 1785, set up a system for surveying western lands into townships six miles square?
items.a: the Land Ordinance of 1785
items.ex: The Land Ordinance of 1785 divided western land into townships six miles square with 36 sections, reserving one section in each for public schools. It let Congress sell land in an orderly way to raise money it could not raise by taxes.
w: the Northwest Ordinance of 1787
The 1787 ordinance set up territorial government and a path to statehood, not the survey grid.
the Homestead Act
The Homestead Act (1862) gave free land to settlers; it came much later.
the Ordinance of 1784
Jefferson's Ordinance of 1784 outlined future states but did not create the township survey system.

alt.q: Which sequence lists the western land ordinances of the Confederation Congress in the correct order?
alt.a: Ordinance of 1784, Land Ordinance, Northwest Ordinance
alt.ex: Jefferson's Ordinance of 1784 proposed dividing the West into future states; the Land Ordinance of 1785 created the survey system; and the Northwest Ordinance of July 13, 1787, set up territorial government and the path to statehood.
w: Land Ordinance, Northwest Ordinance, Ordinance of 1784
The Ordinance of 1784 came first, before the 1785 and 1787 laws.
Northwest Ordinance, Ordinance of 1784, Land Ordinance
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) was the last of the three.
Ordinance of 1784, Northwest Ordinance, Land Ordinance
The Land Ordinance (1785) came before the Northwest Ordinance (1787).

alt.q: What was the most significant achievement of the Confederation Congress under the Articles of Confederation (1781–1789)?
alt.a: organizing and settling the western lands
