alt.ex: The Declaration says people are 'endowed by their Creator' with rights and that governments are instituted 'to secure these rights.'
w: Government creates rights and grants them to its citizens
That describes legal rights; the Declaration says rights come before government.
Government must give up its authority to the individual states
The Declaration is about rights and independence, not federalism.
Government's rights come from the will of the British king
The Declaration rejects the king's authority over the colonies.

items.q: Which power belongs only to the national government?
items.a: coining money
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power to coin money, and Article I, Section 10 forbids the states to do so. Taxing is a concurrent power, while schools and local governments are reserved to the states.
w: levying taxes
Taxing is a concurrent power held by both national and state governments.
establishing public schools
Education is a power reserved to the states.
creating local governments
States create counties and cities under their reserved powers.

alt.q: Why would this agreement be unconstitutional?
alt.a: Article I, Section 10 forbids states to make treaties.
alt.ex: Article I, Section 10 says “No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation.” Foreign affairs belong to the national government.
w: The Tenth Amendment reserves foreign affairs to the states.
Foreign affairs are delegated to the national government, not reserved to the states.
Only state legislatures, not governors, may sign treaties.
No part of a state government may make treaties.
Treaties require approval by a national referendum.
Treaties are made by the President with the consent of two-thirds of the Senate.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: The governor of a state signs a formal agreement with a foreign country promising military cooperation and special trade benefits for the state's ports.

alt.q: Which pair correctly matches each power with the level of government that holds it under the Constitution?
alt.a: declaring war: national; creating local governments: state
alt.ex: Declaring war is a delegated power of Congress, while creating counties and cities is a power reserved to the states.
w: creating local governments: national; declaring war: state
Both powers are matched to the wrong level of government.
coining money: state; setting up public schools: national
Coining money is national and schools are a state power.
making treaties: state; regulating interstate trade: national
States may not make treaties under Article I, Section 10.

items.q: How did problems under the Articles of Confederation influence the federal system created by the Constitution?
items.a: They strengthened the national government but kept the states.
items.ex: Under the Articles, the national government could not tax, regulate trade, or enforce its laws, leaving the states nearly independent. The Constitution created a stronger national government with its own powers while preserving the states.
w: They abolished the states and created a single central government.
The Constitution kept the states and divided power with them.
They let each state override national laws it opposed.
The Supremacy Clause makes valid national law supreme over state law.
They kept the national government unable to collect taxes.
The Constitution gave Congress the power to lay and collect taxes.

alt.q: Which American plan of government had these traits?
alt.a: the Articles of Confederation
alt.ex: The Articles created a weak confederation: Congress had one vote per state, could not levy taxes, and had no separate executive or national court system, leaving most power with the states.
w: the Virginia Plan of 1787
The Virginia Plan proposed a strong national government with representation based on population.
the Constitution of the United States
The Constitution gave Congress taxing power and created an executive and judiciary.
the Northwest Ordinance of 1787
The Northwest Ordinance organized western territory; it did not set up the national government.

sc.title: A certain government is characterized by the following traits:
sc.text:
1. a national legislature with one vote per state
2. no power to levy taxes
3. no separate national executive or judiciary
4. most power held by the states

alt.q: Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787) convinced many American leaders that the federal system needed which change?
alt.a: a stronger national government
alt.ex: The national government under the Articles could not raise an army or money to help Massachusetts put down the uprising. The rebellion helped prompt the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
w: a weaker national government
The rebellion exposed the weakness of the national government, leading leaders to strengthen it.
the elimination of state governments
The Constitution kept state governments in a federal system.
a return to rule by the British
No serious movement sought to return to British rule.

items.q: In South Dakota v. Dole (1987), the Supreme Court upheld a law withholding some federal highway funds from states that allowed people under 21 to buy alcohol. This case shows how the national government can
items.a: influence state policy by attaching conditions to funds
items.ex: Congress did not order states to raise their drinking age, but under its spending power it attached a condition to highway grants. The case shows how federal money shapes federalism in practice.
w: abolish state laws it disagrees with by executive order
The case involved Congress's spending power, not executive orders abolishing state law.
take over state police powers during peacetime
Congress left the drinking age to the states, using funding as an incentive.
directly set the drinking age in every state by statute
The law did not set a national drinking age; it conditioned funds on states doing so.

alt.q: This arrangement is an example of
alt.a: a conditional grant-in-aid
alt.ex: Grants-in-aid are federal funds given to states. When they come with requirements, such as meeting nutrition standards, the national government uses money to influence state policy.
w: the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
Reserved powers belong to states; here the national government is shaping state policy through funding.
the Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause requires states to honor each other's public acts and court judgments.
state nullification of federal law
Nullification is a state's claimed refusal to follow federal law; here the state complies.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress offers states money for school lunch programs, but only if the states meet federal nutrition standards. A state that wants the money changes its rules to meet the standards.

alt.q: Why does the national government often use grants with conditions instead of direct orders to shape state policies?
alt.a: Congress usually cannot command states but may fund them.
alt.ex: The Supreme Court has held that Congress generally may not commandeer state governments, but under its spending power it may offer funds with reasonable conditions, as in South Dakota v. Dole (1987).
w: States are not allowed to raise any tax money on their own.
States have their own taxing power, a concurrent power.
The Constitution forbids Congress to pass laws about states.
Congress passes many laws affecting states under its enumerated powers.
The President must approve each state's laws in advance.
The President has no power to approve state laws.

items.q: Which statement best describes cooperative federalism?
items.a: National and state governments share responsibility for programs.
items.ex: Cooperative, or “marble-cake,” federalism describes national and state governments sharing the funding and administration of programs such as Medicaid and highways. Dual, or “layer-cake,” federalism pictures each level acting in its own separate sphere.
w: National and state governments work in completely separate spheres.
This describes dual federalism.
State governments may ignore national laws they oppose.
This describes nullification, which the Supremacy Clause rejects.
The national government controls all local decisions.
This describes a unitary system, not federalism.

alt.q: This arrangement best illustrates
alt.a: cooperative federalism
alt.ex: Medicaid is jointly funded by the national and state governments, with federal rules and state administration, a classic example of cooperative federalism.
w: dual (layer-cake) federalism
Dual federalism keeps national and state roles separate, but Medicaid blends them.
a unitary system
In a unitary system the central government holds all power; here states run their own programs.
a confederation
In a confederation the central government is weak and depends on the states; here the national government funds and sets rules.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Medicaid provides health coverage to eligible low-income people. The federal government pays a large share of the costs and sets basic rules, while each state runs its own program and decides some details.

alt.q: Political scientists compare dual federalism to a “layer cake” and cooperative federalism to a “marble cake.” What does the marble cake image suggest?
alt.a: Powers and duties of each level are mixed together.
alt.ex: In a marble cake the flavors swirl together, just as national and state governments share funding and responsibilities under cooperative federalism.
w: Each level of government keeps to its own layer.
This describes the layer cake, or dual federalism.
The states have been absorbed by the national government.
States still exist and act; they share responsibilities rather than disappear.
Local governments hold more power than the states.
The image concerns national-state sharing, not local power over states.

items.q: Which advantage of federalism does Brandeis describe?
items.a: States can test new policies that others may copy.
items.ex: Because states have their own powers, each can try different policies. Successes can spread to other states or the nation while failures stay contained, which is why states are called “laboratories of democracy.”
w: States can overturn national laws that they find unwise.
States cannot overturn valid national laws under the Supremacy Clause.
States can conduct foreign relations with other nations.
Foreign relations belong to the national government.
States can avoid all national rules on economic matters.
Brandeis described state experiments, not escape from national law.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Justice Louis Brandeis's dissent in New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann (1932), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“It is one of the happy incidents of the federal system that a single courageous State may, if its citizens choose, serve as a laboratory; and try novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country.”
Source: New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann, 285 U.S. 262 (1932)

alt.q: This pattern best illustrates which idea about federalism?
alt.a: states as laboratories of democracy
alt.ex: A state tries a new policy; when it succeeds, other states adopt it. Justice Brandeis described this as a state serving “as a laboratory.”
w: the supremacy of national law
No national law is involved; the states are acting on their own.
the full faith and credit owed among states
Full faith and credit requires states to honor each other's records, not copy policies.
the reserved powers of the people
The scenario is about states experimenting with policy, not rights retained by individuals.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: One state creates a new program that lets high school students earn college credit. After the program succeeds, several other states pass laws creating similar programs.

alt.q: The phrase “laboratories of democracy” describes the idea that
alt.a: states can experiment with policies on a small scale
alt.ex: The phrase comes from Justice Brandeis's 1932 dissent describing how a single state may “try novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country.”
w: Congress tests laws in the District of Columbia first
The phrase refers to states experimenting, not Congress testing laws in D.C.
federal courts review experimental state laws in advance
Federal courts do not approve state laws before they take effect.
cities must copy the policies of their state governments
The idea is about states trying different policies, not cities copying them.

items.q: Which statement best describes federalism?
items.a: Power is divided between a national government and state governments
items.ex: Federalism divides authority between the national government (delegated powers) and the states (reserved powers, Tenth Amendment), with some concurrent powers.
w: Power is divided among legislative, executive, and judicial branches
That is separation of powers.
Power is held by sovereign states that loosely cooperate together
That is a confederation, like the Articles of Confederation.
Power is concentrated in a single central government for the nation
That is a unitary system.

alt.q: Federalist No. 51 states that "the power surrendered by the people is first divided between two distinct governments, and then the portion allotted to each subdivided among distinct and separate departments." The first division described is
alt.a: federalism
alt.ex: The 'two distinct governments' are the national and state governments (federalism); the later subdivision 'among distinct and separate departments' is separation of powers. Madison called this a 'double security' for rights.
w: separation of powers
Separation of powers is the second division, among departments (branches).
checks and balances
Checks and balances are tools each branch uses to restrain the others.
judicial review
Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down unconstitutional laws.

alt.q: In the U.S., states hold powers that the national government cannot simply take away, unlike a unitary system in which the central government can create or abolish regional governments. This difference reflects
alt.a: federalism
alt.ex: Under federalism the Constitution itself divides power, so states have their own guaranteed authority.
w: popular sovereignty
Popular sovereignty concerns the people as the source of power.
a confederation
In a confederation the states hold nearly all power and the central government is weak, as under the Articles.
separation of powers
Separation of powers divides power among branches, not between levels.

items.q: A state creates its own public school system and sets rules for marriage licenses. Under which constitutional provision does the state hold these powers?
items.a: The Tenth Amendment
items.ex: The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states (or the people) powers not delegated to the United States, such as education and marriage licensing.
w: The Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause gives Congress implied powers; it does not grant powers to states.
The Supremacy Clause
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme over conflicting state law.
The Commerce Clause
The Commerce Clause gives Congress power over interstate commerce.

alt.q: The Tenth Amendment states: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." This amendment most directly supports
alt.a: federalism
alt.ex: By reserving undelegated powers to the states, the Tenth Amendment protects the state side of the federal system.
w: judicial review
Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws.
separation of powers
Separation of powers divides federal power among three branches.
equal protection
Equal protection (Fourteenth Amendment) bars unfair discrimination by states.

alt.q: Which power is concurrent, meaning it is held by both the national and state governments?
alt.a: Levying taxes
alt.ex: Both Congress and the states may tax and borrow; these are concurrent powers.
w: Coining money
Only Congress may coin money; Article I, Section 10 forbids states to do so.
Declaring war
Declaring war is a delegated power of Congress alone.
Making treaties
Treaty-making belongs to the President with Senate consent; states are barred from it.

mt.q: Match each Bill of Rights amendment to what it protects (6th–10th).
pairs: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer
No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail
Rights not listed still belong to the people
Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people
mt.ex: Bill of Rights (1791): 6th Amendment: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer; 7th Amendment: Jury trial in civil cases; 8th Amendment: No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail; 9th Amendment: Rights not listed still belong to the people; 10th Amendment: Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people.

items.q: A state passes a law that directly conflicts with a valid federal law. Under the Constitution, which law controls?
items.a: The federal law, under the Supremacy Clause
items.ex: Article VI makes the Constitution and federal laws made under it 'the supreme Law of the Land,' so valid federal law prevails over conflicting state law.
w: The state law, under the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth reserves undelegated powers but does not let states override valid federal law.
Whichever of the two laws was passed most recently
Timing does not decide federal-state conflicts; the Supremacy Clause does.
Whichever law the state's voters approve
Voter approval cannot make a state law override valid federal law.

alt.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court held that Maryland could not tax the Second Bank of the United States. This ruling strengthened which side of federalism?
alt.a: National power over conflicting state action
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall upheld the bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause and ruled that, under the Supremacy Clause, a state cannot tax a federal institution ('the power to tax involves the power to destroy').
w: State power to regulate national institutions
This states the opposite of the holding; Maryland's tax was struck down.
Individual rights against state interference
The case concerned national versus state power, not individual rights.
Judicial power over presidential decisions
The case did not involve the President; it involved Congress's bank and a state tax.

alt.q: Article VI states: "This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof... shall be the supreme Law of the Land." In a federal system, this clause is needed mainly to
alt.a: settle conflicts between national and state laws
alt.ex: Because federalism creates two levels of lawmaking, the Supremacy Clause tells courts that valid federal law wins when the two conflict.
w: divide power among the three federal branches
That is separation of powers (Articles I-III).
reserve unlisted powers to the individual states
That is the Tenth Amendment.
guarantee each state a republican government
That is the Guarantee Clause of Article IV.

items.q: Which later constitutional provision reflects the same ideas as this passage?
items.a: the First Amendment's religion clauses
items.ex: Thomas Jefferson drafted the statute in 1779, and James Madison guided it through the Virginia legislature in 1786. Its bans on forced support of religion and on punishment for belief foreshadowed the First Amendment's Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses (1791).
w: the Second Amendment's militia clause
The Second Amendment concerns the militia and the right to bear arms, not religion.
the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement
The Fourth Amendment concerns searches and seizures, not religious belief.
the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people; it does not address religion.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…no man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship, place, or ministry whatsoever, nor shall be enforced, restrained, molested, or burthened in his body or goods, nor shall otherwise suffer, on account of his religious opinions or belief…”
Source: Thomas Jefferson Foundation (Monticello)

alt.q: Which founder drafted the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and had it listed on his tombstone as one of his proudest achievements?
alt.a: Thomas Jefferson
alt.ex: Jefferson wrote the statute in 1779; it became law in 1786. His tombstone names him as author of the Declaration of Independence and of the Virginia statute for religious freedom, and father of the University of Virginia.
w: George Washington
Washington supported religious liberty but did not draft the Virginia statute.
John Adams
Adams was from Massachusetts and did not write the Virginia statute.
Alexander Hamilton
Hamilton, a New Yorker, had no role in drafting the Virginia statute.

alt.q: The opponents' view was written into law the next year in which document?
alt.a: the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
alt.ex: After defeating a proposed tax to support teachers of the Christian religion, Virginia passed Jefferson's statute in 1786. It declared that no one may be compelled to support any religious worship or ministry.
w: the Virginia Declaration of Rights of 1776
That document came about a decade earlier, in 1776.
the Northwest Ordinance of 1787
The Northwest Ordinance governed western territory and was a national, not Virginia, law.
the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780
Massachusetts's constitution was adopted earlier and actually allowed public support for churches.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1785, Virginia's legislature considers a tax to pay teachers of the Christian religion. Opponents, led by James Madison, argue that government has no business forcing citizens to support any church.

items.q: Jefferson's phrase “a wall of separation between Church & State” describes his view of which clause?
items.a: the Establishment Clause
items.ex: Jefferson wrote that the First Amendment's ban on laws “respecting an establishment of religion” built a wall of separation between church and state. The Supreme Court later quoted his phrase in Everson v. Board of Education (1947).
w: the Supremacy Clause
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme over state law; it does not concern religion.
the Free Speech Clause
The phrase refers to the religion clauses Jefferson quoted, not to speech.
the Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause concerns Congress's implied powers, not religion.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Thomas Jefferson's 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptist Association, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…I contemplate with sovereign reverence that act of the whole American people which declared that their legislature should ‘make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof,’ thus building a wall of separation between Church & State.”
Source: Library of Congress

alt.q: Which President, in an 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptist Association, described the First Amendment as building “a wall of separation between Church & State”?
alt.a: Thomas Jefferson
alt.ex: Jefferson, then President, wrote the letter on January 1, 1802. His metaphor became a famous description of the Establishment Clause.
w: George Washington
Washington left office in 1797 and died in 1799.
John Adams
Adams left the presidency in 1801, before the letter was written.
James Madison
Madison was Secretary of State in 1802; he became President in 1809.

alt.q: Which principle, described by Jefferson as a “wall of separation,” does this law violate?
alt.a: separation of church and state
alt.ex: An official state church supported by taxes is an establishment of religion. The Establishment Clause, applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, forbids it.
w: separation of powers
Separation of powers divides government among branches; it does not address religion.
the right to petition the government
The law does not limit citizens' ability to petition officials.
the ban on titles of nobility
The law creates an official church, not a title of nobility.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state legislature passes a law naming one Christian denomination as the official state church and using tax money to pay its ministers.

items.q: In Reynolds v. United States (1879), the Supreme Court upheld a federal law against polygamy even though the defendant said his religion required it. What principle did the Court establish?
items.a: Government may regulate religious actions but not beliefs.
items.ex: The Court wrote that laws “cannot interfere with mere religious belief and opinions” but “may with practices.” The Free Exercise Clause fully protects belief, but religiously motivated conduct can be limited by valid laws.
w: Government may regulate religious beliefs but not actions.
This reverses the rule: belief is protected, while conduct may be regulated.
Religious duties excuse people from obeying criminal laws.
The Court upheld Reynolds's conviction, rejecting a religious excuse.
Congress may establish an official national religion.
The Establishment Clause forbids this, and the case did not involve it.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which statement about religious liberty is most accurate?
alt.a: Belief is fully protected, but conduct may be limited.
alt.ex: Reynolds drew a line between belief, which government may not touch, and religious practices, which may be regulated by valid laws.
w: Conduct is fully protected, but belief may be limited.
This reverses the Court's rule.
Both belief and conduct are beyond the reach of law.
The passage says laws may govern practices.
Both belief and conduct may be banned by Congress.
The passage says laws cannot interfere with religious belief.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Supreme Court's opinion in Reynolds v. United States (1879), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Laws are made for the government of actions, and while they cannot interfere with mere religious belief and opinions, they may with practices.”
Source: Reynolds v. United States, 98 U.S. 145 (1879)

alt.q: Applying the principle of Reynolds v. United States (1879), which law is most likely constitutional?
alt.a: the fire safety law, because it regulates conduct
alt.ex: Under Reynolds, government may regulate actions through valid general laws but may not punish religious belief itself. A neutral fire code regulates conduct; a law against holding beliefs does not.
w: the belief law, because states may define acceptable faiths
Government may not punish religious belief or decide which faiths are acceptable.
both laws, because religious groups have no special protection
The Free Exercise Clause fully protects religious belief.
neither law, because churches are exempt from all regulation
Churches must follow valid, neutral laws such as fire codes.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A small religious group holds unusual beliefs about the end of the world. A state passes one law making it a crime to hold those beliefs and another law requiring all public buildings, including churches, to meet fire safety codes.

items.q: In Engel v. Vitale (1962), the Supreme Court ruled that a prayer written by New York officials for daily recitation in public schools was unconstitutional. On what grounds?
items.a: It violated the Establishment Clause.
items.ex: The Court held that government-written prayer recited in public schools violated the Establishment Clause, even though the prayer was nondenominational and students could remain silent or be excused.
w: It violated the Free Speech Clause.
The Court based its ruling on the ban on establishing religion, not on speech.
It violated the Equal Protection Clause.
The case concerned government sponsorship of religion, not unequal treatment.
It violated the Tenth Amendment.
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to states; it was not the basis of the ruling.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case would most likely be used to strike down this policy?
alt.a: Engel v. Vitale
alt.ex: Engel v. Vitale (1962) held that official, government-composed prayer in public schools violates the Establishment Clause, even if students may remain silent.
w: Wisconsin v. Yoder
Yoder (1972) protected Amish parents' free exercise of religion; it did not involve school prayer.
Tinker v. Des Moines
Tinker (1969) protected students' symbolic political speech.
Reynolds v. United States
Reynolds (1879) upheld a law against polygamy despite religious objections.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state board of education writes a short prayer and directs every public school teacher to lead students in reciting it each morning. Students who object may stay silent.

alt.q: Which statement best describes how Engel v. Vitale (1962) affected religious liberty in public schools?
alt.a: Officials may not compose or lead official school prayers.
alt.ex: Engel barred government-sponsored prayer in public schools. It did not forbid students from praying on their own.
w: Students may not pray privately anywhere on school grounds.
Engel limited government-sponsored prayer, not students' private prayer.
Teachers must lead a daily prayer of the students' choice.
Engel forbade official prayer led by school officials.
Schools may require prayer if it favors no single religion.
The prayer in Engel was nondenominational and was still struck down.

items.q: In Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022), the Supreme Court ruled that a public school football coach's brief, personal prayer on the field after games was protected. Which constitutional protections did the Court rely on?
items.a: the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses
items.ex: The Court held 6–3 that the coach's prayer was protected by the First Amendment's Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses, and that the district's concern about the Establishment Clause did not justify disciplining him.
w: the Establishment and Equal Protection Clauses
The school district relied on the Establishment Clause; the Court's ruling for the coach rested on free exercise and free speech.
the Due Process and Supremacy Clauses
Neither clause was the basis of the decision.
the Second and Tenth Amendments
These amendments concern arms and reserved powers, not religious expression.

alt.q: Based on Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022), how would a court most likely rule?
alt.a: The prayer is protected private religious expression.
alt.ex: In Kennedy, the Court held that a coach's short, personal prayer, which did not require student participation, was protected by the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses.
w: The suspension is required by the Establishment Clause.
The Court rejected the argument that allowing the prayer would violate the Establishment Clause.
The prayer is unprotected because he is a public employee.
Public employees keep First Amendment rights when engaged in private expression.
The suspension is valid because schools may ban all prayer.
Schools may not ban private religious expression of this kind.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A public high school coach kneels alone at midfield after a game for a brief, quiet prayer. He does not ask players to join him. The school district suspends him, saying his prayer could look like the school endorsing religion.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the Supreme Court's approach to the Establishment Clause after Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022)?
alt.a: Courts look to historical practices and understandings.
alt.ex: In Kennedy, the Court said it had abandoned the Lemon test and that the Establishment Clause must be interpreted by reference to historical practices and understandings.
w: Courts apply the three-part Lemon test to every case.
The Court said it had long ago abandoned the Lemon test.
Courts forbid any religious expression by public employees.
Kennedy protected a public employee's private religious expression.
Courts let each state decide what the clause means.
The Supreme Court interprets the Establishment Clause, which binds every state.

items.q: Which statement best describes individual liberty as a principle of American democracy?
items.a: People may speak, believe, and act as they choose within the law
items.ex: Individual liberty means freedom from unjust government control over personal, political, and religious life, protected especially by the Bill of Rights.
w: People must follow the religion chosen by their state government
An established church requiring belief is the opposite of religious liberty.
People's freedoms depend on approval by the majority of voters
Basic liberties are protected even from majorities.
People receive freedoms only as rewards for service to the nation
Liberty is treated as a natural right, not a reward.

alt.q: The First Amendment begins: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." These two clauses together protect
alt.a: freedom of belief and worship from government control
alt.ex: The Establishment Clause bars an official church and the Free Exercise Clause protects practicing one's faith; together they secure religious liberty.
w: the right to petition officials to correct wrongs
That is the Petition Clause, later in the First Amendment.
the freedom of reporters to publish without censorship
That is freedom of the press.
equal treatment of people regardless of race
That is equal protection (Fourteenth Amendment).

alt.q: Amish parents refuse, for religious reasons, to send their children to school after eighth grade, and the state prosecutes them. In Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972), the Supreme Court ruled that
alt.a: the Free Exercise Clause protected the parents' choice
alt.ex: Yoder held that requiring Amish children to attend school past eighth grade violated the parents' free exercise of religion.
w: the Establishment Clause required the state to fund Amish schools
The case was about free exercise; no school funding was ordered.
the state's interest in schooling outweighed the parents' beliefs
That is the right case with the wrong holding; the Court sided with the parents.
the Equal Protection Clause required the same rules for everyone
The ruling rested on religious freedom, not equal protection.

items.q: Students wear black armbands to school to protest a war, and the school suspends them even though no disruption occurred. Which case and principle apply?
items.a: Tinker v. Des Moines; students keep free speech rights in school
items.ex: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Court held that students do not 'shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate'; armbands were protected symbolic speech.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier; schools may edit school-sponsored papers
Hazelwood (1988) allowed censorship of a school-sponsored newspaper, not personal expression.
Engel v. Vitale; public schools may not lead official prayers
Engel (1962) is an Establishment Clause case about school prayer.
Texas v. Johnson; burning the U.S. flag is protected speech
Johnson (1989) protected flag burning as symbolic speech, but not in a school setting.

alt.q: Which case held that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate"?
alt.a: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969)
alt.ex: Tinker protected students' armbands protesting the Vietnam War as symbolic speech absent substantial disruption.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988)
Hazelwood let schools control school-sponsored publications.
Engel v. Vitale (1962)
Engel struck down official school prayer under the Establishment Clause.
Texas v. Johnson (1989)
Johnson protected flag burning as political expression.

alt.q: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), what did the Supreme Court decide about students' black armbands?
alt.a: They were protected symbolic speech that caused no real disruption
alt.ex: The Court held schools may limit student expression only if it would substantially disrupt school; silent armbands did not.
w: They could be banned because schools control all student expression
The Court rejected total school control over student speech.
They were protected only because the students wore them off campus
The armbands were worn at school, and they were still protected.
They were school-sponsored speech that officials could freely edit
That is the Hazelwood (1988) standard for school newspapers.

items.q: Which example best illustrates political liberty rather than religious liberty?
items.a: Criticizing the President at a peaceful public rally
items.ex: Political liberty is the freedom to take part in public life and dissent: speech, press, assembly, petition, and voting.
w: Choosing not to attend any house of worship
Choosing whether to worship is religious liberty.
Praying privately during the lunch period at a public school
Private student prayer is free exercise of religion.
Refusing to salute a flag for reasons of faith
Faith-based refusal to salute (Barnette, 1943) involved religious objections.

alt.q: The First Amendment protects "the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances." These freedoms are most important to democracy because they
alt.a: let citizens criticize leaders and influence policy
alt.ex: Speech, press, assembly, and petition allow citizens to debate, organize, and pressure government: the core of political liberty.
w: prevent the government from setting up an official church
That is the Establishment Clause.
guarantee accused persons a fair and speedy trial
That is the Sixth Amendment.
keep soldiers from being housed in private homes
That is the Third Amendment.

alt.q: A group of residents gathers peacefully outside city hall and delivers a signed request asking the council to repair local roads. Which First Amendment freedoms are they exercising?
alt.a: Assembly and petition
alt.ex: Gathering peacefully is assembly; formally asking government to act is petitioning 'for a redress of grievances.'
w: Press and free exercise
Press concerns publishing; free exercise concerns religion.
Religion and the press
Neither religion nor publishing is involved.
Due process and speech
Due process concerns fair procedures before government takes liberty or property.

items.q: Which of the following ancient civilizations established a republican form of government?
items.a: Roman
items.ex: After overthrowing its kings around 509 B.C.E., Rome created a republic in which citizens elected officials such as consuls to govern for them. The Roman Republic, with its Senate and elected magistrates, was a key model for the U.S. framers.
w: Egyptian
Ancient Egypt was ruled by pharaohs, hereditary kings seen as divine, not by elected representatives.
Greek
Athens is known for direct democracy, in which citizens voted on laws themselves in the Assembly, rather than a representative republic.
Persian
The Persian Empire was ruled by an all-powerful hereditary king, not by elected officials.

alt.q: Which ancient state, governed by two consuls elected each year and an advisory Senate, served as a model of republicanism for the U.S. framers?
alt.a: Rome
alt.ex: The Roman Republic (509–27 B.C.E.) was led by two annually elected consuls and a Senate. Framers such as Madison and Hamilton drew on Rome as an example of representative government; they even signed The Federalist as “Publius,” a Roman name.
w: Athens
Athens was a direct democracy where citizens voted on laws in the Assembly; it was not run by consuls.
Sparta
Sparta had two hereditary kings and a council of elders, not elected consuls.
Egypt
Egypt was ruled by hereditary pharaohs, not by elected officials and a Senate.

alt.q: Which term best describes the form of government that ancient Rome established after it overthrew its kings around 509 B.C.E.?
alt.a: republic
alt.ex: After expelling its last king, Rome set up a republic, a government in which power rests with citizens who elect officials to represent them.
w: direct democracy
Direct democracy, in which citizens vote on laws themselves, is associated with Athens, not Rome.
absolute monarchy
Rome had just abolished its monarchy; a republic replaced rule by kings.
theocracy
Rome was not ruled by religious leaders claiming to govern in the name of the gods.

items.q: During the 6th century B.C.E., the ancient Athenians divided the powers of their government between two assemblies and guaranteed certain political rights to all male citizens. How do these political reforms best illustrate how societies develop?
items.a: by limiting government authority
items.ex: Dividing power between two bodies and guaranteeing rights to citizens keeps any single ruler or group from holding unchecked power. These Athenian reforms (associated with Solon and Cleisthenes) are an early example of societies developing limited government, an idea later built into the U.S. Constitution.
w: by choosing government leaders
The reforms described focus on splitting power and guaranteeing rights, not on how leaders are selected.
by improving government services
Nothing in the reforms concerns providing services; they changed who holds power and what rights citizens have.
by reducing government expenditures
The reforms dealt with the distribution of power and rights, not with government spending.

alt.q: Ancient Athenian reforms spread government power among several bodies and guaranteed political rights to male citizens. Which outcome did these reforms most likely produce?
alt.a: No single ruler could hold unchecked power.
alt.ex: Dividing authority and guaranteeing citizens’ rights limited government, so no individual or small group could rule without restraint.
w: Leaders could rule for life without elections.
The reforms widened citizen participation; they did not create lifetime, unelected rulers.
The government gave every citizen free schooling.
The reforms changed political power and rights, not public services such as schooling.
Citizens no longer had to pay any taxes at all.
The reforms concerned the structure of government and political rights, not abolishing taxes.

alt.q: Around 450 B.C.E., the Roman Republic wrote down its laws on the Twelve Tables and displayed them in public so that officials could not apply unwritten rules however they wished. How does this reform best illustrate how societies develop?
alt.a: by limiting government authority
alt.ex: Publishing written laws for all to see restrained officials, who could no longer interpret secret or unwritten customs to suit themselves. Like the Athenian reforms, the Twelve Tables show a society placing limits on those in power.
w: by choosing government leaders
Writing down the laws did not change how Roman officials were chosen.
by improving government services
The Twelve Tables set out legal rules; they did not provide new public services.
by reducing government expenditures
Publishing the laws was about restraining officials, not cutting spending.

items.q: Which modern democratic concept practiced in the United States is most like the democratic process of ancient Greece?
items.a: the referendum
items.ex: Athens practiced direct democracy: citizens voted on laws themselves in the Assembly. A referendum, in which voters directly approve or reject a law or measure, is the modern U.S. practice closest to that.
w: the presidential election
Presidents are chosen indirectly through the Electoral College and serve as representatives, not a direct vote on laws.
the primary election
Primaries choose party nominees for office; voters pick candidates rather than deciding laws directly.
the nominating convention
At conventions party delegates, not all citizens, choose nominees.

alt.q: Which modern practice in the United States most closely resembles the direct democracy of ancient Athens?
alt.a: the New England town meeting
alt.ex: In a town meeting, the town’s voters gather and vote directly on local laws and budgets, much as Athenian citizens voted on laws in the Assembly.
w: the Electoral College system
The Electoral College is an indirect method of choosing the president through electors.
a vote in the U.S. Senate
The Senate is a body of elected representatives, which reflects a republic, not direct democracy.
a session of a state legislature
State legislatures are representative bodies; citizens do not vote on each law themselves.

alt.q: Florida voters cast ballots to approve or reject a proposed amendment to the state constitution that was placed on the ballot by citizen petition. Which ancient practice does this most resemble?
alt.a: Athenians voting on laws in the Assembly
alt.ex: When voters decide a measure themselves, they act directly, as Athenian citizens did in the Assembly. This is direct democracy rather than representative government.
w: Roman senators debating laws in the Senate
Roman senators were a small body acting for others, not ordinary citizens deciding directly.
Persian kings issuing decrees for the empire
Royal decrees involve no vote by citizens at all.
Spartan kings commanding the army in battle
Military command by hereditary kings has nothing to do with citizens voting on laws.

items.q: Which modern process would be supported by the ancient Greeks?
items.a: electing governors
items.ex: Athenian democracy rested on citizens directly taking part in choosing and controlling their leaders, and Athenians elected some officials, such as their generals. Of the choices, only electing governors gives citizens a direct say in who leads them, which fits Greek democratic ideals.
w: hiring press secretaries
A press secretary is staff hired by an official; citizens play no part in the choice.
nominating an ambassador
Ambassadors are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, with no vote by citizens.
appointing a majority leader
A majority leader is chosen by party members in a legislature, not by the citizens at large.

alt.q: Which modern practice best reflects the ancient Athenian idea that ordinary citizens should take part directly in government?
alt.a: serving on a jury
alt.ex: Athens relied on large juries of ordinary citizens to decide cases. Jury service in the United States likewise lets ordinary citizens share directly in exercising government power.
w: appointing Cabinet secretaries
Cabinet secretaries are chosen by the president and confirmed by the Senate, not by ordinary citizens.
confirming federal judges
Only senators vote to confirm federal judges; ordinary citizens take no direct part.
hiring civil service workers
Civil servants are hired by government agencies; this is not citizen participation.

alt.q: Which modern process would ancient Athenians most likely view as consistent with their democratic ideals?
alt.a: voting for a city mayor
alt.ex: Athenian democracy valued citizens having a direct voice in who governs them. Voting for a mayor gives citizens that direct choice, unlike appointment or inheritance.
w: appointing a federal judge for life
Life appointments by officials give citizens no direct say.
inheriting a seat in a legislature
Inherited office is the opposite of democratic choice by citizens.
naming a Cabinet secretary
Cabinet members are named by the president, not chosen by citizens.

items.q: Which statement best describes how laws were made in the democracy of ancient Athens?
items.a: Eligible citizens debated and voted on laws themselves in the Assembly
items.ex: Athens practiced direct democracy: male citizens met in the Assembly (ekklesia) and voted on laws and policy in person rather than through representatives.
w: Citizens elected senators who then voted on all the laws on their behalf
That is representative government, the model of the Roman Republic, not Athenian direct democracy.
A council of hereditary nobles drafted laws for a king to approve
That describes aristocracy or monarchy; democratic Athens had no king making its laws.
Two consuls chosen each year issued the laws for the entire city
Consuls were the chief elected officials of the Roman Republic, not of Athens.

alt.q: In Thucydides' account of Pericles' Funeral Oration (431 B.C.), Pericles says of Athens: "Its administration favors the many instead of the few; this is why it is called a democracy." Which feature of Athenian government does this best reflect?
alt.a: Power rested with the body of citizens rather than with a small elite
alt.ex: Pericles contrasts rule by 'the many' (the citizen body voting in the Assembly) with rule by 'the few'; in Athens, ordinary male citizens held power directly.
w: Power was shared between elected consuls and a Senate serving for life
That is the structure of the Roman Republic, not Athens.
Power was granted to the ruler by divine right and passed to heirs
That is divine-right hereditary monarchy, the opposite of rule by the many.
Power was held by the wealthiest families who owned the most land
That is oligarchy or aristocracy, rule by 'the few' that Pericles contrasts with democracy.

alt.q: A town's adult citizens meet each spring in one hall and vote directly on the budget and local laws, with no elected council. This system most closely resembles which ancient model?
alt.a: The Athenian Assembly, where citizens voted on laws in person
alt.ex: Citizens voting on laws themselves, without representatives, is direct democracy, the system of the Athenian Assembly.
w: The Roman Senate, where members advised the elected magistrates
The Roman Senate was a body of leading citizens advising elected officials, a representative and aristocratic institution.
The Twelve Tables, which put Rome's laws in writing for everyone
The Twelve Tables were a written law code, not a way citizens made decisions.
The Spartan system, in which two hereditary kings shared power
Sparta's dual kingship was hereditary rule, not citizens voting directly on laws.

items.q: Which reform is most associated with Cleisthenes, often called the 'father of Athenian democracy'?
items.a: Reorganizing citizens into ten tribes and creating the Council of 500
items.ex: Cleisthenes' reforms (c. 508-507 B.C.) broke the power of aristocratic clans by regrouping citizens into ten tribes by residence and creating the Council of 500 (boule).
w: Writing Athens' first harsh law code, under which many crimes were capital
That was Draco (c. 621 B.C.), whose severe written code gave us the word 'draconian.'
Canceling debts and ending the enslavement of Athenians for unpaid debt
That was Solon (c. 594 B.C.), an earlier reformer who laid groundwork for democracy.
Paying citizens for jury service so poorer men could take part in government
That was Pericles (mid-400s B.C.), who expanded democracy decades after Cleisthenes.

alt.q: Around 508-507 B.C., an Athenian leader reorganized citizens into ten tribes based on where they lived and created a Council of 500 chosen from them. Who was this leader?
alt.a: Cleisthenes
alt.ex: Cleisthenes' reforms of 508-507 B.C. created the ten tribes and the Council of 500, earning him the title 'father of Athenian democracy.'
w: Peisistratus
Peisistratus was a tyrant who seized power in Athens in the mid-500s B.C., before Cleisthenes' democratic reforms.
Pericles
Pericles led Athens during its golden age (c. 461-429 B.C.), decades after the tribal reforms.
Solon
Solon (c. 594 B.C.) canceled debts and set up wealth-based classes; he did not create the ten tribes.

alt.q: Cleisthenes grouped Athenians into new tribes that mixed people from the city, the coast, and the inland regions. What was the primary purpose of this reform?
alt.a: To weaken the power of old aristocratic clans and regional factions
alt.ex: By mixing citizens from different regions into each tribe, Cleisthenes broke the hold of noble families and local factions and tied citizens to the city as a whole.
w: To create a hereditary class of nobles who would command the army
The reform did the opposite: it reduced the influence of the noble families.
To replace the Assembly with a small group of elected representatives
Athens kept its Assembly of citizens; representative lawmaking is the Roman and American model.
To ensure that only the wealthiest landowners could hold public office
Linking office to wealth classes was Solon's earlier system; Cleisthenes' tribal reform aimed instead at breaking the power of noble clans.

items.q: Which statement best describes who could take part in the Athenian Assembly?
items.a: Only free adult male citizens; women, slaves, and foreigners were excluded
items.ex: Athenian democracy was direct but narrow: only free adult men of citizen birth could vote, so women, enslaved people, and metics (resident foreigners) were left out.
w: All adult residents of Athens, including women and resident foreigners
Women and metics (resident foreigners) could not vote in the Assembly.
Only members of the noble families who owned large estates outside the city
That describes an aristocracy; Athenian democracy let ordinary male citizens, rich or poor, take part.
Only the members of the Senate and the two consuls elected that year
The Senate and consuls were institutions of the Roman Republic, not Athens.

alt.q: A historian argues that Athens was 'less democratic than its name suggests.' Which fact best supports this argument?
alt.a: Most residents, including women and slaves, had no vote at all
alt.ex: Citizenship was limited to free adult males of citizen birth, so the majority of people living in Athens (women, enslaved people, metics) could not participate.
w: Citizens voted on laws directly instead of through representatives
Direct voting by citizens was a highly democratic feature, not a limitation.
Many officials were chosen by drawing lots rather than by election
Selection by lot (sortition) was seen as democratic because it gave every citizen an equal chance.
Leaders could be ostracized by a vote of the assembled citizens
Ostracism was a popular check on powerful leaders, a democratic feature.

alt.q: Which group was allowed to vote in the Athenian Assembly?
alt.a: Free adult men born to Athenian citizen families
alt.ex: Only free adult males of citizen birth could vote; in 451 B.C., Pericles' citizenship law required both parents to be Athenian.
w: Resident foreigners (metics) who paid taxes to the city
Metics paid a special tax and served in the military but could not vote.
Enslaved workers who served in Athenian households
Enslaved people had no political rights in Athens.
Women who were born into Athenian citizen families
Women of citizen families could not vote or hold office in Athens.

items.q: In Athenian democracy, what was the primary purpose of ostracism?
items.a: To let citizens vote to exile a person seen as a threat to the city
items.ex: Ostracism (traditionally credited to Cleisthenes) let citizens write a name on pottery shards (ostraka); the 'winner' was exiled for ten years, a popular check on would-be tyrants.
w: To let citizens elect representatives to a lawmaking Senate
Electing representatives to a Senate describes the Roman Republic, not ostracism.
To choose jurors and officials randomly by drawing lots
That is sortition (selection by lot), a different Athenian practice.
To publish the city's laws on public tablets so all could read them
Posting written laws publicly describes Rome's Twelve Tables, not ostracism.

alt.q: Athenian citizens scratch a politician's name on pottery shards, and the person named most often must leave the city for ten years. This practice best illustrates
alt.a: a check by the people on anyone gaining too much power
alt.ex: This is ostracism: citizens could exile a leader who seemed dangerous, a direct popular check on power.
w: the selection of officials by random lottery among citizens
That is sortition, Athens' method of choosing many officials and jurors.
the election of representatives to make laws for the city
Electing lawmakers is representative government, as in Rome; Athenians voted on laws themselves.
judicial review of laws by an independent court of judges
Judicial review is a U.S. practice established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

alt.q: Which Athenian practice allowed citizens to banish a leader for ten years without a trial?
alt.a: Ostracism
alt.ex: Ostracism let the Assembly exile a citizen for ten years by a vote written on pottery shards; no crime or trial was required.
w: Sortition
Sortition was the selection of officials and jurors by lot.
Impeachment
Impeachment is an English and American process of formally charging an official.
Tribunician veto
The tribune's veto was a Roman power to block actions harming plebeians.

items.q: Which feature of the Roman Republic most directly influenced the framers' choice of a representative government?
items.a: Citizens elected officials to govern and make decisions for them
items.ex: After expelling its kings (509 B.C.), Rome had citizens elect magistrates such as consuls; this republic, or representative government, is the model Article IV guarantees each state.
w: Citizens met in a single assembly to vote on every law themselves
That is direct democracy as practiced in Athens, which the framers rejected for a large nation.
A hereditary king ruled with advice from a council of elders
That describes monarchy, the system Rome abolished when the Republic began in 509 B.C.
A single emperor held all power and chose his own successor
That describes the Roman Empire under Augustus and later emperors, after the Republic fell.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 10, Madison writes: "A republic, by which I mean a government in which the scheme of representation takes place, opens a different prospect, and promises the cure for which we are seeking." Which ancient model does Madison's preferred system most resemble?
alt.a: Rome's government of elected consuls and a Senate
alt.ex: Madison favored a republic, government through elected representatives, like the Roman Republic, over a 'pure democracy' like Athens.
w: Athens' Assembly, where citizens voted on laws in person
Madison argued 'pure democracy' could not cure faction, so this is the model he rejected.
Sparta's system of two kings sharing hereditary rule
Sparta's dual hereditary kingship involved no scheme of representation.
Rome's later empire under a single all-powerful ruler
The Empire replaced the Republic with one-man rule, the opposite of representation.

alt.q: Voters in a city choose a council of nine members, who then pass the city's ordinances. This arrangement reflects which idea inherited from the Roman Republic?
alt.a: Rule through elected representatives
alt.ex: Citizens choosing officials who make the laws is representative government, the core idea of the Roman Republic.
w: Rule by citizens voting on each law directly
That is Athenian direct democracy; here the council, not the voters, passes ordinances.
Rule by a hereditary king and his council
That is monarchy, which the Romans abolished when they founded the Republic.
Rule by a dictator named for an emergency
Rome's dictator was a temporary emergency office, not the regular system of government.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Senate of the Roman Republic?
items.a: A body of leading citizens that advised magistrates and controlled finances
items.ex: The Roman Senate, made up largely of patricians and former magistrates serving for life, advised the consuls and controlled public money and foreign affairs; the U.S. borrowed its name.
w: An assembly of all adult male citizens that voted on every law directly
That describes the Athenian Assembly, a direct-democracy body.
A pair of officials elected each year to run both the government and the army
Those were the two consuls, Rome's chief executives.
A group of officials elected by plebeians who could veto harmful actions
Those were the tribunes of the plebs, protectors of the common people.

alt.q: The framers created an upper chamber of Congress whose members serve longer terms and were meant to bring experience and stability. Which ancient body inspired the name of this chamber?
alt.a: The Roman Senate
alt.ex: The U.S. Senate takes its name and its role as an experienced, deliberative upper body from the Senate of the Roman Republic.
w: The Athenian Assembly
The Assembly was Athens' gathering of all citizens, a direct-democracy body, not an upper chamber.
The Council of 500
The Council of 500 (boule) was Cleisthenes' Athenian council chosen by lot from the ten tribes.
The Roman Tribunate
The tribunes were officials elected by plebeians who could veto actions, not a chamber of elders.

alt.q: Roman senators usually served for life and were drawn mostly from former magistrates and patrician families. Which role did this body mainly play?
alt.a: Advising the consuls and controlling public money
alt.ex: The Senate advised elected magistrates and controlled finances and foreign policy, giving experienced leaders influence over the Republic.
w: Voting directly on laws as an assembly of all citizens
That describes Athens' Assembly, not the Roman Senate.
Vetoing actions of officials that harmed the plebeians
That was the power of the tribunes, elected by plebeians.
Ruling alone during emergencies for up to six months
That was the Roman dictator, a temporary emergency office.

items.q: In the Roman Republic, two consuls served one-year terms and each could veto the other. Which American principle does this arrangement most closely foreshadow?
items.a: Checks and balances that keep any one official from dominating
items.ex: Rome guarded against one-man rule by electing two consuls for one-year terms, each able to block the other, and tribunes who could veto acts harming plebeians: an early form of checks and balances.
w: Federalism dividing power between national and state levels
Federalism divides power between levels of government; the consuls shared one level.
Popular sovereignty, with all authority coming from the people
Popular sovereignty concerns the source of power, not officials blocking each other.
Judicial review of laws by an independent court of judges
Judicial review is a court's power to strike down laws, set out in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

alt.q: Which Roman official, elected by the plebeians, could veto actions of magistrates and the Senate that harmed common citizens?
alt.a: Tribune
alt.ex: Tribunes of the plebs could veto (Latin for 'I forbid') acts harmful to plebeians, a check on the patrician-dominated government.
w: Consul
Consuls were the two chief executives of the Republic; each could block the other, but they did not represent the plebeians.
Censor
Censors took the census and oversaw public morals and the Senate's membership list.
Praetor
Praetors were magistrates in charge of administering justice.

alt.q: Why did the Roman Republic elect two consuls for one-year terms rather than a single ruler for life?
alt.a: To prevent any one person from gaining kinglike power
alt.ex: Having driven out their last king in 509 B.C., Romans split executive power between two consuls with short terms and mutual vetoes so no one could become a king.
w: To make sure the laws were posted in writing for citizens
Written, public law was the purpose of the Twelve Tables.
To let every citizen vote directly on all public matters
That describes Athenian direct democracy, not the consulship.
To give the Senate a hereditary leader for the army
The consuls were elected, not hereditary, and served only one year.

items.q: In Federalist No. 39, Madison defines a republic as "a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior." Which form of government does this describe?
items.a: Rule by elected officials
items.ex: Madison's definition describes representative democracy, or republicanism: power from the people, exercised by officials serving limited terms or during good behavior.
w: Rule by citizens in person
Citizens governing in person is direct democracy, as in Athens.
Rule by a hereditary king
Hereditary rule is monarchy; Madison's offices are held for limited periods.
Rule by a wealthy few
Rule by a wealthy few is oligarchy, not power from 'the great body of the people.'

alt.q: Article IV, Section 4 states: "The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government." This clause requires every state to have
alt.a: a government whose leaders are chosen by the people
alt.ex: The Guarantee Clause requires representative (republican) government in every state, with no monarchy or hereditary rule.
w: a government in which citizens vote on every single law
That is direct democracy, which the clause does not require.
a government led by a governor who serves for life
Life rule would contradict republican government.
a government whose laws match those of every other state
States may have different laws; Full Faith and Credit concerns honoring other states' records.

alt.q: Citizens of a country elect a legislature, which makes laws on their behalf; there is no monarch. Which term best describes this country?
alt.a: A republic
alt.ex: A republic is a government in which citizens elect representatives to make laws, with no hereditary ruler.
w: A direct democracy
In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws themselves rather than through a legislature.
A constitutional monarchy
A constitutional monarchy keeps a monarch with limited powers.
An oligarchy
An oligarchy is rule by a small, privileged group.

items.q: Madison argued in Federalist No. 10 that "a pure democracy, by which I mean a society consisting of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government in person, can admit of no cure for the mischiefs of faction." Which conclusion did Madison draw?
items.a: A large republic with elected representatives can best control factions
items.ex: In Federalist No. 10 (1787), Madison argued that representation and a large republic with many competing interests would keep any single faction from dominating.
w: Factions should be eliminated entirely by restricting freedom of opinion
Madison said removing the causes of faction would destroy liberty, a cure 'worse than the disease.'
Small democracies best protect minorities from majority factions
Madison argued the opposite: small democracies are most easily dominated by a majority faction.
States should stay independent instead of forming a strong union
That is closer to the Anti-Federalist view (e.g., Brutus No. 1).

alt.q: Which Federalist essay argues that a large republic is the best cure for the 'mischiefs of faction'?
alt.a: Federalist No. 10
alt.ex: Madison's Federalist No. 10 explains how a large republic with representation controls the effects of faction.
w: Federalist No. 51
No. 51 explains checks and balances and separation of powers ('Ambition must be made to counteract ambition').
Federalist No. 78
No. 78 (Hamilton) defends an independent judiciary and judicial review.
Brutus No. 1
Brutus No. 1 is an Anti-Federalist essay arguing a large republic could not work.

alt.q: A framer argues that elected representatives will "refine and enlarge the public views" by filtering out the passions of the moment better than a crowd of voters could. This is an argument for
alt.a: republicanism over direct democracy
alt.ex: Madison (Federalist No. 10) argued that passing public views 'through the medium of a chosen body of citizens' improves decisions: the case for a republic.
w: states' rights over national power
The argument concerns representation, not the balance between states and nation.
judicial review over legislative power
The argument concerns elected representatives, not courts.
a monarchy over representative rule
The argument favors elected representatives, not a monarch.

items.q: In the founders' view of republicanism, why was civic virtue important?
items.a: Citizens had to put the common good ahead of private interests
items.ex: Classical republicanism, drawn from Rome, held that a republic survives only if citizens and leaders place the public good above self-interest.
w: Citizens had to obey a hereditary ruler without question
Unquestioning obedience to a hereditary ruler describes monarchy.
Citizens had to vote directly on every single law the state passed
Voting directly on laws is direct democracy, not republican civic virtue.
Citizens had to belong to the official church of their state
Required church membership conflicts with religious liberty.

alt.q: George Washington was praised as a 'modern Cincinnatus' for giving up command of the army in 1783 and returning to private life. This praise reflects the republican value of
alt.a: civic virtue, placing public service above personal power
alt.ex: Like the Roman Cincinnatus, who gave up emergency power to return to his farm, Washington resigned his commission (December 1783), modeling republican virtue.
w: popular sovereignty, letting voters elect the army's leaders
Washington was appointed by Congress, not elected by voters, and the praise is about giving up power.
federalism, letting each state command its own militia
The praise concerns personal restraint, not state-national power.
natural rights, protecting each soldier's private property
The praise is about giving up power, not protecting property.

alt.q: Which Roman figure, who gave up emergency power and returned to his farm, became a symbol of republican virtue for the founders?
alt.a: Cincinnatus
alt.ex: Cincinnatus was named dictator to save Rome, then resigned and returned to his farm; the Society of the Cincinnati and the city of Cincinnati honor him.
w: Julius Caesar
Caesar took power as dictator for life, helping to end the Republic.
Augustus
Augustus became Rome's first emperor, replacing the Republic.
Cicero
Cicero was an orator who defended the Republic, but he is not known for giving up emergency power.

items.q: What is the principal function of a written constitution?
items.a: outlining the structure and powers of a government
items.ex: A written constitution sets up the framework of government: it creates the branches, assigns their powers, and sets limits on them. The U.S. Constitution, for example, creates Congress, the presidency, and the federal courts in Articles I–III.
w: resolving disagreements between competing parties
Disputes are settled by courts, elections, and negotiation; settling them is not a constitution’s main purpose.
confirming resistance to civil disobedience
Constitutions do not exist to oppose civil disobedience; this is not a function of a constitution.
declaring the independence of a state
Declaring independence is the job of a document like the Declaration of Independence, not a constitution.

alt.q: Articles I, II, and III of the U.S. Constitution create Congress, the presidency, and the federal courts and list the powers of each. Which function of a written constitution does this best illustrate?
alt.a: setting up the framework of government
alt.ex: Creating the branches of government and defining their powers is the principal function of a written constitution: it establishes the government’s structure and authority.
w: declaring independence from another nation
That was the purpose of the Declaration of Independence, not Articles I–III.
settling disputes between political parties
Articles I–III establish branches; they do not resolve party disputes.
listing every law that citizens must obey
A constitution sets the framework for making laws; it does not list all laws.

alt.q: Why is a written constitution important to the idea of limited government?
alt.a: It puts the limits on officials’ power in writing.
alt.ex: Because a written constitution states what government may and may not do, officials can be held to those written limits, and courts can enforce them.
w: It lets leaders change the rules whenever needed.
A constitution is hard to change; amending the U.S. Constitution requires supermajorities.
It guarantees that one party controls government.
Constitutions set rules for all parties; they do not guarantee one party’s power.
It removes the need for courts to interpret laws.
Courts still interpret laws and the constitution itself, as in judicial review.

items.q: This requirement best reflects which principle?
items.a: constitutionalism
items.ex: Article VI requires every federal and state legislator, executive, and judge to swear to support the Constitution. Officials pledge loyalty to the supreme written law rather than to a person or party.
w: majority rule
The oath binds officials to the Constitution, not to the wishes of the majority.
direct democracy
The oath concerns officials' duties, not citizens voting directly on laws.
executive privilege
Executive privilege protects presidential communications; the oath binds all officials to the Constitution.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article VI of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Senators and Representatives before mentioned, and the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: The presidential oath in Article II requires the President to “preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States.” What does this oath show about the President's authority?
alt.a: It comes from, and is limited by, the Constitution.
alt.ex: The President swears to defend the Constitution, not to rule by personal will. The office's powers come from the Constitution and must be exercised within its limits.
w: It comes from the political party that won the election.
The President's powers come from the Constitution, not from a party.
It is above the Constitution during emergencies.
No emergency places the President above the Constitution he swears to defend.
It is granted by the Supreme Court each term.
The Court does not grant presidential power; the Constitution does.

alt.q: This practice most directly promotes
alt.a: constitutionalism
alt.ex: Swearing loyalty to a written constitution, rather than to a leader or party, commits officials to govern within the limits of the fundamental law.
w: one-party rule
The practice deliberately avoids loyalty to a ruling party.
absolute monarchy
An absolute monarch is not bound by a constitution.
direct democracy
The practice concerns officials' loyalty to the constitution, not citizens voting directly on laws.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In a new democracy, newly elected officials must publicly swear loyalty to the nation's written constitution before taking office, instead of swearing loyalty to the president or the ruling party.

items.q: How does the U.S. Constitution differ from the British constitution?
items.a: It is a single written document above ordinary law.
items.ex: Britain's constitution is drawn from statutes, court rulings, and conventions, and Parliament can change it by ordinary law. The U.S. Constitution is one written document that ordinary laws cannot override.
w: It can be changed by a simple act of the legislature.
This describes Britain; the U.S. Constitution requires the Article V amendment process.
It is made up mainly of customs and court decisions.
This describes Britain's largely unwritten constitution.
It gives the national legislature unlimited power.
Britain's Parliament is sovereign; the U.S. Congress has only limited, enumerated powers.

alt.q: Which country best fits this description?
alt.a: the United Kingdom
alt.ex: The United Kingdom has no single written constitution; its constitutional rules come from statutes, court decisions, and conventions, and Parliament can change them by ordinary law.
w: the United States
The United States has a single written Constitution that ordinary laws cannot change.
Mexico
Mexico has a single written constitution.
the Federal Republic of Germany
Germany has a written constitution called the Basic Law.

sc.title: A certain country is characterized by the following traits:
sc.text:
1. no single written constitutional document
2. constitutional rules drawn from statutes, court rulings, and customs
3. a legislature that can change constitutional rules by ordinary law

alt.q: Why did Americans in 1787 insist on a written constitution rather than relying on custom, as Britain did?
alt.a: to fix clear, lasting limits on government power
alt.ex: Having seen Parliament claim power over the colonies, Americans wanted a written fundamental law that defined and limited government and could not be changed by ordinary legislation.
w: to make it easier for Congress to change the rules
A written constitution makes the rules harder to change, requiring amendments.
to give the President authority over the states
The Constitution divides power; it does not place states under the President.
to let judges create new rights each term
The goal was clear, stable limits, not rules that change each court term.

items.q: Article I, Section 8 lists the specific powers of Congress, such as taxing, borrowing money, and declaring war. How does this list reflect constitutionalism?
items.a: It limits Congress to powers granted in writing.
items.ex: By granting Congress specific, enumerated powers, the Constitution defines and limits what the national government may do. Powers not delegated are reserved to the states or the people under the Tenth Amendment.
w: It lets Congress act on any issue it chooses.
Listing powers limits Congress; it does not give unlimited authority.
It gives the states control over Congress's agenda.
The list defines Congress's powers; it does not put states in charge of them.
It allows the President to approve each power.
The powers are granted by the Constitution itself, not by the President.

alt.q: Under the principle of limited, enumerated powers, why could a court strike down this law?
alt.a: Congress may act only under powers the Constitution grants.
alt.ex: The national government has only the powers the Constitution delegates. A law that rests on no constitutional power exceeds those limits, however good its purpose.
w: Congress may pass laws only with the states' unanimous consent.
Congress does not need state consent to pass laws within its powers.
Congress may act only after a national vote of the people.
The Constitution provides no national referendum on federal laws.
Congress may legislate only on issues the President proposes.
Congress may legislate on any subject within its powers, whoever proposes it.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law that it admits is based on no particular power listed in the Constitution, only on its belief that the law would be good for the country.

alt.q: Which feature of the U.S. Constitution most directly limits the national government's power?
alt.a: a written list of enumerated powers
