alt.ex: Enumerating Congress's powers in Article I, Section 8, and reserving the rest to the states or the people, defines the boundaries of national authority.
w: the system of electing the President
The method of electing the President does not define the limits of national power.
the census taken every ten years
The census apportions House seats; it does not limit national power.
the President's power to grant pardons
The pardon power is a grant of power, not a limit on the national government.

items.q: Why did the framers require the Constitution to be ratified by special state conventions rather than by state legislatures?
items.a: so it would rest directly on the authority of the people
items.ex: Article VII required ratification by conventions in nine states. Madison and others argued that approval by conventions chosen by the people would make the Constitution a higher law than acts of ordinary legislatures.
w: so state legislatures could amend it before approving it
Ratifying conventions could only accept or reject the Constitution, and the choice bypassed legislatures.
so the Continental Congress could control the outcome
Conventions in each state, not Congress, decided ratification.
so only wealthy landowners could take part in the vote
The goal was a broad popular foundation, not limiting participation to the wealthy.

alt.q: Requiring ratification by conventions rather than by state legislatures was meant to make the Constitution
alt.a: a higher law approved by the people themselves
alt.ex: Conventions elected by the people gave the Constitution an authority above ordinary legislatures, grounding it in popular consent.
w: a temporary agreement among the state governments
The framers sought a lasting fundamental law, not a pact among state governments.
a document that Congress could revise at will
The Constitution can be changed only through the Article V amendment process.
a treaty that any state could later cancel
Ratification by the people was meant to make the Union lasting, not a revocable treaty.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article VII of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Ratification of the Conventions of nine States, shall be sufficient for the Establishment of this Constitution between the States so ratifying the Same.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: This member's reasoning most closely follows the framers' reasoning for
alt.a: ratification by special conventions
alt.ex: The framers had the Constitution ratified by conventions elected for that purpose, so the fundamental law would rest on the people rather than on the legislatures it would limit.
w: election of senators by state legislatures
This original method gave legislatures more power; it was not about approving fundamental law.
the Great Compromise on representation
The Great Compromise settled how states are represented in Congress.
the Supremacy Clause in Article VI
The Supremacy Clause settles conflicts between national and state law.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A group writing a new state constitution debates how to approve it. One member argues that the legislature should not approve the very rules that will limit it, so the document should go to a convention chosen by the people.

items.q: Which statement best describes constitutionalism?
items.a: Government's powers are defined and limited by a supreme fundamental law
items.ex: Constitutionalism means government operates under, and is limited by, a constitution that ranks above ordinary laws and can be changed only by a special process (Article V).
w: Government's powers are divided between the nation and the states
That is federalism.
Government's powers come from the consent of the governed
That is the social contract and popular sovereignty.
Government's powers are exercised by the citizens' elected representatives
That is republicanism.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 78, Hamilton writes: "The interpretation of the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts. A constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges, as a fundamental law." Hamilton's argument supports
alt.a: courts treating the Constitution as superior to ordinary laws
alt.ex: Hamilton argued that judges must prefer the Constitution over conflicting statutes, foreshadowing judicial review in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: Congress overriding the court rulings by a simple majority vote
Hamilton argued courts protect the Constitution against the legislature, not the reverse.
states deciding for themselves which federal laws are valid
That is nullification, which Federalist No. 78 does not support.
the President interpreting the laws without judicial review
Hamilton assigns interpretation to the courts, not the executive.

alt.q: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Supreme Court declared part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 void. This reinforced constitutionalism by establishing that
alt.a: a law conflicting with the Constitution cannot stand
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall held that Section 13 of the Judiciary Act unconstitutionally expanded the Court's original jurisdiction, so the Constitution controls over ordinary law.
w: the President may ignore any Supreme Court ruling
The case asserted courts' power to say what the law is, not presidential defiance.
states may nullify unconstitutional federal laws
Nullification was a states' rights theory (Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions), not the holding.
Congress may expand the Court's original jurisdiction
That is exactly what the Court said Congress could not do.

items.q: A new majority in Congress wants to extend House members' terms from two years to six without changing the Constitution. Why can't Congress simply pass a law to do so?
items.a: The Constitution sets the term, and only an amendment can change it
items.ex: Article I sets two-year House terms; ordinary laws cannot change constitutional provisions, which require the Article V amendment process.
w: The President alone decides the length of congressional terms
The President has no power over congressional terms.
Each state legislature sets the terms of its own U.S. representatives
House terms are set by the Constitution, not by states.
The Supreme Court must approve all laws before they take effect
Courts review laws only in actual cases after passage; they do not pre-approve laws.

alt.q: Which feature most clearly makes the U.S. Constitution a higher law than ordinary statutes?
alt.a: It can be changed only through the special amendment process
alt.ex: Article V requires supermajorities (two-thirds to propose, three-fourths of states to ratify), so the Constitution cannot be altered by ordinary legislation.
w: It can be changed by a simple majority vote in both houses of Congress
That describes ordinary statutes, not the Constitution.
It was written by members of the Continental Congress
It was written at the Constitutional Convention of 1787; authorship does not make it supreme.
It must be renewed by the states every twenty years
The Constitution has no renewal requirement.

alt.q: A state constitution says the governor may serve only two terms. A popular governor's supporters in the legislature pass a statute allowing a third term, and a court strikes it down. The court's reasoning rests on
alt.a: constitutionalism: a constitution limits ordinary lawmaking
alt.ex: A statute cannot override the constitution that creates and limits the legislature; changing the term limit requires amending the constitution.
w: federalism: states may ignore national term limits
The term limit here is in the state constitution; no federal-state conflict exists.
popular sovereignty: voters may choose any candidate they want
Popular sovereignty would not let a statute override the constitution the people adopted.
majority rule: the legislature speaks for the people
Majority rule is limited by the constitution, which is why the statute fails.

items.q: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice Marshall wrote: "It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is." Which power did this decision establish?
items.a: Judicial review
items.ex: Marbury established judicial review, the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional, reinforcing the Constitution as supreme law.
w: Judicial restraint
Judicial restraint is a philosophy that judges should defer to elected branches; it is not a power Marbury created.
Implied powers
Implied powers were upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Selective incorporation
Selective incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to states through the Fourteenth Amendment, case by case.

alt.q: Which case first established judicial review, the power of courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
alt.ex: In Marbury, Chief Justice John Marshall struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing judicial review.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
McCulloch upheld implied powers and barred state taxation of the national bank.
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
Dred Scott was only the second time the Court struck down a federal law, but it did not establish the power.
Baker v. Carr (1962)
Baker held that legislative apportionment can be challenged in federal court.

alt.q: A federal court rules that a statute passed by Congress violates the First Amendment and cannot be enforced. The court is exercising
alt.a: judicial review
alt.ex: Striking down a law as unconstitutional is judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: executive privilege
Executive privilege is a presidential confidentiality claim.
senatorial courtesy
Senatorial courtesy is the custom of consulting home-state senators on nominations.
legislative oversight
Legislative oversight is Congress monitoring executive agencies.

items.q: Based on the passage, how did Madison believe a large republic would protect minority rights?
items.a: Many rival interests make an unjust majority less likely.
items.ex: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that a large republic contains so many factions that no single majority faction could easily unite to oppress others.
w: A strong executive can overrule the majority when needed.
Madison's remedy in the passage is the variety of interests, not executive power.
Small states can block any law passed by large states.
The passage does not discuss small states blocking laws.
Voters in a large nation are wiser than those in small ones.
Madison's point is about the number and diversity of interests, not voters' wisdom.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Federalist No. 10 (1787) by James Madison, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens…”
Source: The Federalist No. 10

alt.q: In Federalist No. 10, James Madison was most concerned about
alt.a: majority factions that violate the rights of others
alt.ex: Madison wrote that a minority faction can be outvoted, but a majority faction could use government to oppress others. He argued that a large republic would control this danger.
w: foreign nations invading the United States
Federalist No. 10 is about factions at home, not foreign invasion.
small states taking control of the national government
Madison's essay focuses on factions, not small states.
the cost of running a large federal government
The essay does not address government costs.

alt.q: According to Madison, why is a minority faction less dangerous than a majority faction?
alt.a: The majority can outvote it in elections.
alt.ex: Madison wrote that a minority faction is checked by “the republican principle,” meaning the majority can defeat it by vote. A majority faction is more dangerous because voting alone cannot stop it.
w: The courts must always rule against it.
Madison relied on voting, not courts, to defeat minority factions.
The President can ban it from organizing.
Madison rejected destroying liberty to cure faction; he did not propose banning factions.
The Constitution forbids minority parties.
The Constitution does not forbid any party or faction.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Federalist No. 10 (1787) by James Madison, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“If a faction consists of less than a majority, relief is supplied by the republican principle, which enables the majority to defeat its sinister views by regular vote.”
Source: The Federalist No. 10

items.q: Which term, used by Alexis de Tocqueville in Democracy in America, describes a majority using its power to oppress those with less support?
items.a: tyranny of the majority
items.ex: Tocqueville, a French observer who toured the United States in the early 1830s, warned that in a democracy the majority's power could become oppressive. Constitutional limits such as the Bill of Rights are designed to prevent this.
w: divine right of kings
Divine right is a theory that monarchs' authority comes from God.
separation of powers
Separation of powers divides government among branches.
dictatorship of the proletariat
This is a Marxist term, not Tocqueville's.

alt.q: This law is an example of which danger?
alt.a: tyranny of the majority
alt.ex: A majority using its voting power to silence an unpopular minority's newspaper is what Tocqueville called the tyranny of the majority. The First Amendment protects the press even against majority votes.
w: rule by a minority faction
Here a large majority, not a minority, is abusing its power.
abuse of judicial review
No court is involved; the voters themselves passed the law.
separation of powers
Separation of powers is a safeguard, not the danger shown here.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In a town, 80 percent of voters approve a law banning a small political group's newspaper because most residents dislike its opinions.

alt.q: Alexis de Tocqueville warned about the “tyranny of the majority.” Which situation best fits this concern?
alt.a: A majority votes to seize one ethnic group's property.
alt.ex: Using majority power to strip rights from a minority group is exactly the tyranny of the majority Tocqueville feared.
w: A minority party wins several seats in a state legislature.
A minority party winning seats is normal democratic competition.
A court strikes down a popular law that limits free speech.
This protects minority rights against the majority.
A President vetoes a bill that most voters support.
A veto is a constitutional check, not majority oppression of a minority.

items.q: In the U.S. Senate, ending debate on most bills requires a cloture vote of 60 senators. How does this rule affect majority rule?
items.a: It lets a large minority delay or block a bill.
items.ex: Under Senate Rule XXII, cloture on most legislation requires three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn (60 of 100). As few as 41 senators can sustain a filibuster, forcing the majority to compromise. This is a Senate rule, not a constitutional requirement.
w: It lets the majority pass bills without any debate.
The rule protects extended debate; it does not let the majority skip debate.
It lets the President end debate whenever needed.
The President has no power to end Senate debate.
It lets the House decide when Senate debate ends.
Each chamber sets its own rules; the House has no say over Senate debate.

alt.q: What is the most likely result under current Senate rules?
alt.a: The bill is stalled because cloture needs 60 votes.
alt.ex: With only 55 supporters, the majority cannot reach the 60 votes needed to invoke cloture on most legislation, so the minority can block a final vote.
w: The bill passes because it has a simple majority.
A simple majority is enough to pass the bill only after debate has ended.
The Vice President ends debate and the bill passes.
The Vice President may break tie votes but cannot end debate.
The bill goes to the Supreme Court for a decision.
The Supreme Court does not decide whether bills pass Congress.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A bill has the support of 55 of the 100 senators. The other 45 senators oppose it and refuse to agree to end debate on the bill.

alt.q: Senate supporters of the filibuster argue that it mainly protects which value?
alt.a: the voice of the minority party in lawmaking
alt.ex: Because cloture requires 60 votes, the minority party can force the majority to negotiate, which supporters say protects minority views from being overridden.
w: the President's power to set the Senate agenda
The filibuster limits the Senate majority; it gives the President no power over the agenda.
the right of states to nullify federal laws
The filibuster is a Senate procedure; it has nothing to do with nullification.
the power of courts to rule on legislation
The filibuster affects lawmaking in the Senate, not judicial review.

items.q: How does equal representation in the U.S. Senate protect a minority interest?
items.a: Small states get the same number of senators as large states.
items.ex: Under Article I, Section 3 and the Great Compromise, every state has two senators regardless of population. This keeps the populous states from fully controlling Congress.
w: Large states get more senators to reflect their larger populations.
Representation by population applies to the House; every state has two senators.
Minority parties are guaranteed half of all Senate seats.
No party is guaranteed any seats.
Each state's governor appoints its two senators.
Senators were originally chosen by state legislatures and, since the Seventeenth Amendment, by voters.

alt.q: This clause most directly protects
alt.a: less populous states from domination by larger states
alt.ex: Article V forbids any amendment that would take away a state's equal vote in the Senate without its consent, permanently protecting small states' equal representation.
w: minority political parties from losing their Senate seats
The clause concerns states' equal representation, not parties.
individual voters from unfair voting districts
District fairness is addressed by equal protection cases, not this clause.
the President from removal by the Senate
The clause does not concern impeachment or removal.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article V of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which constitutional compromise gave every state two senators to protect the interests of small states?
alt.a: the Great Compromise
alt.ex: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise of 1787 created a House based on population and a Senate with equal representation for every state.
w: the Three-Fifths Compromise
This compromise concerned counting enslaved people for representation and taxes.
the Missouri Compromise
The Missouri Compromise (1820) dealt with slavery in new states.
the Compromise of 1850
The Compromise of 1850 dealt with slavery in territories gained from Mexico.

items.q: How does this provision help protect minority rights?
items.a: Judges can rule against majorities without losing their posts.
items.ex: Federal judges serve during good behavior, which in practice means for life unless impeached and removed. Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 78 that this independence lets courts protect individual rights against temporary majority passions.
w: Judges must face voters often, so they follow majority opinion.
Federal judges are appointed, not elected, and do not face voters.
Judges can be removed whenever Congress disagrees with them.
Judges can be removed only through impeachment and conviction, not for their rulings.
Judges serve short terms, so new majorities can replace them.
Federal judges have no fixed terms; they serve during good behavior.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article III of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts, shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which feature of the Constitution allows the judge to make this ruling without fear of losing the job?
alt.a: federal judges serve during good behavior
alt.ex: Article III's good-behavior tenure and protection of judges' pay free federal judges from political pressure, so they can protect unpopular minorities.
w: federal judges are elected for fixed terms
Federal judges are appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
the Senate reviews every federal court ruling
The Senate does not review court rulings.
the President may overturn unpopular rulings
The President has no power to overturn court decisions.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A federal judge strikes down a very popular law because it violates the free speech rights of an unpopular group. Many voters are angry, but they cannot vote the judge out of office.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 78, Alexander Hamilton argued that the permanent tenure of federal judges was important mainly because it
alt.a: frees judges to protect rights against majority pressure
alt.ex: Hamilton argued that judicial independence guards the Constitution and the rights of individuals from temporary passions of the people and their representatives.
w: lets the President direct how judges decide each case
Tenure protects judges from presidential and political pressure.
makes judges answerable to the voters each year
Permanent tenure removes judges from election pressures.
allows Congress to remove judges whose rulings it dislikes
Judges may be removed only by impeachment, not for disliked rulings.

items.q: In his First Inaugural Address (1801), Jefferson said: "though the will of the majority is in all cases to prevail, that will to be rightful must be reasonable; that the minority possess their equal rights, which equal law must protect, and to violate would be oppression." Jefferson is describing
items.a: majority rule limited by the rights of the minority
items.ex: Jefferson summarized the balance at the heart of American democracy: the majority governs, but it may not violate the equal rights of the minority.
w: unlimited majority rule over every question of rights
Jefferson said the majority's will 'to be rightful must be reasonable' and may not oppress the minority.
a minority's power to veto the decisions of the majority
Jefferson said the majority's will is 'in all cases to prevail'; minorities keep their rights, not a veto.
the people's right to abolish a destructive government
That is the right of revolution in the Declaration of Independence.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the principle of majority rule with minority rights?
alt.a: The majority decides, but it cannot violate the basic rights of the few
alt.ex: Decisions are made by majority vote, but constitutional rights limit what any majority may do to a minority.
w: The minority decides whenever the majority's choice is unwise
Minorities do not overrule majorities; they are protected in their rights.
Every public decision must have the unanimous approval of all the citizens
Unanimity is a different rule (the Articles required it for amendments).
The majority decides every question, including individual rights
Unlimited majority rule can become 'tyranny of the majority'; rights are protected.

alt.q: Voters in a town approve, by a large margin, a measure banning one small religious group from holding public meetings. A court strikes down the measure. This outcome illustrates
alt.a: that some rights are protected even against the majority
alt.ex: Free exercise and assembly rights cannot be voted away; courts protect minority rights from majority decisions.
w: that federal courts must follow local voters' wishes
The court overrode the voters, the opposite.
that the majority rules on all matters involving religion
The First Amendment removes religious freedom from majority control.
that towns hold powers reserved by the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers do not allow towns to violate constitutional rights.

items.q: In West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943), the Court wrote: "One's right to life, liberty, and property, to free speech, a free press, freedom of worship and assembly, and other fundamental rights may not be submitted to vote; they depend on the outcome of no elections." This means that
items.a: the Bill of Rights places certain rights beyond majority control
items.ex: Justice Jackson explained that the Bill of Rights places fundamental rights beyond the reach of majorities; the Court struck down a mandatory flag salute.
w: fundamental rights may be changed by a statewide voter referendum
The passage says the opposite: rights may not be submitted to vote.
the states, not voters, decide which rights are fundamental
The Court, applying the Constitution, protected the rights against the state.
elections are the main way to protect individual rights
The passage says rights depend on 'no elections'; courts protect them.

alt.q: Jehovah's Witness students refused, for religious reasons, to salute the flag as their public school required. In 1943, the Supreme Court ruled that
alt.a: the school could not force the students to salute
alt.ex: West Virginia v. Barnette (1943) held that compelling the flag salute violated the First Amendment, overruling Minersville v. Gobitis (1940).
w: the school could require the salute for national unity
That was the holding of Minersville v. Gobitis (1940), which Barnette overruled.
the students could be expelled only after a hearing
A hearing requirement is a due process idea; the Court protected the refusal itself.
the matter should be settled by a school board vote
Barnette held such rights 'may not be submitted to vote.'

alt.q: Which feature of the Constitution most directly protects minority rights from majority rule?
alt.a: The Bill of Rights, which limits what laws may say
alt.ex: The Bill of Rights restricts government even when a majority supports a law, protecting minorities' freedoms.
w: The Electoral College, which counts votes by state
The Electoral College selects the President; it does not protect individual rights.
The census, which apportions House seats by population
The census distributes representation by population, a majoritarian feature.
The House of Representatives, elected by population
The House is the most majoritarian branch.

items.q: The Constitution requires two-thirds of both houses of Congress to propose an amendment and three-fourths of the states to ratify it. Why require more than a simple majority?
items.a: To protect basic rules and minorities from a temporary majority
items.ex: Article V's supermajorities ensure that fundamental law changes only with broad agreement, limiting a temporary majority.
w: To let any single state block a national law that it strongly dislikes
One state could block amendments only under the Articles' unanimity rule, and Article V does not cover ordinary laws.
To give the President final control over amendments
The President has no formal role in the Article V process.
To ensure that the Supreme Court proposes all amendments
Amendments are proposed by Congress or a national convention, not the Court.

alt.q: Which action requires a supermajority rather than a simple majority under the Constitution?
alt.a: Overriding a presidential veto
alt.ex: Article I, Section 7 requires two-thirds of both houses to override a veto.
w: Passing an ordinary bill in the House
Ordinary bills pass by simple majority.
Impeaching an official in the House
Impeachment in the House takes a simple majority; conviction in the Senate takes two-thirds.
Electing the Speaker of the House
The Speaker is chosen by a majority of votes cast.

alt.q: A majority of senators wants to ratify a treaty, but fewer than two-thirds of senators present support it. What happens?
alt.a: The treaty is not ratified
alt.ex: Article II requires the consent of two-thirds of senators present for treaties, protecting against narrow majorities.
w: The treaty is ratified by majority vote
A simple Senate majority is not enough for treaties.
The House decides by majority vote
The House has no constitutional role in ratifying treaties.
The President may ratify it alone
Treaties require Senate consent; the President cannot ratify alone.

items.q: In Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023), the Supreme Court ruled on race-conscious college admissions. What did the Court decide?
items.a: Harvard's and UNC's race-based admissions were unlawful.
items.ex: The Court held that the race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Equal Protection Clause (which applies to Harvard through Title VI of the Civil Rights Act). The ruling effectively ended race-based affirmative action in college admissions.
w: Colleges must reserve a fixed number of seats for minorities.
Racial quotas were already struck down in Bakke (1978), and SFFA ended race-based admissions altogether.
Private colleges are exempt from all federal civil rights laws.
Harvard, a private college, is bound by Title VI because it accepts federal funds.
Each state may decide whether colleges consider race.
The Court ruled that the Equal Protection Clause forbids these programs nationwide.

alt.q: Which 2023 Supreme Court decision held that race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina were unlawful?
alt.a: Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
alt.ex: In Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023), the Court held that the race-conscious admissions programs violated equal protection guarantees.
w: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke
Bakke (1978) struck down racial quotas but allowed race as one factor.
Grutter v. Bollinger
Grutter (2003) upheld a law school's race-conscious admissions program.
Brown v. Board of Education
Brown (1954) struck down segregation in public schools.

alt.q: Under current Supreme Court precedent, this plan would most likely be
alt.a: unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) held that race-based admissions programs violate equal protection, so a public university may not award admissions points based on race.
w: constitutional, as long as no fixed quota is used
This reflects the Bakke-era rule, which SFFA (2023) replaced.
constitutional, because universities set their own rules
Public universities must follow the Equal Protection Clause.
unconstitutional under the Second Amendment
The Second Amendment concerns the right to bear arms, not admissions.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 2026, a public university plans to give applicants extra points in admissions based on their race.

items.q: In Reed v. Reed (1971), the Supreme Court struck down an Idaho law that automatically preferred men over women as administrators of estates. Why was this case significant?
items.a: It first used Equal Protection to strike down a sex-based law.
items.ex: For the first time, the Court held that a state law treating men and women differently violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, extending equal protection to sex-based classifications.
w: It first gave women a constitutional right to vote in all states.
The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) secured women's right to vote.
It first struck down racial segregation in public schools.
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) did this.
It upheld different legal rules for men and for women.
The Court struck down the law treating men and women differently.

alt.q: Which case and clause would be used to strike down this law?
alt.a: Reed v. Reed, under the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Reed v. Reed (1971) struck down an Idaho law preferring men over women as estate administrators, holding that it violated the Equal Protection Clause.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson, under the Equal Protection Clause
Plessy (1896) upheld racial segregation; it did not strike down sex discrimination.
Reed v. Reed, under the Establishment Clause
Reed rested on equal protection, not religion.
Brown v. Board, under the Commerce Clause
Brown involved school segregation and rested on equal protection.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state law says that when two equally qualified relatives apply to manage a deceased person's estate, a man must always be chosen over a woman.

alt.q: Reed v. Reed (1971) expanded the reach of the Equal Protection Clause by applying it to
alt.a: laws that classify people by sex
alt.ex: Reed was the first case in which the Court held that a law discriminating on the basis of sex violated the Equal Protection Clause.
w: laws that classify people by race
Race-based laws had been struck down under equal protection long before 1971.
private businesses that serve the public
The Equal Protection Clause limits government, not private businesses.
actions of foreign governments
The Equal Protection Clause limits U.S. states, not foreign governments.

items.q: In Reynolds v. Sims (1964), the Supreme Court required state legislative districts to have roughly equal populations. Which principle did the Court apply?
items.a: one person, one vote
items.ex: The Court held that the Equal Protection Clause requires both houses of a state legislature to be apportioned substantially by population, so each person's vote carries roughly equal weight.
w: separate but equal
That doctrine, from Plessy v. Ferguson, was about segregation.
winner-take-all voting
Winner-take-all describes how most states award electoral votes.
clear and present danger
That is a free speech test from Schenck v. United States.

alt.q: Under Reynolds v. Sims (1964), why is this arrangement unconstitutional?
alt.a: It gives some votes far more weight than others.
alt.ex: When districts with very different populations each elect one senator, voters in small districts have far more influence. Reynolds held this violates the Equal Protection Clause.
w: It gives the governor too much power over the senate.
The problem is unequal voting weight, not the governor's power.
It violates the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers.
The ruling rested on the Equal Protection Clause.
It lets federal courts choose state senators.
Voters choose state senators; the issue is unequal district populations.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In a state, one state senate district has 600,000 residents and another has 15,000 residents, but each district elects one state senator.

alt.q: Which clause did the Supreme Court rely on in Reynolds v. Sims (1964) to require equally populated state legislative districts?
alt.a: the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Reynolds v. Sims held that the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause requires state legislative districts to be substantially equal in population.
w: the Commerce Clause
The Commerce Clause concerns regulating trade, not voting districts.
the Guarantee Clause
The Court has treated Guarantee Clause claims as political questions; Reynolds rested on equal protection.
the Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause concerns Congress's implied powers.

items.q: When a law treats people differently based on race, how do courts review it under the Equal Protection Clause?
items.a: with strict scrutiny, the most demanding test
items.ex: Courts apply strict scrutiny to racial classifications: the government must show the law is narrowly tailored to serve a compelling interest. Most other classifications, such as those based on age or income, receive only rational basis review.
w: with rational basis review, the most lenient test
Rational basis review applies to ordinary classifications, not race.
with no review, since legislatures decide such matters
Courts review racial classifications closely under the Equal Protection Clause.
with a public vote on whether the law is fair
Courts, not public votes, decide equal protection challenges.

alt.q: Under strict scrutiny, which must the government prove to justify a law that classifies people by race?
alt.a: The law is narrowly tailored to a compelling interest.
alt.ex: Strict scrutiny is the most demanding standard of review: the government must show a compelling interest and that the law is narrowly tailored to achieve it.
w: The law is supported by a majority of voters.
Popularity does not satisfy strict scrutiny.
The law is reasonably related to some legitimate government goal.
This is the rational basis test, the most lenient standard.
The law was passed by both houses of the legislature.
Every law passes the legislature; that alone does not justify a racial classification.

alt.q: How would courts most likely review these two laws?
alt.a: rational basis for the age law; strict scrutiny for the race law
alt.ex: Age-based rules such as a driving age receive rational basis review and are usually upheld. Racial classifications receive strict scrutiny and are rarely upheld.
w: strict scrutiny for the age law; rational basis for the race law
The standards are reversed; race receives the strictest review.
strict scrutiny for both laws
Age is not a suspect classification and receives only rational basis review.
rational basis for both laws
Racial classifications require strict scrutiny.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: One state law sets a minimum age of 16 to obtain a driver's license. Another state law assigns public housing units based on applicants' race.

items.q: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment limits only the states. In Bolling v. Sharpe (1954), how did the Supreme Court apply equal protection to the federal government?
items.a: through the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause
items.ex: Decided the same day as Brown v. Board of Education, Bolling struck down segregation in the public schools of Washington, D.C., which is governed by Congress. The Court found an equal protection guarantee in the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
w: through the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to states; it does not limit federal discrimination.
through the Privileges and Immunities Clause of Article IV
That clause protects citizens traveling between states.
through the Ninth Amendment's unlisted rights
The Court relied on the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

alt.q: Which case struck down this segregation?
alt.a: Bolling v. Sharpe
alt.ex: Bolling v. Sharpe (1954), decided with Brown v. Board of Education, held that school segregation in Washington, D.C., violated the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Brown applied the Fourteenth Amendment to segregation in the states.
Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld segregation.
Sweatt v. Painter
Sweatt (1950) involved a Texas law school, not D.C. public schools.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1954, public schools in Washington, D.C., were segregated by race. Because the District of Columbia is not a state, the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause did not directly apply.

alt.q: Which statement about equal protection in the United States today is most accurate?
alt.a: It limits both state governments and the federal government.
alt.ex: The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause binds the states, and since Bolling v. Sharpe (1954), the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause imposes a similar duty on the federal government.
w: It limits state governments but never the federal government.
Bolling v. Sharpe applied equal protection principles to the federal government.
It limits the federal government but never the states.
The Fourteenth Amendment's clause was written specifically to limit the states.
It limits only private businesses, not governments.
Equal protection limits governments; private businesses are covered by civil rights statutes.

items.q: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) forbids any State to "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws." Relying on this clause, the Supreme Court rejected 'separate but equal' in public schools in which decision?
items.a: Brown v. Board (1954)
items.ex: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) unanimously held that school segregation violates the Equal Protection Clause: 'Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.'
w: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Plessy interpreted the same clause but upheld 'separate but equal'; Brown overturned it for public schools.
Mapp v. Ohio (1961)
Mapp applied the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule to the states.
Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
Miranda rests on the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.

alt.q: "We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal." Which case does this come from?
alt.a: Brown v. Board (1954)
alt.ex: Chief Justice Warren wrote these words for a unanimous Court in Brown v. Board of Education, applying the Equal Protection Clause.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Plessy created the 'separate but equal' doctrine that this passage rejects.
Regents v. Bakke (1978)
Bakke concerned racial quotas in university admissions.
Shaw v. Reno (1993)
Shaw concerned racial gerrymandering of congressional districts.

alt.q: A state requires Black and white children to attend separate public schools, claiming the schools are equal. Under current law, which ruling and clause make this unconstitutional?
alt.a: Brown v. Board, under the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Brown (1954) held that state-mandated school segregation denies equal protection of the laws under the Fourteenth Amendment.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson, under the Equal Protection Clause
Plessy (1896) upheld segregation; it is the case Brown overturned.
Brown v. Board, under the First Amendment
Right case, wrong clause: Brown rested on equal protection, not the First Amendment.
Plessy v. Ferguson, under the Due Process Clause
Plessy upheld segregation, and Brown's holding rests on equal protection.

items.q: A state medical school reserved a fixed number of seats only for minority applicants. In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978), the Supreme Court held that
items.a: racial quotas were unconstitutional, though race could be one factor
items.ex: Bakke struck down the school's fixed quota (16 of 100 seats) but allowed race as one factor in admissions. (Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 2023, later held race-conscious admissions programs unconstitutional.)
w: all consideration of race in admissions was fully permitted
Bakke struck down the quota, so it did not permit every use of race.
racial quotas were required to remedy past discrimination
The Court rejected the quota rather than requiring one.
universities could not consider any factor other than their test scores
Bakke said nothing limiting admissions to test scores.

alt.q: Which 1978 case struck down a medical school's racial quota but allowed race to be considered as one factor in admissions?
alt.a: Regents v. Bakke
alt.ex: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978) rejected fixed racial quotas while permitting race as one 'plus' factor.
w: Grutter v. Bollinger
Grutter (2003) upheld the University of Michigan Law School's holistic admissions; it came 25 years later.
Shaw v. Reno
Shaw (1993) concerned racially drawn congressional districts.
Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal' segregation.

alt.q: A university reviews applicants individually and considers race as one factor among many, without setting aside any seats. Under the 1978 Bakke decision, this approach was treated as
alt.a: permissible, unlike a fixed racial quota
alt.ex: Bakke distinguished quotas (unconstitutional) from considering race as one factor (allowed); in 2023, SFFA v. Harvard held race-conscious admissions unconstitutional.
w: unconstitutional, like any use of race
Under Bakke, race as one factor was allowed; only the quota was struck down.
required by the Equal Protection Clause
Bakke permitted race as a factor but did not require it.
a matter left only to state legislatures
The Court decided the issue under the Constitution and federal law.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Equal Protection Clause?
items.a: States must apply their laws equally and not discriminate unfairly
items.ex: The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause (1868) forbids states from denying any person 'the equal protection of the laws.'
w: States must follow fair procedures before taking a person's liberty
That is the Due Process Clause.
States must honor the public records and court rulings of other states
That is the Full Faith and Credit Clause (Article IV).
States must provide every citizen with an equal amount of income
Equal protection concerns equal treatment under law, not equal income.

alt.q: A state draws an oddly shaped congressional district based almost entirely on race. In Shaw v. Reno (1993), the Court held that such a district
alt.a: may violate the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Shaw v. Reno held that districts drawn mainly by race are subject to strict scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause.
w: is always required by the Voting Rights Act
The Court rejected the idea that the Voting Rights Act automatically justified such districts.
is a political question courts cannot review
Baker v. Carr (1962) had already made districting challenges reviewable.
violates the one-person, one-vote rule
One person, one vote concerns equal population, not racial line-drawing.

alt.q: The Equal Protection Clause appears in which amendment, ratified after the Civil War?
alt.a: The Fourteenth Amendment
alt.ex: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) contains the Citizenship, Due Process, and Equal Protection Clauses.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Thirteenth (1865) abolished slavery.
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote because of race.
The Fifth Amendment
The Fifth (1791) contains a due process clause limiting the federal government, not the Equal Protection Clause.

sections.name: Bill of Rights and Civil Rights/Liberties

items.q: Which idea about civil liberties does this passage express?
items.a: Free speech has limits when it causes serious harm.
items.ex: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote that speech may be punished when it creates a “clear and present danger” of harms Congress may prevent. Today's narrower test, from Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), protects advocacy unless it is directed to and likely to incite imminent lawless action.
w: Free speech protects every statement in every setting.
The passage says even the strongest protection has limits.
Free speech applies only to spoken, not written, words.
The First Amendment protects both speech and the press.
Free speech belongs only to citizens, not to visitors.
The passage is about harmful speech, not who holds the right.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Supreme Court's opinion in Schenck v. United States (1919), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.”
Source: Schenck v. United States, 249 U.S. 47 (1919)

alt.q: Which test did the Supreme Court announce in Schenck v. United States (1919) for when speech may be limited?
alt.a: clear and present danger
alt.ex: Schenck asked whether words are used in circumstances that “create a clear and present danger” of substantive evils Congress has a right to prevent.
w: imminent lawless action
This test comes from Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969).
substantial disruption at school
This standard comes from Tinker v. Des Moines (1969).
actual malice
This libel standard for public officials comes from New York Times v. Sullivan (1964).

alt.q: In the 1919 case based on these facts, how did the Supreme Court rule?
alt.a: It upheld the conviction under the clear and present danger test.
alt.ex: In Schenck v. United States, the Court unanimously upheld the conviction under the Espionage Act, reasoning that in wartime the leaflets created a clear and present danger of obstructing the draft.
w: It overturned the conviction because all political speech is protected.
The Court upheld the conviction, holding that speech rights have limits.
It overturned the conviction because the law was ex post facto.
The law was in force before Schenck acted, and the Court upheld the conviction.
It upheld the conviction because wartime suspends the Bill of Rights.
The Court did not suspend the Bill of Rights; it applied a test for when speech may be punished.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: During World War I, a man mails thousands of leaflets urging drafted men to resist the draft. He is convicted under a federal law, and he argues that the First Amendment protects his leaflets.

items.q: Why is this rule most likely constitutional?
items.a: It neutrally limits the time, place, and manner of speech.
items.ex: Government may impose reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions if they are content-neutral, serve a significant interest such as traffic safety, and leave other ways to communicate. It may not deny permits based on a group's viewpoint.
w: The First Amendment does not protect parades on public streets.
Parades and marches are protected speech and assembly; they may be regulated, not banned.
Cities may block groups whose messages they find offensive.
Viewpoint-based restrictions are unconstitutional.
Free speech rights apply only inside private buildings.
Public streets and parks are traditional places for free expression.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A city requires groups to obtain a permit before holding a parade on public streets. The permit rules set the route and hours to manage traffic and apply equally to all groups, whatever their message.

alt.q: Which restriction on a public demonstration would most likely be upheld?
alt.a: a ban on loudspeakers in neighborhoods late at night
alt.ex: A content-neutral limit on noise at night protects residents and leaves protesters other ways to communicate, so it is a valid time, place, and manner restriction.
w: a ban on any public rally that criticizes the governor
This targets a viewpoint, which the First Amendment forbids.
a ban on all public protests by one political party
This singles out a group for its political views.
a ban on signs that support unpopular political causes
Banning unpopular messages is viewpoint discrimination.

alt.q: Which statement best explains why the government may set some rules for protests?
alt.a: Rights may be limited in neutral ways to protect public safety.
alt.ex: Civil liberties are not absolute. Government may regulate the time, place, and manner of expression to protect safety and order, as long as the rules do not target the message.
w: Rights may be limited whenever officials dislike the message.
Restrictions based on the message are unconstitutional.
Rights apply only to groups that have registered with the state.
First Amendment rights belong to everyone, not only registered groups.
Rights may be limited only by a vote of the people.
Courts apply constitutional standards; a popular vote cannot strip rights.

items.q: Which Supreme Court case held that the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms applies to state and local governments?
items.a: McDonald v. City of Chicago
items.ex: In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), the Court held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense. In McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010), it applied that right to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
w: District of Columbia v. Heller
Heller involved the federal district of Washington, D.C., and did not decide whether the right applies to the states.
Mapp v. Ohio
Mapp (1961) applied the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule to the states.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Gideon (1963) applied the right to counsel to the states.

alt.q: Which case supports the resident's argument?
alt.a: McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010)
alt.ex: McDonald held that the Second Amendment right recognized in Heller is incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment and limits state and local governments.
w: United States v. Lopez (1995)
Lopez limited Congress's commerce power over guns near schools; it did not apply the Second Amendment to states.
Barron v. Mayor of Baltimore (1833)
Barron held that the Bill of Rights limited only the federal government, which undercuts the resident's argument.
Schenck v. United States (1919)
Schenck concerned free speech in wartime.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A city bans almost all residents from keeping handguns in their homes. A resident who wants a handgun for self-defense sues, arguing that the Second Amendment limits cities and states, not just the federal government.

alt.q: Through which process did the Supreme Court apply the Second Amendment to the states in 2010?
alt.a: incorporation through the Fourteenth Amendment
alt.ex: Under selective incorporation, the Court applies Bill of Rights protections to the states one by one through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, as it did for the Second Amendment in McDonald v. City of Chicago.
w: a constitutional amendment ratified by the states
No new amendment was adopted; the Court interpreted the Fourteenth Amendment.
an executive order issued by the President
Executive orders cannot apply constitutional rights to the states.
a federal law passed by Congress
The change came from a Supreme Court decision, not a statute.

items.q: Based on Miranda v. Arizona (1966), what is the most likely result?
items.a: The confession is generally barred from use at trial.
items.ex: Miranda requires police to warn people in custody, before questioning, of the right to remain silent and the right to a lawyer. Statements obtained without these warnings generally cannot be used by the prosecution to prove guilt, protecting the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
w: The suspect must be released and can never be charged.
The remedy is excluding the statement, not ending the prosecution.
The confession is valid because no one forced him to talk.
Miranda treats custodial questioning without warnings as inherently pressured.
The officers must be removed from the police force.
Miranda's remedy concerns the evidence, not officers' employment.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Police arrest a robbery suspect and question him at the station without telling him that he may remain silent or have a lawyer present. He confesses.

alt.q: The Miranda warnings that police give to suspects in custody are based mainly on which constitutional right?
alt.a: the Fifth Amendment protection against self-incrimination
alt.ex: The Fifth Amendment says no person “shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself.” Miranda warnings protect that right during custodial interrogation.
w: the Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches
The Fourth Amendment governs searches and seizures, not questioning.
the Eighth Amendment ban on cruel and unusual punishment
The Eighth Amendment concerns punishment after conviction, bail, and fines.
the First Amendment freedom of speech
Miranda concerns the right not to incriminate oneself, not free speech.

alt.q: Under Miranda v. Arizona (1966), what must police tell a suspect in custody before questioning?
alt.a: that he has the right to remain silent
alt.ex: Miranda warnings tell suspects they have the right to remain silent, that what they say can be used against them, and that they have the right to an attorney.
w: that he has the right to a jury of his choice
Defendants do not choose their jurors, and this is not part of Miranda.
that he has the right to a speedy appeal
Appeals come after trial and are not part of Miranda warnings.
that he has the right to refuse arrest
No one has a right to resist a lawful arrest.

items.q: In Riley v. California (2014), the Supreme Court addressed police searches of cell phones taken from people under arrest. What did the Court decide?
items.a: Police generally need a warrant to search the phone's data.
items.ex: The Court unanimously held that police generally may not search the digital data on a cell phone seized during an arrest without a warrant, because phones hold vast amounts of private information.
w: Police may search any phone without limits after an arrest.
The Court rejected warrantless searches of phone data incident to arrest.
Police may never seize a phone from someone under arrest.
Police may seize the phone; they generally need a warrant to search its data.
Police need the phone company's permission to search it.
The requirement is a judicial warrant, not the phone company's permission.

alt.q: On what constitutional grounds could the driver challenge this search?
alt.a: Fourth Amendment
alt.ex: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. In Riley v. California (2014), the Court held that police generally need a warrant to search a phone seized during an arrest.
w: Fifth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment protects against self-incrimination and guarantees due process; the issue here is a search.
Sixth Amendment
The Sixth Amendment concerns trial rights such as counsel and a jury.
Eighth Amendment
The Eighth Amendment concerns bail, fines, and punishment.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Police arrest a driver after a traffic stop and take his smartphone. Without a warrant, an officer scrolls through his photos and text messages looking for evidence.

alt.q: Riley v. California (2014) best shows that the Bill of Rights
alt.a: is applied by courts to new technologies over time
alt.ex: Riley applied the Fourth Amendment, written in 1791, to smartphones, showing how courts interpret long-standing protections in contemporary settings.
w: no longer applies to searches by state or local police
The Fourth Amendment applies to state and local police through the Fourteenth Amendment.
protects only the rights listed in 1791 exactly
Riley applied old principles to new technology.
can be changed by the Supreme Court without limit
Courts interpret the Bill of Rights; changing its text requires an amendment.

items.q: Which statement best distinguishes civil liberties from civil rights?
items.a: Liberties limit what government may do; rights guarantee equal treatment
items.ex: Civil liberties (speech, religion, fair trial) are freedoms protected from government interference; civil rights are guarantees of equal treatment and freedom from discrimination (equal protection, Civil Rights Act of 1964).
w: Liberties are granted by states; rights are granted by the national government
Both are protected at both levels; the difference is in what they protect.
Liberties apply only to citizens; rights apply to all persons in the country
Most liberties and rights protect 'persons,' not only citizens.
Liberties come from statutes; rights come only from court decisions
Liberties come mainly from the Bill of Rights; civil rights come from amendments, laws, and rulings.

alt.q: A restaurant refuses to serve customers because of their race, and the customers sue under federal law. This dispute is mainly about
alt.a: civil rights
alt.ex: Freedom from discrimination in public accommodations is a civil right, protected by Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
w: civil liberties
Civil liberties are protections against government interference, such as free speech.
natural law
Natural law is the philosophical basis of rights, not the legal category of this dispute.
reserved powers
Reserved powers (Tenth Amendment) belong to states, not individuals.

alt.q: A city arrests a person for criticizing the mayor in a letter to a newspaper. This dispute is mainly about
alt.a: a civil liberty protected by the First Amendment
alt.ex: Freedom of speech and press are civil liberties, limits on what government may do to individuals.
w: a civil right protected by the Civil Rights Act
The Civil Rights Act targets discrimination, not punishment for speech.
a reserved power protected by the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers belong to states; the issue is an individual freedom.
an equal protection claim under the Fourteenth
No unequal treatment of a group is described; the issue is punishment for speech.

items.q: Which statement best describes the original purpose of the Bill of Rights (1791)?
items.a: To limit the national government's power over individual freedoms
items.ex: Demanded by Anti-Federalists and drafted by Madison, the Bill of Rights originally bound only the federal government (Barron v. Baltimore, 1833); it was later applied to states through selective incorporation.
w: To limit state governments' power over individual freedoms
The amendments applied to states only later, through the Fourteenth Amendment.
To guarantee the right to vote regardless of race or sex
Those guarantees came in the Fifteenth (1870) and Nineteenth (1920) Amendments.
To divide powers between the national and the various state governments
That division is federalism, set up in the main body of the Constitution.

alt.q: In 1961, the Supreme Court ruled that evidence from an illegal police search could not be used in a state court. This case applied the Fourth Amendment to the states through
alt.a: the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause
alt.ex: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) incorporated the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule against the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause (selective incorporation).
w: the Fourth Amendment's own text, which names the states
The Bill of Rights originally limited only the federal government.
the Full Faith and Credit Clause of Article IV
That clause requires states to honor each other's records and judgments.
the Privileges and Immunities Clause of Article IV
That clause bars discrimination against citizens of other states.

alt.q: Why did Anti-Federalists insist on adding a Bill of Rights to the Constitution?
alt.a: They feared a strong national government would threaten liberties
alt.ex: Anti-Federalists such as George Mason argued the new, stronger central government needed written limits to protect individual freedoms.
w: They wanted the states to give up their reserved powers
Anti-Federalists wanted to protect state power, not reduce it.
They wanted to guarantee voting rights to all of the adult citizens
Universal suffrage was not part of the 1791 Bill of Rights.
They feared the Constitution gave Congress too little power
That was the Federalists' complaint about the Articles of Confederation.

items.q: Which law is an example of government protecting a civil right?
items.a: A 1964 law banning racial discrimination in public places
items.ex: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public accommodations and employment: a civil rights guarantee.
w: The First Amendment, barring laws that abridge the freedom of speech
Free speech is a civil liberty, a limit on government.
The Fourth Amendment, requiring warrants for most searches and seizures
Protection from unreasonable searches is a civil liberty.
The Tenth Amendment, reserving undelegated powers to the states
The Tenth Amendment concerns federalism, not individual rights.

alt.q: A worker is fired by a private employer because of their religion. Which federal law most directly protects them?
alt.a: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
alt.ex: Title VII bans employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, including by private employers.
w: The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment
The First Amendment limits government, not private employers.
The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
Equal protection limits state action, not private businesses.
The Voting Rights Act of 1965
The Voting Rights Act protects voting, not employment.

alt.q: Which pair correctly classifies the two protections: (1) freedom from unreasonable searches; (2) freedom from racial discrimination in hiring?
alt.a: (1) civil liberty; (2) civil right
alt.ex: Freedom from unreasonable searches limits government (Fourth Amendment), a civil liberty; freedom from job discrimination is equal treatment (Title VII), a civil right.
w: (1) civil right; (2) civil liberty
This reverses the categories.
(1) civil liberty; (2) civil liberty
Hiring discrimination involves equal treatment, a civil right.
(1) civil right; (2) civil right
Search protection limits government power, a civil liberty.

items.q: Florida holds closed primary elections. Which statement best describes a closed primary?
items.a: Only voters registered with a party may vote in its primary.
items.ex: In Florida's closed primaries, only voters registered with a political party may vote in that party's primary. All registered voters may vote in nonpartisan races and in a universal primary contest, when all candidates for an office share a party and the winner will face no opposition in the general election.
w: Any registered voter may vote in whichever party's primary they choose.
This describes an open primary, which Florida does not use.
The top two finishers advance regardless of their party.
This describes a top-two primary, used in some other states.
Party leaders, not voters, choose the party's nominees.
In a primary, voters choose nominees; this describes selection by party leaders or caucuses.

alt.q: In which contest may this voter cast a ballot?
alt.a: the nonpartisan school board race
alt.ex: Florida's partisan primaries are closed, so a voter with no party affiliation cannot vote in the Republican or Democratic primary. All registered voters may vote in nonpartisan races such as school board.
w: the Republican primary for governor
Only registered Republicans may vote in Florida's Republican primary.
the Democratic primary for governor
Only registered Democrats may vote in Florida's Democratic primary.
both parties' primaries for governor
A voter with no party affiliation may vote in neither partisan primary.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A Florida voter is registered with no party affiliation. In August, the state holds a primary election that includes the Republican and Democratic primaries for governor and a nonpartisan school board race.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of a party primary election, compared with the general election?
alt.a: to choose each party's nominee for the general election
alt.ex: In a primary, a party's voters select the candidate who will represent the party. In the general election, held for federal offices on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November, voters choose among the nominees to fill the office.
w: to choose the officeholder who will take office
The general election decides who takes office.
to remove an official from office before the term ends
This describes a recall election.
to approve proposed amendments to the state constitution
Amendments are approved by voters on a ballot measure; that is not the purpose of a party primary.

items.q: Which process are the citizens using?
items.a: initiative
items.ex: An initiative lets citizens propose a law or constitutional amendment by petition and put it to a public vote. In Florida, a citizen initiative may propose amendments to the state constitution.
w: referendum
A referendum is a vote on a measure placed on the ballot, often by the legislature; here citizens started the proposal by petition.
recall
A recall is a vote to remove an official before the term ends.
impeachment
Impeachment is a legislature's process for charging an official.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Citizens in Florida collect enough voter signatures to place a proposed amendment to the state constitution directly on the statewide ballot.

alt.q: Voters in a Florida city sign petitions and then vote to remove a city commissioner from office before the end of the term. This process is called a
alt.a: recall
alt.ex: A recall lets voters remove an elected official before the term ends. Florida law allows recall of members of the governing body of a municipality or charter county.
w: referendum
A referendum is a vote on a measure, not on removing an official.
initiative
An initiative proposes a law or amendment, not the removal of an official.
primary
A primary selects party nominees for an upcoming election.

alt.q: Which statement best describes a referendum?
alt.a: Voters approve or reject a measure placed on the ballot.
alt.ex: In a referendum, voters directly decide whether to approve a measure, often one referred to them by the legislature, such as a legislatively proposed constitutional amendment.
w: Voters remove an elected official from office before the term ends.
This describes a recall.
Voters gather signatures to propose a new law.
This describes the petition stage of an initiative.
Voters choose their party's nominee for an office.
This describes a primary election.

items.q: For most proposed amendments to the Florida Constitution, what share of the votes cast on the amendment must be “yes” votes for it to pass?
items.a: at least 60 percent
items.ex: Under the Florida Constitution, most proposed amendments, whether from the legislature, a citizen initiative, or a commission, must be approved by at least 60 percent of the voters voting on the measure. This supermajority makes the state's fundamental law harder to change than ordinary statutes.
w: a simple majority
Florida raised the threshold above a simple majority in 2006.
at least two-thirds
Two-thirds applies only to amendments that impose a new state tax or fee; most amendments need 60 percent.
at least 75 percent
Seventy-five percent is not the requirement; it echoes the three-fourths of states needed for U.S. constitutional amendments.

alt.q: What is the result?
alt.a: It fails, because it needed at least 60 percent approval.
alt.ex: A proposed amendment to the Florida Constitution must receive at least 60 percent of the votes cast on it to pass. A 57 percent “yes” vote falls short.
w: It passes, because it won a majority of the votes cast.
A simple majority is not enough for a Florida constitutional amendment.
It passes, but only after the governor signs it into law.
Constitutional amendments go to the voters; the governor does not sign them.
It fails, because state amendments need approval by Congress.
Congress plays no role in amending a state constitution.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A proposed amendment to the Florida Constitution appears on the November ballot. It receives 57 percent “yes” votes and 43 percent “no” votes.

alt.q: To place a citizen initiative amendment on Florida's ballot, sponsors must collect valid voter signatures equal to what share of the votes cast in the last presidential election, both statewide and in at least half of the congressional districts?
alt.a: 8 percent
alt.ex: Florida requires initiative petitions signed by voters equal to 8 percent of the votes cast in the last presidential election, statewide and in at least half of the state's congressional districts. Approved amendments then need 60 percent of the vote.
w: 2 percent
Two percent is far below Florida's requirement.
25 percent
Twenty-five percent is far above Florida's requirement.
50 percent
Fifty percent would be nearly impossible to gather and is not the requirement.

items.q: Which requirement must a person meet to register to vote in Florida?
items.a: be a U.S. citizen and a Florida resident
items.ex: To register in Florida, a person must be a U.S. citizen and a Florida resident, be at least 18 (16- and 17-year-olds may preregister), not be adjudicated mentally incapacitated with respect to voting, and not have a felony conviction without restored voting rights.
w: own property in the county where they live
Property ownership is not a requirement to vote.
pass a test on the Florida Constitution
Literacy and knowledge tests for voting are prohibited.
have lived in Florida for at least five years
Florida requires residency, not a five-year waiting period.

alt.q: What does Florida law allow her to do now?
alt.a: preregister, then vote once she turns 18
alt.ex: Florida lets citizens preregister at 16 or 17. They are automatically eligible to vote once they turn 18.
w: vote in local elections only, starting now
No one under 18 may vote in Florida elections.
vote in state elections with a parent's consent
Parental consent does not allow anyone under 18 to vote.
register only after she turns 21
The voting age is 18, and preregistration begins at 16.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A 16-year-old Florida high school student who is a U.S. citizen wants to get ready to vote. She contacts her county's Supervisor of Elections office.

alt.q: A Florida resident wants to vote in an upcoming general election but has not registered. By when must the registration generally be submitted?
alt.a: 29 days before the election
alt.ex: Florida's registration books close 29 days before an election, so a new registration must be submitted by that deadline to vote in that election.
w: on Election Day at the polls
Florida does not offer Election Day registration.
7 days before the election
Seven days is too late; the deadline is 29 days before.
90 days before the election
Ninety days is not the deadline; registrations are accepted until 29 days before.

items.q: After each election, Florida counties must audit the results by checking randomly selected precincts. How does this practice support secure elections?
items.a: It confirms that voting machines counted ballots correctly.
items.ex: Florida law requires every county to conduct a post-election audit, either a public hand count of one race in randomly selected precincts or an automated independent audit of at least 20 percent of precincts. Comparing ballots with machine tallies confirms accuracy and builds public trust.
w: It allows officials to change any votes they believe are wrong.
Audits check counts against ballots; officials cannot change voters' choices.
It lets candidates choose which ballots get counted.
Candidates do not choose which ballots count; precincts are selected randomly.
It replaces the need to count votes on Election Day.
Audits happen after the official count to verify it, not to replace it.

alt.q: Which Florida election safeguard helps ensure that machine vote counts can be checked against a physical record?
alt.a: voters mark paper ballots that are kept after the election
alt.ex: Florida voters mark paper ballots that are scanned and preserved, so results can be audited and recounted. Florida's voting machines are never connected to the internet during voting.
w: voting machines send results to the state over the internet
Florida's voting machines are never connected to the internet during voting.
voters may cast their ballots by text message or email
Florida does not allow voting by text message or email.
poll workers record each vote from memory after polls close
Votes are recorded on ballots, not from poll workers' memory.

alt.q: Which statement best explains why secure elections are essential in a democracy?
alt.a: Citizens must trust that results reflect the votes cast.
alt.ex: Free, fair, and secure elections give government legitimacy because they reflect the consent of the governed. Safeguards such as paper ballots, audits, and accurate voter rolls build public trust.
w: Officials must be able to choose winners when races are close.
Close races are settled by counts and recounts under law, not by officials' choice.
Secure elections let the winners serve without term limits.
Election security has nothing to do with removing term limits.
Security lets the government keep results secret from voters.
Election results are public; transparency is part of secure elections.

items.q: Which statement best describes how the Electoral College selects the President?
items.a: Each state gets electors equal to its House and Senate seats; 270 votes wins
items.ex: Under Article II, each state's electors equal its senators plus representatives; with D.C.'s 3 (Twenty-third Amendment, 1961) there are 538, and a majority of 270 is needed.
w: Each state gets electors equal to its House seats only, and a plurality wins
Electors also include each state's two Senate seats, and a majority, not a plurality, is required.
The candidate with the most popular votes nationwide automatically wins
The national popular vote does not decide the election; electoral votes do.
State legislatures choose the President directly by a majority vote
State legislatures decide how electors are chosen (today by popular vote), but they do not elect the President.

alt.q: Article II states: "Each State shall appoint, in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct, a Number of Electors, equal to the whole Number of Senators and Representatives to which the State may be entitled in the Congress." A state with 2 senators and 8 representatives has how many electors?
alt.ex: Electors equal senators plus representatives: 2 + 8 = 10.
w: That counts only House seats and leaves out the two senators.
That counts only Senate seats.
Electors are not double the House delegation; they equal the total congressional delegation.

alt.q: No presidential candidate wins a majority of electoral votes. Under the Twelfth Amendment, who chooses the President?
alt.a: The House, with one vote per state delegation
alt.ex: If no one has a majority of electoral votes, the House chooses among the top three, each state delegation casting one vote (as in 1824); the Senate chooses the Vice President.
w: The Senate, with one vote per senator
The Senate chooses the Vice President in this situation, not the President.
The Supreme Court, by majority vote
The Court has no constitutional role in choosing the President.
The House, with one vote per individual member
The House votes by state delegation, one vote per state, not one per member.

items.q: In 2016, one candidate won the most popular votes nationwide, but the other won the presidency. How is this possible?
items.a: The winner earned a majority of electoral votes by carrying key states
items.ex: The President is chosen by electoral votes, mostly awarded winner-take-all by state; popular-vote losers also won in 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016.
w: The House overturned the popular vote by a majority decision
The House chooses the President only if no candidate wins an electoral majority.
The Supreme Court awarded the victory after ordering a recount
In Bush v. Gore (2000) the Court halted a recount; it played no such role in 2016.
The Senate rejected the electors sent from several of the largest states
The Senate did not reject electors; the electoral count followed state results.
