alt.q: Most states award all of their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state's popular vote. Which two states use a district-based method instead?
alt.a: Maine and Nebraska
alt.ex: Maine and Nebraska give two electors to the statewide winner and one to the winner of each congressional district.
w: Florida and Texas
Both use winner-take-all.
Iowa and New Hampshire
These states are known for early caucuses and primaries; both use winner-take-all.
California and New York
Both use winner-take-all.

alt.q: Which outcome is possible because most states award electoral votes on a winner-take-all basis?
alt.a: A candidate can lose the national popular vote and still win
alt.ex: Narrow wins in states with many electors can produce an electoral majority without a popular-vote plurality, as in 2000 and 2016.
w: A candidate can win without receiving any of the electoral votes
A candidate must win a majority of electoral votes (270).
A state can split its votes evenly among all candidates
Winner-take-all gives all of a state's votes to one candidate.
A candidate needs only a plurality of electoral votes
A majority of electoral votes is required; otherwise the House decides.

items.q: "The right of citizens of the United States, who are eighteen years of age or older, to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of age." Which amendment is this, and what did it do?
items.a: The 26th, lowering the voting age to 18 in 1971
items.ex: The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, driven by the argument that those drafted for Vietnam should be able to vote.
w: The 19th, giving women the vote in 1920
The Nineteenth bars denial of the vote 'on account of sex.'
The 24th, banning poll taxes in 1964
The Twenty-fourth bans poll taxes in federal elections.
The 15th, barring racial limits on voting in 1870
The Fifteenth bars denial 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.'

alt.q: In 1970, an 18-year-old who could be drafted to serve in Vietnam could not vote in most states. Which amendment changed this?
alt.a: The Twenty-sixth Amendment
alt.ex: Ratified in 1971, the Twenty-sixth Amendment set 18 as the minimum voting age in all elections.
w: The Nineteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth (1920) extended the vote to women.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The Twenty-fourth (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections.
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth (1870) barred racial discrimination in voting.

alt.q: Which statement best explains the main argument for the Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971)?
alt.a: People old enough to be drafted should be old enough to vote
alt.ex: During the Vietnam War, the slogan 'old enough to fight, old enough to vote' drove ratification of the amendment lowering the voting age to 18.
w: Women deserved the same voting rights that men already had
That was the argument for the Nineteenth Amendment (1920).
Poll taxes kept poor citizens from voting in federal elections
That was the argument for the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964).
Residents of the capital deserved electoral votes for President
That was the purpose of the Twenty-third Amendment (1961).

items.q: Which article of the U.S. Constitution grants the power to coin money, make treaties, and levy import duties?
items.a: Article I
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power to coin money and to lay duties (taxes on imports). Article I, Section 10 bars the states from coining money or entering treaties, and from laying import duties without Congress’s consent, leaving these powers to the national government. (The president’s role in making treaties with Senate consent is in Article II.)
w: Article II
Article II covers the executive branch; it does not give the power to coin money or lay import duties.
Article III
Article III establishes the federal courts and their jurisdiction.
Article IV
Article IV deals with relations among the states, such as full faith and credit and admitting new states.

alt.q: Which article of the U.S. Constitution grants the power to declare war, raise armies, and regulate commerce with foreign nations?
alt.a: Article I
alt.ex: All three are powers of Congress listed in Article I, Section 8.
w: Article II
Article II makes the president commander in chief, but declaring war and raising armies belong to Congress in Article I.
Article III
Article III deals with the judicial branch.
Article IV
Article IV deals with relations among the states.

alt.q: Which article of the U.S. Constitution grants the power to grant pardons, receive ambassadors, and command the armed forces?
alt.a: Article II
alt.ex: These are powers of the president, listed in Article II, Sections 2 and 3.
w: Article I
Article I lists the powers of Congress, such as taxing and declaring war.
Article III
Article III deals with the federal courts.
Article IV
Article IV deals with relations among the states.

items.q: Which of the following represents a suitable petition for the suspect in this situation, in regard to their constitutional rights?
items.a: petition for a writ of habeas corpus
items.ex: A writ of habeas corpus, protected by Article I, Section 9, lets a prisoner ask a court to examine whether he or she is being lawfully held. It is the tool for challenging an unreasonable, prolonged detention.
w: petition for a writ of extradition
Extradition (Article IV, Section 2) is the process by which the demanding state gets the fugitive back; it is not a right the prisoner petitions for.
petition for release into their custody
This is not a recognized constitutional remedy; habeas corpus is the way to challenge a detention.
petition for overturning of the charges
Charges are decided at trial; the immediate constitutional issue is the lawfulness of the detention.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A suspect is accused of a crime in one state and flees to another state where they are apprehended. The state is very slow in returning the suspect to the state of origin and keeps them imprisoned.

alt.q: Which constitutional protection allows the person to ask a court to decide whether the detention is lawful?
alt.a: writ of habeas corpus
alt.ex: Habeas corpus requires the government to bring a detained person before a court and justify the detention. Article I, Section 9 protects this privilege.
w: ex post facto ban
The ban on ex post facto laws prevents punishing acts that were legal when done; it does not address detention without charges.
bill of attainder ban
The ban on bills of attainder stops legislatures from punishing people without a trial; it does not let a prisoner challenge custody.
full faith and credit
Full faith and credit requires states to honor one another’s public acts and records.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A person is arrested and held in jail for weeks. The person is never charged with a crime or brought before a judge.

alt.q: Under Article I, Section 9 of the U.S. Constitution, when may the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus be suspended?
alt.a: during rebellion or invasion
alt.ex: Article I, Section 9 says the privilege of the writ may not be suspended unless public safety requires it in cases of rebellion or invasion.
w: whenever the president wishes
The Constitution allows suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion; it is not left to presidential choice.
when a governor requests it
State governors have no power to suspend the federal writ.
during any criminal trial
Trials are not a ground for suspension; habeas corpus protects people during criminal cases.

items.q: Which phrase best describes the power of impeachment?
items.a: the ability of the U.S. House to charge federal officers with a crime or violation
items.ex: Impeachment is the formal charge. Article I, Section 2 gives the House “the sole Power of Impeachment,” which it exercises by majority vote; removal happens only if the Senate convicts.
w: the ability of the U.S. Supreme Court to determine constitutionality of laws
This describes judicial review, not impeachment.
the power of the U.S. Senate to remove federal officers for a crime or violation
The Senate tries impeachments and may convict and remove, but the impeachment itself (the charge) is done by the House.
the power of the U.S. President to enforce decisions of federal courts
This describes executive enforcement, not impeachment.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the role of the U.S. Senate in the impeachment process?
alt.a: It holds the trial and may vote to remove.
alt.ex: Under Article I, Section 3, the Senate tries all impeachments, and a two-thirds vote of senators present is needed to convict and remove the official.
w: It brings the formal charges against the official.
Bringing the charges is impeachment, which is the House’s power.
It reviews the case after the Supreme Court rules.
The Supreme Court does not decide impeachments; the Chief Justice only presides over a president’s trial.
It must approve the House’s decision to investigate.
The House does not need Senate approval to investigate or to impeach.

alt.q: The House of Representatives votes to approve articles of impeachment against a federal judge. What has the House done?
alt.a: formally charged the judge
alt.ex: Approving articles of impeachment means the House has formally accused the official. The judge remains in office unless the Senate convicts by a two-thirds vote.
w: removed the judge from office
Removal requires conviction by the Senate, not just a House vote.
convicted the judge of a crime
The House does not convict; the Senate holds the trial.
declared the judge’s rulings void
Impeachment does not cancel a judge’s past rulings.

items.q: Which set of requirements does Article I set for members of the House of Representatives?
items.a: Age 25, a citizen for 7 years, an inhabitant of the state; 2-year term
items.ex: Article I, Section 2 requires Representatives to be at least 25, citizens for 7 years and inhabitants of their state, and sets two-year terms.
w: Age 30, a citizen for 9 years, an inhabitant of the state; 6-year term
These are the requirements and term for Senators (Article I, Section 3).
Age 35, natural-born citizen, 14 years a resident; 4-year term
These are the requirements and term for the President (Article II, Section 1).
Age 21, a citizen for 5 years, a resident of the district; 2-year term
Article I sets no age-21 rule and no district-residence requirement for the House.

alt.q: A 26-year-old who has been a U.S. citizen for 8 years and lives in Ohio wants to serve in Congress for Ohio. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: They may serve in the House but not yet in the Senate
alt.ex: They meet the House minimums (25 years old, 7 years a citizen) but not the Senate's (30 years old, 9 years a citizen).
w: They may serve in the Senate but not yet in the House
This reverses the rules; the Senate's requirements are stricter than the House's.
They may serve in neither chamber until they turn 30
Age 30 applies only to the Senate; the House minimum is 25.
They may serve in either chamber, since only citizenship matters
Both chambers have age and citizenship-length requirements.

alt.q: “No Person shall be a Representative who shall not have attained to the Age of twenty five Years, and been seven Years a Citizen of the United States…” A person who meets these requirements and wins a seat must face reelection…
alt.a: Every two years
alt.ex: Article I, Section 2 provides that House members are chosen “every second Year,” keeping the House closest to the people.
w: Every four years
Four-year terms belong to the President and Vice President.
Every six years
Six-year terms belong to Senators.
Every three years
No federal elected office has a three-year term.

items.q: Which feature did the framers give the Senate to make it more stable and less swayed by sudden shifts in public opinion than the House?
items.a: Six-year terms, with one-third of seats up every two years
items.ex: Article I, Section 3 sets staggered six-year terms; originally senators were also chosen by state legislatures, until the Seventeenth Amendment (1913).
w: Two-year terms, with every seat up for election at the same time
That describes the House of Representatives.
Seats divided among the states according to population
Population-based seats describe the House; each state has two senators.
Service for life during good behavior, like judges
Life tenure applies to federal judges under Article III, not to senators.

alt.q: Under the original Constitution of 1787, how were U.S. senators chosen?
alt.a: By the legislature of each state
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3 originally had senators “chosen by the Legislature thereof”; the Seventeenth Amendment (1913) switched to direct popular election.
w: By direct popular vote in each state
Direct election came only with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913.
By the Electoral College every 6 years
The Electoral College chooses the President and Vice President.
By the House of Representatives
The House plays no role in choosing senators.

alt.q: In any single federal election year, about how many Senate seats are on the ballot nationwide?
alt.a: About one-third of the seats
alt.ex: Senators are divided into three classes so roughly one-third of the Senate is elected every two years (Article I, Section 3).
w: All one hundred of the seats
Electing every seat at once describes the House, not the Senate.
About one-half of the seats
The Senate is divided into thirds, not halves.
About two-thirds of the seats
Only one class (one-third) is chosen in each two-year cycle.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Great (Connecticut) Compromise of 1787?
items.a: It based the House on population and gave states equal Senate votes
items.ex: Roger Sherman's compromise blended the Virginia Plan (population) and the New Jersey Plan (equality) into a bicameral Congress.
w: It counted three-fifths of enslaved people for House seats and taxes
That was the Three-Fifths Compromise.
It gave each state one vote in a single-chamber legislature
That describes the Articles of Confederation and the New Jersey Plan.
It based seats in both houses of Congress on state population
That was the Virginia Plan, which small states rejected.

alt.q: Small states feared being outvoted, while large states wanted power based on population. Which outcome settled this dispute at the Convention?
alt.a: A two-house Congress mixing population and equal votes
alt.ex: The Great Compromise created a House apportioned by population and a Senate with two members per state.
w: A one-house Congress with one vote for each state
That was the New Jersey Plan, favored by small states.
A two-house Congress with both houses based on population
That was the Virginia Plan, favored by large states.
A three-fifths ratio for counting the enslaved
The Three-Fifths Compromise settled a different, North–South dispute.

alt.q: Which delegate is most closely associated with proposing the Great Compromise?
alt.a: Roger Sherman of Connecticut
alt.ex: Roger Sherman (with Oliver Ellsworth) of Connecticut proposed the plan, which is why it is also called the Connecticut Compromise.
w: James Madison of Virginia
Madison drafted the Virginia Plan, which based both houses on population.
William Paterson of New Jersey
Paterson presented the New Jersey Plan of equal state votes.
Alexander Hamilton of New York
Hamilton proposed a plan with a lifetime executive and senate, which was not adopted.

items.q: “The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen by the Legislature thereof, for six Years…” This provision most directly reflects which demand at the Constitutional Convention?
items.a: Small states' demand for equal representation
items.ex: Equal Senate representation was the small states' half of the Great Compromise, carried over from the New Jersey Plan.
w: Large states' demand for seats based on population
Population-based seats were the large states' demand, met in the House.
Southern states' demand to count enslaved people
That demand was settled by the Three-Fifths Compromise in Article I, Section 2.
Anti-Federalists' demand for a written bill of rights
That demand was met by the Bill of Rights in 1791, not by Senate structure.

alt.q: The idea preserved in this provision, equal votes for every state, had been proposed at the Convention in which plan?
alt.a: The New Jersey Plan
alt.ex: William Paterson's New Jersey Plan kept one vote per state; the Great Compromise preserved that idea in the Senate.
w: The Virginia Plan
The Virginia Plan based representation in both houses on population.
The Hamilton Plan
Hamilton's plan proposed senators serving for life, not equal state votes as such.
The Albany Plan of Union
The Albany Plan of Union (1754) was Benjamin Franklin's colonial proposal, decades earlier.

alt.q: What special protection does Article V give the rule stated in this provision?
alt.a: No state can lose its equal Senate vote without its consent
alt.ex: Article V ends: “no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.”
w: It can be changed only through a national amendment convention
Article V names no such special route for this rule.
It can be changed by a simple majority of the states
Ordinary amendments need three-fourths of the states, and this rule needs the affected state's consent.
It can be changed by Congress through ordinary legislation
Constitutional text cannot be changed by statute.

items.q: “…which shall be determined by adding to the whole Number of free Persons… three fifths of all other Persons.” This clause of Article I most directly determined…
items.a: How many House seats each state would receive
items.ex: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three-fifths of enslaved people when apportioning House seats and direct taxes, boosting Southern power in the House and Electoral College.
w: How many Senate seats each state would receive
Every state receives two senators regardless of population.
Which people were allowed to vote in federal elections
The clause concerned counting population, not voting; states set voter qualifications.
Which states could keep importing enslaved people
The slave-trade clause (Article I, Section 9) barred Congress from ending imports before 1808.

alt.q: What did the Three-Fifths Compromise decide?
alt.a: How enslaved people were counted for seats and taxes
alt.ex: Article I, Section 2 counted “three fifths of all other Persons” for apportioning representatives and direct taxes.
w: How many senators each state would send to Congress
Senate seats were fixed at two per state by the Great Compromise.
Whether Congress could end the slave trade before 1808
That was a separate compromise in Article I, Section 9.
Whether new western states could allow slavery
That issue arose later, e.g., the Missouri Compromise (1820).

alt.q: Which amendment replaced the three-fifths formula by apportioning House seats “counting the whole number of persons in each State”?
alt.a: The Fourteenth Amendment
alt.ex: Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) changed apportionment to count the whole number of persons.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery but did not rewrite the apportionment formula.
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) barred denying the vote on account of race.
The Nineteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) barred denying the vote on account of sex.

items.q: A majority of the House votes to approve articles of impeachment against a federal judge. What happens next under the Constitution?
items.a: The Senate holds a trial; conviction requires a two-thirds vote
items.ex: The House has “the sole Power of Impeachment” (Art. I, §2); the Senate has “the sole Power to try all Impeachments” and conviction needs two-thirds of members present (§3).
w: The judge is removed from office at once by the House's vote
Impeachment is only a formal accusation; removal requires Senate conviction.
The Supreme Court holds a trial and decides by majority vote
The Supreme Court has no role in impeachment trials.
The Senate holds a trial; conviction requires only a simple majority
Conviction requires two-thirds of senators present, not a simple majority.

alt.q: Who presides over the Senate trial when a President has been impeached?
alt.a: The Chief Justice of the United States
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3: “When the President of the United States is tried, the Chief Justice shall preside.”
w: The Vice President of the United States
The Vice President normally presides over the Senate but would gain from a President's removal.
The Speaker of the House of Representatives
The Speaker leads the House, which only brings the charges.
The President pro tempore of the Senate
The President pro tempore presides in the Vice President's absence, not in presidential trials.

alt.q: Which statement best describes “impeachment” as the Constitution uses the term?
alt.a: A formal accusation voted by the House
alt.ex: Impeachment is the House's charge; removal follows only if two-thirds of the Senate votes to convict.
w: Removal from office after a Senate vote to convict
That is conviction and removal, the step after impeachment.
A criminal trial held in a federal district court
Impeachment is a political process in Congress, not a criminal trial.
A recall election held by a state's voters
Recall is a state-level procedure; federal officials cannot be recalled.

items.q: “The House of Representatives shall chuse their Speaker and other Officers; and shall have the sole Power of Impeachment.” Which statement best explains the power in the second half of this sentence?
items.a: Only the House may formally charge federal officials
items.ex: The House alone impeaches (accuses); the Senate alone tries the case and decides on removal.
w: Only the House may remove federal officials from office
Removal requires conviction by two-thirds of the Senate.
Only the House may try impeached officials and rule on them
The Senate has “the sole Power to try all Impeachments.”
Only the House may approve the President's appointments
Approving appointments is the Senate's “Advice and Consent” power.

alt.q: Article II, Section 4 lists which grounds for removing a President after impeachment and conviction?
alt.a: Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors
alt.ex: Article II, Section 4: officers “shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.”
w: Treason, incompetence, or a loss of the public's confidence
Incompetence and unpopularity are not listed grounds.
Any felony conviction in a state or federal court
The Constitution does not tie impeachment to criminal convictions.
Abuse of office as defined by the Supreme Court
The Court does not define impeachable offenses; Congress decides.

alt.q: Andrew Johnson (1868), Bill Clinton (1998) and Donald Trump (2019 and 2021) share which outcome?
alt.a: Impeached by the House but acquitted by the Senate
alt.ex: Each was impeached by a House majority, but the Senate never reached the two-thirds needed to convict; no President has been removed.
w: Removed from office after a Senate conviction
No President has ever been convicted and removed.
Resigned before the full House could vote
That describes Richard Nixon in 1974.
Impeached by the Senate but acquitted by the House
This reverses the roles; the House impeaches and the Senate tries.

items.q: “All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives…” Why did the framers give this power to the House?
items.a: Its members were directly elected by the people
items.ex: The House was the only chamber chosen directly by voters, so the power to start tax bills was placed closest to the people (“no taxation without representation”).
w: Its members served longer and more stable terms
Longer, more stable terms describe the Senate (six years).
It represented the states as equal partners
Equal state representation describes the Senate.
It was smaller and could act on bills more quickly
The House has always been the larger chamber.

alt.q: A senator introduces a bill to raise federal income tax rates. Under Article I, what is the constitutional problem?
alt.a: Revenue bills must begin in the House
alt.ex: Article I, Section 7 (the Origination Clause) requires revenue bills to originate in the House, though the Senate may amend them.
w: Tax bills need the President's approval in advance
The President signs or vetoes bills after passage; there is no prior approval.
Only state governments may levy income taxes
The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) lets Congress tax incomes.
Tax bills need a two-thirds vote in the Senate
Tax bills pass by majority vote; two-thirds is for overrides and treaties.

alt.q: Which power belongs to the House of Representatives alone?
alt.a: Starting bills that raise revenue
alt.ex: Under the Origination Clause, only the House may introduce revenue bills (the House also has the sole power of impeachment).
w: Approving treaties with foreign nations
Treaty approval belongs to the Senate (two-thirds of senators present).
Confirming judges and ambassadors
Confirmation is the Senate's “Advice and Consent” role.
Trying officials who are impeached
The Senate has the sole power to try impeachments.

items.q: Which of the following is an expressed (enumerated) power of Congress listed in Article I, Section 8?
items.a: Declaring war
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power “To declare War,” along with powers such as taxing, coining money and regulating commerce.
w: Chartering a national bank
A national bank is an implied power, upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Issuing drivers' licenses
Licensing drivers is a reserved power of the states.
Granting federal pardons
Pardons belong to the President under Article II, Section 2.

alt.q: Congress passes a law establishing post offices and post roads. This action is best classified as…
alt.a: An expressed power written in Article I
alt.ex: Article I, Section 8 expressly lists the power “To establish Post Offices and post Roads.”
w: An implied power from the Elastic Clause
Implied powers are not written; the postal power is listed word for word.
A reserved power under the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers belong to the states; postal service was delegated to Congress.
A concurrent power shared with the states
States may not run a competing postal system; it is a federal power.

alt.q: Which list contains only powers expressly given to Congress?
alt.a: Coin money, declare war, regulate interstate trade
alt.ex: All three are listed in Article I, Section 8.
w: Coin money, declare war, negotiate foreign treaties
Treaties are made by the President with two-thirds Senate consent (Article II).
Levy taxes, declare war, set up public schools
Public schools are a reserved power of the states.
Raise armies, borrow money, veto bills it dislikes
The veto belongs to the President (Article I, Section 7).

items.q: Congress passes a law declaring a specific, named person guilty of disloyalty and seizing their property without any trial. Which constitutional limit does this violate?
items.a: The ban on bills of attainder
items.ex: Article I, Section 9 says “No Bill of Attainder or ex post facto Law shall be passed”; a bill of attainder punishes a named person or group without a trial.
w: The ban on ex post facto laws
An ex post facto law punishes conduct that was legal when it was done.
The ban on titles of nobility
That clause bars granting titles such as duke or lord.
The limit on suspending habeas corpus
Habeas corpus protects against being held without being brought before a judge.

alt.q: “No Bill of Attainder or ex post facto Law shall be passed.” A bill of attainder is best described as…
alt.a: A law that punishes a named person without a trial
alt.ex: A bill of attainder lets the legislature act as judge and jury, which Article I, Section 9 forbids.
w: A law that punishes acts done before it was passed
That is an ex post facto law, the other item in this sentence.
A court order to bring a prisoner before a judge
That is a writ of habeas corpus.
A law that grants a citizen a title of nobility
Titles of nobility are banned by a separate clause of Section 9.

alt.q: “The Privilege of the Writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion the public Safety may require it.” This clause primarily protects people from…
alt.a: Being jailed without going before a judge
alt.ex: Habeas corpus lets a prisoner demand that a court review the legality of their detention; Lincoln controversially suspended it during the Civil War.
w: Being punished under a law passed after the act
That protection is the ban on ex post facto laws.
Being punished by a legislature without a trial
That protection is the ban on bills of attainder.
Being searched by police without any warrant
Protection from unreasonable searches is in the Fourth Amendment.

items.q: A state legislature votes to print its own paper currency and sign a trade treaty with Canada. Under Article I, Section 10, these actions are…
items.a: Forbidden, since states may not coin money or make treaties
items.ex: Article I, Section 10: “No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation; … coin Money; emit Bills of Credit…”
w: Allowed, since they are reserved powers of the states
Reserved powers cannot include powers the Constitution expressly denies to states.
Allowed, since they are concurrent powers shared with Congress
Concurrent powers include taxing and borrowing, not coining money or treaties.
Forbidden only because the Senate did not ratify the treaty
Even Senate approval could not let a state make a treaty; states also cannot coin money.

alt.q: Which problem from the Articles of Confederation era does Article I, Section 10 most directly address?
alt.a: States printing their own paper money
alt.ex: Under the Articles, states issued their own paper money, causing confusion and inflation; Section 10 bars states from coining money or emitting bills of credit.
w: Congress lacking any power to collect taxes
The taxing problem was fixed by Article I, Section 8, which limits Congress, not states.
No national court system to settle disputes
The lack of national courts was fixed by Article III.
Amendments needing approval of all 13 states
The unanimity problem was fixed by Article V.

alt.q: Which of the following is a power the Constitution denies to the states?
alt.a: Coining money
alt.ex: Article I, Section 10 bars states from coining money; it is an exclusive national power.
w: Collecting taxes
Taxing is a concurrent power held by both states and the national government.
Establishing courts
Both levels of government create courts, making this concurrent.
Conducting elections
Running elections is largely a state power (Article I, Section 4).

items.q: The President vetoes a bill. Which statement best describes how the bill can still become law?
items.a: Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to override
items.ex: Article I, Section 7 lets Congress override a veto by a two-thirds vote in each house.
w: A simple majority of both houses passes it a second time
A simple majority passes a bill originally, but an override needs two-thirds.
The Supreme Court reviews the bill and approves it
Courts review laws only in actual cases; they cannot enact a vetoed bill.
Three-fourths of the state legislatures approve it
Three-fourths of the states is the threshold for ratifying amendments.

alt.q: Congress passes a bill and then adjourns, and the President neither signs nor returns it within ten days (Sundays excepted). What is the result?
alt.a: The bill dies in what is called a pocket veto
alt.ex: Under Article I, Section 7, an unsigned bill becomes law after ten days unless Congress's adjournment prevents its return, in which case it does not become law.
w: The bill becomes law without the President's signature
That happens only if Congress is still in session after ten days.
The bill is sent to the Supreme Court for decision
The Supreme Court plays no role in the lawmaking process.
The bill passes to the next Congress automatically
Bills do not carry over; a new Congress must start again.

alt.q: The veto and the veto override are best described as examples of…
alt.a: Checks and balances between branches
alt.ex: The President checks Congress with the veto, and Congress checks the President with the override.
w: Federalism between nation and states
Federalism concerns national-state relations; the veto involves two federal branches.
Judicial review of acts of Congress
Judicial review is the courts' check, not the President's.
Popular sovereignty through elections
Popular sovereignty means power comes from the people.

items.q: In how a bill becomes a law, which step comes right after “A committee studies it and votes on it”?
items.a: The full chamber debates and votes on it
items.ex: That's step 3 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: The other chamber passes the same bill
That's step 4 of 5.
The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
That's step 1 of 5.
The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.q: Which step comes first in how a bill becomes a law?
alt.a: The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: A committee studies it and votes on it
That's step 2 of 5.
The full chamber debates and votes on it
That's step 3 of 5.
The other chamber passes the same bill
That's step 4 of 5.

alt.q: Which step comes last in how a bill becomes a law?
alt.a: The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
alt.ex: That's step 5 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: The other chamber passes the same bill
That's step 4 of 5.
The full chamber debates and votes on it
That's step 3 of 5.
A committee studies it and votes on it
That's step 2 of 5.

alt.q: In how a bill becomes a law, which step comes right after “The bill is introduced in the House or Senate”?
alt.a: A committee studies it and votes on it
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: The full chamber debates and votes on it
That's step 3 of 5.
The other chamber passes the same bill
That's step 4 of 5.
The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.a: The other chamber passes the same bill

w: The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
That's step 5 of 5.
A committee studies it and votes on it
That's step 2 of 5.
The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
That's step 1 of 5.

alt.q: In how a bill becomes a law, which step comes right after “The other chamber passes the same bill”?
alt.a: The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
alt.ex: That's step 5 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: The full chamber debates and votes on it
That's step 3 of 5.
A committee studies it and votes on it
That's step 2 of 5.
The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
That's step 1 of 5.

alt.a: The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: The full chamber debates and votes on it
That's step 3 of 5.
The other chamber passes the same bill
That's step 4 of 5.
The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.q: In how a bill becomes a law, which step comes right before “The full chamber debates and votes on it”?
alt.a: A committee studies it and votes on it
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
That's step 1 of 5.
The other chamber passes the same bill
That's step 4 of 5.
The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.a: The full chamber debates and votes on it
alt.ex: That's step 3 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: A committee studies it and votes on it
That's step 2 of 5.
The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
That's step 1 of 5.
The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.q: In how a bill becomes a law, which step comes right before “The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)”?
alt.a: The other chamber passes the same bill
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 5. A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
w: The full chamber debates and votes on it
That's step 3 of 5.
A committee studies it and votes on it
That's step 2 of 5.
The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
That's step 1 of 5.

ord.q: Put the steps of how a bill becomes a law in order.
items: The bill is introduced in the House or Senate
A committee studies it and votes on it
The full chamber debates and votes on it
The other chamber passes the same bill
The President signs it into law (or vetoes it)
ord.ex: A bill is introduced, studied by a committee, passed by the full chamber, passed in the same form by the other chamber (a conference committee settles any differences), then sent to the President. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.

items.q: Which limit does Article II place on the President's power to grant pardons?
items.a: It cannot be used in cases of impeachment
items.ex: Article II, Section 2 gives the President power to grant reprieves and pardons for federal offenses “except in Cases of Impeachment,” so a pardon cannot undo an impeachment or removal.
w: It requires approval by two-thirds of the Senate
Senate consent applies to treaties and appointments; the pardon power belongs to the President alone.
It applies only after a person has been convicted
A pardon may be granted before charges or conviction, as when President Ford pardoned Richard Nixon in 1974.
It cannot be used for any federal crime
The reverse is true: the power covers only “Offences against the United States,” meaning federal crimes.

alt.q: Why would the President's pardon in this scenario have no legal effect?
alt.a: The President can pardon only federal crimes
alt.ex: Article II limits the pardon power to “Offences against the United States.” A conviction under state law can be pardoned only through that state's own clemency process, such as by its governor or pardon board.
w: Pardons need the advice and consent of the Senate
The Senate has no role in pardons; Article II gives that power to the President alone.
Only the Supreme Court may pardon state crimes
Courts do not grant pardons; state crimes are pardoned under state law, by state officials.
Pardons may be given only to federal officials
Pardons can go to any person convicted of or charged with a federal offense, not just officials.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A man is convicted of robbery under state law in a state court. The President, a longtime friend of his family, announces a presidential pardon for him.

alt.q: Which action falls OUTSIDE the power described in this passage?
alt.a: Undoing the Senate's removal of an impeached judge
alt.ex: The pardon power excludes “Cases of Impeachment,” so the President cannot reverse an impeachment conviction or restore an officer the Senate has removed.
w: Shortening the prison sentence of a federal inmate
Reducing (commuting) a federal sentence is part of the pardon power and has been used by many Presidents.
Pardoning a person before federal charges are filed
A pardon may come before any charges, as with President Ford's 1974 pardon of Richard Nixon.
Delaying the scheduled execution of a federal inmate
A delay of punishment is a reprieve, which the passage expressly allows.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“he shall have Power to grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offences against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

items.q: According to this passage, what must happen before a President can be removed from office?
items.a: Impeachment and conviction for serious offenses
items.ex: Article II, Section 4 provides for removal “on Impeachment for, and Conviction of” treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors. The House impeaches and the Senate tries the case, with two-thirds needed to convict.
w: A vote of no confidence by a majority of Congress
No-confidence votes belong to parliamentary systems; the Constitution provides only impeachment and conviction.
A ruling against the President by the Supreme Court
The Court does not remove officials; the Chief Justice only presides at a President's Senate trial.
A recall election held by voters in every state
The Constitution contains no recall procedure for federal officials.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article II, Section 4 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The President, Vice President and all civil Officers of the United States, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which grounds for removing a President are listed in Article II?
alt.a: Treason, bribery, or high crimes and misdemeanors
alt.ex: Article II, Section 4 lists “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.” The framers rejected vaguer grounds such as “maladministration” so that removal would not depend on policy disputes.
w: Poor job performance or low public approval ratings
Unpopularity is not a ground for removal; voters judge performance at elections.
Policy disagreements with a majority of Congress
The framers deliberately avoided grounds that would let Congress remove a President over policy.
Loss of his party's support in midterm elections
Election results have no bearing on removal; the President serves a fixed four-year term.

alt.q: Under the Constitution, how can this judge be removed from office?
alt.a: Impeachment by the House, conviction by the Senate
alt.ex: Article II, Section 4 applies to “all civil Officers,” and federal judges serve during good behavior, so they can be removed only by impeachment and conviction. Judge Thomas Porteous, for example, was removed this way in 2010.
w: Dismissal by the President who appointed the judge
Presidents cannot fire federal judges; life tenure during good behavior protects judicial independence.
A majority vote of the Supreme Court's justices
The Supreme Court has no power to remove lower-court judges.
A recall election held by the state's voters
Federal judges are appointed, not elected, and no recall process exists for them.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A federal district judge is found to have accepted bribes and other payments from lawyers with cases pending before the judge's court. Members of the public demand that the judge be removed.

items.q: This clause from Article II assigns the President which main role?
items.a: Enforcing the laws Congress passes
items.ex: The Take Care Clause (Article II, Section 3) makes the President responsible for carrying out and enforcing federal law, the core job of the executive branch.
w: Writing the laws of the nation
Article I vests lawmaking power in Congress, not the President.
Deciding whether laws are constitutional
Interpreting laws and judging their constitutionality is the role of the courts.
Approving state laws before they take effect
The President has no power to approve or reject state laws.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article II, Section 3 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…he shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: The Attorney General directs federal prosecutors to enforce a newly passed federal law. This carries out which Article II duty of the President?
alt.a: Ensuring the laws are faithfully executed
alt.ex: Article II, Section 3 says the President “shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” Executive departments such as the Justice Department carry out that duty on the President's behalf.
w: Giving Congress information on the State of the Union
This Section 3 duty involves reporting to Congress, not enforcing laws.
Receiving ambassadors and other public ministers
This Section 3 duty concerns diplomacy, not law enforcement.
Recommending measures for Congress to consider
This Section 3 duty involves proposing legislation, not enforcing laws already passed.

alt.q: Which presidential duty is found in Article II, Section 3?
alt.a: Seeing that laws are faithfully executed
alt.ex: Article II, Section 3 lists the President's duties, including that he “shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” along with giving State of the Union information and receiving ambassadors.
w: Declaring war against foreign nations
Article I, Section 8 gives the power to declare war to Congress.
Setting uniform rules of naturalization
Article I, Section 8 gives the naturalization power to Congress.
Deciding cases that arise under federal law
Article III gives this judicial power to the federal courts.

items.q: Which person would be constitutionally eligible to serve as President?
items.a: A 36-year-old natural-born citizen who has lived in the U.S. 15 years
items.ex: Article II, Section 1 requires a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and 14 years a resident of the United States.
w: A 40-year-old naturalized citizen who has lived in the U.S. 30 years
Naturalized citizens are not eligible; the President must be natural-born.
A 33-year-old natural-born citizen who has lived in the U.S. 33 years
This person is younger than the minimum age of 35.
A 50-year-old natural-born citizen who has lived in the U.S. 10 years
This person falls short of the 14-year residency requirement.

alt.q: “…neither shall any Person be eligible to that Office who shall not have attained to the Age of thirty five Years, and been fourteen Years a Resident within the United States.” Which other requirement does Article II add for this office?
alt.a: Being a natural-born citizen
alt.ex: Article II, Section 1 also requires the President to be “a natural born Citizen” (or a citizen when the Constitution was adopted).
w: Owning property in one's home state
The Constitution sets no property requirement for any federal office.
Prior service in Congress or the military
No prior office or military service is required.
Being a citizen for at least nine years
Nine years of citizenship is the requirement for Senators.

alt.q: Which minimum ages, in order, does the Constitution set for Representative, Senator and President?
alt.ex: Article I sets 25 for the House and 30 for the Senate; Article II sets 35 for the President.
w: These numbers are each one step too low.
This reverses the House and Senate ages.
Eighteen is the voting age under the Twenty-sixth Amendment, not an office minimum.

items.q: How does Article II determine the number of presidential electors each state receives?
items.a: It equals the state's senators plus its representatives
items.ex: Each state gets electors “equal to the whole Number of Senators and Representatives” it has in Congress.
w: It equals only the state's number of House seats
This leaves out the two electors that match each state's senators.
It is two per state, regardless of population
Two per state matches Senate seats only, not the full elector count.
It is set by each state's share of the national popular vote
Elector numbers are fixed by congressional seats, not vote totals.

alt.q: “Each State shall appoint, in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct, a Number of Electors…” Under this clause, who decides how a state's electors are chosen?
alt.a: The state's legislature
alt.ex: Article II, Section 1 leaves the method of choosing electors to each state legislature; today every state uses a popular vote.
w: The United States Congress
Congress sets the day electors are chosen, not the method.
The U.S. Supreme Court
The Court resolves disputes but does not set each state's method.
The national party conventions
Parties nominate candidates; the Constitution gives the choice of method to legislatures.

alt.q: If no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, who chooses the President?
alt.a: The House, with one vote per state delegation
alt.ex: Under Article II and the Twelfth Amendment (1804), the House picks the President with each state delegation casting one vote (as in 1800 and 1824).
w: The Senate, with one vote cast by each senator
The Senate chooses the Vice President in that situation.
The House, with one vote for each member
Votes are cast by state delegations, one per state.
The Supreme Court, by a majority of justices
The Court has no constitutional role in choosing the President.

items.q: “He shall have Power, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties, provided two thirds of the Senators present concur…” This clause best illustrates…
items.a: Power shared between the President and the Senate
items.ex: The treaty power is split: the President negotiates, and two-thirds of senators present must consent, a check and balance.
w: Exclusive executive control over all foreign affairs
The clause requires Senate consent, so control is not exclusive.
Cooperation between federal and state governments
States have no role in treaties; Article I, Section 10 bars them from making treaties.
The House's role in approving foreign agreements
The House has no formal role in approving treaties.

alt.q: The President negotiates a treaty with another nation. What must happen before the treaty takes effect for the U.S.?
alt.a: Two-thirds of senators present must consent
alt.ex: Article II, Section 2 requires the consent of two-thirds of the senators present.
w: A majority of both houses must approve it
Treaties go to the Senate only, and need two-thirds, not a majority.
Three-fourths of the states must ratify it
State ratification applies to constitutional amendments.
The Supreme Court must review it in advance
The Court does not pre-approve treaties.

alt.q: The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles (1919–1920) is an example of which constitutional check?
alt.a: The Senate's treaty-consent power
alt.ex: President Wilson signed the treaty, but it never won two-thirds approval in the Senate, so the U.S. never ratified it.
w: Congress's power to declare war
Declaring war was not at issue; the treaty ended a war.
The House's power over revenue bills
The House has no formal role in treaties.
Judicial review of executive actions
No court was involved in the treaty's defeat.

items.q: A President nominates someone to fill a Supreme Court vacancy. What must happen for the nominee to take the seat?
items.a: A majority of the Senate must confirm the nominee
items.ex: Article II, Section 2 gives the President the power to appoint judges “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate”; confirmation is by majority vote.
w: Two-thirds of the Senate must confirm the nominee
Two-thirds is the threshold for treaties, not appointments.
Both the House and the Senate must confirm the nominee
The House has no role in confirming appointments.
The sitting justices must vote to accept the nominee
Justices have no constitutional role in choosing colleagues.

alt.q: Which officials does Article II say the President appoints with the Senate's “Advice and Consent”?
alt.a: Ambassadors and Supreme Court justices
alt.ex: Article II, Section 2 lists “Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court” and other officers.
w: Senators and members of the House
Members of Congress are elected, not appointed.
State governors and state judges
State officials are chosen under state law.
The presidential electors of each state
Electors are chosen as each state legislature directs.

alt.q: Senate confirmation hearings for a cabinet nominee are an example of…
alt.a: The legislative branch checking the executive
alt.ex: Requiring Senate consent for executive appointments lets Congress check the President.
w: The judicial branch checking the legislative branch
Courts are not involved in confirmations.
The executive branch checking the judiciary
A cabinet post is executive; the check here comes from the Senate.
The states checking the national government
Confirmation is a power of the U.S. Senate, not the states.

items.q: “The President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States…” Which war-related power did the framers give to Congress instead, dividing control over war?
items.a: The power to declare war
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power “To declare War” and to raise and fund armies, while the President commands them.
w: The power to direct military strategy
Directing the armed forces is part of the President's role as Commander in Chief.
The power to negotiate peace treaties
The President negotiates treaties, subject to Senate consent.
The power to pardon military deserters
Pardons belong to the President under Article II.

alt.q: The War Powers Resolution (1973) was Congress's attempt to address tension between which two constitutional provisions?
alt.a: The Commander in Chief power and Congress's war power
alt.ex: After the Vietnam War, Congress sought to limit how long a President could commit troops without a declaration of war or authorization.
w: The treaty power and the Supremacy Clause of Article VI
These concern treaties as law, not the commitment of troops.
Congress's war power and the Senate's treaty power
Treaties were not at issue; the Resolution targets presidential troop deployments without congressional approval.
The appointment power and Senate confirmation
These concern filling offices, not military action.

alt.q: Which statement best describes how the Constitution divides military power?
alt.a: Congress declares war and funds forces; the President commands them
alt.ex: Article I gives Congress the power to declare war and raise armies; Article II makes the President Commander in Chief.
w: The President declares war; Congress commands the military
This reverses the roles of the two branches.
Congress both declares war and directly commands the military forces
Command belongs to the President.
The states declare war; the President commands the military
Article I, Section 10 bars states from engaging in war unless invaded.

items.q: Which constitutional provision would the man most likely cite to keep his trial in Florida?
items.a: Article III's rule on where criminal trials are held
items.ex: Article III, Section 2 requires that criminal trials be by jury and “held in the State where the said Crimes shall have been committed.” Because the alleged crime took place in Florida, the trial belongs there.
w: Article I, which lets Congress punish counterfeiting
This clause allows Congress to make counterfeiting a crime but says nothing about where trials are held.
Article IV, which requires return of fugitives
The Extradition Clause concerns returning people who flee across state lines, not the place of a federal trial.
Article VI, which makes federal law supreme
The Supremacy Clause settles federal–state conflicts, not the location of a criminal trial.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A man is accused of counterfeiting U.S. currency in Miami, Florida. Federal prosecutors want to hold his trial in Boston, Massachusetts, where they believe a jury would be tougher on him.

alt.q: Which right does this passage from Article III protect?
alt.a: A jury trial in the state of the crime
alt.ex: This clause of Article III, Section 2 requires a jury for all federal criminal trials (except impeachments) and requires that the trial be held in the state where the crime was committed.
w: A speedy trial with the help of a lawyer
Speedy trial and counsel rights come from the Sixth Amendment, not this Article III clause.
Protection from being tried twice
Protection against double jeopardy comes from the Fifth Amendment.
A grand jury indictment for felonies
The grand jury requirement comes from the Fifth Amendment.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article III, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Trial of all Crimes, except in Cases of Impeachment, shall be by Jury; and such Trial shall be held in the State where the said Crimes shall have been committed;…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which kind of trial is NOT covered by Article III's requirement of trial by jury?
alt.a: Impeachment trials
alt.ex: Article III, Section 2 says “The Trial of all Crimes, except in Cases of Impeachment, shall be by Jury.” Impeachments are tried by the Senate under Article I, Section 3.
w: Treason trials
Treason is a crime, so it must be tried by a jury; Article III even sets special proof rules for it.
Counterfeiting trials
Counterfeiting is a federal crime, so the jury requirement applies.
Piracy trials
Piracy is a federal crime and falls under the jury requirement.

items.q: Why would this proposed law be unconstitutional?
items.a: Article III bars cutting sitting judges' pay
items.ex: Article III, Section 1 says federal judges receive a compensation “which shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office,” so Congress cannot punish judges by lowering their salaries.
w: Article III lets only the President set judges' pay
Congress, not the President, sets judicial salaries by law; it just may not lower them for sitting judges.
Judges' exact salaries are fixed in the Constitution
The Constitution sets no dollar amount; Congress decides pay, subject to the no-reduction rule.
Only the Supreme Court may change any judge's pay
The Supreme Court has no power over salaries; Congress controls them by statute.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Angry about a ruling, several members of Congress propose a law cutting the salaries of the federal judges who decided the case, so the judges will think twice before ruling against Congress again.

alt.q: Under Article III, which change to federal judges' pay is allowed?
alt.a: Raising the salaries of sitting judges
alt.ex: Article III, Section 1 forbids only diminishing a judge's compensation during the judge's time in office. Congress may raise judicial pay.
w: Lowering the salaries of sitting judges
This is exactly what Article III forbids for judges in office.
Halting pay for judges who rule against Congress
Stopping pay would diminish compensation and attack judicial independence.
Cutting pay for judges named by a rival party
Any reduction for sitting judges is barred, whatever the reason.

alt.q: Which officials are protected by this provision of Article III?
alt.a: Federal judges
alt.ex: The clause in Article III, Section 1 applies to “The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts,” so it protects federal judges, not legislators, the President, or state judges.
w: Members of Congress
Congressional pay is governed by Article I and the Twenty-seventh Amendment, not Article III.
The President
The President's pay is covered by a separate clause in Article II.
State court judges
Article III governs only the federal judiciary; state judges' pay is set by state law.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article III, Section 1 of the U.S. Constitution, describing federal judges, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…a Compensation, which shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

items.q: Based on the passage, which case could be heard in a federal court?
items.a: A claim that a city violated the First Amendment
items.ex: Article III, Section 2 extends federal judicial power to cases “arising under this Constitution, the Laws of the United States, and Treaties.” A First Amendment claim arises under the Constitution.
w: A contract dispute between two Florida businesses
This raises only state law between parties from the same state, so it belongs in state court.
A divorce between two residents of the same state
Divorce is a matter of state law and is handled by state courts.
A traffic ticket issued under a city ordinance
A local ordinance is not federal law, so the case does not arise under the Constitution or federal law.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article III, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The judicial Power shall extend to all Cases, in Law and Equity, arising under this Constitution, the Laws of the United States, and Treaties made, or which shall be made, under their Authority;…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which lawsuit falls under federal judicial power because of WHO the parties are, rather than which law is involved?
alt.a: A dispute between citizens of different states
alt.ex: Article III, Section 2 extends the judicial power to controversies “between Citizens of different States,” so federal courts can hear such cases even when only state law is at issue.
w: A dispute between a city and its own residents
Parties from the same state do not create federal jurisdiction based on who they are.
A divorce between two residents of Ohio
A divorce between residents of the same state is a state-court matter.
A dispute between two Florida businesses
Two businesses from the same state do not trigger Article III's party-based jurisdiction.

alt.q: Why may a federal court hear this case?
alt.a: Article III covers cases arising under treaties
alt.ex: Article III, Section 2 extends federal judicial power to cases arising under “Treaties made, or which shall be made, under their Authority,” so a treaty-based claim can be heard in federal court.
w: Article IV requires full faith and credit for treaties
Full Faith and Credit concerns states honoring each other's acts and rulings, not treaties or federal court power.
Article V gives courts the power to amend treaties
Article V concerns amending the Constitution; courts cannot amend treaties.
Article VII ties all treaties to ratification by states
Article VII concerns ratifying the Constitution; treaties need Senate consent, not state ratification.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A company claims that a state law conflicts with a treaty the United States has signed with another nation. The state argues that only its own courts may hear the dispute.

items.q: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” According to this excerpt, who creates the federal courts below the Supreme Court?
items.a: Congress
items.ex: Article III creates only the Supreme Court and leaves lower federal courts to Congress, which first set them up in the Judiciary Act of 1789.
w: The President
The President nominates judges but does not create courts.
The Supreme Court
The Supreme Court decides cases; it does not establish other courts.
The states
States create their own courts, not federal courts.

alt.q: Which statement about the federal court system is accurate under Article III?
alt.a: Only the Supreme Court is required; Congress sets up lower courts
alt.ex: Article III names one Supreme Court and lets Congress “ordain and establish” inferior courts.
w: The Constitution itself names every federal court that must exist
Only the Supreme Court is named; the rest are left to Congress.
States create the lower federal courts within their borders
Federal courts are created by Congress, not by states.
The President creates lower courts by executive order
Creating courts is a legislative power, not an executive one.

alt.q: Congress abolishes one federal appeals circuit and creates two new ones in its place. Under Article III, this action is…
alt.a: Permitted, since Congress establishes the lower courts
alt.ex: Congress may reorganize lower courts; for example, it split the Fifth Circuit in 1980, creating the Eleventh Circuit.
w: Forbidden, since only the Supreme Court can organize courts
The Supreme Court has no constitutional power to create or abolish courts.
Permitted only after the President issues an executive order
No executive order is needed; Congress acts by statute.
Forbidden, since Article III fixes the number of courts
Article III sets no number of lower courts.

items.q: “The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts, shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour…” The main purpose of this provision, along with protected salaries, is to…
items.a: Protect judges' independence from political pressure
items.ex: Tenure “during good Behaviour” (effectively life) and salaries that cannot be cut free judges from fear of the other branches and of voters.
w: Keep judges accountable to the voters who elect them
Federal judges are appointed, not elected, and life tenure reduces accountability to voters.
Let Congress remove judges who rule against it
Judges can be removed only by impeachment and conviction.
Give the President control over the courts' decisions
Life tenure means the President cannot fire judges after appointment.

alt.q: In practice, the “good Behaviour” clause of Article III means federal judges…
alt.a: Serve until death, resignation or removal
alt.ex: Federal judges have no fixed term; they leave office only by death, resignation, retirement, or impeachment and conviction.
w: Serve fixed terms of ten years each
Article III sets no fixed terms.
Must retire when they reach age 70
The Constitution sets no retirement age.
Face reconfirmation by the Senate periodically
Once confirmed, judges never face the Senate again.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 78, Alexander Hamilton defended life tenure for judges by arguing that the judiciary…
alt.a: Is “the least dangerous” branch and needs independence
alt.ex: Hamilton wrote that the judiciary “will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution,” having neither sword nor purse.
w: Commands the military and must be kept stable
The military belongs to the executive.
Holds the power of the purse and must be watched
The power of the purse belongs to the legislature.
Is elected by the people and must stay answerable to them
Federal judges are appointed, not elected.

items.q: Where does the federal courts' power of judicial review come from?
items.a: The ruling in Marbury v. Madison (1803)
items.ex: Judicial review is not stated in the Constitution; Chief Justice John Marshall established it in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: An explicit grant of power in Article III, Section 2
Article III defines jurisdiction but never mentions judicial review.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), on implied powers
McCulloch upheld the national bank and federal supremacy, not judicial review.
Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789
Marbury actually struck down part of Section 13 as unconstitutional.

alt.q: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” This sentence was written by which Chief Justice, in which case?
alt.a: John Marshall, in Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: Marshall wrote these words in Marbury v. Madison (1803), establishing judicial review.
w: John Marshall, in McCulloch v. Maryland
Right Chief Justice, wrong case; McCulloch (1819) concerned the national bank.
Roger Taney, in Dred Scott v. Sandford
Taney's Dred Scott opinion (1857) concerned slavery and citizenship.
John Jay, in Chisholm v. Georgia
Jay's era case (1793) concerned suits against states, leading to the Eleventh Amendment.

alt.q: A federal court rules that a law passed by Congress violates the First Amendment and cannot be enforced. The court is exercising…
alt.a: Judicial review
alt.ex: Judicial review is the power to declare laws or government acts unconstitutional, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: Original jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction is the power to hear a case first, not to void laws.
Executive privilege
Executive privilege is a President's claim to withhold information (U.S. v. Nixon, 1974).
Selective incorporation
Incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to the states; this was a federal law.

items.q: Texas sues New Mexico in a dispute over water from a river the two states share. Where does this case begin?
items.a: In the Supreme Court, under its original jurisdiction
items.ex: Article III, Section 2 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases “in which a State shall be Party,” so state-versus-state suits start there.
w: In a federal district court, followed by appeals
Most federal cases start there, but state-versus-state suits go straight to the Supreme Court.
In the Supreme Court, under its appellate jurisdiction
Appellate jurisdiction means reviewing a lower court; here no lower court is involved.
In the state courts of the defending state
A state court could not neutrally decide a dispute against another state.

alt.q: “In all Cases affecting Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, and those in which a State shall be Party, the supreme Court shall have original Jurisdiction.” Original jurisdiction means the Supreme Court…
alt.a: Hears the case first, acting as a trial court
alt.ex: In original jurisdiction cases, the Supreme Court is the first and only court to hear the dispute.
w: Reviews decisions already made by lower courts
That is appellate jurisdiction, which covers most of the Court's cases.
Chooses which appeals it will agree to hear
That is the certiorari process, a part of appellate review.
Gives advisory opinions when Congress asks
The Supreme Court does not issue advisory opinions.

alt.q: Most cases reach the U.S. Supreme Court under which type of jurisdiction?
alt.a: Appellate jurisdiction
alt.ex: Article III, Section 2 gives the Court appellate jurisdiction in “all the other Cases,” and nearly all of its cases arrive on appeal.
w: Original jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction covers only a few cases, such as those involving states or ambassadors.
Concurrent jurisdiction
Concurrent jurisdiction means two court systems may hear the same type of case.
Exclusive state jurisdiction
Cases solely under state law end in state courts.

items.q: “Treason against the United States, shall consist only in levying War against them, or in adhering to their Enemies, giving them Aid and Comfort.” Why did the framers define treason this narrowly?
items.a: To keep it from being used against political critics
items.ex: English rulers had used broad treason laws against opponents; Article III limits treason to two acts and requires two witnesses or a confession in open court.
w: To make treason easier to prosecute during times of war
A narrow definition and strict proof make treason harder, not easier, to prove.
To let Congress redefine treason as it chooses
The definition is fixed in the Constitution; Congress sets only the punishment.
To let each state try treason on its own terms
This clause defines treason against the United States.

alt.q: Which conduct would fit the Constitution's definition of treason?
alt.a: Secretly arming a country at war with the U.S.
alt.ex: Giving “Aid and Comfort” to enemies during war is one of the two forms of treason in Article III, Section 3.
w: Publicly criticizing the President's foreign policy
Criticism is protected speech, not treason.
Refusing to pay federal income taxes owed
Tax evasion is a crime but not treason.
Organizing a peaceful march against a war
Peaceful protest is protected by the First Amendment.

alt.q: A person is charged with treason. Under Article III, which evidence would be enough to convict?
alt.a: Two witnesses to the same overt act
alt.ex: Article III, Section 3 requires “the Testimony of two Witnesses to the same overt Act, or … Confession in open Court.”
w: One witness plus strong circumstantial evidence
The Constitution specifically requires two witnesses to the same act.
A confession made privately to police officers
A confession must be made in open court.
A grand jury indictment by itself alone
An indictment is only a formal charge, not proof for conviction.

sections.name: Article IV: Full Faith and Credit & New States

items.q: Which constitutional provision gives Congress authority to govern U.S. territories such as Guam and Puerto Rico?
items.a: The Territory Clause of Article IV
items.ex: Article IV, Section 3 gives Congress power to “make all needful Rules and Regulations respecting the Territory or other Property belonging to the United States.”
w: The Commerce Clause of Article I
The Commerce Clause covers trade with foreign nations, among states, and with tribes, not governing territories.
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
The Supremacy Clause ranks federal law over state law; it grants no power over territories.
The Guarantee Clause of Article IV
The Guarantee Clause promises a republican government to the states, not to territories.

alt.q: Which action is most directly supported by this passage?
alt.a: Congress making rules for national parks
alt.ex: This Territory (or Property) Clause of Article IV, Section 3 lets Congress make rules for territories and other federal property, such as national parks and federal lands.
w: A state taxing goods brought in from other states
This clause concerns federal territory and property; it sets no rule about state taxes on goods from other states.
The President making treaties with other nations
Treaty-making is an Article II power of the President with Senate consent.
A state admitting a territory as a new state
Only Congress may admit new states, under a different clause of Article IV, Section 3.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article IV, Section 3 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Congress shall have Power to dispose of and make all needful Rules and Regulations respecting the Territory or other Property belonging to the United States;…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Before becoming a state in 1845, Florida was governed as a U.S. territory. Which body had authority under Article IV to make rules for it?
alt.a: Congress
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 3 gives Congress power to make all needful rules for U.S. territories. Congress organized the Territory of Florida in 1822 and admitted Florida as a state in 1845.
w: The President alone
The President carries out territorial laws, but Article IV gives the rule-making power to Congress.
The Supreme Court
Courts decide cases; they do not make rules to govern territories.
The neighboring states
No state has power over a federal territory; that authority belongs to Congress.

items.q: Based on this passage, when may the national government step in to stop domestic violence, such as a riot, within a state?
items.a: When the state legislature or governor requests it
items.ex: Article IV, Section 4 promises protection against domestic violence “on Application of the Legislature, or of the Executive (when the Legislature cannot be convened).”
w: Only after the state's voters approve a referendum
The passage requires a request from state officials, not a public vote.
Only if the Supreme Court first approves the action
The passage gives the courts no role in such requests.
Only when the violence spreads into another state
The passage applies to violence within a single state when that state asks for help.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article IV, Section 4 of the U.S. Constitution, describing the duties of the United States toward the states, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…and shall protect each of them against Invasion; and on Application of the Legislature, or of the Executive (when the Legislature cannot be convened) against domestic Violence.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which promise does Article IV, Section 4 make to every state?
alt.a: Protection against invasion
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 4 says the United States shall guarantee each state a republican form of government “and shall protect each of them against Invasion.”
w: A share of federal tax revenue
The Constitution does not promise states any share of federal revenue.
Equal funding for public schools
Public education is a reserved state power and is not guaranteed in Article IV.
Equal seats in the House
House seats are divided by population under Article I; equal representation is in the Senate.

alt.q: Which constitutional provision most directly supports the governor's request?
alt.a: Article IV's domestic violence clause
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 4 commits the United States to protect each state against domestic violence on request of its legislature, or of its executive when the legislature cannot be convened.
w: Article III's guarantee of trial by jury
Jury trials concern prosecuting crimes, not sending help to restore order.
Article IV's Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause makes states honor each other's acts and rulings; it says nothing about federal aid.
Article VI's oath requirement for officials
The oath clause binds officials to support the Constitution but does not provide federal protection.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: During widespread rioting, a state's governor, whose legislature is out of session and cannot be convened in time, formally asks the federal government to send help to restore order.

items.q: Which Article IV provision was made obsolete by the Thirteenth Amendment (1865)?
items.a: The Fugitive Slave Clause
