items.ex: Article IV, Section 2 required that people escaping slavery be returned on claim of their enslavers. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, ending any effect of that clause.
w: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause, requiring states to honor each other's acts and rulings, remains in force today.
The Extradition Clause
States still must return people charged with crimes who flee to another state.
The Privileges and Immunities Clause
This clause still protects citizens' basic rights when they are in other states.

alt.q: This clause of Article IV required states to…
alt.a: Return enslaved people who escaped
alt.ex: The Fugitive Slave Clause of Article IV, Section 2 required that a person “held to Service or Labour” who escaped to another state be delivered up to the person claiming that service. The Thirteenth Amendment ended it.
w: Grant citizenship to people escaping slavery
The clause did the opposite; it denied freedom to people who escaped.
Pay enslavers for people who escaped
The clause required returning people, not paying compensation.
Let new states decide on slavery by popular vote
Popular sovereignty over slavery came from laws like the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), not Article IV.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article IV, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“No Person held to Service or Labour in one State, under the Laws thereof, escaping into another,…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 was passed to enforce which constitutional provision?
alt.a: Article IV's Fugitive Slave Clause
alt.ex: The Fugitive Slave Acts of 1793 and 1850 put into effect Article IV's requirement that escaped enslaved people be returned. The clause was ended by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865.
w: Article I's Commerce Clause
The act relied on Article IV's fugitive clause, not Congress's power to regulate trade.
Article IV's Extradition Clause
The Extradition Clause concerns people charged with crimes, not people escaping slavery.
The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause
The 1850 act was criticized for denying due process, such as jury trials, to accused people.

items.q: Which state practice is generally permitted despite this clause?
items.a: Limiting voting in state elections to residents
items.ex: The Privileges and Immunities Clause protects fundamental rights of out-of-state citizens, but voting in a state's elections is a right of that state's own residents, so states may limit it to them.
w: Barring nonresidents from suing in its courts
Access to a state's courts is a protected privilege that nonresidents share.
Refusing nonresidents care at public hospitals
The Court has held that states may not deny basic medical services to nonresidents.
Banning nonresidents from owning property there
The right to buy and hold property is a basic privilege states must extend to nonresidents.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article IV, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: In Hicklin v. Orbeck (1978), the Supreme Court struck down this law. Which constitutional provision did it violate?
alt.a: The Privileges and Immunities Clause
alt.ex: In Hicklin v. Orbeck (1978), the Court held that “Alaska Hire” discriminated against citizens of other states in pursuing work, violating Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause.
w: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause concerns honoring other states' acts and court judgments, not hiring rules.
The Republican Guarantee Clause
This clause promises representative government and is not about discrimination against nonresidents.
The Extradition Clause of Article IV
This clause concerns returning people charged with crimes who flee to another state, not hiring rules.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Alaska passed a law requiring companies working on its oil and gas projects to hire qualified Alaska residents ahead of residents of other states.

alt.q: A Florida resident visits Georgia on vacation. Under Article IV, Georgia generally must…
alt.a: Give the visitor the basic rights its citizens have
alt.ex: The Privileges and Immunities Clause entitles citizens of each state to the basic privileges of citizens in every other state, so Georgia may not discriminate against the visitor in fundamental rights.
w: Allow the visitor to vote in Georgia's next election
Voting in state elections may be limited to that state's residents.
Apply Florida law, not Georgia law, to the visitor
Visitors must follow the laws of the state they are in.
Exempt the visitor from paying Georgia's sales taxes
Visitors pay the same taxes residents pay; the clause bars discrimination, not taxes.

items.q: A U.S. territory votes to seek statehood. Under Article IV, who has the power to admit it as a new state?
items.a: Congress
items.ex: Article IV, Section 3: “New States may be admitted by the Congress into this Union.”
w: The President
The President signs admission laws but cannot admit a state alone.
The Supreme Court
The Court has no role in admitting states.
Three-fourths of the states
Three-fourths of the states ratify amendments, not new states.

alt.q: Residents of one region of a state want to break away and form a new state. Article IV requires consent from…
alt.a: The state's legislature and Congress
alt.ex: No new state may be formed within another state without consent of the legislatures concerned and of Congress (Art. IV, §3); West Virginia (1863) is the classic case.
w: Only the residents of the breakaway region
Local residents alone cannot create a state.
Only Congress, acting by itself
The existing state's legislature must also agree.
The President and the Supreme Court
Neither has a role in forming new states.

alt.q: Which article of the Constitution deals with relations among the states and the admission of new states?
alt.a: Article IV
alt.ex: Article IV covers full faith and credit, privileges and immunities, extradition, new states and the republican-government guarantee.
w: Article I
Article I sets up Congress and its powers.
Article V
Article V describes the amendment process.
Article VI
Article VI covers supremacy, debts and oaths.

items.q: A state charges out-of-state residents a much higher fee than its own residents for a commercial fishing license, and the law is challenged. Which Article IV provision is most directly at issue?
items.a: The Privileges and Immunities Clause
items.ex: Article IV, Section 2 entitles citizens of each state to “all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States,” limiting discrimination against out-of-staters.
w: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause requires states to honor other states' public acts, records and court judgments.
Article IV's Republican Guarantee Clause
That clause promises each state a republican form of government.
The Extradition Clause
That clause requires states to return people who flee criminal charges.

alt.q: A person charged with a crime in Georgia flees to Alabama. Under Article IV, Alabama generally must…
alt.a: Return the person to Georgia on demand
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 2's Extradition Clause requires a fugitive to be delivered up on demand of the state they fled.
w: Try the person in Alabama's own courts
Crimes are tried in the state where they were committed.
Grant the person asylum if they request it
States may not shelter fugitives from other states.
Refer the matter to the Supreme Court first
Extradition is handled between the states' executives.

alt.q: “The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government…” This clause promises each state…
alt.a: A government run by elected representatives
alt.ex: The Guarantee Clause (Article IV, Section 4) promises republican, representative government and protection from invasion.
w: Equal representation in the United States Senate
Equal Senate representation is in Article I and protected by Article V.
Freedom from all forms of federal taxation
States receive no such protection.
A government chosen by the national political parties
Parties are not mentioned in the Constitution.

items.q: A Florida court orders a person to pay $20,000 in damages. The person moves to Georgia to avoid paying. Which clause requires Georgia's courts to enforce the Florida judgment?
items.a: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
items.ex: Article IV, Section 1 requires each state to give full faith and credit to the “judicial Proceedings of every other State.”
w: The Privileges and Immunities Clause
That clause protects out-of-state citizens from discrimination, not judgments.
The Supremacy Clause
That clause settles federal-state conflicts, not state-to-state ones.
The Extradition Clause
That clause returns people fleeing criminal charges; this is a civil judgment.

alt.q: A couple married in Alabama moves to Oregon, which recognizes their marriage. Which constitutional provision most directly supports this recognition?
alt.a: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
alt.ex: Full Faith and Credit requires states to respect the “public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings” of other states, such as marriage records.
w: Article IV's Republican Guarantee Clause
That clause promises a republican form of government.
Article VI's Supremacy Clause
That clause makes federal law supreme over state law.
Article I's Commerce Clause
That clause gives Congress power over trade.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of the Full Faith and Credit Clause?
alt.a: To make states respect each other's laws and rulings
alt.ex: It keeps the states from acting like foreign countries toward each other's official acts and court judgments.
w: To make states treat visitors like their own citizens
That is the purpose of the Privileges and Immunities Clause.
To make state laws yield to valid federal laws
That is the purpose of the Supremacy Clause.
To make states return people who flee criminal charges
That is the purpose of the Extradition Clause.

items.q: “Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State.” Which situation best illustrates this clause?
items.a: Nevada enforcing a child-support order issued in Utah
items.ex: A child-support order is a judicial proceeding, so other states must give it full faith and credit.
w: Nevada letting Utah residents buy land on equal terms
Equal treatment of out-of-staters is Privileges and Immunities.
Nevada sending a fugitive back to Utah for trial
Returning fugitives is the Extradition Clause.
Nevada following a federal law over its own statute
Federal law prevailing over state law is the Supremacy Clause.

alt.q: This clause appears in which article of the Constitution?
alt.a: Article IV, on interstate relations
alt.ex: Full Faith and Credit is Article IV, Section 1, the article on interstate relations.
w: Article I, on the powers of Congress
Article I creates Congress and lists its powers.
Article III, on the federal courts
Article III creates the judiciary.
Article VI, on federal supremacy
Article VI contains the Supremacy Clause, oaths and debts.

alt.q: The Full Faith and Credit Clause and the Privileges and Immunities Clause share which main goal?
alt.a: Uniting the states as one nation, not rivals
alt.ex: Both Article IV clauses keep states from treating one another and one another's citizens as foreign.
w: Strengthening the President's power over the states
Neither clause involves the President.
Protecting people from searches by state police
Search protections come from the Fourth Amendment.
Letting each state ignore the others' laws
Both clauses do the opposite.

items.q: What formal role does the President have in amending the Constitution?
items.a: None; proposed amendments do not go to the President
items.ex: Article V gives the amendment process to Congress (or a convention) and the states. In Hollingsworth v. Virginia (1798), the Court confirmed that proposed amendments need not be presented to the President.
w: The President must sign each proposed amendment
Unlike ordinary bills, proposed amendments do not require the President's signature, as the Court confirmed in Hollingsworth v. Virginia (1798).
The President may veto amendments, subject to override
The veto applies only to bills and resolutions under Article I, not to Article V amendments.
The President calls conventions to ratify amendments
Article V lets Congress, not the President, choose ratification by state conventions.

alt.q: What effect does the President's veto have?
alt.a: None; the amendment still goes to the states
alt.ex: Article V gives the President no role in amendments, so a presidential “veto” has no legal effect. Once two-thirds of both houses propose an amendment, it goes to the states for ratification.
w: It blocks the amendment unless Congress overrides it
The veto-override process applies to ordinary bills, not proposed amendments.
It sends the amendment to the Supreme Court for review
The Court does not review proposed amendments before ratification.
It requires approval by all fifty states instead
Article V always requires three-fourths of the states; a veto cannot change that.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress approves a proposed constitutional amendment by a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate. The President strongly opposes the amendment and announces a veto.

alt.q: Which participants have a formal role in the amendment process under Article V?
alt.a: Congress and the states
alt.ex: Under Article V, amendments are proposed by Congress (or a convention requested by the states) and ratified by state legislatures or state conventions. The President and courts have no formal role.
w: The President and Congress
The President has no formal role; proposed amendments do not require a presidential signature.
The Supreme Court and the states
The Court has no part in proposing or ratifying amendments.
The President and the Supreme Court
Neither takes part in the Article V process.

items.q: According to this passage, who decides whether an amendment is ratified by state legislatures or by state conventions?
items.a: Congress
items.ex: Article V lets ratification happen by legislatures or by conventions in three-fourths of the states, “as the one or the other Mode of Ratification may be proposed by the Congress.”
w: The President
Article V gives the President no role in amendments.
Each state's governor
Governors have no role in choosing the ratification method.
The Supreme Court
The courts do not choose how amendments are ratified.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article V of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…when ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States, or by Conventions in three fourths thereof, as the one or the other Mode of Ratification may be proposed by the Congress;…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Who is correct?
alt.a: Congress, which chooses the ratification method
alt.ex: Article V gives Congress the choice between ratification by state legislatures and by state conventions. Congress chose conventions only once, for the Twenty-first Amendment (1933).
w: The governor, since states choose their own method
Article V gives this choice to Congress, not to each state.
The governor, since conventions are not allowed
Article V expressly allows ratification by state conventions.
Neither, since voters must decide by referendum
In Hawke v. Smith (1920), the Court held that a state referendum cannot ratify an amendment.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress proposes a constitutional amendment and specifies that it must be ratified by special conventions in the states. A governor insists that her state's legislature should vote on it instead.

alt.q: Which two methods of ratifying an amendment does Article V allow?
alt.a: Legislatures or conventions in three-fourths of the states
alt.ex: Article V requires ratification by the legislatures of three-fourths of the states or by conventions in three-fourths of the states, whichever method Congress chooses.
w: Votes by two-thirds of the states or by a national popular vote
Ratification requires three-fourths of the states, and Article V provides for no national vote.
A national referendum or a unanimous vote of the state governors
Neither a referendum nor the governors play any part in Article V ratification.
Approval by a majority of states and then by the President
A majority is not enough, and the President has no role in amendments.

items.q: This part of Article V protects which feature of the Constitution?
items.a: Each state's equal vote in the Senate
items.ex: Article V forbids any amendment that would take away a state's “equal Suffrage in the Senate” without that state's consent, protecting the Great Compromise's guarantee of two senators per state.
w: Each state's share of House seats
House seats depend on population and change after each census.
Each state's number of electors
Electoral votes change with a state's House seats and are not protected by Article V.
Each state's right to leave the Union
The Constitution provides no right to secede, and this clause concerns only the Senate.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article V of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“…and that no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Why could this amendment not take effect against a small state that objects?
alt.a: Article V bars taking a state's equal Senate vote
alt.ex: Article V says no state, “without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.” Ratification by three-fourths of the states is not enough to override that protection.
w: Article I fixes the Senate's size forever
Article I sets two senators per state, but the permanent protection comes from Article V.
Article IV guarantees each state a republic
The Guarantee Clause promises representative government, not equal Senate seats.
The Tenth Amendment reserves Senate seats to states
The Tenth Amendment concerns reserved powers, not Senate representation.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A proposed amendment would give large states three senators each and small states one. Supporters say that if three-fourths of the states ratify it, every state must accept it.

alt.q: Besides equal Senate representation, Article V protected which provision from amendment until 1808?
alt.a: The bar on Congress banning the slave trade
alt.ex: Article V barred amendments before 1808 that affected the first and fourth clauses of Article I, Section 9, including the clause preventing Congress from banning the importation of enslaved people before 1808.
w: The President's power to make foreign treaties
Article V gave no special protection to the treaty power.
The location of the national capital
The Constitution did not fix the capital's location; Congress chose it by law.
The number of Supreme Court justices
The Constitution does not set the number of justices; Congress does by law.

items.q: The Twenty-seventh Amendment was proposed in 1789 but not ratified until 1992. What does this history show about Article V?
items.a: Article V itself sets no deadline for ratification
items.ex: Article V contains no time limit. Congress may set one, but it set none for the congressional pay amendment, so states could still ratify it more than 200 years later.
w: Amendments need unanimous approval of the states
Article V requires three-fourths of the states, not all of them.
Congress must propose amendments again every decade
Nothing in Article V requires re-proposing amendments.
Amendments take effect only after court review
No court review is part of the Article V process.

alt.q: Which amendment, first proposed alongside the Bill of Rights in 1789, was finally ratified in 1992?
alt.a: The Twenty-seventh Amendment
alt.ex: The Twenty-seventh Amendment, which delays changes in congressional pay until after the next House election, was proposed in 1789 and ratified in 1992.
w: The Twenty-sixth Amendment
The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age to 18 and was ratified within months.
The Twenty-fifth Amendment
The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) deals with presidential disability and succession.
The Twenty-second Amendment
The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limits Presidents to two elected terms.

alt.q: Congress has often included a seven-year time limit when proposing amendments. Which statement about such limits is accurate?
alt.a: Congress may set them, though Article V has none
alt.ex: Article V contains no deadline. In Dillon v. Gloss (1921), the Court upheld Congress's power to set a reasonable time limit, as it did for the Eighteenth Amendment.
w: Article V requires ratification within seven years
Article V has no deadline; the Twenty-seventh Amendment took over 200 years.
Only the states, not Congress, may set time limits
The Court has upheld Congress's power to set time limits.
The Twenty-seventh Amendment banned all time limits
That amendment concerns congressional pay, not ratification deadlines.

items.q: Which statement about the 27 amendments to the Constitution is accurate?
items.a: All were proposed by Congress, not a convention
items.ex: Every one of the 27 amendments was proposed by a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress. The convention method in Article V has never been used.
w: Most were ratified by special state conventions
Only the Twenty-first Amendment was ratified by state conventions; the rest by legislatures.
Each was proposed by a convention of the states
No national convention to propose amendments has ever been held.
Some took effect without any state ratification
Every amendment required ratification by three-fourths of the states.

alt.q: Which part of the Article V process has never been used?
alt.a: A convention to propose amendments
alt.ex: All 27 amendments were proposed by Congress. Although states have applied for one, no convention for proposing amendments has ever been called.
w: Ratification by special state conventions
This method was used once, for the Twenty-first Amendment in 1933.
Ratification by the state legislatures
This method has been used for 26 of the 27 amendments.
A two-thirds vote of Congress to propose
Congress proposed all 27 amendments this way.

alt.q: Which correction to the student's claim is accurate?
alt.a: Congress proposed it; state legislatures ratified it
alt.ex: James Madison introduced the amendments in the First Congress in 1789. Congress proposed them by a two-thirds vote, and state legislatures ratified ten of them by December 15, 1791.
w: The President proposed it, and Congress ratified it
The President has no formal role in amendments, and ratification is done by the states.
The Supreme Court wrote it, and the states approved it
The Supreme Court has no role in writing or proposing amendments.
Voters proposed it through a national referendum
The Constitution provides no national referendum for any purpose.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A student claims that the Bill of Rights was written by a second constitutional convention that the states called in 1789.

items.q: Which pair correctly describes the two ways Article V allows amendments to be proposed?
items.a: Two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or a convention called at the request of two-thirds of the states
items.ex: Proposal: two-thirds of both houses, or a national convention on application of two-thirds of state legislatures; ratification: three-fourths of the states.
w: Three-fourths of both houses of Congress, or a convention called at the request of three-fourths of the states
Three-fourths is the ratification threshold, not the proposal threshold.
A majority of both houses of Congress, or a convention called at the request of a majority of the state governors
Article V requires two-thirds, and it gives governors no role.
Two-thirds of the Senate acting alone, or a national referendum called by the President of the United States
The House must also vote, and Article V has no national referendum or presidential role.

alt.q: After an amendment has been proposed, what does Article V require to ratify it?
alt.a: Approval by three-fourths of the states
alt.ex: Ratification requires the legislatures of, or conventions in, three-fourths of the states (38 of 50 today).
w: Approval by two-thirds of the states
Two-thirds is the threshold for proposing, not ratifying.
Approval by a majority of voters nationwide
The Constitution has no national referendum.
Approval by the President and the Supreme Court
Neither has a formal role in ratification.

alt.q: “The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution, or, on the Application of the Legislatures of two thirds of the several States, shall call a Convention for proposing Amendments…” Which statement about this process is accurate?
alt.a: Every amendment so far has been proposed by Congress
alt.ex: All 27 amendments were proposed by two-thirds of Congress; the convention route has never been used.
w: Most amendments were proposed by a national convention
No national convention for proposing amendments has ever been called.
The President must sign each proposed amendment
The President has no formal role in proposing amendments.
Amendments take effect once Congress proposes them
Proposed amendments must still be ratified by three-fourths of the states.

items.q: The Twenty-first Amendment (1933), which repealed Prohibition, is unique among the amendments because it was…
items.a: Ratified by state conventions, not legislatures
items.ex: Article V allows ratification by legislatures or conventions in three-fourths of the states; the Twenty-first is the only amendment ratified by conventions.
w: Proposed by a national convention, not by Congress
Congress proposed it; no amendment has come from a national convention.
Ratified by a national popular referendum
Article V provides no national referendum.
Adopted without the President's signature
No amendment needs a President's signature, so this is not unique.

alt.q: Thirty-five of the fifty states have ratified a proposed amendment. What is its status?
alt.a: Not yet ratified; 38 states are needed
alt.ex: Three-fourths of 50 states is 37.5, so 38 states must ratify.
w: Ratified, since two-thirds of the states approved
Two-thirds is the threshold for proposing, not ratifying.
Ratified, since a majority of the states approved
A simple majority of states is not enough.
Not yet ratified; 45 states are needed
Article V requires three-fourths (38), not 90 percent.

alt.q: The amendment process is often described as “federal” in character because…
alt.a: Both national and state bodies take part
alt.ex: Congress (or a convention) proposes and the states ratify, so both levels of government participate.
w: Only the national government may change it
Ratification requires action by three-fourths of the states.
Only the states may propose any change
Congress has proposed every amendment so far.
The Supreme Court must approve each change
The Court has no formal role in amending the Constitution.

items.q: Why did the framers make amending the Constitution difficult but still possible?
items.a: To allow change but guard against hasty changes
items.ex: Supermajority thresholds (two-thirds to propose, three-fourths to ratify) make change deliberate, while avoiding the Articles' unanimity rule.
w: To prevent the Constitution from ever being changed
Article V exists precisely so the Constitution can change.
To let Congress alone update it whenever needed
The states must ratify every amendment.
To make sure no group of states could block a change
Just 13 of the 50 states can block ratification, since 38 are needed.

alt.q: Which weakness of the Articles of Confederation did Article V correct?
alt.a: Amendments needed all thirteen states' approval
alt.ex: Under the Articles, amendments required unanimity, so one state could block reform; Article V lowered this to three-fourths.
w: Congress could not regulate trade among the states
Trade was fixed by the Commerce Clause in Article I.
No national executive existed to enforce the laws
That was fixed by Article II.
Each state had one vote in the Congress
That was addressed by the Great Compromise in Article I.

alt.q: Supporters of a balanced-budget amendment, frustrated with Congress, urge state legislatures to apply for a convention. Which Article V route are they using?
alt.a: A convention on application of two-thirds of the states
alt.ex: Article V lets two-thirds of state legislatures require Congress to call a convention to propose amendments; this route has never been completed.
w: A proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress
That is the congressional route these supporters are bypassing.
Ratification by conventions in three-fourths of the states
That is a ratification method, used only after an amendment is proposed.
A national referendum called by the state governors
Article V provides no referendum and no role for governors.

items.q: In the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V), which step comes right after “The proposed amendment is sent to the states”?
items.a: Three-fourths of the states ratify it
items.ex: That's step 3 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: It becomes part of the Constitution
That's step 4 of 4.
Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
That's step 1 of 4.

alt.q: Which step comes first in the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V)?
alt.a: Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: The proposed amendment is sent to the states
That's step 2 of 4.
Three-fourths of the states ratify it
That's step 3 of 4.
It becomes part of the Constitution
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: Which step comes last in the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V)?
alt.a: It becomes part of the Constitution
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: Three-fourths of the states ratify it
That's step 3 of 4.
The proposed amendment is sent to the states
That's step 2 of 4.
Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
That's step 1 of 4.

alt.q: In the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V), which step comes right after “Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it”?
alt.a: The proposed amendment is sent to the states
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: Three-fourths of the states ratify it
That's step 3 of 4.
It becomes part of the Constitution
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V), which step comes right after “Three-fourths of the states ratify it”?
alt.a: It becomes part of the Constitution
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: The proposed amendment is sent to the states
That's step 2 of 4.
Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
That's step 1 of 4.

alt.q: In the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V), which step comes right before “The proposed amendment is sent to the states”?
alt.a: Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: Three-fourths of the states ratify it
That's step 3 of 4.
It becomes part of the Constitution
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V), which step comes right before “Three-fourths of the states ratify it”?
alt.a: The proposed amendment is sent to the states
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
That's step 1 of 4.
It becomes part of the Constitution
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In the usual way the Constitution is amended (Article V), which step comes right before “It becomes part of the Constitution”?
alt.a: Three-fourths of the states ratify it
alt.ex: That's step 3 of 4. Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
w: The proposed amendment is sent to the states
That's step 2 of 4.
Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
That's step 1 of 4.

ord.q: Put the steps of the usual amendment process in order.
items: Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to propose it
The proposed amendment is sent to the states
Three-fourths of the states ratify it
It becomes part of the Constitution
ord.ex: Article V: an amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.

items.q: In the United States, how are conflicts between state laws and federal laws generally resolved?
items.a: The conflict must be resolved using the Supremacy Clause.
items.ex: Article VI’s Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution and federal laws made under it “the supreme Law of the Land,” so a valid federal law overrides a conflicting state law.
w: The conflict must be resolved by the U.S. attorney general.
The attorney general heads the Justice Department and can bring lawsuits, but courts decide conflicts using the Supremacy Clause.
The conflict must be resolved by a national referendum.
The United States has no national referendum process.
The conflict must be resolved using the Tenth Amendment.
The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states; it does not let state law override valid federal law.

alt.q: Which part of the U.S. Constitution declares that the Constitution and federal laws made under it “shall be the supreme Law of the Land”?
alt.a: Article VI
alt.ex: The Supremacy Clause appears in Article VI, Clause 2. It requires state judges to follow the Constitution and federal law even when state laws conflict.
w: Article I
Article I creates Congress and lists its powers.
Article III
Article III establishes the federal courts.
Article V
Article V describes how the Constitution is amended.

alt.q: A state law allows factories to dump a chemical into rivers that a valid federal law bans. If the conflict reaches the courts, which outcome is most likely?
alt.a: The federal law prevails over the state law.
alt.ex: Under the Supremacy Clause, a valid federal law overrides a conflicting state law, so the state law would be preempted.
w: The state law prevails inside that state.
State law cannot override a valid federal law, even within the state.
Voters in the state settle it by referendum.
A state referendum cannot override federal law.
Congress must vote on the law a second time.
Courts resolve the conflict; Congress does not have to pass the law again.

items.q: Based on this passage, when is a federal law NOT part of the supreme law of the land?
items.a: When it violates the Constitution
items.ex: Article VI makes supreme only the federal laws “made in Pursuance” of the Constitution. A federal law that violates the Constitution is not supreme and can be struck down.
w: When most state legislatures vote to reject it
States cannot void federal law by voting against it; that idea is nullification.
When a governor declares it harmful to the state
Governors have no power to cancel federal laws.
When it conflicts with a state constitution
Article VI says federal law controls even over conflicting state constitutions.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article VI of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties made, or which shall be made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land;…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which statement correctly ranks sources of law under Article VI?
alt.a: The Constitution, then federal law, then state law
alt.ex: The Constitution is the highest law; federal laws made in pursuance of it and treaties come next; and state constitutions and laws give way when they conflict with either.
w: Federal law, then the Constitution, then state law
No law can override the Constitution; laws must be made in pursuance of it.
State constitutions, then federal law, then treaties
Article VI places state constitutions below federal law and treaties.
Treaties, then state law, then the Constitution
The Constitution stands above treaties, and state law is lowest.

alt.q: Why does the Supremacy Clause NOT require the state court to apply this law?
alt.a: Only constitutional federal laws are supreme
alt.ex: Article VI makes supreme only laws “made in Pursuance” of the Constitution. A law punishing criticism of the President would violate the First Amendment, so it is not valid supreme law.
w: State courts never have to apply federal laws
Article VI expressly binds state judges to apply valid federal law.
Only treaties, not statutes, are supreme law
Article VI names the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties as supreme.
State judges may ignore federal laws they dislike
State judges must follow valid federal law regardless of their views.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law making it a crime for newspapers to criticize the President. A state court refuses to enforce the law, ruling that it is unconstitutional.

items.q: Under Article VI, how would this conflict most likely be resolved?
items.a: The treaty and law prevail as supreme law
items.ex: Article VI makes treaties made under the authority of the United States part of the supreme law of the land. In Missouri v. Holland (1920), the Court upheld a migratory bird treaty and law over a state's objection.
w: The state prevails under the Tenth Amendment
The Court rejected this argument because valid treaties override conflicting state powers.
The President settles it by executive order
Executive orders do not resolve conflicts between treaties and state powers; Article VI does.
Canada's courts decide, since it is a party
U.S. courts decide cases about U.S. law; a foreign nation's courts have no such power.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: The United States signs a treaty to protect birds that migrate between the U.S. and Canada, and Congress passes a law to carry it out. A state objects that only it may regulate hunting within its borders.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case held that a valid treaty, and a federal law carrying it out, override a state's claimed power over wildlife?
alt.a: Missouri v. Holland (1920)
alt.ex: In Missouri v. Holland (1920), the Court upheld the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, ruling that a valid treaty is supreme law under Article VI even in an area states claimed under the Tenth Amendment.
w: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Gibbons concerned steamboat licenses and Congress's commerce power, not treaties.
Marbury v. Madison (1803)
Marbury established judicial review; it did not involve treaties or wildlife.
Printz v. United States (1997)
Printz limited federal power, barring Congress from commandeering state officers.

alt.q: Which three kinds of law does Article VI name as the supreme law of the land?
alt.a: The Constitution, federal laws, and treaties
alt.ex: Article VI declares that “This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties… shall be the supreme Law of the Land.”
w: The Constitution, state laws, and treaties
State laws are not supreme; they give way when they conflict with federal law.
Federal laws, state constitutions, and court rulings
State constitutions are expressly subordinate under Article VI.
The Constitution, executive orders, and state laws
Article VI does not mention executive orders, and state laws are not supreme.

items.q: Which weakness of the Articles of Confederation did the Supremacy Clause most directly address?
items.a: States could defy national laws and treaties
items.ex: Under the Articles, Congress had no way to make states obey its acts or treaties. Article VI made federal law and treaties binding on state judges over any conflicting state law.
w: Each state had only one vote in Congress
Representation was addressed by the Great Compromise in Article I, not Article VI.
Amendments required approval by all thirteen states
This problem was solved by Article V's three-fourths rule.
There was no national executive branch
This weakness was addressed by creating the presidency in Article II.

alt.q: Which constitutional provision was designed to prevent this problem?
alt.a: The Supremacy Clause
alt.ex: Article VI makes treaties part of “the supreme Law of the Land” and binds state judges to them, so states could no longer block obligations under treaties such as the 1783 Treaty of Paris.
w: The No Religious Test Clause
This clause bars religious tests for federal office; it says nothing about treaties.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause makes states honor each other's acts and judgments, not national treaties.
The Privileges and Immunities Clause
This clause protects citizens visiting other states, not treaty obligations.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: After the American Revolution, several states passed laws blocking British creditors from collecting prewar debts, even though the 1783 Treaty of Paris promised that such debts could be collected. Congress under the Articles of Confederation could do nothing to stop them.

alt.q: Which statement best explains why the framers included the Supremacy Clause?
alt.a: To make federal law override conflicting state law
alt.ex: The framers wanted a national government whose laws states could not ignore, as they had under the Articles. Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties supreme over state law.
w: To let states veto national laws they oppose
The clause does the opposite; it denies states power to override federal law.
To place the courts above the Constitution
The Constitution itself is supreme; courts must follow it.
To give the President control over state governors
The clause ranks laws; it gives the President no authority over governors.

items.q: “…no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.” This clause most directly means that…
items.a: Federal officials cannot be required to hold a faith
items.ex: Article VI bars religious qualifications for federal office, at a time when many states required officeholders to hold Christian beliefs.
w: Congress may not establish an official national church
That is the First Amendment's Establishment Clause.
People may freely practice any religion they choose
That is the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause.
States must keep organized prayer out of public schools
That comes from Engel v. Vitale (1962) under the Establishment Clause.

alt.q: Before the Bill of Rights was added, which part of the Constitution addressed religion and government office?
alt.a: Article VI, banning religious tests
alt.ex: The original Constitution's main reference to religion is Article VI's ban on religious tests for federal office.
w: Article I, barring a national church
The ban on an established church is in the First Amendment (1791).
Article III, protecting free worship
Article III concerns the courts; free exercise is in the First Amendment.
The Preamble, invoking God's blessing
The Preamble does not mention God or religion.

alt.q: A federal agency requires applicants for a senior post to swear that they believe in God. Which provision of the original Constitution does this most directly violate?
alt.a: Article VI's ban on religious tests
alt.ex: Requiring a profession of belief as a condition of federal office is exactly what Article VI forbids.
w: Article I's ban on titles of nobility
That clause bars granting noble titles, not religious oaths.
Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause
That clause protects out-of-state citizens from discrimination by states.
Article II's presidential oath of office
The President's oath has no religious requirement and does not govern other posts.

items.q: A newly elected state legislator takes an oath of office. Under Article VI, that oath must include a promise to…
items.a: Support the Constitution of the United States
items.ex: Article VI requires federal and state legislators, executives and judges to be bound “by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution.”
w: Support only the constitution of their own state
State officials must also support the U.S. Constitution.
Support the policies of the current President
Oaths run to the Constitution, not to any officeholder.
Support the platform of their political party
The Constitution never mentions political parties.

alt.q: “…the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution…” Why is it significant that state officials are included?
alt.a: It binds state officials to the national Constitution
alt.ex: Requiring state officers to swear to support the Constitution reinforces federal supremacy within the states.
w: It lets state officials overrule federal laws they oppose
Article VI does the opposite, making federal law supreme.
It makes state officials employees of the federal government
State officials remain state officers; the oath binds them to the Constitution.
It requires state officials to belong to a religious faith
Article VI forbids religious tests for federal office.

alt.q: Which promise in Article VI reassured creditors and foreign nations in 1787?
alt.a: Debts from before the Constitution remained valid
alt.ex: Article VI: “All Debts contracted and Engagements entered into, before the Adoption of this Constitution, shall be as valid against the United States…”
w: States could print money to repay their debts
Article I, Section 10 bars states from coining money or emitting bills of credit.
Congress would cancel all Revolutionary War debts
The Constitution kept those debts valid.
Creditors could sue the President for repayment
No such provision exists.

items.q: A state law directly conflicts with a valid federal statute that Congress passed under its commerce power. A court will most likely rule that…
items.a: The federal statute controls under Article VI
items.ex: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution, federal laws made under it, and treaties “the supreme Law of the Land,” overriding conflicting state law.
w: The state law controls under the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment reserves only undelegated powers; commerce power was delegated.
Both laws apply, and residents may choose one
When laws truly conflict, the federal law preempts the state law.
Whichever law was passed more recently controls
Timing does not matter; federal supremacy does.

alt.q: “This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties made, or which shall be made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land…” This excerpt is known as…
alt.a: The Supremacy Clause
alt.ex: This is the Supremacy Clause of Article VI.
w: The Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause (Article I, Section 8) lets Congress pass laws to carry out its powers.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause (Article IV) requires states to honor each other's acts and judgments.
The Commerce Clause
That clause (Article I, Section 8) gives Congress power over interstate and foreign trade.

alt.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Maryland's tax on the Second Bank of the United States was struck down mainly because…
alt.a: A state may not tax a valid federal institution
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall reasoned that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy” and that federal supremacy bars states from burdening federal operations.
w: No power of Congress supported creating the bank
The Court held the bank valid as an implied power under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
Only Congress may levy taxes of any kind at all
States may tax; taxing is a concurrent power.
The tax violated the Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns respect among the states, not state taxes on federal entities.

items.q: “…and the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding.” This part of Article VI means state judges must…
items.a: Apply federal law over conflicting state law
items.ex: State judges are bound by the U.S. Constitution, federal laws and treaties even when their own state's constitution or laws say otherwise.
w: Apply state law over conflicting federal law
This reverses the Supremacy Clause.
Refer every federal question to the Supreme Court
State courts decide federal questions themselves, subject to review.
Be appointed by the President and the Senate
State judges are chosen under state law.

alt.q: Which historical claim most directly conflicts with the Supremacy Clause?
alt.a: Nullification, the claim a state may void federal law
alt.ex: South Carolina's nullification of federal tariffs (1832) contradicted the Supremacy Clause, and President Jackson rejected it.
w: Judicial review, the claim courts may void laws
Judicial review is consistent with the Supremacy Clause.
Popular sovereignty, the claim power comes from the people
This principle underlies the Preamble, not a challenge to supremacy.
Federalism, the claim power is divided by level
Federalism includes federal supremacy within delegated powers.

alt.q: After Brown v. Board of Education, Arkansas officials claimed they were not bound by the ruling. In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), the Supreme Court relied mainly on…
alt.a: The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
alt.ex: The Court held that its interpretation of the Constitution in Brown was the supreme law of the land and binding on state officials.
w: The Commerce Clause of Article I
The Commerce Clause concerns Congress's power over trade.
The Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
Arkansas's states'-rights argument was rejected, not relied on.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause governs respect among states, not federal-state conflict.

items.q: Which state was the first to ratify the Constitution, on December 7, 1787?
items.a: Delaware
items.ex: Delaware's convention ratified the Constitution unanimously on December 7, 1787, which is why it calls itself “The First State.”
w: Pennsylvania
Pennsylvania ratified second, on December 12, 1787.
Virginia
Virginia ratified in June 1788, after nine states had already approved.
Massachusetts
Massachusetts ratified sixth, in February 1788.

alt.q: Delaware's nickname, “The First State,” refers to which event?
alt.a: Being first to ratify the Constitution
alt.ex: Delaware ratified the Constitution on December 7, 1787, before any other state, earning the nickname “The First State.”
w: Founding the first English colony
The first permanent English colony was Jamestown, Virginia (1607).
Hosting the First Continental Congress
The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 1774.
Hosting the Constitutional Convention
The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 1787.

alt.q: Which pair correctly names the first and the ninth states to ratify the Constitution?
alt.a: Delaware and New Hampshire
alt.ex: Delaware ratified first (December 7, 1787), and New Hampshire became the ninth state on June 21, 1788, meeting Article VII's requirement.
w: Pennsylvania and Virginia
Pennsylvania was second, and Virginia was tenth.
Delaware and New York
Delaware was first, but New York was eleventh, in July 1788.
Massachusetts and Rhode Island
Massachusetts was sixth, and Rhode Island was the last of the thirteen, in 1790.

items.q: Which of the original thirteen states was the last to ratify the Constitution, in May 1790?
items.a: Rhode Island
items.ex: Rhode Island ratified on May 29, 1790, by a vote of 34 to 32, more than a year after the new government had begun.
w: North Carolina
North Carolina ratified in November 1789, before Rhode Island.
New York
New York ratified in July 1788 as the eleventh state.
Virginia
Virginia ratified in June 1788 as the tenth state.

alt.q: When George Washington took office in April 1789, which two states had not yet ratified the Constitution?
alt.a: North Carolina and Rhode Island
alt.ex: North Carolina did not ratify until November 1789 and Rhode Island until May 1790, both after Washington's inauguration on April 30, 1789.
w: New York and Virginia
Both ratified in the summer of 1788.
Delaware and Georgia
Both ratified in December 1787 and January 1788.
Massachusetts and South Carolina
Both ratified in the first half of 1788.

alt.q: Rhode Island, the last of the thirteen states to ratify, had also refused to take part in which event?
alt.a: The Constitutional Convention
alt.ex: Rhode Island never sent delegates to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787, and it held out on ratification until May 1790.
w: The First Continental Congress of 1774
Rhode Island sent delegates to the First Continental Congress.
The signing of the Declaration of Independence
Rhode Island's delegates, Stephen Hopkins and William Ellery, signed the Declaration.
The ratification of the Articles of Confederation
Rhode Island ratified the Articles of Confederation in 1778.

items.q: In February 1788, Massachusetts ratified the Constitution by a close vote. Which approach helped Federalists win there?
items.a: Ratifying while recommending later amendments
items.ex: Massachusetts ratified 187 to 168 while recommending amendments for the new Congress to consider. Several later states, including Virginia and New York, followed this model.
w: Ratifying only after a bill of rights was added
The Bill of Rights was not added until 1791, long after Massachusetts ratified.
Promising to keep the Articles as a backup plan
Ratification replaced the Articles; no such promise was made.
Agreeing to move the national capital to Boston
No such deal was made; the capital was later placed on the Potomac.

alt.q: The “Massachusetts Compromise” during ratification most directly led to which later development?
alt.a: The adoption of the Bill of Rights
alt.ex: Under the Massachusetts Compromise, states ratified while recommending amendments. These recommendations pressured the First Congress to propose the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791.
w: The adoption of the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were adopted years earlier, in 1781.
The Great Compromise on representation
The Great Compromise was reached at the Constitutional Convention in 1787, before ratification.
The Three-Fifths Compromise
The Three-Fifths Compromise was also reached at the Convention in 1787.

alt.q: Which solution did several states, beginning with Massachusetts, use to resolve this kind of standoff?
alt.a: Ratify now and recommend amendments for later
alt.ex: Beginning with Massachusetts in February 1788, several conventions ratified the Constitution unconditionally while proposing amendments for the new Congress to consider.
w: Reject it until a second convention was held
Massachusetts ratified; no second national convention was ever held.
Ratify only some articles of the Constitution
Article VII required ratification of the whole Constitution, not parts of it.
Wait until Congress had amended it first
The Constitution could not be amended under Article V until after it took effect.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: At a state ratifying convention in 1788, delegates are closely divided. Some will vote yes only if the Constitution is changed to protect individual rights; others refuse to make ratification conditional on any changes.

items.q: This closing passage, which follows Article VII, records which event?
items.a: The signing of the Constitution in 1787
items.ex: The closing of the Constitution records that it was done in the Convention on September 17, 1787, when the delegates signed it. Ratification by nine states came in 1788.
w: Ratification by the ninth state in 1788
New Hampshire's ratification in June 1788 is not recorded in the document's text.
The adoption of the Bill of Rights in 1791
The Bill of Rights was added as amendments after the main text.
The signing of the Declaration in 1776
The Declaration of Independence is a separate document signed in 1776.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the closing of the U.S. Constitution, following Article VII, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“done in Convention by the Unanimous Consent of the States present the Seventeenth Day of September…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which fact best explains the careful wording “States present” in this passage?
alt.a: Rhode Island never sent delegates
alt.ex: Rhode Island never took part in the Convention, so the document claimed only the unanimous consent of the states present, not of all thirteen states.
w: Every delegate signed the document that day
Several delegates, including George Mason, Edmund Randolph, and Elbridge Gerry, refused to sign.
The states had already ratified it unanimously
Ratification by state conventions came later, beginning in December 1787.
Article VII required only nine states to sign
Article VII required nine states to ratify, not to sign at the Convention.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the closing of the U.S. Constitution, following Article VII, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“done in Convention by the Unanimous Consent of the States present the Seventeenth Day of September…”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which date, now observed as Constitution Day, marks the signing of the Constitution?
alt.a: September 17, 1787
alt.ex: Delegates signed the Constitution in Philadelphia on September 17, 1787, the date recorded at the end of the document.
w: July 4, 1776
This is the date the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
This is when New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify.
December 15, 1791
This is when the Bill of Rights was ratified.

items.q: After New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify in June 1788, why did approval by Virginia and New York still matter greatly?
items.a: A Union without these large states would be weak
items.ex: Nine states were enough legally under Article VII, but Virginia and New York were large and powerful. A new nation without them would have been weak and divided.
w: Article VII required those two states by name
Article VII names no states; any nine conventions were sufficient.
Their votes were needed to reach nine states
New Hampshire had already been the ninth state to ratify.
The Supreme Court had ruled their votes mandatory
The Supreme Court did not yet exist in 1788.

alt.q: Which large state ratified the Constitution in July 1788, after Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote The Federalist essays to win support there?
alt.a: New York
alt.ex: The Federalist essays were addressed “To the People of the State of New York.” New York ratified on July 26, 1788, by a close 30-to-27 vote.
w: Virginia
Virginia ratified in June 1788; The Federalist essays were aimed at New York.
Pennsylvania
Pennsylvania ratified in December 1787, before most of the essays appeared.
Massachusetts
Massachusetts ratified in February 1788.

alt.q: Virginia ratified the Constitution in June 1788 after a heated debate. Which leading Anti-Federalist spoke out against ratification at Virginia's convention?
alt.a: Patrick Henry
alt.ex: Patrick Henry argued at Virginia's convention that the Constitution would create a dangerous national government without protections for rights. Virginia ratified 89 to 79 and recommended amendments.
w: James Madison
Madison led the Federalist side at Virginia's convention.
George Washington
Washington supported ratification and was not a delegate to Virginia's convention.
Alexander Hamilton
Hamilton was a New York Federalist, not a member of Virginia's convention.

items.q: Once enough states had ratified, which body set March 4, 1789, as the date for the new government to begin?
items.a: The Confederation Congress
items.ex: In September 1788, the Congress under the Articles of Confederation set dates for choosing electors and set March 4, 1789, for the new government to begin, allowing an orderly transition.
w: The Constitutional Convention
The Convention adjourned in September 1787, before ratification.
The first U.S. Senate
The Senate did not exist until the new government began.
The U.S. Supreme Court
The Supreme Court was created only after the new government began.

alt.q: Which sequence of events is in the correct order?
alt.a: Signing, ratification by nine states, Washington's inauguration
alt.ex: The Constitution was signed on September 17, 1787, ratified by the ninth state on June 21, 1788, and George Washington was inaugurated on April 30, 1789.
w: Ratification by nine states, signing, Washington's inauguration
The Constitution had to be signed and sent to the states before they could ratify it.
Signing, Washington's inauguration, ratification by nine states
Washington could not take office until the Constitution was in effect.
Washington's inauguration, signing, ratification by nine states
The presidency did not exist until the Constitution was signed and ratified.

alt.q: What best explains why North Carolina and Rhode Island had no members in the First Congress when it began in 1789?
alt.a: They had not yet ratified the Constitution
alt.ex: Article VII made the Constitution binding only on the states that ratified it. North Carolina joined in November 1789 and Rhode Island in May 1790.
w: They were still territories, not states
Both were among the original thirteen states.
Article VII gave seats only to the first nine
Article VII says nothing about seats; every ratifying state was represented.
Congress had expelled them over unpaid taxes
No state was ever expelled from Congress.

items.q: “The Ratification of the Conventions of nine States, shall be sufficient for the Establishment of this Constitution between the States so ratifying the Same.” Why did the framers adopt this rule instead of requiring all thirteen states?
items.a: Unanimity had made the Articles nearly unamendable
items.ex: Because amending the Articles required all 13 states, the framers let nine states put the Constitution into effect; New Hampshire became the ninth in June 1788.
w: Nine states already held a majority of the population
Population was not the basis for the rule; it counted states.
Rhode Island had already promised to ratify it
Rhode Island boycotted the Convention and ratified last, in 1790.
Only nine states had sent delegates to Philadelphia
Twelve states sent delegates; only Rhode Island did not.

alt.q: Which state's ratification in June 1788 made it the ninth, putting the Constitution into effect?
alt.a: New Hampshire
alt.ex: New Hampshire ratified on June 21, 1788, the ninth state; Virginia and New York followed soon after.
w: Delaware
Delaware ratified first, in December 1787.
Massachusetts
Massachusetts ratified sixth, in February 1788.
Rhode Island
Rhode Island ratified last, in May 1790.

alt.q: Article VII called for ratification by special state conventions rather than by state legislatures. The main reason was to…
alt.a: Base its authority directly on the people
alt.ex: Conventions elected for the purpose reflected popular sovereignty and bypassed legislatures that might resist losing power.
w: Let state legislatures keep control of the decision
Using conventions deliberately took the decision away from legislatures.
Speed approval by avoiding any public debate
Ratification produced intense public debate, such as the Federalist Papers.
Allow Congress to choose the convention delegates
Delegates were chosen in the states, not by Congress.

items.q: According to Article VII, how was the Constitution to be put into effect?
items.a: Approval by conventions in nine of the thirteen states
items.ex: Article VII: "The Ratification of the Conventions of nine States, shall be sufficient for the Establishment of this Constitution between the States so ratifying the Same."
w: Approval by the state legislatures of all thirteen states
That was the Articles' rule for amendments, which the framers bypassed.
Approval by two-thirds of the Confederation Congress
Congress merely sent the Constitution to the states.
Approval by three-fourths of the state legislatures
Three-fourths is the Article V rule for ratifying amendments.

alt.q: Why was the ratification method in Article VII a sharp break from the Articles of Confederation?
alt.a: It needed nine states, not the unanimity required by the Articles
alt.ex: Changing the Articles required all thirteen legislatures; Article VII required only nine state conventions.
w: It required all states, not just the nine needed to pass major laws
This reverses the rules.
It let Congress alone approve the new plan of government
Ratification was by state conventions, not Congress.
It let state governors approve the Constitution by decree
Governors had no role; elected conventions decided.

alt.q: In June 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the Constitution, though Virginia and New York had not yet voted. What was the effect?
alt.a: The Constitution took effect among the ratifying states
alt.ex: Under Article VII, nine ratifications established the Constitution among those states; Virginia and New York ratified soon after.
w: The Constitution failed until all thirteen states ratified
Article VII required nine, not thirteen.
The Constitution took effect only after the Bill of Rights
The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791, after the government began in 1789.
The Constitution still needed two-thirds of Congress
Congress had no ratifying vote under Article VII.

items.q: Which statement best defines expressed powers?
items.a: Powers specifically listed in the Constitution
items.ex: Expressed (also called enumerated) powers are written out in the Constitution, such as Congress's powers in Article I, Section 8 to tax, coin money, and declare war.
w: Powers reasonably drawn from listed powers
This describes implied powers, based on the Necessary and Proper Clause.
Powers shared by national and state governments
This describes concurrent powers.
Powers kept by the states or the people
This describes reserved powers under the Tenth Amendment.

alt.q: Which power of Congress is an expressed power, written directly in Article I, Section 8?
alt.a: Declaring war
alt.ex: Article I, Section 8 expressly gives Congress the power “To declare War.”
w: Creating a national bank
A national bank is an implied power, upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Setting a minimum driving age
Driving rules are reserved state powers, not listed congressional powers.
Running public schools
Public education is a reserved power of the states.

alt.q: Article I, Section 8 lists powers such as laying taxes, coining money, and regulating commerce with foreign nations. These are best classified as…
alt.a: Enumerated powers
alt.ex: Powers written out in the Constitution, such as the list in Article I, Section 8, are enumerated (expressed) powers delegated to the national government.
w: Implied powers
Implied powers are not listed; they are drawn from the listed ones.
Reserved powers
Reserved powers belong to the states or the people, not to Congress.
Inherent powers
Inherent powers are not written in the Constitution; these powers are listed.

items.q: Which idea does the passage support?
items.a: Congress has implied powers beyond its list
items.ex: Marshall reasoned that Congress may use any appropriate means, not prohibited by the Constitution, to carry out its legitimate ends, the basis for implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: States may tax any federal institution freely
McCulloch held the opposite: Maryland could not tax the national bank.
Congress may act only on powers expressly listed
Marshall rejected this strict reading of Congress's powers.
Courts may not review acts of Congress
The passage is itself a court reviewing an act of Congress; judicial review dates to Marbury v. Madison (1803).

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the Constitution, and all means which are appropriate, which are plainly adapted to that end, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the Constitution, are Constitutional.”
Source: McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. 316 (1819)

alt.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court held that Congress could create a national bank because…
alt.a: it was a necessary and proper way to use listed powers
alt.ex: The Court held that the bank was a reasonable means of carrying out Congress's expressed powers, such as taxing, borrowing, and supporting armies, under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: Article I expressly lists a power to charter banks
No banking power is listed; that is why the case turned on implied powers.
the states had voted to give Congress that power
No state vote was involved; the power came from the Constitution.
banking is a power reserved to the national government
Reserved powers belong to the states or the people under the Tenth Amendment.

alt.q: Which clause would supporters of the bank most likely cite to show that Congress had power to create it?
alt.a: The Necessary and Proper Clause
alt.ex: The Necessary and Proper (Elastic) Clause of Article I, Section 8 lets Congress make laws needed to carry out its listed powers, which supports creating a bank as a means to those ends.
w: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
This Article IV clause concerns states honoring each other's acts and rulings.
The Privileges and Immunities Clause
This Article IV clause protects citizens traveling to other states.
The Republican Guarantee Clause
This Article IV clause promises representative government to the states.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress creates a national bank to help it collect taxes, borrow money, and pay the army. A state argues that the bank is unconstitutional because the Constitution never mentions a bank.

items.q: In 1791, Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson disagreed over whether Congress could charter a national bank. Which statement best describes Hamilton's position?
items.a: Read the Constitution loosely to allow implied powers
items.ex: Hamilton argued that the Necessary and Proper Clause allowed any means reasonably related to Congress's listed powers, a loose (broad) construction later echoed in McCulloch v. Maryland.
w: Read the Constitution strictly, allowing only listed powers
This strict construction was Jefferson's position.
Leave all banking to the states as a reserved power
Jefferson argued the power was reserved to the states; Hamilton disagreed.
Let the President charter banks without Congress
Both men assumed the bank would be chartered by an act of Congress.

alt.q: Thomas Jefferson argued that the national bank was unconstitutional because the Constitution did not list such a power. This view is known as…
alt.a: strict construction
alt.ex: Jefferson read “necessary” narrowly, meaning truly indispensable, and argued Congress could not go beyond its listed powers. This is called strict construction.
w: loose construction
Loose construction was Hamilton's view, allowing broad implied powers.
judicial review
Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws, not a view of Congress's powers.
popular sovereignty
Popular sovereignty means government rests on the people's consent.

alt.q: Which pair correctly matches each leader with his view of the Necessary and Proper Clause in the 1791 national bank debate?
alt.a: Hamilton: broad reading; Jefferson: narrow reading
alt.ex: Hamilton read the clause broadly to support the bank, while Jefferson read it narrowly and opposed the bank. President Washington sided with Hamilton and signed the bank bill.
w: Hamilton: narrow reading; Jefferson: broad reading
This reverses their positions.
Both Hamilton and Jefferson: a narrow reading
Hamilton argued for a broad reading to justify the bank.
Both Hamilton and Jefferson: a broad reading
Jefferson argued for a narrow reading and opposed the bank.

items.q: Which power does the Constitution deny to BOTH the national government and the states?
items.a: Passing ex post facto laws
items.ex: Article I, Section 9 bars Congress, and Article I, Section 10 bars the states, from passing ex post facto laws or bills of attainder.
w: Coining and printing money
Coining money is denied to the states but is an expressed power of Congress.
Making treaties with other nations
Treaties are denied to the states but may be made by the President with Senate consent.
Collecting taxes on income
Taxing is a concurrent power used by both levels of government.

alt.q: The rule in this passage is best classified as…
alt.a: a power denied to Congress
alt.ex: Article I, Section 9 lists limits on Congress, including this ban on bills of attainder and ex post facto laws. These are denied (prohibited) powers.
w: a power delegated to Congress
The passage forbids Congress from acting; it grants nothing.
a power reserved to the states
Article I, Section 10 also denies these powers to the states.
a power implied by the Elastic Clause
Implied powers are things Congress may do; this passage says what it may not do.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article I, Section 9 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“No Bill of Attainder or ex post facto Law shall be passed.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Why is this law unconstitutional?
alt.a: It is an ex post facto law, barred to states
alt.ex: An ex post facto law punishes an act that was legal when it was done. Article I, Section 10 forbids states to pass such laws.
w: It violates the Full Faith and Credit Clause
Full Faith and Credit concerns honoring other states' acts and rulings, not retroactive punishment.
Only Congress may pass laws that punish past acts
Congress is also forbidden to pass ex post facto laws under Article I, Section 9.
It denies a jury trial guaranteed by Article III
The problem is the law's retroactive punishment, not the trial procedure.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state legislature passes a law making it a crime to have sold a certain product last year, when selling it was legal, and orders that past sellers be fined.

items.q: Congress created the U.S. Air Force in 1947, though Article I mentions only armies and a navy. This action is best classified as an example of…
items.a: An implied power
items.ex: The power comes from the listed powers to raise armies and maintain a navy, combined with the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: An expressed power
Expressed powers are written out; an air force is not mentioned in the text.
A reserved power
Reserved powers belong to the states under the Tenth Amendment.
A concurrent power
Concurrent powers are shared by state and national governments; states cannot raise air forces.

alt.q: Which statement best defines implied powers?
alt.a: Unlisted powers reasonably drawn from listed ones
alt.ex: Implied powers are not written in the Constitution but are reasonably inferred from enumerated powers through the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: Powers specifically written in Article I, Section 8
That defines expressed (enumerated) powers.
Powers kept by the states under the Tenth Amendment
That defines reserved powers.
Powers used by both national and state governments
That defines concurrent powers.

alt.q: Which clause of Article I is the main textual basis for implied powers?
alt.a: The Necessary and Proper Clause
alt.ex: The final clause of Article I, Section 8 lets Congress make all laws “necessary and proper” for carrying out its listed powers.
w: The Interstate Commerce Clause
The Commerce Clause is itself an enumerated power over trade.
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme over conflicting state law.
The Origination Clause
The Origination Clause requires revenue bills to begin in the House.

items.q: Both Florida and the national government collect taxes and run court systems. These are examples of…
items.a: Concurrent powers
items.ex: Concurrent powers are held by both levels of government at the same time, such as taxing, borrowing and establishing courts.
w: Reserved powers
Reserved powers belong to the states alone under the Tenth Amendment.
Implied powers
Implied powers are unlisted federal powers drawn from the Necessary and Proper Clause.
Enumerated powers
Enumerated powers are those listed for the national government, mainly in Article I, Section 8.

alt.q: Which power is best described as concurrent?
alt.a: Borrowing money
alt.ex: Both the states and the national government may borrow money, so it is a concurrent power.
w: Declaring war
Declaring war is an expressed power of Congress alone.
Coining money
Coining money is national only; Article I, Section 10 denies it to states.
Issuing marriage licenses
Marriage licensing is a reserved power of the states.

alt.q: Which statement best defines concurrent powers?
