items.q: The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) protects the vote for President, Vice President, presidential electors, Senator, or Representative, which "shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any State by reason of failure to pay any poll tax or other tax." Its ban applied to
items.a: federal elections only
items.ex: The 24th covered elections for President, Vice President, and Congress; Harper v. Virginia (1966) later barred poll taxes in state elections.
w: state and local elections only
State elections were reached by Harper v. Virginia, not the amendment.
every election at all levels
The text lists only federal offices.
primary elections only
It covers primaries and general elections for federal office.

alt.q: In 1965, Virginia still charged a poll tax to vote in state elections. In Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966), the Supreme Court struck it down using
alt.a: the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Harper held that making wealth or fee payment a voting qualification violates the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
w: the Twenty-fourth Amendment
The 24th covered only federal elections.
the Fifteenth Amendment
The 15th concerns race; Harper rested on equal protection.
the Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause gives Congress implied powers.

alt.q: Poll taxes were used mainly to
alt.a: keep poor and Black citizens from voting
alt.ex: Poll taxes in Jim Crow states disenfranchised Black and poor white voters until the 24th Amendment and Harper v. Virginia ended them.
w: pay for printing ballots and polling places
Their main effect, and often purpose, was disenfranchisement.
fund state schools for new voters
Revenue was not their main purpose.
reduce fraud by verifying citizenship
Paying a tax does not verify citizenship.

items.q: During the Vietnam War, many 18-year-olds could be drafted but could not vote. Which amendment responded to this argument?
items.a: Twenty-sixth Amendment
items.ex: The 26th Amendment (1971) bars denying the vote to citizens 18 or older on account of age.
w: Twenty-fourth Amendment
The 24th banned poll taxes in federal elections.
Twenty-third Amendment
The 23rd gave D.C. electoral votes for President.
Nineteenth Amendment
The 19th barred sex discrimination in voting.

alt.q: "The right of citizens of the United States, who are eighteen years of age or older, to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of age." This 1971 amendment was a response mainly to
alt.a: young people drafted to fight in Vietnam
alt.ex: "Old enough to fight, old enough to vote" drove ratification of the 26th Amendment in about 100 days.
w: women's demands after World War I
That led to the 19th Amendment (1920).
poll taxes used in the Jim Crow South
That led to the 24th Amendment (1964).
D.C. residents lacking any electoral votes
That led to the 23rd Amendment (1961).

alt.q: Oregon v. Mitchell (1970) held that Congress could set an 18-year-old voting age only for federal elections. How was the resulting confusion resolved?
alt.a: The 26th Amendment set age 18 for all elections
alt.ex: Rather than run separate federal and state voter rolls, states quickly ratified the 26th Amendment in 1971.
w: Congress passed a law forcing every state to comply
Mitchell had just held Congress could not do that by statute.
The Court reversed itself the following year
The Court did not reverse Mitchell; an amendment was needed.
Each state chose its own age for state elections
The 26th Amendment set a uniform national rule.

mt.q: Match each amendment to what it did.
pairs: No poll taxes in federal elections
mt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.

items.q: Which amendment is correctly matched to the group of voters it protected?
items.a: Twenty-sixth: citizens aged 18 to 20
items.ex: The 26th lowered the voting age to 18; the 15th covered race, the 19th sex, and the 24th poll taxes.
w: Nineteenth: formerly enslaved men
The 19th covered sex; race was the 15th.
Fifteenth: women of all races
The 15th covered race; women got the vote in the 19th.
Twenty-third: citizens too poor to pay
The 23rd gave D.C. electoral votes; poll taxes were the 24th.

alt.q: What do the 15th, 19th, 24th, and 26th Amendments have in common?
alt.a: Each bars denying the vote on a specific basis
alt.ex: Each says the right to vote "shall not be denied or abridged" because of race, sex, failure to pay a tax, or age (18+).
w: Each gives Congress sole power over voter rules
States still run elections within these limits.
Each makes voting mandatory for adult citizens
None requires anyone to vote.
Each was ratified during the Reconstruction era
Only the 15th (1870) was from Reconstruction.

alt.q: In 1968, a 19-year-old in Ohio could not vote, and a voter in 1962 Texas had to pay a fee to vote for Congress. Which amendments later removed these barriers?
alt.a: The 26th and the 24th
alt.ex: The 26th (1971) set the voting age at 18, and the 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections.
w: The 19th and the 15th
The 19th covered sex and the 15th race.
The 23rd and the 25th
The 23rd gave D.C. electoral votes; the 25th covers succession.
The 17th and the 16th
The 17th made senators popularly elected; the 16th allowed an income tax.

items.q: What did the 17th Amendment do?
items.a: Direct election of senators
items.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: Women's right to vote
That goes with 19th Amendment.
No poll taxes in federal elections
That goes with 24th Amendment.
Voting age lowered to 18
That goes with 26th Amendment.

alt.q: What did the 19th Amendment do?
alt.a: Women's right to vote
alt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: Direct election of senators
That goes with 17th Amendment.
No poll taxes in federal elections
That goes with 24th Amendment.
Voting age lowered to 18
That goes with 26th Amendment.

alt.q: What did the 24th Amendment do?
alt.a: No poll taxes in federal elections
alt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: Direct election of senators
That goes with 17th Amendment.
Women's right to vote
That goes with 19th Amendment.
Voting age lowered to 18
That goes with 26th Amendment.

alt.q: What did the 26th Amendment do?
alt.a: Voting age lowered to 18
alt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: Direct election of senators
That goes with 17th Amendment.
Women's right to vote
That goes with 19th Amendment.
No poll taxes in federal elections
That goes with 24th Amendment.

alt.q: Which amendment did this: “Direct election of senators”?
alt.a: 17th Amendment
alt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: 19th Amendment
19th Amendment: Women's right to vote.
24th Amendment
24th Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections.
26th Amendment
26th Amendment: Voting age lowered to 18.

alt.q: Which amendment did this: “Women's right to vote”?
alt.a: 19th Amendment
alt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: 17th Amendment
17th Amendment: Direct election of senators.
24th Amendment
24th Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections.
26th Amendment
26th Amendment: Voting age lowered to 18.

alt.q: Which amendment did this: “No poll taxes in federal elections”?
alt.a: 24th Amendment
alt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: 17th Amendment
17th Amendment: Direct election of senators.
19th Amendment
19th Amendment: Women's right to vote.
26th Amendment
26th Amendment: Voting age lowered to 18.

alt.q: Which amendment did this: “Voting age lowered to 18”?
alt.a: 26th Amendment
alt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
w: 17th Amendment
17th Amendment: Direct election of senators.
19th Amendment
19th Amendment: Women's right to vote.
24th Amendment
24th Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections.

mt.q: Match each amendment to what it did.
pairs: No poll taxes in federal elections
mt.ex: 17th (1913) senators elected directly by voters; 19th (1920) women's right to vote; 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.

items.q: In Ramos v. Louisiana (2020), the Supreme Court held that…
items.a: state convictions for serious crimes need unanimous juries
items.ex: The Court held that the Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial, incorporated against the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, requires a unanimous verdict to convict of a serious offense.
w: states may set any jury vote they choose for serious crimes
Ramos held that a non-unanimous verdict violates the Sixth Amendment in state courts.
juries are not required in state murder trials
The right to a jury trial in serious state criminal cases was incorporated in 1968.
only federal courts must provide juries in criminal cases
The Sixth Amendment jury right applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Evangelisto Ramos was convicted of murder in Louisiana after a jury voted 10 to 2 to convict him, which state law then allowed. He appealed, arguing that the Constitution requires a unanimous verdict.

alt.q: Which case applied the Sixth Amendment's requirement of a unanimous jury verdict to state criminal trials?
alt.a: Ramos v. Louisiana (2020)
alt.ex: In Ramos v. Louisiana (2020), the Court held that the incorporated Sixth Amendment requires unanimous juries to convict for serious offenses in state courts.
w: Timbs v. Indiana (2019)
Timbs incorporated the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause.
Gideon v. Wainwright (1963)
Gideon required states to provide lawyers to poor defendants in felony cases.
Mapp v. Ohio (1961)
Mapp applied the exclusionary rule for illegally seized evidence to the states.

alt.q: Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) is an example of selective incorporation because the Court…
alt.a: applied a Sixth Amendment rule to state trials
alt.ex: Selective incorporation applies Bill of Rights protections to the states one by one through the Fourteenth Amendment. Ramos applied the Sixth Amendment's unanimity requirement to state trials.
w: applied the Bill of Rights only to Congress
That was the rule of Barron v. Baltimore (1833), which incorporation moved away from.
let each state choose its own jury voting rule
Ramos took that choice away by requiring unanimity.
applied a state jury rule to the federal courts
Incorporation applies federal rights to the states, not state rules to federal courts.

items.q: Which statement best describes selective incorporation?
items.a: Applying Bill of Rights protections to states case by case
items.ex: Through the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause, the Court has applied most Bill of Rights guarantees to the states one right at a time.
w: Applying every Bill of Rights protection to states at once
That is total incorporation, urged by Justice Hugo Black but never adopted.
Letting states choose which federal laws they will follow
That is nullification, which the Constitution rejects.
Adding new rights to the Constitution by amendment
Amendments follow Article V; incorporation is done by court rulings.

alt.q: Through which constitutional provision has the Supreme Court applied most of the Bill of Rights to the states?
alt.a: The 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause
alt.ex: The Court reads the "liberty" protected by the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause to include fundamental Bill of Rights guarantees.
w: The 10th Amendment's reserved powers
The 10th protects state power; it does not apply rights to states.
The 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause
That clause defines citizenship; incorporation runs through due process.
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
Supremacy makes federal law prevail but did not itself apply the Bill of Rights to states.

alt.q: A defendant in a state court argues that a Bill of Rights guarantee binds the state because it has been "incorporated." What must the Supreme Court have found about that right?
alt.a: It is fundamental to liberty and justice
alt.ex: A right is incorporated when the Court finds it fundamental to the scheme of ordered liberty, protected by the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause.
w: It is listed in the state's own constitution
State constitutions do not decide federal incorporation.
It was approved by a majority of the states
Incorporation is done by Court decisions, not state votes.
It applies only to federal criminal trials
A right limited to federal trials would by definition not be incorporated.

items.q: In Barron v. Baltimore (1833), the Supreme Court held that the Bill of Rights
items.a: limited only the federal government, not states
items.ex: Chief Justice Marshall ruled the Bill of Rights restrained only the national government, which is why later incorporation through the 14th Amendment mattered.
w: applied fully to the states through due process
There was no 14th Amendment until 1868.
limited the states but not the federal government
This reverses Barron's holding.
protected only rights also listed in state charters
Barron did not tie federal rights to state constitutions.

alt.q: In 1833, a wharf owner claimed the city of Baltimore destroyed the value of his wharf without just compensation. The Court ruled he had no federal claim because
alt.a: the 5th Amendment bound only the national government
alt.ex: Barron v. Baltimore (1833) held the Takings Clause, like the rest of the Bill of Rights, did not limit state or city governments.
w: the Takings Clause covered only land, not wharves
The Court did not rest on the type of property.
the city had already paid him fair market value
Barron received nothing; the case turned on whom the Bill of Rights binds.
property rights were reserved to the state governments alone
The ruling was about the reach of the Bill of Rights, not the Tenth Amendment.

alt.q: Why was the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) essential for later incorporation decisions?
alt.a: It limited the states with a due process guarantee
alt.ex: Its command that no State shall deprive any person of liberty without due process became the vehicle for applying the Bill of Rights to states.
w: It repealed the Bill of Rights' limits on Congress
The Bill of Rights still limits the federal government.
It gave Congress power to approve state laws
Congress has no general veto over state laws.
It listed every right that states must protect
It did not list them; the Court identified them case by case.

items.q: The Court assumed that freedom of speech and of the press "are among the fundamental personal rights and 'liberties' protected by the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment from impairment by the States." This 1925 statement came from
items.a: Gitlow v. New York
items.ex: Gitlow (1925) first assumed that First Amendment speech and press rights apply to the states, beginning selective incorporation.
w: Schenck v. United States
Schenck (1919) was a federal case creating the clear-and-present-danger test.
Barron v. Baltimore
Barron (1833) held the Bill of Rights did not apply to states.
Near v. Minnesota
Near (1931) later applied press freedom against prior restraint by a state.

alt.q: Gitlow v. New York (1925) is significant because the Court
alt.a: began applying free speech rights to the states
alt.ex: Although it upheld Gitlow's conviction, the Court assumed free speech is protected against states by the 14th Amendment.
w: first created the clear and present danger test
That was Schenck v. United States (1919).
struck down all state laws against sedition
Gitlow upheld New York's criminal anarchy law.
applied the exclusionary rule to state courts
That was Mapp v. Ohio (1961).

alt.q: A man was convicted under a New York criminal anarchy law for publishing a radical manifesto. The Court upheld the conviction but assumed free speech limits the states. This illustrates
alt.a: the start of selective incorporation
alt.ex: Gitlow v. New York (1925) is the first case applying a First Amendment right to the states through due process.
w: the doctrine of full or total incorporation
Total incorporation would apply all rights at once; the Court never adopted it.
the clear and present danger test
That test came from Schenck (1919), a federal case.
the dual-sovereignty rule of federalism
Dual sovereignty concerns separate state and federal prosecutions.

items.q: Chicago banned most handgun possession by residents. Two years after Heller, the Court ruled in 2010 that
items.a: the Second Amendment applies to state and city laws
items.ex: McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010) incorporated the Second Amendment against states and localities through the 14th Amendment.
w: the Second Amendment applies only to federal areas
That was the open question after Heller, which McDonald answered the other way.
cities may ban handguns under their police powers
McDonald struck down Chicago's ban.
the Tenth Amendment reserves gun laws to the states
States may regulate guns, but within Second Amendment limits.

alt.q: Which case incorporated the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms against the states?
alt.a: McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010)
alt.ex: McDonald (2010) applied Heller's individual right to state and local governments.
w: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008)
Heller involved D.C., a federal district, so it did not reach states.
United States v. Lopez (1995)
Lopez limited the Commerce Clause.
Printz v. United States (1997)
Printz barred commandeering local sheriffs.

alt.q: Why did D.C. v. Heller (2008) not settle whether state and city gun laws were bound by the Second Amendment?
alt.a: D.C. is a federal district, not a state
alt.ex: Because Washington, D.C., is under federal authority, Heller did not decide incorporation; McDonald (2010) did.
w: Heller involved only rifles, not handguns
Heller struck down a handgun ban.
Heller was decided under the Tenth Amendment
Heller was a Second Amendment case.
Heller applied only to members of militias
Heller recognized an individual right not tied to militias.

items.q: Cleveland police forced their way into a woman's home without a valid warrant and found obscene materials, which were used to convict her. In 1961 the Court ruled that
items.a: illegally seized evidence is barred in state courts
items.ex: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) applied the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule to the states.
w: illegally seized evidence may be used if it's reliable
Mapp held such evidence must be excluded.
suspects must be warned of their right to silence
That was Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
states must provide lawyers for poor defendants
That was Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).

alt.q: The exclusionary rule, applied to the states in Mapp v. Ohio (1961), means that
alt.a: illegally obtained evidence is barred from trial
alt.ex: Evidence gathered in violation of the Fourth Amendment generally cannot be used to convict.
w: illegally detained suspects must be freed at once
The rule concerns evidence, not release from custody.
certain groups may be excluded from jury service
Excluding jurors by race violates equal protection.
any illegal search requires dismissing the case
Only the tainted evidence is excluded; the case may continue.

alt.q: Which case extended the exclusionary rule for illegally seized evidence to state courts?
alt.a: Mapp v. Ohio (1961)
alt.ex: Mapp (1961) overruled the part of Wolf v. Colorado that let states use illegally seized evidence.
w: Wolf v. Colorado (1949)
Wolf applied the Fourth Amendment to states but declined to require exclusion.
Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
Miranda concerned confessions and warnings.
Katz v. U.S. (1967)
Katz defined a search by reasonable expectation of privacy.

items.q: Which Bill of Rights guarantee has the Supreme Court NOT applied to the states?
items.a: The Seventh Amendment's civil jury right
items.ex: The Seventh Amendment civil jury right, the Fifth's grand jury clause, and the Third Amendment remain unincorporated.
w: The Sixth Amendment's right to counsel
Incorporated in Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
The Eighth Amendment's excessive fines ban
Incorporated in Timbs v. Indiana (2019).
The Second Amendment's right to bear arms
Incorporated in McDonald v. Chicago (2010).

alt.q: A person sues their neighbor in a state court for $5,000 in property damage, and the state's rules provide no jury for such cases. Why doesn't the Seventh Amendment require one?
alt.a: It has not been incorporated against the states
alt.ex: The Seventh Amendment binds only federal courts; states set their own civil jury rules.
w: It applies only to suits worth under twenty dollars
It applies to suits over twenty dollars.
It covers only criminal, not civil, trials
The Seventh is specifically about civil suits.
It was repealed by the Fourteenth Amendment
No part of the Bill of Rights has been repealed.

alt.q: Which pair of rights remain unincorporated, so they bind only the federal government?
alt.a: Grand jury indictment; civil jury trial
alt.ex: Hurtado v. California (1884) declined to incorporate the grand jury clause, and the Seventh Amendment has not been applied to states.
w: Right to counsel; a speedy public trial
Both Sixth Amendment rights have been incorporated.
Free exercise; protection from takings
Both have been incorporated (Cantwell 1940; Chicago, B&Q R.R. 1897).
Excessive fines; unanimous jury verdict
Both were incorporated recently (Timbs 2019; Ramos 2020).

items.q: Indiana seized a man's $42,000 Land Rover after he pleaded guilty to a drug sale carrying a maximum fine of $10,000. In Timbs v. Indiana (2019), the Court held that
items.a: the Excessive Fines Clause applies to the states
items.ex: Timbs unanimously incorporated the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause through the 14th Amendment.
w: the Takings Clause required paying him for the car
Forfeiture as punishment is analyzed as a fine, not a taking.
forfeiture is never allowed in criminal cases
Forfeiture is allowed if it is not grossly disproportional.
the Fourth Amendment barred seizing the car
The case turned on the Eighth Amendment.

alt.q: Timbs v. Indiana (2019) is an example of selective incorporation because it
alt.a: applied an Eighth Amendment clause to the states
alt.ex: Timbs made the Excessive Fines Clause binding on states, one more right added case by case.
w: applied the Seventh Amendment to state courts
The Seventh remains unincorporated.
applied the Bill of Rights to all states at once
That would be total incorporation.
held that states must follow federal sentencing
States set their own sentences within constitutional limits.

alt.q: Which case incorporated the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause against the states?
alt.a: Timbs v. Indiana (2019)
alt.ex: Timbs (2019) involved forfeiture of a Land Rover worth far more than the maximum fine.
w: Robinson v. California (1962)
Robinson incorporated the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause.
Roper v. Simmons (2005)
Roper barred the juvenile death penalty.
Ramos v. Louisiana (2020)
Ramos required unanimous juries in state criminal trials.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Federalists during the ratification debate of 1787–1788?
items.a: Backers of ratification and a stronger central government
items.ex: Federalists such as Hamilton, Madison and Jay argued the new Constitution would fix the Articles' weaknesses while protecting liberty.
w: Opponents who feared a strong and distant central government
That describes the Anti-Federalists.
Supporters of keeping the Articles with only small changes
Revising the Articles was closer to the Anti-Federalist view.
Members of Jefferson's Democratic-Republican Party
That party formed in the 1790s, after ratification.

alt.q: Which writers produced The Federalist Papers under the pen name “Publius”?
alt.a: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
alt.ex: The 85 essays appeared in New York newspapers in 1787–1788; Hamilton wrote most, Madison about 29 and Jay five.
w: Patrick Henry, George Mason and Richard Henry Lee
These were prominent Anti-Federalists from Virginia.
Thomas Jefferson, John Adams and Benjamin Franklin
Jefferson and Adams were abroad; none of the three wrote the essays.
Robert Yates, Mercy Otis Warren and George Clinton
These were Anti-Federalists from New York and Massachusetts.

alt.q: The Federalist Papers were first published mainly to…
alt.a: Persuade New York to ratify the Constitution
alt.ex: The essays ran in New York newspapers to win over a state where opposition was strong.
w: Persuade Britain to recognize American independence
Britain recognized independence in the Treaty of Paris (1783).
Persuade Congress to add a bill of rights
Hamilton argued in No. 84 that a bill of rights was unnecessary.
Persuade Virginia to give up western lands
Western land cessions happened under the Articles.

items.q: Which group of leaders is most closely associated with the Anti-Federalist cause?
items.a: Patrick Henry, George Mason and Mercy Otis Warren
items.ex: Henry and Mason led opposition in Virginia, and Warren wrote against ratification as “A Columbian Patriot.”
w: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
These were the Federalist authors of The Federalist Papers.
George Washington, Benjamin Franklin and James Wilson
All three supported ratification.
John Marshall, John Adams and Roger Sherman
All three were Federalists or supported the Constitution.

alt.q: George Mason refused to sign the Constitution in 1787 mainly because it…
alt.a: Contained no declaration or bill of rights
alt.ex: Mason, author of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), began his written objections by noting there was no declaration of rights.
w: Gave the small states too much power in the House
The House is based on population, favoring large states.
Created a presidency that was much too weak
Anti-Federalists feared the presidency was too strong.
Abolished the state legislatures entirely
The Constitution kept the state legislatures.

alt.q: Patrick Henry, who refused to attend the Philadelphia Convention, opposed ratification in Virginia chiefly because he believed the Constitution…
alt.a: Endangered the states and individual liberty
alt.ex: Henry warned that the consolidated government, lacking a bill of rights, would swallow the states and threaten liberty.
w: Left the national government too weak to act
That was the Federalists' complaint about the Articles.
Failed to create any national court system
Article III created a Supreme Court, which Anti-Federalists feared.
Made the President an elected rather than hereditary office
Henry did not favor a hereditary executive.

items.q: Which argument was most typical of the Anti-Federalists?
items.a: A large republic would endanger liberty and states
items.ex: Anti-Federalists, drawing on Montesquieu, believed republics must be small and that a distant national government would threaten liberty.
w: A large republic best controls the effects of faction
That is Madison's Federalist argument in Federalist No. 10.
A bill of rights is unnecessary and even dangerous
That is Hamilton's Federalist argument in Federalist No. 84.
A single energetic executive ensures good government
That is Hamilton's Federalist argument in Federalist No. 70.

alt.q: “In a republic, the manners, sentiments, and interests of the people should be similar. If this be not the case, there will be a constant clashing of opinions…” This argument from Brutus No. 1 claims that…
alt.a: A republic as large as the U.S. could not succeed
alt.ex: Brutus (October 1787) argued that a vast, diverse nation could not be governed as a free republic.
w: A large republic would best control faction
This is Madison's opposite argument in Federalist No. 10.
A republic needs a strong executive to settle disputes
Brutus feared, rather than favored, strong national power.
A bill of rights would protect minority opinions
This passage concerns size and diversity, not a bill of rights.

alt.q: Which document is the best-known Anti-Federalist essay warning against a consolidated national government?
alt.a: Brutus No. 1
alt.ex: Brutus No. 1 (1787), published in New York, argued that the Constitution would create one consolidated government.
w: Federalist No. 10
Federalist No. 10 is Madison's pro-ratification essay on factions.
Federalist No. 51
Federalist No. 51 is Madison's pro-ratification essay on checks and balances.
Common Sense
Common Sense (1776) by Thomas Paine argued for independence.

items.q: “Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens…” Which argument does Madison make here?
items.a: A large republic makes oppressive majorities rarer
items.ex: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that a large, diverse republic controls the effects of faction because no single faction can easily form a majority.
w: A small republic best protects the rights of minorities
That was the Anti-Federalist view Madison was answering.
Separate branches should check one another's ambition
That is Madison's argument in Federalist No. 51.
A bill of rights is needed to protect citizens' rights
That was the Anti-Federalist demand, not this passage's point.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argues that the causes of faction cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so the best remedy is to…
alt.a: Control their effects with a large republic
alt.ex: Since faction is “sown in the nature of man,” Madison proposed controlling its effects through representation in an extended republic.
w: Ban political parties by passing a federal law
Madison said removing causes would destroy liberty.
Give each state a veto over national laws
Madison wanted to strengthen, not weaken, the national government.
Elect a strong executive to suppress them
Federalist No. 10 relies on size and representation, not the executive.

alt.q: Which group most directly rejected this argument, insisting that free republics must be small?
alt.a: Anti-Federalists, such as Brutus
alt.ex: Brutus No. 1 argued that a republic must be small with similar interests, directly opposing Madison's extended republic.
w: Federalists, such as Hamilton
Hamilton co-wrote The Federalist and supported the extended republic.
Loyalists, such as Thomas Hutchinson
Loyalists sided with Britain during the Revolution.
Framers who backed the Virginia Plan
Virginia Plan supporters wanted a strong national government.

items.q: “For why declare that things shall not be done which there is no power to do?” In Federalist No. 84, Alexander Hamilton used this question to argue that…
items.a: A bill of rights was unneeded in the Constitution
items.ex: Hamilton argued that because Congress had only enumerated powers, listing restrictions was unnecessary and could even be dangerous.
w: The President should not hold a veto over Congress
Hamilton defended the veto elsewhere; No. 84 is about a bill of rights.
Congress should list every right it may not violate
This is the opposite of Hamilton's argument.
The Supreme Court should not review acts of Congress
Hamilton defended judicial review in Federalist No. 78.

alt.q: Which amendment answered the concern that listing some rights might imply that unlisted rights were unprotected?
alt.a: The Ninth Amendment
alt.ex: The Ninth Amendment says the enumeration of certain rights “shall not be construed to deny or disparage others retained by the people.”
w: The Tenth Amendment
The Tenth reserves powers, not rights, to the states or the people.
The First Amendment
The First protects religion, speech, press, assembly and petition.
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth (1868) limits the states through due process and equal protection.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the Federalist position on a bill of rights in 1787–1788?
alt.a: Unneeded, since Congress held only listed powers
alt.ex: Federalists argued that a government of enumerated powers had no authority to violate rights in the first place.
w: Essential, since Congress held unlimited powers
That reflects Anti-Federalist fears.
Needed only to restrain the state governments
Federalists did not argue this.
Needed to protect slavery in the Southern states
The ratification debate over a bill of rights did not turn on this.

items.q: Why did Federalists promise to add a bill of rights after ratification?
items.a: To win votes in divided states like Massachusetts and Virginia
items.ex: Federalists accepted recommended amendments to secure ratification; Madison then introduced the amendments in 1789, and they were ratified in 1791.
w: To satisfy a demand made by the British government
Britain played no role in ratification.
Because Article VII required one before the Constitution took effect
Article VII required only nine state conventions.
To give the national government more power over the states
A bill of rights limits, rather than expands, national power.

alt.q: Which leader, once doubtful that a bill of rights was needed, introduced the proposed amendments in the First Congress in 1789?
alt.a: James Madison
alt.ex: Madison kept his ratification-campaign promise and drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights (ratified 1791).
w: Alexander Hamilton
Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 84 that a bill of rights was unnecessary.
George Mason
Mason demanded a bill of rights but did not serve in the First Congress.
Thomas Jefferson
Jefferson urged a bill of rights by letter but was minister to France.

alt.q: The “Massachusetts Compromise” of February 1788 helped secure ratification by…
alt.a: Ratifying while recommending amendments for later
alt.ex: Massachusetts ratified and attached recommended amendments; other states, including Virginia and New York, followed this model.
w: Making ratification depend on a second convention
Conditional ratification was rejected in favor of recommendations.
Giving Massachusetts extra seats in the Senate
Every state receives two senators.
Delaying a vote until a bill of rights was adopted
Massachusetts ratified before any bill of rights existed.

items.q: At a 1788 ratifying convention, a delegate warns that the Necessary and Proper Clause and the Supremacy Clause will let Congress swallow up the state governments. This delegate is most likely…
items.a: An Anti-Federalist opposing ratification
items.ex: Anti-Federalists feared these clauses would create a consolidated government and destroy state sovereignty.
w: A Federalist defending ratification
Federalists defended these clauses as needed for an effective government.
A delegate seeking stronger national power
This delegate fears, not seeks, national power.
A delegate favoring an end to the states
The delegate wants to protect the states.

alt.q: Which features of the Constitution did Anti-Federalists most often cite as threats to the states?
alt.a: The Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses
alt.ex: Brutus and others argued these clauses gave Congress nearly unlimited power and made federal law override the states.
w: The ban on religious tests for federal office
This was not a central Anti-Federalist complaint about state power.
Equal representation of the states in the Senate
Equal Senate votes protected the states' role.
The rule requiring nine states to ratify
This concerned adoption, not ongoing federal power.

alt.q: The Tenth Amendment is best understood as a response to which concern?
alt.a: Anti-Federalist fears of national power
alt.ex: The Tenth Amendment reassured critics that powers not delegated remained with the states or the people.
w: Federalist fears of disorder like Shays' Rebellion
That concern led to a stronger national government, not the Tenth.
Small-state fears about representation in the House
That was settled by the Great Compromise.
Southern fears about ending the slave trade
That was addressed by Article I, Section 9.

items.q: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” Madison used this argument in Federalist No. 51 to defend…
items.a: Checks and balances among separate branches
items.ex: Federalist No. 51 argues each branch must have the means and motive to resist encroachment by the others.
w: A large republic to control the effects of faction
That is the argument of Federalist No. 10.
Life tenure for judges as the least dangerous branch
That is Hamilton's argument in Federalist No. 78.
A single executive with energy and unity
That is Hamilton's argument in Federalist No. 70.

alt.q: Federalist No. 51 argues that liberty in the American “compound republic” is protected because power is divided…
alt.a: Between two levels and among the branches
alt.ex: Madison described a “double security”: power split between national and state governments and then among separate departments.
w: Only among the three national branches
This omits the division between national and state governments.
Only between the states and the nation
This omits the separation of branches.
Among the people, the states and the churches
Churches play no role in Madison's scheme.

alt.q: Which famous line comes from Federalist No. 51?
alt.a: “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.”
alt.ex: Madison used this line to argue that government must be controlled by internal checks as well as by the people.
w: “These are the times that try men's souls.”
Thomas Paine wrote this in The American Crisis (1776).
“Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition…”
Hamilton wrote this in Federalist No. 70.
“the power to tax involves the power to destroy”
John Marshall wrote this in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).

items.q: What is generally considered the Anti-Federalists' most lasting contribution to American government?
items.a: Pressure that produced the Bill of Rights
items.ex: Although they lost the ratification fight, Anti-Federalist demands produced the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791.
w: Defeat of the Constitution in most of the states
All thirteen states eventually ratified.
Creation of the Electoral College system
The Electoral College was designed at the 1787 Convention.
Writing of the essays in The Federalist Papers
Federalists Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote those essays.

alt.q: North Carolina and Rhode Island did not ratify until 1789 and 1790. Their delay best shows that…
alt.a: Concerns about rights and state power persisted
alt.ex: North Carolina ratified in November 1789 after amendments were proposed, and Rhode Island in May 1790, under pressure.
w: The Constitution needed unanimous approval to begin
Article VII required only nine states.
Federalists controlled every state convention
Anti-Federalists controlled those two states' decisions.
Most states opposed adding a bill of rights
Most states had recommended amendments.

alt.q: Which state ratified the Constitution last, in May 1790, after the Bill of Rights had been proposed?
alt.a: Rhode Island
alt.ex: Rhode Island, which had boycotted the Convention, ratified on May 29, 1790.
w: North Carolina
North Carolina ratified in November 1789.
New York
New York ratified in July 1788.
Virginia
Virginia ratified in June 1788 as the tenth state.

items.q: “Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government.” Hamilton used this line in Federalist No. 70 to argue for…
items.a: A single, vigorous President, not a council
items.ex: Hamilton argued that unity in one executive brings decisiveness and clear accountability, against proposals for a plural executive.
w: A plural executive shared among several officials
This is the idea Hamilton opposed.
A President chosen directly by Congress
The Convention rejected congressional selection in favor of electors.
A President limited to only a single term
The Constitution set no term limit until the 22nd Amendment (1951).

alt.q: In which essay did Alexander Hamilton argue that a single, energetic President would make government decisive and accountable?
alt.a: Federalist No. 70
alt.ex: Hamilton wrote the essays on the executive; No. 70 argues that unity in the executive brings “energy” and clear responsibility.
w: Federalist No. 10
Madison's No. 10 argues that a large republic controls the effects of faction.
Federalist No. 51
Madison's No. 51 defends checks and balances: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.”
Federalist No. 78
Hamilton's No. 78 defends judicial independence and calls the judiciary the “least dangerous” branch.

alt.q: Anti-Federalists who criticized the presidency most often feared it would…
alt.a: Grow into an elected form of monarchy
alt.ex: Critics warned that a powerful President with command of the army and no term limits could become a king.
w: Be too weak to enforce the national laws
That was the Federalists' concern about the Articles.
Be chosen far too often to remain stable
Four-year terms were not a central objection.
Be filled by citizens born in other countries
The natural-born requirement addressed that.

items.q: In Wickard v. Filburn (1942), the Supreme Court upheld federal limits on wheat a farmer grew only for use on his own farm. What reasoning did the Court use?
items.a: Many farmers' combined actions substantially affect interstate commerce
items.ex: The Court admitted one farmer's home-grown wheat had a tiny effect, but held that wheat grown for home use by many farmers, taken together, substantially affects the national wheat market. This “aggregate effects” reasoning greatly widened Congress's Commerce Clause power.
w: Any wheat grown on a farm will eventually be sold to buyers in other states
The Court did not rely on the wheat crossing state lines; it relied on the combined effect of home-grown wheat on the national market.
Farming is a form of navigation between the several states
Navigation was the issue in Gibbons v. Ogden (1824); Wickard was about the effect of farming on the interstate wheat market.
The states had agreed to give Congress control over their farms
No such state consent was involved; the Court relied on Congress's own commerce power.

alt.q: Based on Wickard v. Filburn (1942), how would the Supreme Court most likely rule?
alt.a: for the government, since home-grown wheat affects the wheat market
alt.ex: In Wickard v. Filburn (1942), the Court upheld a penalty on a farmer who grew more wheat than his quota allowed, even though he used it on his own farm. Wheat grown for home use, added up across many farms, substantially affects interstate commerce.
w: for the farmer, because his extra wheat never entered interstate trade
The Court rejected this exact argument; the combined effect of home-grown wheat on the market was enough.
for the farmer, because agriculture is reserved to the states
Wickard held that Congress may regulate farm production that substantially affects interstate commerce.
for the government, because the quota is a valid tax on farmers
The Court upheld the wheat quota under the Commerce Clause, not the taxing power.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A federal law limits how much wheat each farmer may plant in order to stabilize prices. A farmer plants about twice his allowed amount and argues that federal law cannot reach the extra wheat because he feeds it to his own animals and never sells it.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case held that Congress may regulate a local activity because the combined, nationwide effect of many such activities on interstate commerce is substantial?
alt.a: Wickard v. Filburn (1942)
alt.ex: Wickard v. Filburn (1942) upheld federal wheat quotas applied to wheat a farmer grew for his own use, reasoning that the total effect of many farmers doing the same thing substantially affects interstate commerce.
w: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Gibbons held that commerce includes navigation between states; it did not involve local farm production.
United States v. Lopez (1995)
Lopez limited the commerce power, striking down a federal ban on guns in school zones.
Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918)
Hammer struck down a federal child labor law under a narrow view of the commerce power; it was later overruled.

items.q: In Gonzales v. Raich (2005), the Supreme Court ruled that federal drug law could be enforced against Californians who grew marijuana at home for medical use allowed by state law. Which statement best explains the ruling?
items.a: Local growing is part of a national market Congress may regulate
items.ex: Relying on Wickard v. Filburn (1942), the Court held 6–3 that the Commerce Clause, together with the Necessary and Proper Clause, lets Congress ban local cultivation and use because home-grown marijuana affects the national market for the drug.
w: California's medical marijuana law violated the Due Process Clause
The case was about the reach of Congress's commerce power, not whether California's law violated due process.
The Tenth Amendment gives drug policy solely to the national government
The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people; it gives nothing to the national government.
Marijuana grown at home counts as commerce with foreign nations
The Court treated the activity as part of a national (interstate) market, not foreign commerce.

alt.q: Gonzales v. Raich (2005) shows that, even after United States v. Lopez (1995), the Supreme Court
alt.a: still let Congress regulate local economic activity
alt.ex: Lopez (1995) struck down a law regulating gun possession, which was not economic activity. In Raich (2005), the Court distinguished Lopez and upheld federal power over home-grown marijuana because growing a marketable drug is economic activity tied to a national market.
w: returned all regulation of drugs to the states
Raich upheld federal drug law over a conflicting state medical marijuana law.
overruled Lopez and restored unlimited federal power
Raich distinguished Lopez rather than overruling it; limits on the commerce power remain.
ended the use of the Commerce Clause for criminal laws
Raich upheld the federal Controlled Substances Act, a criminal law, under the Commerce Clause.

alt.q: Based on Gonzales v. Raich (2005), which conclusion is most accurate?
alt.a: Federal law applies, since Congress regulates the national market
alt.ex: In Gonzales v. Raich (2005), the Court held that Congress's commerce power reaches plants grown at home for personal use when Congress regulates a national market for that product, even where state law allows it.
w: State law controls, because the plants were never sold to anyone
Raich rejected this argument, relying on Wickard v. Filburn's reasoning about goods produced for one's own use.
Federal law applies only if the plants were carried across a state line
The Court upheld federal power over plants that never left the state.
State law controls under the Full Faith and Credit Clause
Full Faith and Credit concerns states honoring one another's records and judgments, not conflicts with federal law.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state allows residents to grow a certain plant at home for personal medical use. A federal law bans growing that plant anywhere in the country. Federal agents seize plants that a resident grew at home and never sold.

items.q: In United States v. Morrison (2000), the Supreme Court struck down a part of the Violence Against Women Act that let victims sue attackers in federal court. What was the Court's main Commerce Clause reason?
items.a: Gender-motivated violence is not economic activity
items.ex: In a 5–4 decision following United States v. Lopez (1995), the Court held that gender-motivated violent crime is not economic activity, so Congress could not reach it under the Commerce Clause, even with findings about its overall economic effects.
w: Congress may never create federal crimes or civil remedies
Congress creates many federal crimes and remedies; the problem was the lack of a link to economic activity.
The law violated the accused's Sixth Amendment rights
The case was decided on the limits of Congress's powers, not on the rights of accused persons.
Only the President may regulate violence between states
The Constitution gives lawmaking power to Congress; the issue was the scope of that power.

alt.q: Which pair of Supreme Court cases both limited Congress's Commerce Clause power by ruling that the conduct being regulated was not economic activity?
alt.a: United States v. Lopez and United States v. Morrison
alt.ex: Lopez (1995) struck down a ban on guns in school zones and Morrison (2000) struck down a federal civil remedy for gender-motivated violence; in both, the Court said the regulated conduct was not economic activity.
w: Gibbons v. Ogden and Wickard v. Filburn
Both of these cases expanded or affirmed Congress's commerce power.
Heart of Atlanta Motel and Gonzales v. Raich
Both of these cases upheld federal laws under the Commerce Clause.
McCulloch v. Maryland and NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel
McCulloch upheld the national bank and Jones & Laughlin upheld federal labor law; neither limited the commerce power.

alt.q: Which reasoning from United States v. Morrison (2000) best supports the court's decision?
alt.a: Noneconomic violent crime is not commerce Congress can regulate
alt.ex: In Morrison (2000), the Court refused to let Congress add up the effects of noneconomic violent crime to reach it under the Commerce Clause, leaving such crimes mainly to the states.
w: Victims must file in state courts because of the Seventh Amendment
The Seventh Amendment concerns civil jury trials, not which court hears a case.
Congress is not allowed to study the national economy
Congress may make findings; the Court simply held the findings could not turn noneconomic crime into commerce.
The law took attackers' property without just compensation
The Takings Clause was not the basis of the decision.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law letting victims of gender-motivated violent crimes sue their attackers in federal court. Congress argues that such crimes, added up nationwide, reduce travel and business. A court strikes down the law.

items.q: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), Chief Justice John Roberts concluded that the Affordable Care Act's requirement to buy health insurance was not a valid use of the commerce power. Why?
items.a: Congress may regulate commerce but not compel people to engage in it
items.ex: Roberts wrote that the Commerce Clause lets Congress regulate existing commercial activity, not force people who are inactive to buy a product. The mandate was nonetheless upheld as a tax.
w: Health care is not an economic activity that crosses state lines at all
The Court did not say health care is noneconomic; it objected to compelling people to enter the market.
Insurance companies sell policies only within one state at a time
The ruling did not rest on where insurance is sold.
The mandate was never approved by the Senate as the Constitution requires
The Affordable Care Act passed both houses of Congress; the issue was the scope of Congress's power.

alt.q: Although the Court in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) rejected the Commerce Clause argument, it upheld the individual health insurance mandate under which power of Congress?
alt.a: the power to lay and collect taxes
alt.ex: The Court treated the payment owed by people without insurance as a tax, so the mandate was upheld under Congress's taxing power even though it failed under the Commerce Clause.
w: the power to regulate foreign commerce
The Court held the mandate could not be upheld as a regulation of commerce of any kind.
the power to establish post offices
The postal power has nothing to do with health insurance.
the power to coin money
The coinage power concerns currency, not health insurance.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the limit on the commerce power described in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012)?
alt.a: Congress can regulate activity but cannot force people into commerce
alt.ex: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), Chief Justice Roberts reasoned that the power to regulate commerce assumes existing commercial activity; it does not include the power to compel people to buy a product.
w: Congress can regulate only goods that physically cross over state lines
The Court has long allowed Congress to regulate local activity that substantially affects interstate commerce.
Congress can regulate only businesses with more than fifty workers
No such size rule exists in the Constitution or in the decision.
Congress can regulate commerce only with the consent of the states
The Commerce Clause does not require state consent.

items.q: Before 1937, the Supreme Court often treated manufacturing and labor as local matters beyond Congress's reach. In NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp. (1937), the Court changed course by holding that Congress may regulate
items.a: local activity closely tied to interstate commerce
items.ex: Upholding the National Labor Relations Act, the Court said Congress may regulate intrastate activities that have a close and substantial relation to interstate commerce. This began a long era of broad Commerce Clause rulings, such as Wickard (1942) and Heart of Atlanta Motel (1964).
w: only goods while they are moving between states
That was closer to the older, narrow view the Court moved away from in 1937.
any activity at all, with no constitutional limit of any kind
The Court said effects that are too indirect or remote remain beyond federal power.
only factories owned by the federal government
Jones & Laughlin was a private steel company.

alt.q: Which statement best summarizes how the Supreme Court's reading of the Commerce Clause changed during the 20th century?
alt.a: Narrow early on, much broader after 1937, then some limits in 1995
alt.ex: Early 1900s cases such as Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918) read the power narrowly; from 1937 (Jones & Laughlin) through Wickard (1942) and Heart of Atlanta (1964) it grew much broader; United States v. Lopez (1995) set new limits.
w: Broad early on, much narrower after 1937, then unlimited in 1995
This reverses the actual pattern; 1937 began the broad era and Lopez (1995) imposed limits.
Unchanged throughout the century, as first defined in Gibbons
The Court's reading changed significantly over the century.
Broad until 1995, when the Court limited it to goods in transit only
Lopez limited the power but still allowed regulation of activities that substantially affect interstate commerce.

alt.q: Which law did the Supreme Court uphold in NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp. (1937), a turning point in Commerce Clause interpretation?
alt.a: the National Labor Relations Act
alt.ex: Jones & Laughlin (1937) upheld the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, which protected workers' rights to organize, ruling that labor disputes at a large steel plant could disrupt interstate commerce.
w: the Civil Rights Act of 1964
The Civil Rights Act's public accommodations section was upheld in Heart of Atlanta Motel (1964).
the Gun-Free School Zones Act
This law was struck down in United States v. Lopez (1995).
the Violence Against Women Act of 1994
Part of this law was struck down in United States v. Morrison (2000).

items.q: Which problem under the Articles of Confederation most directly led the framers to include the Commerce Clause in the Constitution?
items.a: States taxed and restricted one another's trade
items.ex: Under the Articles, Congress had no power to regulate trade, and states placed taxes and restrictions on goods from other states and foreign nations, causing conflict. The Commerce Clause gave Congress power to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among the states, and with Indian tribes.
w: Congress imposed heavy taxes on trade between states
Under the Articles, Congress had no power to tax or to regulate trade.
The President refused to sign trade treaties with Europe
The Articles created no President or separate executive branch.
National courts kept striking down state trade laws
The Articles created no national court system to strike down state laws.

alt.q: Which weakness of the Articles of Confederation did this clause correct?
alt.a: Congress's lack of power to regulate trade
alt.ex: The Commerce Clause (Article I, Section 8) gave Congress the power over trade that it lacked under the Articles, ending the confusion of separate state trade policies.
w: Congress's lack of power to declare war
Congress under the Articles could declare war; this clause concerns commerce.
the absence of any national legislature
The Articles did create a national legislature, the Confederation Congress.
Congress's lack of power to make foreign treaties
Congress under the Articles could make treaties; this clause concerns commerce.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article I, Section 8 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes;”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which constitutional provision gives Congress the power to address this problem today?
alt.a: the Commerce Clause
alt.ex: The Commerce Clause gives Congress power to regulate commerce “among the several States,” which lets it prevent states from waging trade wars against each other, a major problem under the Articles of Confederation.
w: the Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause requires states to respect one another's public acts, records, and court rulings, not to regulate trade.
the Foreign Emoluments Clause
This clause bars federal officers from taking foreign gifts without Congress's consent.
the Guarantee Clause
This clause promises each state a republican form of government.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Two neighboring states each place heavy taxes on goods brought in from the other. Merchants in both states suffer, and the national legislature has no power to stop the states. This was a common complaint in the 1780s.

items.q: “To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes…” Congress relied on this power to pass which law, upheld in Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964)?
items.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
items.ex: The Court upheld the Act's ban on discrimination in public accommodations because such discrimination burdened interstate travel and commerce.
w: The Voting Rights Act of 1965
That law enforced the Fifteenth Amendment's voting protections.
The Pendleton Act of 1883
That law created merit-based civil service hiring.
The Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990
That law was struck down as beyond the commerce power in U.S. v. Lopez (1995).

alt.q: A motel serving mostly interstate travelers refuses to rent rooms to Black guests. Congress's power to ban this discrimination was upheld under…
alt.a: The Commerce Clause
alt.ex: In Heart of Atlanta Motel v. U.S. (1964), the Court held that racial discrimination by businesses serving travelers affected interstate commerce.
w: The Equal Protection Clause
That clause limits state action; the motel was a private business.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns states honoring one another's acts and rulings.
The Emoluments Clause
That clause bars officials from taking unapproved payments or gifts.

alt.q: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) is a key Commerce Clause case because the Court held that…
alt.a: Congress's commerce power covers navigation between states
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall read “commerce” broadly to include navigation and struck down New York's steamboat monopoly as it conflicted with a federal license.
w: States may grant monopolies over interstate waterways
The Court struck down New York's monopoly.
Congress may not regulate trade within any state's borders
The ruling expanded, not restricted, federal power.
Commerce means only the buying and selling of goods
Marshall rejected this narrow definition.

items.q: In United States v. Lopez (1995), the Supreme Court struck down a federal ban on guns in school zones mainly because…
items.a: Congress overstepped its interstate commerce power
items.ex: The Court held that carrying a gun near a school is not economic activity substantially affecting interstate commerce, the first such limit since 1937.
w: The ban violated the Second Amendment right to bear arms
The case was decided on Commerce Clause grounds, not the Second Amendment.
The ban conflicted with the Supremacy Clause of Article VI
Supremacy concerns valid federal law over state law; the law here was invalid.
Congress has no power to regulate any firearms at all
Congress regulates firearms in commerce; Lopez was narrower.

alt.q: Which case was the first in nearly sixty years to limit Congress's power under the Commerce Clause?
alt.a: United States v. Lopez (1995)
alt.ex: Lopez ended a long line of decisions since 1937 that had upheld nearly every use of the commerce power.
w: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Gibbons expanded the commerce power.
Heart of Atlanta Motel v. U.S. (1964)
Heart of Atlanta upheld the Civil Rights Act under the commerce power.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
McCulloch concerned implied powers and a national bank.

alt.q: Congress makes it a federal crime to have a gun within 1,000 feet of a school, arguing that school violence harms the economy. The strongest objection, as in Lopez, is that…
alt.a: Gun possession is not commerce Congress can regulate
alt.ex: Lopez held that simple possession near a school is not commercial activity, so the commerce power could not reach it.
w: The law is an unconstitutional bill of attainder
A bill of attainder punishes named persons without trial; this law is general.
The law violates the Full Faith and Credit Clause of Article IV
That clause concerns interstate respect for records and judgments.
The law is an ex post facto law punishing past acts
The law applies only to future conduct.

items.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), after upholding Congress's power to create a national bank, the Supreme Court also ruled that Maryland
items.a: could not tax the bank, because federal law is supreme
items.ex: The unanimous Court held that a state may not tax or otherwise control a lawful federal institution. Chief Justice Marshall reasoned that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy,” and federal law is supreme under the Supremacy Clause.
w: could tax the bank, because states have equal power to tax
The Court struck down Maryland's tax on the bank.
could close the bank, because it was not in the Constitution
The Court upheld the bank as a valid use of implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
could regulate the bank, because it operated in Maryland
The Court held states may not control the lawful operations of the federal government.

alt.q: Chief Justice John Marshall used this reasoning in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) to conclude that
alt.a: states may not tax an agency of the federal government
alt.ex: Because a tax could be used to destroy what Congress lawfully created, Marshall held that Maryland's tax on the Bank of the United States was unconstitutional.
w: Congress may not tax the citizens of any individual state
Congress has the power to tax; the case limited state taxation of federal institutions.
states may not tax the property of their own citizens at all
Marshall noted that states may still tax ordinary property in the state, including the bank's real estate.
the federal government may not create corporations
The Court upheld Congress's power to charter the bank.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That the power to tax involves the power to destroy; that the power to destroy may defeat and render useless the power to create…”
Source: McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. 316 (1819)

alt.q: Which two constitutional provisions were central to the Supreme Court's decision in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)?
alt.a: the Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses
alt.ex: The Court used the Necessary and Proper Clause to uphold the national bank and the Supremacy Clause to strike down Maryland's tax on it.
w: the Commerce Clause and the Foreign Emoluments Clause
Neither clause was the basis of the decision.
the Due Process Clause and the Equal Protection Clause
These are in the Fourteenth Amendment, which was not ratified until 1868.
the Contract Clause and the Republican Guarantee Clause
Neither clause was the basis of the decision.

items.q: Powers that Congress exercises under the Necessary and Proper Clause, though not specifically listed in the Constitution, are called
items.a: implied powers
items.ex: Implied powers are not spelled out in the Constitution but are reasonably related to carrying out Congress's listed (enumerated) powers. McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) confirmed them.
w: reserved powers
Reserved powers belong to the states or the people under the Tenth Amendment.
concurrent powers
Concurrent powers, such as taxing, are held by both the national and state governments.
denied powers
Denied powers are things the Constitution forbids government to do.

alt.q: Which of the following is an implied power of Congress rather than an enumerated (listed) power?
alt.a: creating a national bank
alt.ex: The Constitution never mentions a bank. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court held that Congress could create one under the Necessary and Proper Clause as a means of carrying out its powers to tax, borrow, and spend.
w: coining money
Article I, Section 8 expressly gives Congress the power to coin money.
declaring war
Article I, Section 8 expressly gives Congress the power to declare war.
establishing post offices
Article I, Section 8 expressly gives Congress the power to establish post offices.

alt.q: Which constitutional provision best supports this law?
alt.a: the Necessary and Proper Clause
alt.ex: The law is a means of carrying out an enumerated power (the postal power), so it rests on the Necessary and Proper Clause, which lets Congress pass laws needed to carry out its listed powers.
w: the Supremacy Clause
The Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law supreme, but it does not itself give Congress power to pass laws.
the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people.
the Domestic Emoluments Clause of Article II
This clause concerns the President's salary.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: The Constitution gives Congress the power to establish post offices and post roads. To protect the mail, Congress makes stealing mail a federal crime, even though the Constitution never mentions mail theft.

items.q: In United States v. Comstock (2010), the Supreme Court relied on the Necessary and Proper Clause to uphold a federal law allowing
items.a: civil commitment of sexually dangerous federal prisoners
items.ex: The Court held 7–2 that because Congress may create federal crimes and run federal prisons, it may also provide for the continued custody of mentally ill, sexually dangerous federal prisoners as a reasonable means of carrying out those powers.
w: federal regulation of guns near public schools
That law was struck down under the Commerce Clause in United States v. Lopez (1995).
a requirement that all individuals buy health insurance coverage
In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), the mandate failed under the Necessary and Proper Clause and was upheld only as a tax.
federal civil suits for gender-motivated violence
That remedy was struck down in United States v. Morrison (2000).

alt.q: In United States v. Comstock (2010), the Supreme Court explained that the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress pass laws that are
alt.a: reasonably related to carrying out its listed powers
alt.ex: Comstock confirmed the broad McCulloch view: a law is valid if it is a reasonable means of carrying out an enumerated power. It is not limited to absolutely essential laws, but it does not give Congress a general police power.
w: absolutely essential to the survival of the nation
McCulloch and Comstock both rejected a strict “absolutely necessary” reading.
approved in advance by most state legislatures
The clause does not require state approval.
related to any goal that Congress considers beneficial
The Court said the clause must be tied to enumerated powers and creates no general police power.

alt.q: Which reasoning did the Supreme Court use to uphold such a law in United States v. Comstock (2010)?
alt.a: It is a reasonable means of carrying out powers Congress already has
alt.ex: The Court held that the law was a reasonable extension of Congress's powers to create federal crimes and run federal prisons, so it was valid under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: It falls under a general police power that the Constitution gives Congress
Congress has no general police power; the Court stressed the law was tied to existing federal powers.
It is required by the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel punishment
The Eighth Amendment limits punishment; it does not authorize civil commitment.
It was ratified by the states under the Article V process
Article V governs constitutional amendments, not ordinary laws.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress has created federal crimes, federal courts, and federal prisons. It then passes a law allowing federal officials to keep certain mentally ill, sexually dangerous prisoners in custody after their sentences end, while allowing a state to take custody of them if it wishes.

items.q: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that the Necessary and Proper Clause could not save the requirement to buy health insurance. Which principle about the clause does this reflect?
items.a: It carries out listed powers but cannot create new ones
items.ex: Roberts concluded the mandate was not a “proper” means because it would let Congress reach people outside its enumerated commerce power. The clause helps carry out listed powers but does not expand them; the mandate survived only as a tax.
w: It applies only to laws that Congress passed before the year 1819
The clause applies to all laws; there is no time limit.
It may be used only with the approval of the states
The clause does not require state approval.
It gives Congress unlimited power over the economy
The ruling shows the opposite: the clause has limits.

alt.q: Which statement best describes a limit on the Necessary and Proper Clause?
alt.a: Laws must be tied to a power the Constitution grants
alt.ex: The clause authorizes laws “for carrying into Execution” the powers the Constitution grants. Laws that do not serve an enumerated power, or that are not “proper,” are not authorized, as in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012).
w: Laws must be approved by two-thirds of both houses
Ordinary laws need only a majority in each house, plus presidential approval or a veto override.
Laws must be ratified by three-fourths of the states
That rule applies to constitutional amendments, not laws.
Laws must expire after ten years unless renewed
The Constitution sets no such time limit on laws (except two-year limits on army funding).

alt.q: Based on NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), how would the Supreme Court most likely view this argument?
alt.a: reject it, because the mandate is not a proper means
alt.ex: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), the Court held that a mandate to buy a product was not a “proper” use of the Necessary and Proper Clause because it would reach people beyond Congress's enumerated commerce power.
w: accept it, because the clause has no limits
The Court held the clause is limited to proper means of carrying out enumerated powers.
reject it, because the clause applies only to the President
The clause gives power to Congress to carry out powers of every branch.
accept it, because most states consented to the law
State consent is not required and was not the basis of the decision.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law requiring every adult to buy a particular product, arguing that the requirement is necessary and proper to make its rules for that industry work. Opponents argue that the law reaches people who are not engaged in that commerce at all.

items.q: Which interpretation of the Constitution does this passage best represent?
items.a: a broad view of congressional power
items.ex: Marshall held that Congress may use any appropriate means to reach a legitimate constitutional end, a broad (loose) construction of the Necessary and Proper Clause associated with Alexander Hamilton.
w: a strict view of congressional power
A strict view, held by Thomas Jefferson, would allow only absolutely essential means.
a view favoring state nullification
Nullification claimed states could void federal laws; McCulloch upheld federal supremacy.
a view rejecting judicial review
In McCulloch the Court exercised its power to interpret the Constitution.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution, and all means which are appropriate, which are plainly adapted to that end, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the constitution, are constitutional.”
Source: McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. 316 (1819)

alt.q: Chief Justice John Marshall's reading of the Necessary and Proper Clause in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) most closely followed the view of which founder?
alt.a: Alexander Hamilton
alt.ex: As Treasury Secretary, Hamilton argued in 1791 that the clause allowed Congress to create a national bank as a useful means to its powers. Marshall's broad reading in McCulloch followed this view.
w: Thomas Jefferson
Jefferson read the clause strictly and opposed the bank.
Patrick Henry
Henry was an Anti-Federalist who feared broad national power.
George Mason
Mason refused to sign the Constitution and feared the clause would allow unlimited federal power.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case most directly rejected this student's view?
alt.a: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
alt.ex: McCulloch held that Congress has implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause, such as creating a national bank, even though such powers are not listed in the Constitution.
w: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
Marbury established judicial review; it did not address implied powers of Congress.
Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Gibbons interpreted an enumerated power (commerce), not implied powers.
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
Dred Scott concerned slavery and citizenship, and it limited congressional power.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: During a class debate, a student says, “If the Constitution does not specifically list a power, Congress cannot use it, period. The bank, for example, is nowhere in the text.”

items.q: The Articles of Confederation limited Congress to powers “expressly delegated” to it, while the Constitution added the Necessary and Proper Clause. What was the main effect of this difference?
items.a: Congress could use means not specifically listed
items.ex: The Articles confined Congress to expressly delegated powers. The Necessary and Proper Clause allows Congress to choose means, such as a national bank, that are not listed but help carry out its enumerated powers.
w: States gained the power to veto federal laws they opposed
The Constitution gave states no veto over federal laws.
Congress lost its power to declare war on other nations
The Constitution expressly gives Congress the power to declare war.
The President gained the power to write laws
Lawmaking remains with Congress; the President signs or vetoes bills.

alt.q: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers “not delegated” to the United States but, unlike the Articles of Confederation, does not say “expressly” delegated. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Chief Justice Marshall treated this difference as evidence that
alt.a: the national government can have implied powers
alt.ex: Marshall noted that the Tenth Amendment, unlike the Articles, omits “expressly,” leaving room for powers implied from the enumerated ones, such as creating a bank.
w: states may veto any federal laws that they dislike
McCulloch rejected state control over federal laws and institutions.
the Bill of Rights applies to the states
The Court held the Bill of Rights limited only the federal government in Barron v. Baltimore (1833).
Congress may not charter any banks or corporations
McCulloch upheld Congress's power to charter the bank as a corporation.

alt.q: According to this clause, Congress may make laws to carry out the powers of
alt.a: any part of the national government
alt.ex: The clause covers the “foregoing Powers” of Congress and “all other Powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department or Officer thereof.”
w: Congress only, not the other branches
The clause also covers powers vested in the government as a whole and in any department or officer.
the state governments and their officers
The clause refers to the Government of the United States, not the states.
foreign governments allied with the nation
The clause concerns powers vested by the Constitution, not foreign governments.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article I, Section 8 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers, and all other Powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department or Officer thereof.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

items.q: “To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers…” In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court relied on this clause to uphold…
items.a: Congress's creation of a national bank
items.ex: Marshall held that the bank was a legitimate means of carrying out powers to tax, borrow and regulate commerce, even though banks are not listed.
w: A state's tax on a federal bank branch
McCulloch struck down Maryland's tax under the Supremacy Clause.
A federal ban on guns near schools
That law was struck down in United States v. Lopez (1995).
The Court's own power of judicial review
Judicial review came from Marbury v. Madison (1803).

alt.q: The Necessary and Proper Clause is often called the “Elastic Clause” because it…
alt.a: Stretches Congress's powers to meet new needs
