Checks and balances concern the branches checking each other, not national and state powers.
executive privilege
Executive privilege concerns presidential confidentiality.

alt.q: Thomas Paine compared his proposed “Continental Charter” to the Magna Carta. Which document first put his idea of a written charter for the united colonies into practice?
alt.a: the Articles of Confederation
alt.ex: The Articles of Confederation, approved by Congress in 1777 and ratified in 1781, were the first written charter of government for the united states, as Paine had urged in 1776.
w: the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration announced independence but did not set up a plan of government.
the Mayflower Compact
The Mayflower Compact (1620) created a government for one colony, long before Paine wrote.
the Northwest Ordinance
The Northwest Ordinance governed the territories; it was not a charter for the union.

items.q: Which idea in the Declaration of Independence shares the outlook of this sentence?
items.a: All men are endowed with unalienable rights.
items.ex: Paine presented the American cause as universal, not just local. The Declaration likewise claims rights for “all men,” not only for colonists or Englishmen.
w: The king has kept standing armies in peacetime.
This is a specific grievance against the king, not a universal claim.
The colonists have petitioned the king in vain.
This describes colonial efforts at redress, not a universal principle.
The colonies may levy war and make alliances.
This lists powers of the new states, not rights of all people.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind.”
Source: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776), Project Gutenberg

alt.q: When Paine wrote that “the cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind,” he meant that
alt.a: American liberty mattered to people everywhere
alt.ex: Paine argued that the struggle for American independence was about universal principles of liberty, so its outcome would affect people around the world, not only the colonists.
w: America should conquer other nations
Paine did not call for conquest.
all nations should stay loyal to Britain
Paine urged a break with Britain.
only Americans truly deserved natural rights
Paine's point was that the cause concerned all mankind, not Americans only.

alt.q: This speaker is echoing which claim from Common Sense?
alt.a: America's cause is the cause of all mankind.
alt.ex: Paine wrote that “the cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind,” meaning the principles of the Revolution applied to all peoples. The speaker applies them to another country.
w: Government is at best a necessary evil.
This Paine claim concerns the nature of government, not the universal reach of the Revolution.
An island should not govern a continent.
This claim concerns Britain ruling America specifically.
Reconciliation with Britain is still possible.
Paine argued reconciliation was impossible.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A speaker at a rally in another country in the 1790s argues that the American Revolution proved that any people, anywhere, may claim natural rights and throw off tyranny.

items.q: Which development in the years after 1776 best reflects Paine's advice in this passage?
items.a: Americans wrote new state and national constitutions.
items.ex: Paine urged Americans to form “a constitution of our own in a cool deliberate manner.” States wrote constitutions after 1776, and the nation adopted the Articles of Confederation and then the Constitution of 1787.
w: Americans asked the British Parliament to write their laws.
Paine called self-government a natural right and rejected Parliament's authority.
Americans chose a king from among their leaders.
Paine rejected monarchy, and Americans created republics.
Americans relied on unwritten customs alone.
Paine called for a written constitution, and Americans wrote them.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“A government of our own is our natural right: And when a man seriously reflects on the precariousness of human affairs, he will become convinced, that it is infinitely wiser and safer, to form a constitution of our own in a cool deliberate manner, while we have it in our power, than to trust such an interesting event to time and chance.”
Source: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776), Project Gutenberg

alt.q: Paine wrote in Common Sense that it is “infinitely wiser and safer, to form a constitution of our own in a cool deliberate manner.” Which later event best fits this advice?
alt.a: the Constitutional Convention of 1787
alt.ex: At the Constitutional Convention, delegates deliberated for months to draft a new frame of government, the kind of careful constitution-making Paine recommended instead of leaving government “to time and chance.”
w: the Boston Tea Party protest of 1773
The Tea Party was a protest, not the deliberate writing of a constitution.
the Battle of Saratoga in 1777
Saratoga was a military victory, not constitution-making.
Shays' Rebellion in 1786–1787
Shays' Rebellion was an armed uprising, the opposite of calm deliberation.

alt.q: In Common Sense, Paine wrote that “a government of our own is our natural right.” This argument draws most directly on which Enlightenment idea?
alt.a: the people's right to create their own government
alt.ex: Following John Locke, Paine argued that people have a natural right to form a government of their own. The Declaration of Independence states the same idea: the people may institute new government.
w: the divine right of kings to rule
Divine right says rulers get power from God; Paine attacked monarchy.
the duty of colonies to obey Parliament
Paine argued the colonies should break from Parliament and the king.
the authority of the church over the government
Paine's argument concerns self-government, not church power.

items.q: Common Sense attacked hereditary monarchy and aristocracy. Which provision of the U.S. Constitution reflects this same rejection?
items.a: the ban on titles of nobility
items.ex: Article I, Section 9 says “No Title of Nobility shall be granted by the United States,” reflecting the republican rejection of hereditary rank that Paine championed.
w: the power to coin money
Coining money is an economic power unrelated to hereditary rank.
the Full Faith and Credit Clause
This clause concerns states honoring each other's records.
the power to regulate commerce
The Commerce Clause concerns trade, not hereditary rank.

alt.q: Which constitutional provision best reflects Paine's argument in Common Sense that America should be a republic rather than a monarchy?
alt.a: the guarantee of a republican form of government to every state
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 4 says the United States shall guarantee to every state a republican form of government, putting into the Constitution the rejection of monarchy that Paine urged.
w: the requirement that the president be a natural-born citizen
This is a qualification for office, not a guarantee of republican government.
the rule that each state has two senators in Congress
Equal Senate representation concerns the states' role, not monarchy versus republic.
the power of Congress to admit new states to the Union
Admitting states concerns expansion, not the form of government.

alt.q: These delegates are applying Paine's argument against
alt.a: hereditary rule
alt.ex: In Common Sense, Paine attacked monarchy and hereditary succession as contrary to reason. The U.S. Constitution likewise bans titles of nobility and makes every office elective or appointive.
w: separation of powers
Paine did not oppose separating powers; the delegates' rules target inherited status.
written constitutions
Paine favored a written charter; the delegates are writing one.
popular elections
Paine favored elected, representative government.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A newly independent nation is writing a constitution. Delegates who have read Common Sense insist that no public office may be inherited and that no citizen may receive a title such as “duke” or “lord.”

items.q: What was the main purpose of Thomas Paine's Common Sense (January 1776)?
items.a: To persuade ordinary colonists to support independence
items.ex: Written in plain language, Common Sense attacked monarchy and argued for separation from Britain; it sold widely and swayed public opinion.
w: To explain formally to foreign nations why the colonies left
That was the purpose of the Declaration of Independence (July 1776).
To argue for ratifying the new federal Constitution
That was the purpose of The Federalist Papers (1787–1788).
To urge colonists to reconcile with the king and Parliament
Paine argued against reconciliation.

alt.q: "...there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island." This argument for independence appeared in —
alt.a: Thomas Paine's Common Sense
alt.ex: Paine used plain, common-sense reasoning in 1776 to argue that America should be independent of Britain.
w: Jefferson's Declaration of Independence
The Declaration argues from natural rights and grievances, not this comparison.
Madison's Federalist No. 14
No. 14 (1787) defends a large republic, not independence.
John Locke's Second Treatise
Locke wrote in 1689 about government generally, not American independence.

alt.q: Which feature made Common Sense especially influential in early 1776?
alt.a: Its plain language reached ordinary readers
alt.ex: Paine wrote for farmers and artisans rather than lawyers, helping turn public opinion toward independence months before July 1776.
w: Its legal arguments convinced Parliament
Parliament was not persuaded; the pamphlet was aimed at colonists.
Its plan of government became the Articles
The Articles were drafted by John Dickinson and Congress.
Its author was a leading member of Congress
Paine was a recent immigrant writer, not a member of Congress.

items.q: "For as in absolute governments the King is law, so in free countries the law ought to be King; and there ought to be no other." In Common Sense, Thomas Paine uses this idea to argue that —
items.a: America should reject monarchy and be ruled by law
items.ex: Paine attacked hereditary monarchy and argued that in a free America, law—not a king—should rule.
w: America should choose a king who obeys the law
Paine argued against having any king at all.
Parliament should be supreme over the British king
Paine rejected British rule entirely, including Parliament.
each colony should crown its own governor
Paine called for a republic, not local monarchs.

alt.q: In Common Sense, Thomas Paine attacked which institution as contrary to reason and the source of British oppression?
alt.a: Hereditary monarchy
alt.ex: Paine ridiculed kingship and hereditary succession, arguing that "the law ought to be King" in a free country.
w: Representative assemblies
Paine supported representative government.
Written constitutions
Paine proposed a written continental charter.
Trial by jury
Paine did not attack jury trials.

alt.q: A colonist in early 1776 reads a pamphlet arguing that kings are unnecessary, that hereditary rule is absurd, and that "the law ought to be King." Which pamphlet is it?
alt.a: Thomas Paine's Common Sense
alt.ex: Published in January 1776, Common Sense attacked monarchy and urged independence.
w: John Dickinson's Letters from a Farmer
Dickinson's letters (1767–1768) opposed the Townshend duties but did not reject monarchy.
James Otis's Rights of the British Colonies
Otis's 1764 pamphlet argued for colonists' rights within the empire.
The Olive Branch Petition
This 1775 petition asked King George III for reconciliation.

items.q: Which principle of the U.S. Constitution most directly reflects this section?
items.a: popular sovereignty
items.ex: Section 2 says all power is “derived from, the people” and officials are their servants. This is popular sovereignty, expressed in the Constitution's opening words, “We the People.”
w: federalism
Federalism divides power between national and state governments; Section 2 concerns the source of power.
judicial review
Judicial review is the courts' power to void laws; Section 2 does not mention courts.
separation of powers
Separation of powers appears in Section 5, not in this passage.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Section 2 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That all power is vested in, and consequently derived from, the people; that magistrates are their trustees and servants and at all times amenable to them.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which phrase from the Preamble to the U.S. Constitution best expresses the idea, found in the Virginia Declaration of Rights, that all power is “derived from, the people”?
alt.a: “We the People”
alt.ex: Section 2 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights says all power is vested in and derived from the people. The Preamble begins “We the People of the United States,” making the people the source of the Constitution's authority.
w: “provide for the common defence”
This phrase states a purpose of government, not its source of power.
“insure domestic Tranquility”
This phrase states a goal of internal peace, not the source of power.
“establish Justice”
This phrase states a purpose of government, not who grants its authority.

alt.q: Which idea from the Virginia Declaration of Rights most directly contradicts the governor?
alt.a: Officials are the people's trustees and servants.
alt.ex: Section 2 declares that all power comes from the people and that magistrates are “their trustees and servants and at all times amenable to them.” A governor cannot claim to answer only to party leaders.
w: A free press is one of the great bulwarks of liberty.
This Section 12 idea concerns the press, not to whom officials answer.
Excessive bail ought not to be required.
This Section 9 idea concerns criminal justice, not officials' accountability.
General warrants are grievous and oppressive.
This Section 10 idea concerns searches, not officials' accountability.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A governor declares that because he was nominated by party leaders, he answers only to them and need not respect the wishes of the ordinary voters of his state.

items.q: Which requirement in the Fourth Amendment most directly reflects this section?
items.a: warrants must describe the place and items
items.ex: Section 10 condemned general warrants that did not name persons or describe offenses. The Fourth Amendment requires warrants supported by probable cause and “particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.”
w: soldiers may not be housed in homes
This is the Third Amendment and concerns quartering, not warrants.
the accused must be informed of the charges
This is a Sixth Amendment right at trial.
excessive fines may not be imposed
This is an Eighth Amendment protection.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Section 10 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That general warrants, whereby an officer or messenger may be commanded to search suspected places without evidence of a fact committed, or to seize any person or persons not named, or whose offense is not particularly described and supported by evidence, are grievous and oppressive and ought not to be granted.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: The Fourth Amendment requires warrants to be supported by “probable cause” and to particularly describe “the place to be searched.” Which 1776 document condemned general warrants as “grievous and oppressive”?
alt.a: the Virginia Declaration of Rights
alt.ex: Section 10 of George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 1776) declared that general warrants “are grievous and oppressive and ought not to be granted,” an important model for the Fourth Amendment.
w: the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration of Independence does not mention general warrants.
Common Sense
Common Sense argued for independence and did not address warrants.
the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were not adopted in 1776 and contained no bill of rights.

alt.q: Which constitutional protection was designed to prevent this kind of search?
alt.a: the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement
alt.ex: Writs of assistance and other general warrants let officers search anywhere without evidence. Virginia's Declaration of Rights (Section 10) condemned them, and the Fourth Amendment requires specific warrants based on probable cause.
w: the Fifth Amendment's ban on double jeopardy
Double jeopardy concerns repeated trials, not searches.
the Sixth Amendment's right to counsel
The right to counsel concerns legal help at trial.
the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel punishment
This concerns punishment after conviction, not searches.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A customs officer in 1770 carries a document allowing him to enter any house he suspects of hiding smuggled goods. The document does not name any owner or describe any evidence.

items.q: Which phrase in the First Amendment uses language taken from this section?
items.a: “the free exercise thereof”
items.ex: Section 16 declared that all men are “equally entitled to the free exercise of religion.” The First Amendment bars Congress from “prohibiting the free exercise thereof,” using the same phrase.
w: “an establishment of religion”
Section 16 speaks of free exercise; the passage does not use establishment language.
“the freedom of speech”
Section 16 concerns religion, not speech.
“peaceably to assemble”
Section 16 does not address assembly.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Section 16 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“… and therefore all men are equally entitled to the free exercise of religion, according to the dictates of conscience; and that it is the mutual duty of all to practise Christian forbearance, love, and charity toward each other.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Section 16 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776) declared that all men are “equally entitled to the free exercise of religion.” Which part of the Bill of Rights carries this idea forward?
alt.a: the First Amendment
alt.ex: The First Amendment forbids Congress to make any law prohibiting the free exercise of religion, the same protection George Mason's Virginia declaration had stated in 1776.
w: the Third Amendment
The Third Amendment concerns quartering soldiers.
the Ninth Amendment
The Ninth Amendment protects unlisted rights, not religion specifically.
the Fourth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment concerns searches and seizures.

alt.q: Which right, declared in the Virginia Declaration of Rights and later in the First Amendment, does this law violate?
alt.a: free exercise of religion
alt.ex: Section 16 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights declared all men equally entitled to the free exercise of religion. The First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause protects the right to worship.
w: freedom of the press
The law restricts worship, not publishing.
the right to bear arms
The law has nothing to do with weapons.
protection from quartering
The law has nothing to do with housing soldiers.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state law forbids members of one small religious group from holding worship services in their homes, though members of other faiths may do so.

items.q: Which statement in the Declaration of Independence expresses the same idea?
items.a: “it is the Right of the People to alter or to abolish it”
items.ex: Section 3 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 12, 1776) said a majority may “reform, alter, or abolish” a government that fails its purposes. Weeks later the Declaration of Independence stated that the people may “alter or to abolish” a destructive government.
w: “For imposing Taxes on us without our Consent”
This is a specific grievance about taxation, not the right to change a government.
“For depriving us in many cases, of the benefits of Trial by Jury”
This is a grievance about jury trials, not the right of revolution.
“For Quartering large bodies of armed troops among us”
This is a grievance about quartering, not the right of revolution.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Section 3 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“… and that, when any government shall be found inadequate or contrary to these purposes, a majority of the community has an indubitable, inalienable, and indefeasible right to reform, alter, or abolish it, in such manner as shall be judged most conducive to the public weal.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Section 3 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights, adopted in June 1776, said a majority has a right to “reform, alter, or abolish” a government that fails its purposes. This idea was repeated weeks later in which document?
alt.a: the Declaration of Independence
alt.ex: Adopted July 4, 1776, the Declaration of Independence says that when government becomes destructive of its ends, “it is the Right of the People to alter or to abolish it, and to institute new Government.”
w: the Articles of Confederation
(The Articles, first drafted in July 1776 and approved by Congress in 1777, created a league of states; they did not restate the right of revolution.)
the Northwest Ordinance
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) organized western territories.
the Treaty of Paris
The Treaty of Paris (1783) ended the Revolutionary War.

alt.q: Which Enlightenment idea is expressed in the Virginia Declaration of Rights' claim that the people may “reform, alter, or abolish” a government that fails to serve them?
alt.a: the right of revolution
alt.ex: John Locke argued that people may change or overthrow a government that violates its trust. Section 3 of the Virginia declaration and the Declaration of Independence both state this right of revolution.
w: the divine right of kings
Divine right holds that rulers answer only to God, the opposite of this claim.
the balance of trade
The balance of trade is an economic idea from mercantilism.
the separation of church and state
Section 3 concerns changing a government, not religion.

items.q: Which amendment in the U.S. Bill of Rights most closely follows this section?
items.a: the Sixth Amendment
items.ex: Section 8 gave the accused the right to know the accusation, confront witnesses, call evidence, and have a speedy trial by an impartial jury. The Sixth Amendment guarantees nearly the same rights “in all criminal prosecutions.”
w: the Fourth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment concerns searches and seizures, not trial rights.
the Seventh Amendment
The Seventh Amendment concerns jury trials in civil suits; this passage covers criminal prosecutions.
the Eighth Amendment
The Eighth Amendment concerns bail, fines, and punishments.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Section 8 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That in all capital or criminal prosecutions a man has a right to demand the cause and nature of his accusation, to be confronted with the accusers and witnesses, to call for evidence in his favor, and to a speedy trial by an impartial jury of twelve men of his vicinage …”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the accused “a speedy and public trial, by an impartial jury.” Which 1776 document, written by George Mason, contained a similar guarantee?
alt.a: the Virginia Declaration of Rights
alt.ex: Section 8 of Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776) guaranteed “a speedy trial by an impartial jury.” Madison drew on it when he drafted the Bill of Rights in 1789.
w: the Declaration of Independence
The Declaration of Independence was drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson and only complained about the loss of jury trials.
Common Sense
Common Sense was written by Thomas Paine and contained no list of rights.
the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were drafted mainly by John Dickinson and had no bill of rights.

alt.q: Which protection, found in Section 8 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights and later in the Bill of Rights, is being violated?
alt.a: the privilege against self-incrimination
alt.ex: Section 8 said an accused person cannot “be compelled to give evidence against himself.” The Fifth Amendment protects the same right: no person shall be compelled in a criminal case to be a witness against himself.
w: the right to a speedy trial
The trial is underway; the problem is forced testimony, not delay.
the right to confront witnesses
Nothing prevents the defendant from questioning witnesses.
the protection against double jeopardy
The defendant is not being tried a second time.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: At a criminal trial, a judge orders the defendant to take the witness stand and answer the prosecutor's questions about the crime, over his objection.

mt.q: Match each Bill of Rights amendment to what it protects (6th–10th).
pairs: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer
No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail
Rights not listed still belong to the people
Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people
mt.ex: Bill of Rights (1791): 6th Amendment: Speedy, public trial with a lawyer; 7th Amendment: Jury trial in civil cases; 8th Amendment: No cruel and unusual punishment or excessive bail; 9th Amendment: Rights not listed still belong to the people; 10th Amendment: Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people.

items.q: This section repeated language from an earlier document and was later adopted nearly word for word in the U.S. Bill of Rights. Which pair correctly identifies both documents?
items.a: English Bill of Rights; Eighth Amendment
items.ex: Section 9 copied the English Bill of Rights (1689) word for word. The Eighth Amendment (1791) uses nearly the same language: excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.
w: Magna Carta; Fourth Amendment
The wording comes from 1689, and the Fourth Amendment concerns searches.
Mayflower Compact; Fourteenth Amendment
The Mayflower Compact has no such language, and the Fourteenth Amendment concerns citizenship, due process, and equal protection.
Common Sense; Fifth Amendment
Common Sense has no such language, and the Fifth Amendment concerns due process and self-incrimination.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Section 9 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That excessive bail ought not to be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which sequence correctly traces the ban on “cruel and unusual punishments” through three documents?
alt.a: English Bill of Rights, Virginia Declaration of Rights, Eighth Amendment
alt.ex: The phrase appears in the English Bill of Rights (1689), was copied into Section 9 of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), and became part of the Eighth Amendment (1791).
w: Virginia Declaration of Rights, English Bill of Rights, Eighth Amendment
The English Bill of Rights (1689) came before Virginia's declaration (1776).
Eighth Amendment, Virginia Declaration of Rights, English Bill of Rights
This reverses the order; the Eighth Amendment (1791) came last.
English Bill of Rights, Eighth Amendment, Virginia Declaration of Rights
Virginia's declaration (1776) came before the Eighth Amendment (1791).

alt.q: Which right is the historian describing?
alt.a: freedom from cruel and unusual punishment
alt.ex: The English Bill of Rights (1689), Section 9 of George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), and the Eighth Amendment proposed by Madison in 1789 all forbid excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments in almost identical words.
w: the freedom of the press from censorship
Virginia's declaration protected the press, but the English Bill of Rights did not.
the right to petition the government
The English Bill of Rights protected petitioning, but Virginia's declaration did not.
trial by a jury of twelve neighbors
Virginia's declaration required twelve jurors, but this was not a provision of the English Bill of Rights.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A historian notes that George Mason's 1776 list of rights repeated a 1689 English guarantee word for word, and that James Madison borrowed nearly the same wording for an amendment he proposed in 1789.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 1776)?
items.a: Mason's list of rights that shaped later bills of rights
items.ex: Adopted June 12, 1776, Mason's declaration influenced the Declaration of Independence's preamble and Madison's Bill of Rights.
w: Thomas Jefferson's list of grievances against King George III
That describes the Declaration of Independence.
James Madison's plan for a new national government in 1787
That describes the Virginia Plan (1787).
Patrick Henry's speech urging Virginia to arm itself for war
That was Henry's "Give me liberty" speech (1775).

alt.q: "That all men are by nature equally free and independent and have certain inherent rights..." This line, adopted in Virginia in June 1776, most directly influenced the opening of —
alt.a: the Declaration of Independence
alt.ex: Weeks later, Jefferson's draft echoed Mason's words: "all men are created equal" with "unalienable Rights."
w: the Articles of Confederation
The Articles begin with a league of states, not a statement of natural rights.
the Mayflower Compact
The Compact (1620) came long before 1776.
the English Bill of Rights of 1689
The English Bill of Rights (1689) came long before 1776.

alt.q: George Mason refused to sign the U.S. Constitution in 1787 mainly because —
alt.a: it lacked a bill of rights like the one he wrote
alt.ex: Mason, author of the Virginia Declaration of Rights, objected that the Constitution had no declaration of rights.
w: it gave small states too little power in Congress
Small states won equal Senate representation.
it created no executive to enforce national laws
The Constitution created a president in Article II.
it ended the foreign slave trade immediately
The slave trade was protected until 1808.

items.q: "That the freedom of the press is one of the great bulwarks of liberty, and can never be restrained but by despotic governments." This 1776 statement from the Virginia Declaration of Rights later influenced which part of the U.S. Constitution?
items.a: The First Amendment
items.ex: Section 12 of Mason's declaration was a model for the First Amendment's protection of the press.
w: The Fourth Amendment
The Fourth concerns searches and seizures.
The Ninth Amendment
The Ninth protects unlisted rights.
The Tenth Amendment
The Tenth reserves powers to the states or the people.

alt.q: Which document, written by George Mason in 1776, served as a major model for the Bill of Rights that James Madison proposed in 1789?
alt.a: The Virginia Declaration of Rights
alt.ex: Mason's declaration protected press freedom, religious exercise, jury trial, and barred excessive bail—rights Madison carried into the amendments.
w: The English Bill of Rights
This 1689 act also influenced the Bill of Rights, but Mason did not write it.
The Massachusetts Declaration of Rights
John Adams drafted this in 1779 for the 1780 state constitution.
The Declaration of Independence
Jefferson wrote it; it lists grievances, not enforceable rights.

alt.q: Members of the First Congress compare Madison's proposed amendments with a 1776 state document that already protected a free press, religious exercise, and jury trials. Which document were they most likely consulting?
alt.a: The Virginia Declaration of Rights
alt.ex: Madison, a Virginian, drew heavily on Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776).
w: The Northwest Ordinance
The 1787 ordinance protected rights in a territory, not as a 1776 state document.
The Massachusetts State Constitution
Massachusetts adopted its constitution in 1780, not 1776.
The Articles of Confederation
The Articles contained no bill of rights.

mt.q: Match each Bill of Rights amendment to what it protects (1st–5th).
pairs: Freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition
Right to keep and bear arms
No forced quartering of soldiers in homes
Due process; no self-incrimination or double jeopardy
mt.ex: Bill of Rights (1791): 1st Amendment: Freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition; 2nd Amendment: Right to keep and bear arms; 3rd Amendment: No forced quartering of soldiers in homes; 4th Amendment: No unreasonable searches and seizures; 5th Amendment: Due process; no self-incrimination or double jeopardy.

items.q: Madison's argument in this passage was a response to which Anti-Federalist claim?
items.a: A republic cannot succeed over a large territory.
items.ex: Brutus No. 1, drawing on Montesquieu, argued that a free republic could not work over a country as large as the United States. In Federalist No. 10, Madison answered that a large republic includes so many interests that no single faction can easily dominate.
w: The president would become an elected king.
Some Anti-Federalists feared this, but the passage addresses the size of the republic, not the presidency.
The federal courts would overpower state courts.
Brutus raised this in later essays, but the passage concerns factions in a large republic.
The Senate would form a dangerous aristocracy.
This was an Anti-Federalist fear, but the passage does not address the Senate.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from The Federalist No. 10 (1787) by James Madison, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens; or if such a common motive exists, it will be more difficult for all who feel it to discover their own strength, and to act in unison with each other.”
Source: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School

alt.q: Which Federalist essay most directly answered this argument by claiming that a large republic better controls factions?
alt.a: The Federalist No. 10
alt.ex: Brutus argued that a large republic with diverse interests would suffer constant clashing. In Federalist No. 10, Madison replied that extending the sphere takes in more interests, making it harder for any one faction to form an oppressive majority.
w: The Federalist No. 78
No. 78 defends the judiciary and judicial independence.
The Federalist No. 84
No. 84 argues that a bill of rights is unnecessary.
The Federalist No. 70
No. 70 argues for an energetic single executive.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Brutus No. 1 (October 1787), an Anti-Federalist essay, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“In a republic, the manners, sentiments, and interests of the people should be similar. If this be not the case, there will be a constant clashing of opinions …”
Source: The Founders' Constitution, University of Chicago Press

alt.q: Which pair correctly identifies writers whose views match Delegate A and Delegate B?
alt.a: Brutus; James Madison
alt.ex: Brutus No. 1 warned that a large republic with dissimilar interests would face constant clashing. Madison's Federalist No. 10 answered that many interests in a large republic make it hard for a faction to form an oppressive majority.
w: James Madison; Brutus
This reverses the writers: Madison defended the large republic and Brutus opposed it.
Brutus; Thomas Paine
Paine's Common Sense (1776) was not part of the 1787–1788 debate over a large republic.
John Jay; Brutus
Jay was a Federalist, and Brutus did not argue that diversity protects liberty.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Two delegates debate in 1788. Delegate A says a country as large as the United States contains so many different interests that its representatives will constantly clash. Delegate B replies that so many different interests will make it hard for any single faction to form a majority and oppress others.

items.q: Which of the following is the most lasting result of the Anti-Federalists' arguments during the ratification debate?
items.a: the addition of the Bill of Rights
items.ex: Although the Constitution was ratified, Anti-Federalist demands for protection of individual rights and state powers led the First Congress to propose amendments in 1789; ten were ratified as the Bill of Rights in 1791.
w: the rejection of the Constitution by New York
New York ratified the Constitution in July 1788.
the return to the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were replaced, not restored.
the creation of the Electoral College
The Electoral College was designed at the Constitutional Convention, not won by Anti-Federalists.

alt.q: Although the Anti-Federalists lost the ratification debate, which amendment most clearly reflects their concern for preserving state power?
alt.a: the Tenth Amendment
alt.ex: Anti-Federalists feared a consolidated national government that would swallow the states. The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the national government to the states or the people.
w: the Sixteenth Amendment
The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) let Congress tax incomes, expanding national power.
the Seventeenth Amendment
The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) took the choice of senators away from state legislatures.
the Fourteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) placed new limits on the states.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the Anti-Federalists' view of the Constitution as written in 1787?
alt.a: It made the national government too strong and listed no rights.
alt.ex: Anti-Federalists such as Brutus, George Mason, and Patrick Henry warned that the Constitution created a powerful central government that would overwhelm the states and that it lacked a bill of rights.
w: It left the national government too weak to collect taxes.
That was the Federalists' criticism of the Articles of Confederation.
It gave the states too much power over interstate trade.
Anti-Federalists feared national power, not state power over trade.
It protected individual rights but made the president too weak.
The original Constitution lacked a bill of rights, and Anti-Federalists feared a strong president.

items.q: Which feature of the proposed Constitution was Brutus criticizing?
items.a: federal judges' service during good behavior
items.ex: Under Article III, federal judges hold office during good behavior and their salaries cannot be cut. Brutus warned that this made them answerable to no one. Hamilton answered in Federalist No. 78 that the judiciary would be the “least dangerous” branch.
w: the election of House members every two years
Brutus's complaint is about judges being independent of the people, not House elections.
the president's power to veto bills
The passage describes judges, not the president.
the equal representation of states in the Senate
The passage describes judges, not Senate representation.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Brutus No. 15 (March 1788), an Anti-Federalist essay describing federal judges under the proposed Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“In short, they are independent of the people, of the legislature, and of every power under heaven.”
Source: The Founders' Constitution, University of Chicago Press

alt.q: Alexander Hamilton's Federalist No. 78, which called the judiciary the “least dangerous” branch, responded to Anti-Federalist fears like those of Brutus that federal judges would be
alt.a: too independent and beyond the people's control
alt.ex: Brutus warned that federal judges would be “independent of the people, of the legislature, and of every power under heaven.” Hamilton replied that the judiciary, with neither force nor will but only judgment, would be the least dangerous branch.
w: too weak to enforce their own decisions
This was Hamilton's point in defending the courts, not the Anti-Federalist fear.
too closely tied to the president who named them
Brutus feared judges would answer to no one, not to the president.
too easily removed by the state legislatures
State legislatures cannot remove federal judges; Brutus feared judges could not be checked.

alt.q: This warning best matches the arguments of
alt.a: Brutus, an Anti-Federalist
alt.ex: In his later essays (Nos. 11–15), Brutus warned that independent federal judges with final say over the Constitution would expand national power at the states' expense.
w: Publius in The Federalist No. 78
Federalist No. 78 defended judicial independence as a protection, not a danger.
John Marshall in Marbury v. Madison
Marshall's 1803 opinion upheld judicial review rather than warning against it.
Thomas Paine in Common Sense
Common Sense (1776) argued for independence and did not discuss federal judges.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A writer in 1788 warns that because federal judges cannot be removed for their decisions, cannot have their salaries reduced, and will have the final say on the meaning of the Constitution, they will gradually expand national power at the expense of the states.

items.q: The speaker's objection reflects which Anti-Federalist fear about the Constitution?
items.a: a national government that would swallow the states
items.ex: At the Virginia ratifying convention in June 1788, Patrick Henry objected that the Constitution spoke for one national people rather than for the states, showing the Anti-Federalist fear of a consolidated government that would overwhelm state sovereignty.
w: a national government too weak to pay its debts
That weakness was a Federalist complaint about the Articles of Confederation.
a union in which large states held too little power
Henry's objection concerns the people versus the states, not large versus small states.
a president chosen by the state legislatures
The passage concerns the Preamble's wording, not presidential selection.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a speech by Patrick Henry at the Virginia ratifying convention (June 4, 1788), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Who authorized them to speak the language of, We, the people, instead of, We, the states?”
Source: The Founders' Constitution, University of Chicago Press

alt.q: Which statement best explains this objection to the Constitution?
alt.a: The union should be formed by the states, not one national people.
alt.ex: Henry argued the Philadelphia delegates had no authority to speak for a single American people. He wanted the union to remain a compact among sovereign states, as under the Articles of Confederation.
w: The union should be formed by one national people, not the states.
This reverses Henry's view; he objected to “We, the people.”
The union should be formed by Parliament, not the states.
Henry, a leading patriot, did not want Parliament involved.
The union should be formed by the king, not the people.
Henry opposed monarchy and royal authority.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a speech by Patrick Henry at the Virginia ratifying convention (June 4, 1788), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Who authorized them to speak the language of, We, the people, instead of, We, the states?”
Source: The Founders' Constitution, University of Chicago Press

alt.q: Who is this speaker?
alt.a: Patrick Henry
alt.ex: Patrick Henry declined to attend the Philadelphia Convention and led the Anti-Federalists at the Virginia ratifying convention in 1788, where he asked who authorized the delegates to say “We, the people” instead of “We, the states.”
w: James Madison
Madison led the Federalists at the Virginia convention and helped write the Constitution.
Alexander Hamilton
Hamilton was a New York Federalist who signed the Constitution.
John Jay
Jay was a New York Federalist and co-author of The Federalist.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: At a 1788 state ratifying convention, a famous orator who had refused to attend the Philadelphia Convention attacks the Constitution's opening words. He says the delegates had no right to speak for one national people instead of for the states.

items.q: Which statement best summarizes the main argument of Brutus No. 1 (October 1787)?
items.a: One republic over so large a country would end in tyranny
items.ex: Brutus argued, citing thinkers like Montesquieu, that "a free republic cannot succeed over a country of such immense extent," and that the plan would consolidate the states.
w: A large republic controls faction by multiplying interests
That is Madison's argument in Federalist No. 10, which answered such critics.
A new national government needs an unlimited taxing power
That is Hamilton's argument in Federalist No. 31; Brutus feared that power.
The colonies should break from Britain and form a republic
That is the argument of Paine's Common Sense (1776).

alt.q: "...a free republic cannot succeed over a country of such immense extent, containing such a number of inhabitants, and these increasing in such rapid progression as that of the whole United States." This argument appeared in —
alt.a: Brutus No. 1, an Anti-Federalist essay
alt.ex: Brutus No. 1, addressed to the citizens of New York on October 18, 1787, argued that a single republic could not govern so vast a country.
w: Federalist No. 10, a pro-Constitution essay
Madison argued the opposite: a large republic is safer from faction.
Federalist No. 14, a Federalist essay
Madison argued a republic can extend over a large region.
Common Sense, a Patriot pamphlet
Paine's 1776 pamphlet argued for independence, not about the Constitution.

alt.q: A New Yorker in 1787 worries that in one huge republic, voters would know few of their rulers and could not easily remove them. This concern matches which writer?
alt.a: Brutus, an Anti-Federalist
alt.ex: Brutus argued that in a republic "of the extent of this continent," the people would know few of their rulers and lose confidence in them.
w: Publius, a Federalist writer
Publius (Hamilton, Madison, Jay) defended the large republic.
Thomas Paine, a Patriot
Paine wrote Common Sense in 1776 for independence.
John Jay, a Federalist
Jay was a co-author of The Federalist, which supported ratification.

items.q: Brutus No. 1 warned that the Necessary and Proper Clause "may receive a construction to justify the passing almost any law." His main fear was that this clause would —
items.a: let Congress expand its power until the states were swallowed
items.ex: Brutus argued that broad implied powers, combined with federal supremacy, would lead to a consolidated government that absorbed the states.
w: let the president make laws without the formal consent of Congress
Brutus's concern was the legislature's broad powers, not presidential lawmaking.
let the courts strike down any law passed by Congress
Brutus feared Congress's power growing, not courts limiting it.
let the states ignore any national law they disliked
This is the opposite of his fear.

alt.q: Which constitutional clause did Brutus No. 1 warn "may receive a construction to justify the passing almost any law"?
alt.a: The Necessary and Proper Clause
alt.ex: Brutus warned that the power to make all laws "necessary and proper" for executing federal powers was so general it could justify almost anything.
w: The Commerce Clause
Brutus's warning here focused on the general lawmaking clause, not commerce.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
This Article IV clause requires states to honor each other's records and judgments.
The Emoluments Clause
This clause bars officials from accepting gifts or titles from foreign states.

alt.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court held that Congress could create a national bank as a "necessary and proper" means of carrying out its listed powers. Which Anti-Federalist prediction did this ruling seem to confirm?
alt.a: Brutus's warning that implied powers would grow very broad
alt.ex: Brutus had warned the clause "may receive a construction to justify the passing almost any law"; McCulloch read it broadly.
w: Brutus's warning that Congress could never tax without states
Brutus feared Congress's taxing power was too broad, not too narrow.
Madison's warning about factions in small republics
This is a Federalist argument from No. 10, not an Anti-Federalist prediction.
Hamilton's warning that national powers were too weak
Hamilton was a Federalist and supported broad implied powers.

items.q: Brutus No. 1 objected that, under the Supremacy Clause, "the constitution and laws of every state are nullified and declared void" whenever they conflict with federal law. What does this objection reveal about Anti-Federalist fears?
items.a: They feared a consolidated government would absorb the states
items.ex: Brutus argued that federal supremacy plus broad powers would leave state governments with little real authority.
w: They feared the states would overpower the national government
That was the problem under the Articles, which Federalists stressed.
They feared judges would be too weak to enforce federal laws
Brutus feared federal power was too strong, not too weak.
They feared treaties would be made without Senate approval
Treaties require two-thirds Senate approval; this was not his objection.

alt.q: Which clause of the Constitution did Brutus warn would make state constitutions and laws void whenever they conflicted with federal law?
alt.a: The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
alt.ex: Article VI declares the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties "the supreme Law of the Land," which Brutus said would nullify conflicting state law.
w: The Commerce Clause of Article I
The Commerce Clause grants power over trade; it is not the source of federal supremacy.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause of Article IV
This clause concerns states honoring one another's records.
The Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment did not exist in 1787 and concerns fair procedures.

alt.q: A state law conflicts with a federal statute, and a court rules the state law invalid. An Anti-Federalist in 1787 would most likely have pointed to this outcome as proof that —
alt.a: the Constitution would reduce the states to near nothing
alt.ex: Brutus argued federal supremacy would nullify state laws and leave states with little power.
w: the Articles had given Congress far too much power
Anti-Federalists defended state power under the Articles; they did not say Congress had too much.
the Bill of Rights shielded states from federal laws
There was no Bill of Rights in 1787, and it protects individuals.
the states would soon come to control the national government
This reverses the Anti-Federalist fear.

items.q: Which statement best describes Brutus No. 1?
items.a: An Anti-Federalist essay urging New York to reject the Constitution
items.ex: Published October 18, 1787, and addressed "To the Citizens of the State of New-York," it is probably the work of Robert Yates.
w: A Federalist essay defending the Constitution's taxing power
That describes Hamilton's Federalist No. 31.
A Patriot pamphlet urging the thirteen colonies to declare independence
That describes Paine's Common Sense (1776).
A Federalist reply to critics who said the republic was too large
That describes Madison's Federalist Nos. 10 and 14.

alt.q: The Anti-Federalist essays signed "Brutus" and addressed "To the Citizens of the State of New-York" are generally believed to have been written by —
alt.a: Robert Yates
alt.ex: Yates, a New York delegate who left the Philadelphia Convention early, is generally assumed to be Brutus.
w: Patrick Henry
Henry opposed the Constitution in speeches at Virginia's ratifying convention.
George Mason
Mason wrote "Objections to this Constitution of Government" and the Virginia Declaration of Rights.
John Jay
Jay was a Federalist and co-author of The Federalist.

alt.q: Why were Brutus's essays and The Federalist Papers both aimed at readers in New York?
alt.a: New York's ratification was crucial and closely contested
alt.ex: New York was large, commercially vital, and divided; Brutus and Publius competed for its ratifying convention's votes.
w: New York was the only state that never signed the Articles
All thirteen states ratified the Articles by 1781.
New York's legislature alone would decide on ratification
Ratification was by state conventions under Article VII.
New York was the first state scheduled to vote on it
Delaware ratified first, on December 7, 1787.

items.q: Which Supreme Court case established the precedent described in the opinion?
items.a: Marbury v. Madison
items.ex: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall reasoned that when a law conflicts with the Constitution, courts must follow the Constitution, which established judicial review, the power to declare laws unconstitutional.
w: Bush v. Gore
Bush v. Gore (2000) ended the Florida recount in the presidential election.
Miranda v. Arizona
Miranda (1966) required police to inform suspects of their rights.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Dred Scott (1857) denied citizenship to Black Americans and struck down the Missouri Compromise.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“So if a law be in opposition to the constitution; if both the law and the constitution apply to a particular case, so that the court must either decide that case conformably to the law, disregarding the constitution; or conformably to the constitution, disregarding the law; the court must determine which of these conflicting rules governs the case.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case established the precedent described in the opinion?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote these words in Marbury v. Madison (1803), asserting the courts’ power of judicial review over acts of Congress.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch (1819) upheld the national bank and barred states from taxing it.
Gibbons v. Ogden
Gibbons (1824) upheld Congress’s broad power to regulate interstate commerce.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Dred Scott (1857) denied citizenship to Black Americans.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which power is the court using, and which case established it?
alt.a: judicial review, from Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: Striking down an act of Congress as unconstitutional is judicial review, which the Supreme Court first claimed in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: judicial review, from McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch upheld an act of Congress; judicial review was established earlier, in Marbury.
executive privilege, from United States v. Nixon
Executive privilege belongs to the president, not the courts.
implied powers, from Gibbons v. Ogden
Implied powers belong to Congress, and the idea is tied to McCulloch, not Gibbons.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A federal court finds that a section of a law passed by Congress violates the Constitution. The court declares that section void and refuses to enforce it.

items.q: Which branch of the federal government gained the most power as a result of Marbury v. Madison?
items.a: the judicial branch
items.ex: By establishing judicial review in 1803, Marbury v. Madison let federal courts strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution, making the judiciary a coequal check on Congress and the President.
w: the executive branch
Madison never had to deliver the commission, but the case's lasting effect was to give courts power to review laws, not to expand presidential power.
the legislative branch
Marbury actually limited Congress: the Court voided part of the Judiciary Act of 1789.
the state governments
The case concerned federal courts and an act of Congress; it did not shift power to the states.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which statement best describes the relationship between the Constitution and ordinary acts of Congress?
alt.a: The Constitution outranks ordinary acts of Congress
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall reasoned that the Constitution is a 'superior, paramount law,' so a statute that conflicts with it cannot stand; this ranking of the Constitution above statutes is the basis of judicial review.
w: The Constitution and acts of Congress carry equal weight
Marshall rejected this; equal weight would let the legislature alter the Constitution at will.
Congress may change the Constitution by passing ordinary acts
This is the alternative Marshall rejected; the Constitution can be changed only through the amendment process.
The states decide whether a law or the Constitution prevails
Marbury placed the power to decide conflicts with the federal courts, not the states.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Constitution is either a superior, paramount law, unchangeable by ordinary means, or it is on a level with ordinary legislative acts, and, like other acts, is alterable when the legislature shall please to alter it.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: The court's action is an example of which check and balance?
alt.a: the judiciary checking the other two branches
alt.ex: Using judicial review, first claimed in Marbury v. Madison (1803), a court can refuse to enforce a law passed by Congress and signed by the President, checking both political branches.
w: the executive checking the judicial branch
The court, not the President, acted here; an executive check would be something like appointing judges.
the legislative branch checking the judicial branch
Congress passed the law; the court checked Congress, not the other way around.
the states checking the national government
A federal court acted, not a state, and the states have no power to void federal laws.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law and the President signs it. Later, in a lawsuit, a federal court rules that the law conflicts with the Constitution and refuses to enforce it.

items.q: After losing the election of 1800, President John Adams appointed a justice of the peace whose commission was never delivered. The appointee asked the Supreme Court to order the new Secretary of State to deliver it. Which case arose from this dispute?
items.a: Marbury v. Madison
items.ex: Marbury v. Madison (1803) began when William Marbury, a last-minute Adams appointee, sought a writ of mandamus against Madison; Chief Justice John Marshall used the case to establish judicial review.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
1819 case on the national bank and a state tax, not an undelivered commission.
United States v. Nixon
1974 case ordering President Nixon to hand over the Watergate tapes.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
1857 case denying Black citizenship and striking down the Missouri Compromise.

alt.q: Which case first established that federal courts may declare an act of Congress unconstitutional and therefore void?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: In Marbury v. Madison (1803) the Court struck down Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, the first time it voided an act of Congress, establishing judicial review.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
Upheld an act of Congress (the bank charter) and struck down a state tax.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Struck down the Missouri Compromise in 1857, but Marbury had already set the precedent.
Gibbons v. Ogden
1824 Marshall Court case defining Congress's power over interstate commerce.

alt.q: "It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is." In which case did Chief Justice John Marshall write this?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: This line from Marbury v. Madison (1803) is the classic statement of judicial review; the Court later quoted it in United States v. Nixon (1974).
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
Also by Marshall, but known for 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy.'
United States v. Nixon
Quoted this Marbury line in 1974; it did not originate it.
Gibbons v. Ogden
Marshall's 1824 opinion on the Commerce Clause and steamboat licenses.

items.q: Which principle did Marbury v. Madison establish?
items.a: Judicial review of laws for constitutionality
items.ex: Marbury (1803) held that a law conflicting with the Constitution is void and that courts decide such conflicts, establishing judicial review.
w: Implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Established by McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Executive privilege limited by due process
The holding of United States v. Nixon (1974).
Selective incorporation of the Bill of Rights
Developed in 20th-century cases such as Gideon and Mapp.

alt.q: In Marbury v. Madison, why did the Court refuse to order Madison to deliver the commission, even though it said Marbury had a right to it?
alt.a: The statute granting that power violated Article III
alt.ex: Marshall held that Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 unconstitutionally expanded the Court's original jurisdiction beyond Article III, so the Court could not issue the writ.
w: Marbury's appointment was never confirmed by the Senate
False: the Senate had confirmed him; only delivery was missing.
Delivering commissions was a political question for Congress
Marshall held delivery was a ministerial legal duty courts could review, not a political matter.
The President held an absolute executive privilege over it
Absolute executive privilege was rejected in United States v. Nixon (1974).

alt.q: Chief Justice Marshall concluded in 1803 that "a law repugnant to the constitution is void." Which idea does this statement express?
alt.a: Courts may void laws that conflict with the Constitution
alt.ex: This Marbury v. Madison reasoning is the basis of judicial review: the Constitution is supreme over ordinary statutes, and courts enforce that supremacy.
w: States may void federal laws they find unconstitutional
That is nullification (Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions), which Marbury did not endorse.
Congress may pass laws needed to carry out its powers
That is the Necessary and Proper Clause, interpreted in McCulloch.
The President may refuse to enforce unconstitutional laws
Marbury gave the power of review to the courts, not the President.

items.q: Marbury v. Madison and McCulloch v. Maryland were both written by Chief Justice John Marshall. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: Marbury set up judicial review; McCulloch upheld implied powers
items.ex: Marbury (1803) established judicial review; McCulloch (1819) upheld the national bank under implied powers and barred Maryland's tax on it.
w: Marbury upheld implied powers; McCulloch set up judicial review
Reverses the two holdings.
Marbury voided a state tax; McCulloch voided a federal statute
Reversed: Marbury voided part of a federal statute; McCulloch voided a state tax.
Marbury upheld the national bank; McCulloch ordered a commission delivered
Mixes up the facts of the two cases.

alt.q: Which pairing correctly matches a Marshall Court case with the law it held unconstitutional?
alt.a: Marbury: part of the Judiciary Act of 1789
alt.ex: Marbury (1803) voided Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789; McCulloch (1819) voided Maryland's tax on the Second Bank of the United States.
w: Marbury: Maryland's tax on the national bank
That tax was struck down in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
McCulloch: the charter of the Second Bank
McCulloch upheld the bank's charter as a valid implied power.
Marbury: the Judiciary Act of 1801's new judgeships
That act was repealed by Congress in 1802, not voided in Marbury.

alt.q: A student writes: 'Marshall's Court first claimed the power to strike down federal laws, and sixteen years later used federal supremacy to stop a state from taxing a federal institution.' Which cases are described, in order?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison, then McCulloch v. Maryland
alt.ex: Marbury (1803) established judicial review; McCulloch (1819) used the Supremacy Clause to bar Maryland's tax on the national bank.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland, then Marbury v. Madison
Correct cases in the wrong order: Marbury came first.
Marbury v. Madison, then Gibbons v. Ogden
Gibbons (1824) concerned interstate commerce, not a state tax on a federal bank.
Fletcher v. Peck, then McCulloch v. Maryland
Fletcher (1810) voided a state law under the Contract Clause; it did not establish review of federal laws.

items.q: How did McCulloch v. Maryland affect the balance of power between the national government and the states?
items.a: It strengthened national authority over the states
items.ex: McCulloch (1819) upheld Congress's implied power to charter a national bank and, under the Supremacy Clause, barred Maryland from taxing it, strengthening the national government relative to the states.
w: It let states tax and regulate federal institutions
The Court ruled the opposite: Maryland could not tax the Bank of the United States.
It limited Congress strictly to its listed powers
McCulloch upheld implied powers beyond those specifically listed.
It gave the states power to void federal laws
No case gave states this nullification power; McCulloch affirmed federal supremacy.

alt.q: Which constitutional principle does this passage most directly support?
alt.a: federal supremacy
alt.ex: Marshall's statement that the national government is 'supreme within its sphere of action' reflects the Supremacy Clause (Article VI): valid federal law prevails over conflicting state law.
w: states' rights
The passage stresses the national government's supremacy, the opposite of a states'-rights view.
popular sovereignty
Popular sovereignty means power comes from the people; the passage is about federal law outranking the states.
separation of powers
Separation of powers divides power among branches; the passage concerns national versus state power.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Supreme Court's opinion in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“...the Government of the Union, though limited in its powers, is supreme within its sphere of action.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that expanded the power of the federal government relative to the states?
alt.a: McCulloch v. Maryland
alt.ex: McCulloch (1819) read the Necessary and Proper Clause broadly and held that states may not tax a federal institution, expanding national power at the states' expense.
w: United States v. Lopez
Lopez (1995) did the opposite: it limited Congress's commerce power in favor of the states.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Dred Scott limited Congress, holding it could not ban slavery in the federal territories.
Wisconsin v. Yoder
Yoder concerned an individual's free exercise of religion against a state law, not federal power.

items.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland, how did Chief Justice Marshall interpret the word ‘necessary’ in the Necessary and Proper Clause?
items.a: as useful or convenient, not absolutely essential
items.ex: Marshall wrote that 'necessary' 'frequently imports no more than that one thing is convenient, or useful, or essential to another,' a loose reading that supports Congress's implied powers.
w: as absolutely indispensable to a listed power
This was Maryland's strict reading, which Marshall rejected; he noted the framers used 'absolutely necessary' elsewhere but not here.
as limited to powers the states agree to grant
Marshall held that the national government's powers come from the people, not from the consent of the states.
as covering only actions taken during times of war
Nothing in the clause or the ruling limits it to war; the case concerned a national bank in peacetime.

alt.q: Which argument did the Supreme Court reject in McCulloch v. Maryland?
alt.a: Congress may pass only indispensable laws
alt.ex: Maryland argued that 'necessary' meant absolutely indispensable; the Court rejected this strict construction and upheld the national bank as a reasonable means to carry out enumerated powers.
w: Congress may charter a national bank
The Court accepted this, holding the bank a valid exercise of implied powers.
Federal law prevails over conflicting state law
The Court accepted this under the Supremacy Clause.
States may not tax federal institutions
The Court accepted this, reasoning that 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy.'

alt.q: Which approach to interpreting the Constitution does this passage support?
alt.a: a flexible reading that allows implied powers
alt.ex: Marshall described a Constitution meant 'to endure for ages to come' and adapt to new crises, which supports a broad (loose) reading of Congress's powers through the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: a strict reading limited to listed powers
A Constitution 'adapted to the various crises of human affairs' implies flexibility, not strict limits to the text.
a reading that lets states veto federal laws
The passage says nothing about state vetoes, and McCulloch affirmed federal supremacy.
a reading that requires frequent formal amendments
Marshall's point was that a flexible reading lets the Constitution adapt without constant amendment.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Supreme Court's opinion in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“...a Constitution intended to endure for ages to come, and consequently to be adapted to the various crises of human affairs.”
Source: United States Reports

items.q: In 1818 a state taxed a local branch of the Second Bank of the United States, and the branch's cashier refused to pay. Which case resulted?
items.a: McCulloch v. Maryland
items.ex: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819): the Court unanimously held that Congress could charter the bank and that Maryland could not tax it.
w: Marbury v. Madison
1803 case about an undelivered judicial commission that established judicial review.
Gibbons v. Ogden
1824 case about steamboat licenses and the Commerce Clause.
United States v. Lopez
1995 case limiting the Commerce Clause in a school gun law.

alt.q: Which case held that Congress may create a national bank under its implied powers and that a state may not tax that bank?
alt.a: McCulloch v. Maryland
alt.ex: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Marshall read the Necessary and Proper Clause broadly and used the Supremacy Clause to strike Maryland's tax.
w: Marbury v. Madison
Established judicial review in 1803; it did not involve the bank.
Gibbons v. Ogden
Defined 'commerce' broadly in 1824; it did not involve a bank tax.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
1857 case on slavery in the territories and Black citizenship.

alt.q: Chief Justice Marshall reasoned "that the power to tax involves the power to destroy." What did the Court conclude from this reasoning?
alt.a: Maryland could not tax the Bank of the United States
alt.ex: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Marshall reasoned that a state tax could destroy a federal institution, which the Supremacy Clause forbids.
w: Congress could not tax banks chartered by the states
Reverses the case: the issue was a state taxing a federal bank.
Congress lacked power to create a national bank
That was Maryland's losing argument; the Court upheld the bank.
States could tax federal banks at equal rates
The Court barred the state tax entirely, not only unequal ones.

items.q: Which constitutional provisions were central to McCulloch v. Maryland?
items.a: Necessary and Proper Clause and Supremacy Clause
items.ex: Marshall read 'necessary' broadly, as useful or conducive rather than absolutely necessary, to uphold the bank, and used the Supremacy Clause to strike Maryland's tax (1819).
w: Commerce Clause and the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
Central to United States v. Lopez (1995), not McCulloch.
Article III original jurisdiction and the Judiciary Act
Central to Marbury v. Madison (1803).
General Welfare Clause and the Full Faith and Credit Clause
Neither was the basis of McCulloch's holding.

alt.q: Congress creates a federal agency that is not mentioned anywhere in the Constitution, reasoning that it helps carry out the power to regulate commerce. Which doctrine from McCulloch v. Maryland best supports this?
alt.a: Implied powers drawn from the Necessary and Proper Clause
alt.ex: McCulloch (1819) held that Congress may use means not listed in the Constitution if they are appropriate to carry out an enumerated power.
w: Reserved powers kept by the states under the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers limit federal action; they do not authorize it.
Concurrent powers shared equally by states and the nation
Concurrent powers (like taxing) were not the basis for creating the bank.
Inherent powers held by the President in foreign affairs
McCulloch concerned Congress's powers, not presidential foreign-affairs power.

alt.q: "Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution, and all means which are appropriate ... are constitutional." Which idea does this passage support?
alt.a: A broad reading of Congress's implied powers
alt.ex: Marshall's line in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) is the classic statement of loose construction of the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: A strict reading limited to enumerated powers
That was the Jeffersonian view Marshall rejected.
The states' reserved power to tax federal banks
The same case held Maryland could not tax the bank.
The courts' power to void unconstitutional laws
That is judicial review from Marbury v. Madison (1803).

items.q: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) and United States v. Lopez (1995) both concerned the reach of federal power. Which statement correctly contrasts them?
items.a: McCulloch expanded federal power; Lopez set a limit on it
items.ex: McCulloch upheld broad implied powers; Lopez struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act as beyond the Commerce Clause.
w: McCulloch limited federal power; Lopez expanded federal power
Reverses the two outcomes.
Both cases struck down federal laws as exceeding Article I
McCulloch upheld the federal bank and struck a state tax.
Both cases upheld federal laws under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Lopez struck down the federal law.

alt.q: A student confuses McCulloch v. Maryland with United States v. Lopez. Which holding belongs only to Lopez?
alt.a: Congress exceeded its Commerce Clause power
alt.ex: Lopez (1995) held that carrying a gun near a school is not economic activity that Congress may regulate under the Commerce Clause.
w: A state could not tax a federal institution
That was McCulloch's holding on Maryland's bank tax.
Congress may use means not listed in the Constitution
That is McCulloch's implied-powers holding.
Federal law is supreme over conflicting state law
McCulloch applied the Supremacy Clause; Lopez did not turn on it.

alt.q: Which pairing correctly matches each case to the clause it mainly interpreted?
alt.a: McCulloch – Necessary and Proper; Lopez – Commerce
alt.ex: McCulloch (1819) interpreted the Necessary and Proper Clause; Lopez (1995) interpreted the Commerce Clause.
w: McCulloch – Commerce; Lopez – Necessary and Proper
Reverses the two clauses.
McCulloch – Supremacy; Lopez – Second Amendment
Lopez was a Commerce Clause case, not a gun-rights case.
McCulloch – Tenth Amendment; Lopez – Due Process
McCulloch rejected the Tenth Amendment argument; Lopez did not rest on due process.

items.q: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) was only the second time the Supreme Court had done which of the following?
items.a: struck down a federal law as unconstitutional
items.ex: By ruling that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, Dred Scott voided the Missouri Compromise, the first act of Congress struck down since Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: overruled one of its own earlier decisions
Dred Scott did not overrule an earlier precedent; it struck down an act of Congress.
decided a case involving slavery
The Court had ruled in slavery-related cases before 1857, such as the Amistad case (1841).
settled a legal dispute between two state governments
Dred Scott was a freedom suit by an individual, not a dispute between states.

alt.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that limited the power of Congress over the federal territories?
alt.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
alt.ex: Dred Scott (1857) held that Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories, voiding the Missouri Compromise and narrowing congressional power over federal land.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch expanded congressional power through implied powers; it did not concern territories.
United States v. Lopez
Lopez limited the commerce power regarding guns near schools, not power over territories.
Marbury v. Madison
Marbury voided part of the Judiciary Act concerning the Court's jurisdiction, not territorial power.

alt.q: Which statement about judicial review is best illustrated by Dred Scott v. Sandford?
alt.a: It can restrict rights as well as protect them
alt.ex: In Dred Scott the Court used judicial review to strike down the Missouri Compromise and deny Black Americans citizenship, showing that the power can restrict rights as well as protect them.
w: It can be used only to protect individual rights
Dred Scott used judicial review to take away rights, so this is false.
It applies only to state laws, not federal laws
Dred Scott struck down a federal law, the Missouri Compromise.
It requires approval from Congress to take effect
Court rulings do not need congressional approval; Congress's law was voided over its objection.

items.q: Which Supreme Court case contains this passage?
items.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
items.ex: Chief Justice Taney wrote in Dred Scott (1857) that people of African descent were not 'citizens' under the Constitution, a holding later reversed by the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause (1868).
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) came after the 14th Amendment made Black Americans citizens; it upheld segregation, not denial of citizenship.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu involved Japanese Americans who were U.S. citizens; it upheld wartime exclusion, not denial of citizenship.
Brown v. Board of Education
Brown expanded civil rights by ending school segregation.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“We think they are not, and that they are not included, and were not intended to be included, under the word ‘citizens’ in the Constitution, and can therefore claim none of the rights and privileges which that instrument provides for and secures to citizens of the United States.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: By what process was Dred Scott v. Sandford's ruling on Black citizenship overturned?
alt.a: constitutional amendment
