alt.ex: Because Dred Scott rested on the Constitution, it was overturned by amending the Constitution: the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) declares all persons born or naturalized in the United States to be citizens.
w: Supreme Court decision
The Court never had to reverse Dred Scott; the 14th Amendment superseded it first.
presidential proclamation
The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed enslaved people in Confederate areas but did not grant citizenship.
state legislation
States cannot override a federal constitutional ruling; a national amendment was required.

alt.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that denied citizenship to an entire group of Americans?
alt.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
alt.ex: Dred Scott (1857) held that people of African descent, enslaved or free, could not be U.S. citizens.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy upheld segregation but did not deny citizenship, which the 14th Amendment had already guaranteed.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu upheld the exclusion of Japanese Americans, most of whom remained U.S. citizens.
Shaw v. Reno
Shaw concerned racially drawn election districts, not citizenship.

items.q: An enslaved man who had lived for years in a free state and in a free federal territory sued in federal court for freedom after returning to Missouri. Which case arose?
items.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
items.ex: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled 7–2 that Scott was not a citizen and could not sue.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
1896 case upholding segregated railroad cars.
Prigg v. Pennsylvania
1842 case on fugitive slave recovery, not a freedom suit by residence.
Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case striking down school segregation.

alt.q: Which case held that people of African descent could not be U.S. citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories?
alt.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
alt.ex: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) denied Black citizenship and declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Upheld 'separate but equal' in 1896; it did not deny citizenship.
McCulloch v. Maryland
1819 case on the national bank and implied powers.
Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case ending school segregation.

alt.q: Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote that Black Americans "had no rights which the white man was bound to respect." This statement comes from which case?
alt.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
alt.ex: Taney's majority opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) contains this line; the 14th Amendment (1868) overturned its citizenship ruling.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Its majority, by Justice Henry Billings Brown, upheld segregation in 1896.
Korematsu v. United States
1944 case upholding Japanese American exclusion.
Brown v. Board of Education
1954 opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren ending school segregation.

items.q: Which constitutional change most directly overturned the Dred Scott decision's ruling on citizenship?
items.a: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868)
items.ex: The 14th Amendment (1868) declares that all persons born or naturalized in the United States are citizens, reversing Dred Scott's citizenship holding.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment (1865)
It abolished slavery but did not define citizenship.
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870)
It barred race-based denial of the vote; it did not define citizenship.
The Emancipation Proclamation (1863)
An executive order, not a constitutional change, and it addressed slavery in Confederate-held areas.

alt.q: Which part of the Dred Scott ruling most intensified sectional conflict before the Civil War?
alt.a: It declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional
alt.ex: By holding that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, Dred Scott (1857) voided the Missouri Compromise and angered the North.
w: It upheld the Missouri Compromise's ban on slavery
The Court struck the Compromise down.
It required Northern states to return fugitive slaves
That was the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, a law of Congress.
It struck down the Kansas-Nebraska Act's popular sovereignty
The Court did not rule on the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

alt.q: On what constitutional basis did Chief Justice Taney argue that Congress could not ban slavery in the federal territories?
alt.a: The Fifth Amendment's protection of property
alt.ex: Taney treated enslaved people as property and held that banning slavery in the territories deprived owners of property without due process (1857).
w: The Tenth Amendment's reserved powers of states
Taney's territorial holding rested on property rights, not reserved powers.
The Commerce Clause's limits on federal power
The commerce power was not the basis of the ruling.
Article IV's Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns honoring other states' records, not slavery.

mt.q: Match each Reconstruction Amendment to what it did.
pairs: Citizenship, due process and equal protection
Race can't be used to deny the vote
mt.ex: Reconstruction Amendments: 13th (1865) abolished slavery; 14th (1868) defined citizenship and guaranteed due process and equal protection; 15th (1870) barred denying the vote because of race.

items.q: Dred Scott v. Sandford and Plessy v. Ferguson are often confused. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: Dred Scott denied Black citizenship; Plessy upheld segregation
items.ex: Dred Scott (1857) said Black Americans could not be citizens; Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal' segregation.
w: Dred Scott upheld segregation; Plessy denied Black citizenship
Reverses the two holdings.
Dred Scott ended slavery in territories; Plessy ended segregation
Both cases went the other way.
Both cases were overturned by the Thirteenth Amendment
Dred Scott was overturned by the 13th and 14th Amendments; Plessy by Brown (1954).

alt.q: Which case came after the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified and so had to interpret its Equal Protection Clause?
alt.a: Plessy v. Ferguson
alt.ex: Plessy (1896) interpreted the 14th Amendment (1868) to allow segregation; Dred Scott (1857) came before that amendment existed.
w: Dred Scott v. Sandford
Decided in 1857, before the 14th Amendment was written.
Prigg v. Pennsylvania
Decided in 1842 on the Fugitive Slave Clause.
Marbury v. Madison
Decided in 1803 on judicial review.

alt.q: A history student writes: 'This decision ruled that Congress could not keep slavery out of federal territories, helping push the nation toward civil war.' Which case is described, and what reversed its key holdings?
alt.a: Dred Scott; reversed by the 13th and 14th Amendments
alt.ex: Dred Scott (1857) was undone by constitutional amendments: the 13th (1865) ended slavery and the 14th (1868) made Black Americans citizens.
w: Plessy; reversed by Brown v. Board of Education
Plessy upheld segregation; it did not involve the territories.
Dred Scott; reversed by Brown v. Board of Education
Brown overturned Plessy, not Dred Scott.
Plessy; reversed by the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments
Plessy came after these amendments and was overturned by Brown.

items.q: The U.S. Supreme Court enabled which government practices to continue in its ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson?
items.a: segregating public facilities
items.ex: In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Court upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers, approving “separate but equal” and allowing segregation of public facilities until Brown v. Board of Education (1954) rejected it for schools.
w: prohibiting monopoly formation
Plessy concerned racial segregation, not antitrust law.
establishing immigration quotas
Immigration quotas came from laws such as the 1924 Immigration Act, not Plessy.
regulating financial markets
Plessy did not involve financial regulation.

alt.q: Which doctrine did the Supreme Court approve in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)?
alt.a: separate but equal
alt.ex: Plessy upheld racial segregation as long as the separate facilities were supposedly equal, giving legal cover to Jim Crow laws.
w: one person, one vote
This principle came from 1960s cases such as Reynolds v. Sims about legislative districts.
clear and present danger
This free-speech test came from Schenck v. United States (1919).
the exclusionary rule
This rule bars illegally obtained evidence; it was applied to the states in Mapp v. Ohio (1961).

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case rejected the doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson as applied to public schools?
alt.a: Brown v. Board of Education
alt.ex: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Court unanimously held that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, violating the Equal Protection Clause.
w: Dred Scott v. Sandford
Dred Scott (1857) held that Black Americans could not be citizens; it came before Plessy.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu (1944) upheld the wartime removal of Japanese Americans.
Marbury v. Madison
Marbury (1803) established judicial review.

items.q: Based on the passage, how did the Court interpret the Fourteenth Amendment in Plessy v. Ferguson?
items.a: as requiring legal equality but allowing segregation
items.ex: The Plessy majority (1896) said the 14th Amendment guaranteed equality 'before the law' but not 'social' equality, so state-required segregation was allowed if facilities were 'equal.'
w: as requiring the integration of all public facilities
That was Brown v. Board's view (1954) for schools; Plessy upheld segregated rail cars.
as applying only to the federal government
The 14th Amendment limits the states; Plessy reviewed a Louisiana law under it.
as banning all racial distinctions in the law
This was Justice Harlan's dissenting view ('Our Constitution is color-blind'), not the majority's.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The object of the amendment was undoubtedly to enforce the absolute equality of the two races before the law, but, in the nature of things, it could not have been intended to abolish distinctions based upon color, or to enforce social, as distinguished from political, equality, or a commingling of the two races upon terms unsatisfactory to either.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that restricted civil rights by narrowly interpreting the Fourteenth Amendment?
alt.a: Plessy v. Ferguson
alt.ex: Plessy (1896) read the Equal Protection Clause to allow 'separate but equal' segregation, giving legal cover to Jim Crow laws.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Brown read the 14th Amendment broadly to strike down school segregation, expanding civil rights.
Baker v. Carr
Baker used the 14th Amendment to let courts review unequal districts, expanding voting rights.
McDonald v. City of Chicago
McDonald used the 14th Amendment to apply the Second Amendment to the states, expanding a right.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court precedent would a court at that time most likely follow?
alt.a: Plessy v. Ferguson
alt.ex: From 1896 until Brown v. Board (1954), Plessy's 'separate but equal' doctrine let states require segregated facilities such as rail cars and waiting rooms.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Brown was not decided until 1954, and it addressed public schools.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Dred Scott (1857) predated the 14th Amendment and concerned citizenship and slavery in the territories.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu was decided in 1944 and concerned wartime exclusion, not segregated facilities.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1910, a state law requires separate waiting rooms for Black and white passengers at train stations. A Black traveler challenges the law under the Equal Protection Clause.

items.q: A man who was one-eighth African American sat in a railroad car reserved for white passengers in Louisiana, refused to move, and was arrested under a state law. Which case resulted?
items.a: Plessy v. Ferguson
items.ex: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld Louisiana's Separate Car Act 7–1, creating the 'separate but equal' doctrine.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case that rejected 'separate but equal' in schools.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
1857 case denying Black citizenship.
Korematsu v. United States
1944 case on Japanese American exclusion.

alt.q: Which case created the 'separate but equal' doctrine by upholding state-required racial segregation?
alt.a: Plessy v. Ferguson
alt.ex: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) held that segregation did not violate the 14th Amendment if facilities were equal.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Rejected the doctrine for public schools in 1954.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
1857 ruling on citizenship and slavery in the territories.
Korematsu v. United States
Upheld wartime exclusion of Japanese Americans in 1944.

alt.q: A majority opinion called it a fallacy to assume "that the enforced separation of the two races stamps the colored race with a badge of inferiority." Which case is this, and how did it rule?
alt.a: Plessy; it upheld segregated rail cars
alt.ex: Justice Henry Billings Brown wrote this for the majority in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), upholding Louisiana's Separate Car Act.
w: Brown; it struck down segregated schools
Brown (1954) found that segregation does create a feeling of inferiority.
Plessy; it struck down segregated rail cars
Right case, wrong outcome: Plessy upheld the law.
Dred Scott; it denied Black citizenship
Dred Scott (1857) predates segregation laws and the 14th Amendment.

items.q: In Plessy v. Ferguson, the Court held that state-mandated segregation did not violate which constitutional provision?
items.a: The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
items.ex: Plessy (1896) held that 'separate but equal' facilities satisfied the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
w: The Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment
That clause binds the federal government; Plessy challenged a state law.
The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment
Concerns government and religion, not race.
The Privileges and Immunities Clause of Article IV
Concerns treatment of out-of-state citizens, not the basis of Plessy.

alt.q: "Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens." Who wrote this, and where?
alt.a: Justice Harlan, dissenting in Plessy v. Ferguson
alt.ex: John Marshall Harlan was the lone dissenter in Plessy (1896); his view was later vindicated by Brown (1954).
w: Chief Justice Warren, for the Court in Brown v. Board
Warren wrote 'Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.'
Justice Brown, for the majority in Plessy v. Ferguson
The Plessy majority upheld segregation.
Justice Murphy, dissenting in Korematsu v. U.S.
Murphy dissented against 'this legalization of racism' in 1944.

alt.q: What was the main impact of Plessy v. Ferguson?
alt.a: It gave legal cover to Jim Crow segregation laws
alt.ex: Plessy (1896) allowed 'separate but equal,' supporting segregation for nearly 60 years until Brown (1954).
w: It ended segregation in public schools nationwide
That was Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
It denied citizenship to people of African descent
That was Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).
It required states to provide equal voting access
Plessy did not concern voting; see the 15th Amendment and Voting Rights Act.

items.q: How did Brown v. Board of Education (1954) relate to Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)?
items.a: Brown rejected Plessy's 'separate but equal' in public schools
items.ex: Brown held unanimously that 'in the field of public education' separate but equal has no place, overturning Plessy for schools.
w: Brown applied Plessy's 'separate but equal' rule to public schools
Brown rejected the rule.
Brown overturned Plessy by applying the Thirteenth Amendment
Brown rested on the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
Brown upheld Plessy but required equal funding for schools
Earlier cases demanded equal facilities; Brown ended segregation itself.

alt.q: Which choice correctly pairs each case with its holding?
alt.a: Plessy: segregation allowed; Brown: school segregation unequal
alt.ex: Plessy (1896) upheld separate but equal; Brown (1954) declared separate schools 'inherently unequal.'
w: Plessy: segregation unequal; Brown: school segregation allowed
Reverses the two holdings.
Plessy: citizenship denied; Brown: segregation allowed if equal
Citizenship was denied in Dred Scott; Brown ended segregation.
Plessy: rail segregation struck; Brown: busing required
Plessy upheld rail segregation; busing was approved in Swann (1971).

alt.q: In 1950 a state argues its separate schools for Black and white students are legal because the buildings and teacher salaries are equal. Which earlier case does the state rely on, and which later case rejected that argument?
alt.a: Plessy v. Ferguson; Brown v. Board of Education
alt.ex: The state relies on Plessy's 'separate but equal' (1896); Brown (1954) held separate schools inherently unequal.
w: Dred Scott v. Sandford; Brown v. Board of Education
Dred Scott concerned citizenship, not segregated facilities.
Brown v. Board of Education; Plessy v. Ferguson
Reverses the order and roles of the cases.
Plessy v. Ferguson; Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg
Swann (1971) approved busing to carry out Brown; it did not make the core ruling.

items.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that limited freedom of speech in prioritization of national security?
items.a: Schenck v. United States
items.ex: In Schenck (1919), the Court unanimously upheld a conviction for antidraft leaflets during World War I, reasoning that speech creating a 'clear and present danger' can be punished.
w: Tinker v. Des Moines
Tinker expanded speech rights by protecting students' antiwar armbands.
Texas v. Johnson
Johnson protected flag burning as symbolic speech.
New York Times v. United States
The Court rejected the government's national security claim and let the newspapers publish.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the impact of Schenck v. United States on free speech?
alt.a: It showed that speech rights are not absolute
alt.ex: Schenck's 'clear and present danger' test showed that the First Amendment does not protect all speech; government may punish speech that creates a serious danger, especially in wartime.
w: It barred most prior restraints on the press
Limits on prior restraint come from cases such as New York Times v. United States, not Schenck.
It protected symbolic protest by students
Student symbolic speech was protected in Tinker v. Des Moines (1969).
It first applied freedom of speech to the states
Schenck involved a federal law; the Court first treated free speech as binding on states in Gitlow v. New York (1925).

alt.q: Which Supreme Court precedent most strongly supports the government's position?
alt.a: Schenck v. United States
alt.ex: Schenck (1919) upheld a wartime Espionage Act conviction for leaflets obstructing the draft, holding that speech posing a 'clear and present danger' may be punished.
w: New York Times v. United States
This case favored the press over the government's security claims.
Tinker v. Des Moines
Tinker protected student antiwar expression, which supports the speaker, not the government.
Texas v. Johnson
Johnson protected offensive political expression, which supports the speaker.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: During a declared war, Congress makes it a crime to mail pamphlets urging soldiers to desert. A person convicted under the law argues that it violates the First Amendment.

items.q: Schenck v. United States tested the constitutionality of which type of law?
items.a: a federal statute passed by Congress
items.ex: Schenck was convicted under the Espionage Act of 1917, a federal law; the First Amendment ('Congress shall make no law') limits Congress directly.
w: a state criminal statute
Schenck was prosecuted by the United States, not by a state.
an executive order issued by the President
The conviction rested on an act of Congress, not an executive order.
a local school district policy
School policies were at issue in cases like Tinker, not Schenck.

alt.q: Charles Schenck was convicted under which law?
alt.a: the Espionage Act of 1917
alt.ex: Schenck, a Socialist Party official, was convicted under the Espionage Act of 1917 for mailing leaflets urging resistance to the draft during World War I.
w: the Sedition Act of 1798
The 1798 Sedition Act expired in 1801, more than a century before Schenck's case.
the Smith Act of 1940
The Smith Act came two decades later and targeted advocacy of overthrowing the government.
the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001
The PATRIOT Act was passed after the 9/11 attacks, long after Schenck.

alt.q: Why could Schenck rely on the First Amendment directly, without the Fourteenth Amendment applying it to the states?
alt.a: He was prosecuted by the federal government
alt.ex: The First Amendment restricts Congress, and Schenck was charged under a federal law (the Espionage Act), so no incorporation was needed; free speech was not applied to the states until Gitlow v. New York (1925).
w: The First Amendment had already been incorporated
Free speech was not treated as binding on the states until 1925, six years after Schenck.
The Fourteenth Amendment was not yet ratified
The 14th Amendment was ratified in 1868, long before 1919.
He was serving in the U.S. armed forces
Schenck was a civilian Socialist Party official, not a soldier.

items.q: During World War I, a Socialist Party official mailed leaflets urging draft-age men to resist conscription and was convicted under the Espionage Act. Which case resulted?
items.a: Schenck v. United States
items.ex: Schenck v. United States (1919) unanimously upheld the conviction; Justice Holmes introduced the 'clear and present danger' test.
w: Tinker v. Des Moines
1969 case protecting students' antiwar armbands.
New York Times v. United States
1971 case rejecting prior restraint of the Pentagon Papers.
Korematsu v. United States
1944 case on Japanese American exclusion, not speech.

alt.q: Which case created the 'clear and present danger' test for limits on speech?
alt.a: Schenck v. United States
alt.ex: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes announced the clear and present danger test in Schenck v. United States (1919).
w: Brandenburg v. Ohio
1969 case that replaced it with the 'imminent lawless action' test.
Tinker v. Des Moines
Created the 'substantial disruption' test for schools in 1969.
New York Times v. United States
1971 case on prior restraint of the press.

alt.q: "The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic." In which case did Justice Holmes write this?
alt.a: Schenck v. United States
alt.ex: Holmes used this analogy in Schenck v. United States (1919) to explain why some speech, like Schenck's antidraft leaflets, may be punished.
w: Abrams v. United States
Also 1919, but there Holmes dissented in favor of the speakers.
New York Times v. United States
1971 case rejecting prior restraint of the press.
Tinker v. Des Moines
1969 student speech case.

items.q: What test did Schenck v. United States establish for when government may limit speech?
items.a: Clear and present danger of a substantive evil
items.ex: Schenck (1919) asked whether words create 'a clear and present danger' of evils Congress has a right to prevent.
w: Material and substantial disruption of school
The Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) standard for students.
Imminent lawless action that is likely to be produced
The Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) test that replaced Schenck's.
Heavy presumption against any prior restraint
The rule applied in New York Times v. United States (1971).

alt.q: Why did the Court uphold Schenck's conviction despite the First Amendment?
alt.a: Wartime speech obstructing the draft posed real danger
alt.ex: Holmes reasoned that in wartime, leaflets urging draft resistance created a clear and present danger Congress could prevent (1919).
w: The First Amendment did not apply to federal laws in 1919
The First Amendment has always limited Congress.
The government may block any publication before it is printed
Schenck was punished after the fact; this was not prior restraint.
Speech by members of minor parties is not protected
Party membership was not the basis of the ruling.

alt.q: "The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger..." Which statement best explains this standard?
alt.a: Context decides whether speech can be punished
alt.ex: In Schenck (1919), Holmes said the same words may be protected in peacetime but punishable in wartime, depending on circumstances.
w: All political speech is fully protected in wartime
Schenck upheld punishment of wartime political speech.
Speech may be stopped only after actual violence
Schenck required only a clear and present danger, not actual violence.
Only spoken words, not printed ones, can be punished
Schenck's words were printed leaflets.

items.q: Schenck v. United States (1919) and New York Times v. United States (1971) both weighed free expression against national security. How did their outcomes differ?
items.a: Schenck upheld a conviction; NYT barred a prior restraint
items.ex: Schenck upheld punishment of antidraft leaflets; NYT v. U.S. (6–3) refused to block publication of the Pentagon Papers.
w: Schenck barred a prior restraint; NYT upheld a conviction
Reverses the outcomes.
Both upheld government limits on wartime publication
NYT v. U.S. rejected the government's attempt to block publication.
Both struck down the Espionage Act as unconstitutional
Schenck upheld the Espionage Act; NYT did not strike it down.

alt.q: Which feature of New York Times v. United States sets it apart from Schenck v. United States?
alt.a: The government sought to stop publication in advance
alt.ex: NYT v. U.S. (1971) involved prior restraint, which carries a heavy presumption against it; Schenck involved punishment after speech.
w: The speaker was punished after urging draft resistance
That describes Schenck.
The Court applied the clear and present danger test
That test came from Schenck.
The Court deferred to Congress in wartime
That deference describes Schenck; NYT ruled against the government.

alt.q: A newspaper obtains a classified history of a war and the government sues to block publication (A); separately, an activist is jailed for leaflets urging people to dodge the draft (B). Which cases match A and B?
alt.a: NYT v. United States; Schenck v. United States
alt.ex: A matches New York Times v. U.S. (1971, prior restraint rejected); B matches Schenck v. U.S. (1919, conviction upheld).
w: Schenck v. United States; NYT v. United States
Reverses the matches.
NYT v. United States; Tinker v. Des Moines
Tinker concerned student armbands, not draft leaflets.
Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier; Schenck v. United States
Hazelwood concerned a school newspaper, not a national newspaper.

items.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that undermined civil rights and liberties in prioritization of national security?
items.a: Korematsu v. United States
items.ex: In Korematsu v. United States (1944), the Court upheld the World War II exclusion of Japanese Americans from the West Coast, citing military necessity. The Court later repudiated the decision in Trump v. Hawaii (2018).
w: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke
Bakke (1978) concerned racial quotas in university admissions, not national security.
Brown v. Board of Education
Brown (1954) expanded civil rights by ending legal school segregation.
District of Columbia v. Heller
Heller (2008) protected an individual right to keep a handgun at home.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case upheld the forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast during World War II?
alt.a: Korematsu v. United States
alt.ex: Fred Korematsu was convicted for refusing to leave a military exclusion zone; in 1944 the Court upheld the exclusion order as a wartime necessity.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld racial segregation on railroad cars.
Brown v. Board of Education
Brown (1954) ended legal segregation in public schools.
Schenck v. United States
Schenck (1919) concerned antidraft leaflets in World War I, not Japanese Americans.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case upheld the conviction of a man who distributed leaflets urging resistance to the military draft during World War I?
alt.a: Schenck v. United States
alt.ex: In Schenck v. United States (1919), the Court ruled that speech posing a “clear and present danger” during wartime could be punished, limiting free speech in the name of national security.
w: Tinker v. Des Moines
Tinker (1969) protected students’ right to wear armbands protesting the Vietnam War.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu (1944) concerned the exclusion of Japanese Americans, not antidraft leaflets.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Gideon (1963) guaranteed counsel to poor criminal defendants.

items.q: Which later action acknowledged the injustice of the wartime policy upheld in Korematsu v. United States?
items.a: the Civil Liberties Act of 1988
items.ex: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 formally apologized for the removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II and provided $20,000 to each eligible survivor.
w: the Civil Rights Act of 1964
This law banned discrimination in public accommodations and employment; it did not address wartime incarceration.
the Voting Rights Act of 1965
This law protected voting rights; it did not address Japanese American incarceration.
the National Origins Act of 1924
This law restricted immigration, including from Japan; it came before the war and offered no apology.

alt.q: This apology addressed a policy that the Supreme Court had upheld in which case?
alt.a: Korematsu v. United States
alt.ex: In 1988 Congress apologized for the exclusion and incarceration of Japanese Americans, the policy under Executive Order 9066 that the Court upheld in Korematsu (1944).
w: Schenck v. United States
Schenck upheld a wartime speech conviction, not the removal of Japanese Americans.
Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy upheld racial segregation of rail cars, not wartime exclusion.
Brown v. Board of Education
Brown ended school segregation; it did not involve wartime policy.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1988 federal law, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“For these fundamental violations of the basic civil liberties and constitutional rights of these individuals of Japanese ancestry, the Congress apologizes on behalf of the Nation.”
Source: Civil Liberties Act of 1988, 50 U.S.C. § 4202

alt.q: What does this congressional action show about Korematsu v. United States?
alt.a: The nation later rejected the policy the Court upheld
alt.ex: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized and paid redress for Japanese American incarceration, showing that the nation came to reject the policy Korematsu (1944) had upheld.
w: Congress overruled the decision by passing a statute
Congress cannot overrule a constitutional ruling by statute; the Act apologized but did not reverse the case.
The Court had ruled against the government in the case
Korematsu upheld the government's exclusion order, 6–3.
The policy was later found constitutional again
The Court has since called Korematsu 'gravely wrong' (Trump v. Hawaii, 2018).

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Decades after a wartime Supreme Court ruling upheld the forced removal of a group of American citizens from their West Coast homes, Congress formally apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving person who had been removed.

items.q: During World War II, a U.S. citizen of Japanese descent refused to leave a West Coast military zone and was convicted. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction. Which case?
items.a: Korematsu v. United States
items.ex: Korematsu v. United States (1944) upheld the exclusion order under Executive Order 9066 by a 6–3 vote.
w: Schenck v. United States
1919 case on antidraft leaflets during World War I.
Ex parte Milligan
1866 case limiting military trials of civilians.
Hirabayashi v. United States
1943 case upholding a curfew, not the exclusion order.

alt.q: Which case upheld the wartime exclusion of Japanese Americans from the West Coast authorized by Executive Order 9066?
alt.a: Korematsu v. United States
alt.ex: Justice Hugo Black's majority in Korematsu (1944) upheld exclusion as a military necessity.
w: Ex parte Endo
Decided the same day in 1944, it held loyal citizens could not be detained.
Schenck v. United States
Upheld limits on wartime speech in 1919.
Hirabayashi v. United States
Upheld a 1942 curfew order, not exclusion.

alt.q: A justice wrote, "I dissent, therefore, from this legalization of racism." This dissent responded to a ruling that
alt.a: upheld removal of Japanese Americans in wartime
alt.ex: Justice Frank Murphy wrote this dissent in Korematsu v. United States (1944).
w: upheld 'separate but equal' rail cars in Louisiana
That was Plessy (1896); Justice Harlan was the dissenter.
denied citizenship to people of African descent
That was Dred Scott (1857); Justices Curtis and McLean dissented.
upheld a conviction for antidraft leaflets in wartime
Schenck (1919) was unanimous; no one dissented.

items.q: Although Korematsu upheld the exclusion order, the Court stated that legal restrictions curtailing the civil rights of a single racial group are
items.a: immediately suspect and subject to rigid scrutiny
items.ex: Justice Black wrote that such restrictions 'are immediately suspect' and courts must give them 'the most rigid scrutiny,' an early form of strict scrutiny.
w: presumed valid if Congress has approved them
Congressional approval supported the ruling but was not the stated standard.
allowed if separate facilities are equal
That is Plessy's 'separate but equal' rule.
permitted under the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
The case concerned federal war powers, not state reserved powers.

alt.q: How does the Supreme Court view Korematsu today?
alt.a: It was disavowed as 'gravely wrong' in Trump v. Hawaii
alt.ex: In Trump v. Hawaii (2018), Chief Justice Roberts wrote that 'Korematsu was gravely wrong the day it was decided.'
w: It remains binding precedent for wartime orders
The Court expressly repudiated it in 2018.
It was overruled by Brown v. Board of Education
Brown (1954) concerned school segregation.
It was reversed by Congress in the Civil Liberties Act
The 1988 Act apologized and paid reparations; Congress cannot reverse a Court ruling.

alt.q: The government's argument in Korematsu rested mainly on which justification?
alt.a: Military necessity to guard against espionage
alt.ex: The Court accepted the claim that exclusion was needed to protect the West Coast from espionage and sabotage (1944).
w: Equal protection for all wartime residents
Equal protection was the dissenters' argument against the order.
The Commerce Clause power over West Coast trade
Commerce was not the basis of the exclusion order.
Congress's power to define naturalization
Korematsu was a native-born citizen; naturalization was not at issue.

items.q: Schenck (1919) and Korematsu (1944) both involved wartime limits on liberty. Which statement correctly contrasts them?
items.a: Schenck limited speech; Korematsu limited where a group could live
items.ex: Schenck upheld punishment of antidraft leaflets; Korematsu upheld removing Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
w: Schenck limited where a group could live; Korematsu limited speech
Reverses the two cases.
Schenck struck down a war law; Korematsu upheld one
Both cases upheld the government's wartime action.
Both were later overruled by Brown v. Board of Education
Brown concerned school segregation, not wartime powers.

alt.q: Executive Order 9066 and Korematsu v. United States are often confused. What is the difference?
alt.a: One was a presidential directive; the other a ruling upholding it
alt.ex: FDR signed EO 9066 in February 1942; the Supreme Court upheld exclusion under it in Korematsu (1944).
w: One was a court ruling; the other a law of Congress overturning it
EO 9066 was an executive order, and Korematsu upheld rather than overturned it.
One ordered internment; the other struck it down
Korematsu upheld the exclusion.
One applied to Germans; the other to Japanese Americans
Both concerned people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast.

alt.q: Which case, like Korematsu, upheld a government restriction on civil liberties during wartime?
alt.a: Schenck v. United States
alt.ex: Schenck (1919) upheld Espionage Act convictions in World War I; Korematsu (1944) upheld exclusion in World War II.
w: New York Times v. United States
Ruled against the government's attempt to block publication during Vietnam.
Ex parte Milligan
Ruled against military trials of civilians where courts were open (1866).
Ex parte Endo
Ordered the release of a loyal Japanese American citizen (1944).

items.q: Brown v. Board of Education best illustrates which power of the Supreme Court?
items.a: overturning its own earlier precedents
items.ex: Brown (1954) rejected the 'separate but equal' doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), showing that the Court can reverse its own precedents.
w: enforcing its rulings with federal troops
The Court has no troops; President Eisenhower, the executive, sent soldiers to Little Rock.
amending the Constitution directly
Only the Article V amendment process can change the Constitution's text.
vetoing acts passed by Congress
The veto belongs to the President; Brown reviewed state school laws.

alt.q: What did the Court do in this sentence?
alt.a: set aside part of an earlier precedent
alt.ex: With this sentence, Brown (1954) rejected Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' reasoning as applied to public education.
w: reaffirmed an earlier precedent
The Court rejected Plessy's reasoning; it did not reaffirm it.
asked Congress to amend the Constitution
The Court acted on its own interpretation; no amendment was involved.
ordered a new trial for the plaintiffs
Brown was a civil case about school segregation, not a criminal trial.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Supreme Court's opinion in Brown v. Board of Education (1954), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Any language in Plessy v. Ferguson contrary to this finding is rejected.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that expanded civil rights by rejecting an earlier precedent that had allowed segregation?
alt.a: Brown v. Board of Education
alt.ex: Brown (1954) unanimously held school segregation unconstitutional, rejecting Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine in public education.
w: Regents of the Univ. of California v. Bakke
Bakke concerned racial quotas in admissions; it did not reject a segregation precedent.
Shaw v. Reno
Shaw concerned racial gerrymandering and did not overrule a segregation case.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu restricted civil rights by upholding wartime exclusion.

items.q: Based on the passage, why did the Court find segregated public schools unconstitutional?
items.a: Separation itself harmed Black children
items.ex: Brown (1954) held that even with equal buildings and teachers, separating children by race 'generates a feeling of inferiority,' so separate schools are 'inherently unequal.'
w: Black schools always had fewer books
The Court accepted that tangible factors might be equal; its point was that separation itself caused harm.
Congress had banned segregated schools
No federal law banned school segregation in 1954; the ruling rested on the 14th Amendment.
The schools violated the Commerce Clause
Brown rested on the Equal Protection Clause, not the Commerce Clause.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“To separate them from others of similar age and qualifications solely because of their race generates a feeling of inferiority as to their status in the community that may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Under the reasoning of Brown v. Board of Education, the arrangement is
alt.a: unconstitutional, because separation itself is unequal
alt.ex: Brown held that segregated schools are 'inherently unequal' even when tangible factors such as buildings and salaries are equal.
w: constitutional, because the facilities are equal
This was the Plessy 'separate but equal' standard that Brown rejected for schools.
constitutional, because education is reserved to the states
States run schools, but they must still obey the Equal Protection Clause.
unconstitutional, because teachers are paid unequally
The scenario states that teacher pay is equal; the problem is separation itself.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state builds a new school for Black students that matches the nearby white school in buildings, books, and teacher pay, but it continues to assign students to schools by race.

alt.q: Besides legal precedent, Brown v. Board of Education relied on which type of evidence?
alt.a: studies of segregation's psychological effects
alt.ex: Brown cited 'modern authority' in psychology (including Kenneth Clark's research) showing that segregation harmed Black children's sense of their status.
w: data on school building construction costs
The Court did not rest its ruling on building costs; it focused on intangible harms.
records proving the framers banned segregation
The Court found the history of the 14th Amendment inconclusive on school segregation.
national polls of opinion on integration
The Court did not rely on public opinion polls.

items.q: A Black student in Topeka, Kansas, had to attend a distant segregated school even though a white school was close to home. The family's lawsuit led to which ruling?
items.a: Brown v. Board of Education
items.ex: Brown v. Board of Education (1954), decided 9–0, held that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Upheld segregated rail cars in 1896.
Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg
Approved busing to desegregate schools in 1971.
Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
1978 case on affirmative action quotas in admissions.

alt.q: Which unanimous case held that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause?
alt.a: Brown v. Board of Education
alt.ex: Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the unanimous opinion in Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Upheld 'separate but equal' in 1896.
Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg
Dealt with busing as a remedy in 1971.
Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
Dealt with university admissions quotas in 1978.

alt.q: "We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal." Which case and author?
alt.a: Brown v. Board, by Chief Justice Earl Warren
alt.ex: Warren wrote this for a unanimous Court in Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
w: Plessy v. Ferguson, by Justice Harlan in dissent
Harlan wrote 'Our Constitution is color-blind.'
Brown v. Board, by Justice Thurgood Marshall
Marshall argued Brown as an NAACP lawyer; he joined the Court in 1967.
Sweatt v. Painter, by Chief Justice Fred Vinson
Sweatt (1950) ordered a Black student admitted to a Texas law school without overruling Plessy.

items.q: Brown v. Board of Education was decided under which constitutional provision?
items.a: The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
items.ex: Brown (1954) held that state-segregated schools deny Black children the equal protection of the laws.
w: The Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment
Used in the companion case Bolling v. Sharpe for Washington, D.C.
The Thirteenth Amendment's ban on badges of slavery
Brown did not rest on the 13th Amendment.
The Fifteenth Amendment's guarantee of voting rights
The 15th Amendment concerns voting, not schools.

alt.q: What was a major impact of Brown v. Board of Education?
alt.a: It overturned 'separate but equal' in public education
alt.ex: Brown (1954) reversed Plessy for public schools; carrying it out took years of resistance and enforcement.
w: It immediately integrated every Southern school by 1955
Brown II (1955) called for 'all deliberate speed,' and resistance lasted years.
It banned racial discrimination in hotels and restaurants
That was the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
It required affirmative action quotas in colleges
Quotas were struck down in Bakke (1978).

alt.q: In 1957, after Brown, the governor of Arkansas used the National Guard to block nine Black students from Little Rock Central High School. What did President Eisenhower do?
alt.a: Sent federal troops to enforce court-ordered integration
alt.ex: Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne to Little Rock in 1957 to enforce federal court desegregation orders based on Brown.
w: Issued an order desegregating the armed forces
That was Truman's Executive Order 9981 (1948).
Signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to end school segregation
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was signed by Lyndon Johnson.
Asked the Court to reconsider its Brown decision
Eisenhower enforced Brown; he did not seek to undo it.

items.q: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978) both applied the Equal Protection Clause to race in education. Which statement correctly contrasts them?
items.a: Brown ended school segregation; Bakke struck down racial quotas
items.ex: Brown held segregated schools unconstitutional; Bakke struck down a fixed racial quota but allowed race as one admissions factor.
w: Brown struck down racial quotas; Bakke ended school segregation
Reverses the two holdings.
Brown upheld separate schools; Bakke required racial quotas
Both parts are false.
Both cases banned any use of race in college admissions
Bakke allowed race as one factor among many.

alt.q: Which correctly distinguishes Brown v. Board (1954) from the follow-up ruling known as Brown II (1955)?
alt.a: The first set the rule; the second set the pace
alt.ex: Brown I declared school segregation unconstitutional; Brown II ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed.'
w: The first set the pace; the second set the rule
Reverses the two decisions.
The first covered colleges; the second covered K-12
Both concerned public elementary and secondary schools.
The first was unanimous; the second overturned it
Brown II implemented Brown I; it did not overturn it.

alt.q: A student claims, 'Brown v. Board overturned Plessy v. Ferguson for every public place, including trains and restaurants.' What is the most accurate correction?
alt.a: Brown applied only to public schools; other laws followed
alt.ex: Brown limited its holding to 'the field of public education'; later rulings and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 reached other facilities.
w: Brown applied only to colleges and graduate schools
Brown concerned elementary and secondary public schools.
Brown upheld Plessy outside of the South
Brown applied nationwide; it did not uphold Plessy anywhere for schools.
Brown applied only to federal schools in Washington, D.C.
D.C. schools were addressed in the companion case Bolling v. Sharpe.

items.q: Before Mapp v. Ohio (1961), the Constitution was held to require the exclusionary rule in which courts?
items.a: only federal courts
items.ex: Weeks v. United States (1914) applied the exclusionary rule to federal prosecutions, and Wolf v. Colorado (1949) declined to require it of the states; Mapp overruled Wolf and extended it to state courts.
w: only state courts
The rule began in federal courts (Weeks, 1914); Mapp was the case that extended it to states.
only military courts
The early exclusionary rule applied to federal criminal prosecutions, not just military courts.
all courts nationwide
If it already applied everywhere, Mapp would not have been needed.

alt.q: Mapp v. Ohio is an example of which constitutional process?
alt.a: selective incorporation
alt.ex: Mapp applied the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, one right at a time, which is selective incorporation.
w: nullification
Nullification is the discredited idea that states can void federal law; Mapp did the reverse.
the formal amendment process
No amendment was adopted; the Court interpreted the 14th Amendment.
implied powers
Implied powers concern Congress's authority (McCulloch), not individual rights against states.

alt.q: How did Mapp v. Ohio affect federalism?
alt.a: It bound state courts to a federal constitutional rule
alt.ex: Mapp made the exclusionary rule binding on state courts through the 14th Amendment, so states lost the option to admit evidence seized in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
w: It let states ignore Supreme Court rulings on searches
Mapp did the opposite, binding state courts to a federal rule.
It moved all criminal trials into the federal courts
State courts still try state crimes; they must now exclude illegally seized evidence.
It gave Congress power to write state search laws
Mapp was a court ruling about the Constitution, not a grant of power to Congress.

items.q: The U.S. Supreme Court ended which government practice in its ruling in Mapp v. Ohio?
items.a: states using illegally seized evidence
items.ex: Mapp (1961) held that evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible in state courts, ending states' use of such evidence in criminal trials.
w: police questioning suspects without warnings
Unwarned custodial questioning was addressed in Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
trying poor defendants without lawyers
Trials without appointed counsel were ended by Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
public schools leading official prayers
School-sponsored prayer was struck down in Engel v. Vitale (1962).

alt.q: Which rule does this passage defend?
alt.a: the exclusionary rule
alt.ex: In Mapp (1961), the Court argued that excluding illegally seized evidence is required because government must obey its own Constitution, even if a guilty person goes free.
w: the right to counsel
The passage concerns police obeying the law in gathering evidence, not lawyers at trial.
the Miranda warnings
Miranda warnings concern questioning suspects; the passage defends excluding unlawfully obtained evidence.
the ban on double jeopardy
Double jeopardy bars a second trial for the same offense; it is not the subject here.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The criminal goes free, if he must, but it is the law that sets him free. Nothing can destroy a government more quickly than its failure to observe its own laws, or worse, its disregard of the charter of its own existence.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Which case expanded the rights of the accused by limiting how police may gather physical evidence?
alt.a: Mapp v. Ohio
alt.ex: Mapp (1961) barred state courts from using physical evidence seized in an unconstitutional search, giving police a strong reason to follow Fourth Amendment rules.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Miranda concerns confessions from custodial questioning, not physical evidence from searches.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Gideon guarantees counsel at trial; it does not regulate police searches.
Schenck v. United States
Schenck restricted speech in wartime and did not involve searches.

items.q: Police searching a home for a bombing suspect without a valid warrant found obscene materials, and the homeowner was convicted in state court based on that evidence. Which case reversed the conviction?
items.a: Mapp v. Ohio
items.ex: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) held 6–3 that evidence from an unconstitutional search is inadmissible in state court.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
1966 case on warnings before custodial questioning.
Gideon v. Wainwright
1963 case on the right to appointed counsel.
Terry v. Ohio
1968 case allowing brief stop-and-frisk searches on reasonable suspicion.

alt.q: Which case applied the exclusionary rule to state courts?
alt.a: Mapp v. Ohio
alt.ex: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) extended the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule to the states through the 14th Amendment.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Excludes unwarned confessions, a Fifth Amendment rule.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Guarantees appointed counsel; it is not an exclusionary rule.
Weeks v. United States
Created the exclusionary rule for federal courts only (1914).

alt.q: "We hold that all evidence obtained by searches and seizures in violation of the Constitution is, by that same authority, inadmissible in a state court." This holding is known as
alt.a: the exclusionary rule applied to the states
alt.ex: Justice Tom Clark wrote this in Mapp v. Ohio (1961), applying the exclusionary rule to state prosecutions.
w: the Miranda rule for custodial interrogation
Miranda (1966) concerns confessions, not physical evidence from searches.
the right to counsel for poor defendants
That is Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
the exigent-circumstances exception to warrants
An exception allowing warrantless searches, the opposite of this holding.

items.q: Mapp v. Ohio applied which amendment's protection to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment?
items.a: Fourth Amendment (searches and seizures)
items.ex: Mapp (1961) incorporated the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule against the states.
w: Fifth Amendment (self-incrimination)
The basis of Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
Sixth Amendment (assistance of counsel)
The basis of Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
Eighth Amendment (cruel and unusual punishment)
Concerns punishments, not searches.

alt.q: Police enter a home without a warrant or any recognized exception, seize drugs, and the state prosecutor wants to use them at trial. Under Mapp v. Ohio, what should the judge do?
alt.a: Exclude the drugs because the search was illegal
alt.ex: Mapp (1961) requires state courts to exclude evidence obtained through unconstitutional searches.
w: Admit the drugs because state courts are not bound
That was the pre-Mapp rule under Wolf v. Colorado (1949).
Exclude the drugs only if no Miranda warning was given
Miranda warnings concern questioning, not searches.
Admit the drugs if the defendant had a lawyer present
Having counsel (Gideon) does not cure an illegal search.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of the exclusionary rule applied in Mapp?
alt.a: To deter police from conducting illegal searches
alt.ex: By barring illegally seized evidence, Mapp (1961) removes the incentive for police to violate the Fourth Amendment.
w: To ensure poor defendants receive a lawyer
That is the purpose of Gideon v. Wainwright.
To tell suspects of their rights before questioning
That is the purpose of Miranda warnings.
To stop states from punishing protected speech
That is a First Amendment concern, not the exclusionary rule.

items.q: Mapp, Gideon, and Miranda are all criminal-procedure cases. Which correctly matches each to its subject?
items.a: Mapp–searches; Gideon–counsel; Miranda–warnings
items.ex: Mapp (1961): illegal searches; Gideon (1963): appointed counsel; Miranda (1966): warnings before custodial questioning.
w: Mapp–warnings; Gideon–searches; Miranda–counsel
Scrambles all three cases.
Mapp–counsel; Gideon–warnings; Miranda–searches
Scrambles all three cases.
Mapp–searches; Gideon–warnings; Miranda–counsel
Mapp is right, but Gideon and Miranda are swapped.

alt.q: Which case would a defendant cite to exclude a confession given in custody without warnings, as opposed to physical evidence from an illegal search covered by Mapp?
alt.a: Miranda v. Arizona
alt.ex: Miranda (1966) excludes unwarned custodial statements (Fifth Amendment); Mapp (1961) excludes illegally seized evidence (Fourth Amendment).
w: Gideon v. Wainwright
Requires counsel at trial; it does not govern confessions.
Terry v. Ohio
Allows brief stop-and-frisk searches.
Weeks v. United States
Created the federal exclusionary rule for searches.

alt.q: Which amendments do Mapp v. Ohio and Miranda v. Arizona mainly rest on, respectively?
alt.a: Fourth Amendment; Fifth Amendment
alt.ex: Mapp rests on the Fourth Amendment (searches); Miranda rests on the Fifth Amendment (self-incrimination).
w: Fifth Amendment; Fourth Amendment
Reverses the two amendments.
Fourth Amendment; Sixth Amendment
Miranda rests mainly on the Fifth Amendment; the Sixth is Gideon's.
Sixth Amendment; Fifth Amendment
Mapp concerns searches (Fourth), not counsel (Sixth).

items.q: Which group gained the most political influence as a result of Baker v. Carr and the reapportionment cases that followed?
items.a: urban and suburban voters
items.ex: Before Baker (1962), many legislatures had not redrawn districts as cities grew, overweighting rural votes; reapportionment based on population shifted power toward urban and suburban areas.
w: rural voters
Rural areas had been overrepresented and lost influence when districts were equalized by population.
voters in U.S. territories
Baker concerned state legislative districts, not the territories.
state political party leaders
The ruling empowered voters in growing areas, not party leaders.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the impact of Baker v. Carr on state legislatures?
alt.a: Many had to redraw districts to reflect population
alt.ex: Baker (1962) let courts hear apportionment claims, and Reynolds v. Sims (1964) then required both houses of state legislatures to be apportioned by population, forcing redistricting nationwide.
w: They lost all power to draw their own districts
Legislatures still draw districts; they must now make them roughly equal in population.
They had to give every county an equal number of seats
The rulings required equal population, which often meant ending equal seats per county.
They had to elect all members statewide
Baker did not require at-large elections; it addressed unequal district populations.

alt.q: After Baker v. Carr and the decisions that followed, what would most likely happen?
alt.a: Courts could order districts based on population
alt.ex: Baker made apportionment claims justiciable under the Equal Protection Clause, and later cases required districts of roughly equal population, so courts could order fair redistricting.
w: Courts would refuse, calling it a political question
Before 1962 courts often refused; Baker rejected that approach.
Congress would redraw the state's legislative districts
Congress does not draw state legislative districts; states do, under court review.
The city would lose its state senator entirely
Equalizing districts would give the city more representation, not less.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1960, a state senator from a rural county represents about 4,000 people, while a state senator from a large city represents about 400,000. The legislature has refused to redraw its districts for decades.

items.q: Justice Felix Frankfurter dissented in Baker v. Carr, arguing that courts should stay out of apportionment and leave the problem to the political process. His view is an example of
items.a: judicial restraint
items.ex: Frankfurter (joined by Harlan) urged judicial restraint: courts should defer to legislatures on districting. The 6–2 majority rejected this and held apportionment claims justiciable.
w: judicial activism
Activism describes courts stepping into policy areas, which is what the majority, not Frankfurter, was accused of.
strict scrutiny
Strict scrutiny is a test for reviewing laws, such as racial classifications, not a philosophy of staying out.
selective incorporation
Incorporation applies Bill of Rights protections to states; it is unrelated to Frankfurter's argument.

alt.q: Critics who call Baker v. Carr an example of judicial activism mean that the Court
alt.a: entered an area long left to elected lawmakers
alt.ex: Before 1962, courts treated apportionment as a 'political question' for legislatures; Baker's willingness to hear such cases led critics to call it activist.
w: refused to hear a constitutional challenge
Refusing to hear a case would be restraint; Baker agreed to hear the challenge.
deferred to the state legislature's choices
Deferring would be restraint; Baker allowed courts to review the legislature's map.
asked Congress to settle the apportionment dispute
The Court did not refer the matter to Congress; it held that courts could decide it.

alt.q: Supporters of the decision in Baker v. Carr argued that court action was necessary because
alt.a: legislatures would not redraw their own districts
alt.ex: Tennessee had not reapportioned since 1901; lawmakers elected from overrepresented rural districts had little reason to give up power, so voters turned to the courts.
w: Congress had ordered courts to redraw districts
No federal law directed courts to redraw state districts.
the Constitution assigns district maps to the judges
The Constitution leaves districting to legislatures; courts review it for equal protection violations.
rural voters had asked the courts to step in
The plaintiffs were underrepresented voters from urban areas such as Memphis.

items.q: Tennessee had not redrawn its state legislative districts since 1901, leaving urban voters badly underrepresented. Voters sued in federal court. Which case resulted?
items.a: Baker v. Carr
items.ex: Baker v. Carr (1962), 6–2, held that legislative apportionment is a justiciable question federal courts may decide.
w: Shaw v. Reno
1993 case on racially drawn congressional districts.
Reynolds v. Sims
1964 case applying 'one person, one vote' to both houses of state legislatures.
Bush v. Gore
2000 case on the Florida presidential recount.

alt.q: Which case held that federal courts may hear challenges to how states apportion legislative seats?
alt.a: Baker v. Carr
alt.ex: Justice William Brennan's opinion in Baker v. Carr (1962) held that apportionment claims under the Equal Protection Clause are justiciable.
w: Shaw v. Reno
Concerned race-based districting in 1993.
Reynolds v. Sims
Built on Baker in 1964 to require equal-population districts.
Colegrove v. Green
1946 case that had treated apportionment as a nonjusticiable political question.

alt.q: Before 1962, federal courts usually refused to hear complaints about unequal legislative districts. Which ruling changed that, and on what reasoning?
alt.a: Baker v. Carr; apportionment was justiciable
alt.ex: Baker v. Carr (1962) held apportionment is not a 'political question' barred from judicial review.
w: Shaw v. Reno; racial districts were bizarre
Shaw (1993) addressed racial gerrymandering after courts were already open to such claims.
Baker v. Carr; it was a political question
Right case, reversed reasoning: Baker rejected the political-question argument.
Bush v. Gore; equal protection applied to votes
Bush v. Gore (2000) concerned a recount, not apportionment.

items.q: Baker v. Carr opened the door to the 'one person, one vote' principle. On which constitutional clause did the voters base their claim?
items.a: The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
items.ex: The Baker (1962) plaintiffs argued that unequal districts denied them equal protection of the laws.
w: The Guarantee Clause of Article IV
The Court treated Guarantee Clause claims as nonjusticiable.
The Fifteenth Amendment's ban on race-based voting limits
The claim was about population, not race.
The Necessary and Proper Clause of Article I
Concerns congressional power, not state districting.

alt.q: In Baker v. Carr, the Court rejected the argument that apportionment was a 'political question.' What did that mean for the case?
alt.a: Courts could decide it rather than leave it to lawmakers
alt.ex: Rejecting the political-question doctrine, Baker (1962) allowed federal courts to review apportionment.
w: Only Congress could redraw a state's legislative map
Baker said courts, not only legislatures, could address the issue.
The issue had to be settled by a statewide referendum
No referendum was required.
Only the President could enforce fair districts in a state
The executive played no role in the holding.

alt.q: Which later principle grew most directly out of Baker v. Carr?
alt.a: One person, one vote in drawing districts
alt.ex: After Baker (1962), cases such as Reynolds v. Sims (1964) required districts of roughly equal population.
w: Strict limits on racial gerrymandering
Came from Shaw v. Reno (1993).
Equal counting standards in recounts
Came from Bush v. Gore (2000).
Unlimited independent spending by corporations
Came from Citizens United v. FEC (2010).

items.q: Baker v. Carr (1962) and Shaw v. Reno (1993) both involved drawing districts. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: Baker: unequal population; Shaw: districts drawn by race
items.ex: Baker addressed malapportionment; Shaw held that bizarrely shaped race-based districts may be challenged under Equal Protection.
w: Baker: districts drawn by race; Shaw: unequal population
Reverses the two cases.
Baker: partisan gerrymanders; Shaw: presidential recounts
Neither case is described correctly.
Baker: voter ID laws; Shaw: unequal population
Neither case concerned voter ID.

alt.q: A state draws a snake-like congressional district that follows a highway mainly to group voters of one race together. Which case applies most directly?
alt.a: Shaw v. Reno
alt.ex: Shaw v. Reno (1993) held that such a district may be challenged as racial gerrymandering under Equal Protection.
w: Baker v. Carr
Concerned unequal district populations, not race.
Reynolds v. Sims
Required equal-population state legislative districts.
Bush v. Gore
Concerned recount standards in 2000.

alt.q: Which case addressed malapportionment (districts with very different populations) rather than racial gerrymandering?
alt.a: Baker v. Carr
alt.ex: Baker v. Carr (1962) involved Tennessee districts unchanged since 1901 despite population shifts.
w: Shaw v. Reno
A racial gerrymandering case (1993).
Miller v. Johnson
A 1995 racial gerrymandering case following Shaw.
Shelby County v. Holder
A 2013 Voting Rights Act preclearance case.

items.q: Why could the Establishment Clause be applied to New York's Board of Regents in Engel v. Vitale?
items.a: The 14th Amendment applies it to the states
items.ex: The First Amendment originally limited only Congress; the Court in Engel (1962) treated the religion clauses as 'operative against the States by virtue of the Fourteenth Amendment.'
w: New York had copied it into its own state law
The ruling rested on the U.S. Constitution as applied through the 14th Amendment, not on New York law.
Congress had passed a ban on school prayer
No federal statute banned school prayer; the case was decided under the Constitution.
Public schools are run by the federal government
Public schools are run by state and local governments, which is why incorporation mattered.

alt.q: Engel v. Vitale limited the authority of which government body?
alt.a: a state education agency
alt.ex: Engel (1962) struck down a prayer composed by the New York State Board of Regents, a state agency, applying the Establishment Clause to the states through the 14th Amendment.
w: the U.S. Congress
Congress did not write or require the Regents' prayer.
the U.S. Department of Education
The prayer came from New York's Board of Regents; no federal agency was involved.
a federal court
Federal courts decided the case; they were not the government body being limited.

alt.q: Which response is most accurate under Engel v. Vitale?
alt.a: The 14th Amendment applies the clause to the states
alt.ex: Engel held that a state-composed school prayer violates the Establishment Clause, which binds the states through the Fourteenth Amendment (selective incorporation).
w: The state is right that the clause binds only Congress
That was true before incorporation, but by 1962 the religion clauses applied to the states.
The prayer is allowed if students may leave the room
Engel held that voluntary participation does not save a government-written prayer.
Only a federal statute could ban this kind of prayer
The Constitution itself, enforced by the courts, forbids it; no statute is needed.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state legislature requires every public school to begin the day with a teacher-led prayer written by state officials. A parent sues. The state argues that the First Amendment begins ‘Congress shall make no law’ and therefore limits only the federal government.

items.q: Which activity in a public school remains permitted after Engel v. Vitale?
items.a: a student praying silently on her own
items.ex: Engel (1962) barred government-written, school-sponsored prayer; it did not stop students from praying privately, which is their own free exercise of religion.
w: a teacher leading the class in prayer
A teacher acts for the school, so leading prayer is government sponsorship of religion.
a principal reading a state-written prayer
This is close to the exact practice Engel struck down.
a school board requiring a daily prayer
A government-required prayer violates the Establishment Clause.

alt.q: A critic claims that Engel v. Vitale ‘banned prayer from public schools.’ Which correction is most accurate?
alt.a: It barred official prayers, not private ones
alt.ex: Engel held that government may not compose or sponsor prayers for students; students remain free to pray on their own.
w: It barred only prayers that name a religion
The Regents' prayer was nondenominational and was still struck down.
It barred prayer only for students under 18
Age played no role; the problem was government sponsorship.
It barred prayer only when participation was mandatory
Engel struck down the prayer even though participation was voluntary.

alt.q: Under the reasoning of Engel v. Vitale, this activity is most likely
alt.a: allowed, because government is not sponsoring it
alt.ex: Engel forbids government-composed or government-led prayer; prayer that students start and lead on their own is private religious expression.
w: banned, because it takes place on school grounds
Location alone does not make private prayer government-sponsored.
banned, because the prayer is not neutral
Engel concerned government authorship, not the content of students' own prayers.
allowed only if the school writes the prayer
A school-written prayer is exactly what Engel prohibited.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Before the first bell, several students gather on their own at their public school's flagpole to pray. No teachers or staff members lead, organize, or require the gathering.

items.q: New York's Board of Regents wrote a short, nondenominational prayer that public school students could recite voluntarily each morning. Parents sued. Which case resulted?
items.a: Engel v. Vitale
items.ex: Engel v. Vitale (1962), 6–1, held that the Regents' prayer violated the Establishment Clause.
w: Wisconsin v. Yoder
1972 Free Exercise case on Amish schooling.
Abington School District v. Schempp
1963 case striking down school Bible reading.
Lemon v. Kurtzman
1971 case on state aid to religious schools.

alt.q: Which case held that a state-written prayer in public schools violates the Establishment Clause even when participation is voluntary?
alt.a: Engel v. Vitale
alt.ex: Justice Hugo Black wrote for the Court in Engel v. Vitale (1962).
w: Wisconsin v. Yoder
Granted Amish families an exemption under Free Exercise.
Abington School District v. Schempp
Struck down Bible reading, not a state-written prayer.
Lemon v. Kurtzman
Created a three-part test for government aid to religion.

alt.q: "...it is no part of the business of government to compose official prayers for any group of the American people to recite as a part of a religious program carried on by government." This statement reflects which clause?
alt.a: The Establishment Clause
alt.ex: Justice Black wrote this in Engel v. Vitale (1962) under the First Amendment's Establishment Clause.
w: The Free Exercise Clause
Protects individuals' practice of religion; it was the basis of Yoder.
The Free Speech Clause
Protects expression generally, not the issue here.
The Equal Protection Clause
A 14th Amendment clause on equal treatment.

items.q: Why did the Court in Engel v. Vitale strike down the Regents' prayer even though students could remain silent or leave?
items.a: Government itself wrote and sponsored the prayer
items.ex: Engel (1962) held that a government-composed prayer is an establishment of religion regardless of voluntariness.
w: It favored one Christian denomination over others
The prayer was deliberately nondenominational.
It forced students to violate their own faith
Coercion of belief is a Free Exercise concern; the prayer was voluntary.
It took instructional time away from lessons
Instructional time was not the constitutional issue.

alt.q: What is the lasting impact of Engel v. Vitale?
alt.a: Public schools may not lead official prayers
alt.ex: Engel (1962) bars school-sponsored prayer; students may still pray privately.
w: Students may not pray on their own at school
A common misconception; private student prayer is protected.
Religious clubs are banned from public schools
Student religious clubs are allowed under the Equal Access Act (1984).
Public schools must teach about every religion
Engel imposed no curriculum requirement.

alt.q: A public school principal begins each day by reading a prayer over the loudspeaker and invites students to join. Which principle is most clearly at issue?
alt.a: Government establishment of religion
alt.ex: Under Engel v. Vitale (1962), school-led prayer violates the Establishment Clause.
w: Students' free exercise of religion
Free exercise protects students' own practice; the issue is government sponsorship.
School officials' freedom of speech
A principal speaking for the school acts as government.
The right to peaceably assemble at school
Assembly is not at issue in a school-led prayer.

items.q: Engel v. Vitale (1962) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) both involved religion and schools. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: Engel turned on establishment; Yoder on free exercise
items.ex: Engel struck down a state-written prayer (Establishment); Yoder exempted Amish teens from compulsory schooling (Free Exercise).
w: Engel turned on free exercise; Yoder on establishment
Reverses the two clauses.
Both upheld the state's power over school religion
Both ruled against the state.
Engel involved Amish families; Yoder a school prayer
Reverses the facts.

alt.q: Which outcome pairing is correct?
alt.a: Engel: school prayer struck; Yoder: Amish exemption granted
alt.ex: Engel (1962) struck down the Regents' prayer; Yoder (1972) let Amish parents end schooling after eighth grade.
w: Engel: school prayer upheld; Yoder: Amish exemption denied
Both outcomes are reversed.
Engel: Amish exemption granted; Yoder: school prayer struck
Swaps the facts of the cases.
Engel: Bible reading upheld; Yoder: Amish exemption denied
Bible reading was struck in Schempp (1963); Yoder granted the exemption.

alt.q: Two disputes: (1) a state writes a prayer for public school students; (2) a state forces Amish teens to attend high school against their faith. Which clauses apply, in order?
alt.a: Establishment Clause; Free Exercise Clause
alt.ex: (1) is Engel v. Vitale (Establishment); (2) is Wisconsin v. Yoder (Free Exercise).
w: Free Exercise Clause; Establishment Clause
Reverses the clauses.
Free Speech Clause; Equal Protection Clause
Neither dispute turns on these clauses.
Establishment Clause; Due Process Clause
Yoder was decided under the Free Exercise Clause.

items.q: A person is charged with felony breaking and entering. During the court proceedings, the defendant requested an attorney and was denied the right to counsel. Which Supreme Court case overturned the trial court’s decision, due to lack of counsel?
items.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
items.ex: Clarence Earl Gideon was charged with breaking and entering a Panama City, Florida pool hall and denied a lawyer. In Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), the Court unanimously held that the Sixth Amendment requires states to provide counsel to defendants in felony cases who cannot afford one.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Miranda (1966) requires police to warn suspects of their rights before questioning, not to provide counsel at trial.
Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld racial segregation.
McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch (1819) upheld the national bank and federal implied powers.

alt.q: Which constitutional amendment was at the center of the Supreme Court’s decision in Gideon v. Wainwright?
alt.a: Sixth Amendment
alt.ex: Gideon held that the Sixth Amendment right to the assistance of counsel applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, so poor defendants charged with felonies must be given a lawyer.
w: Fourth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment concerns searches and seizures.
Fifth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment covers self-incrimination and double jeopardy, not the right to a lawyer at trial.
Eighth Amendment
The Eighth Amendment concerns bail and punishments.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case would best support excluding the confession?
alt.a: Miranda v. Arizona
alt.ex: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires police to warn suspects in custody of their right to remain silent and to an attorney before questioning; statements obtained without these warnings generally cannot be used at trial.
w: Gideon v. Wainwright
Gideon guarantees a lawyer at trial for poor felony defendants; it does not address police warnings.
Mapp v. Ohio
Mapp (1961) excludes evidence from illegal searches, not confessions without warnings.
Marbury v. Madison
Marbury (1803) established judicial review.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A man is arrested and questioned by police for several hours. Officers never tell him that he has the right to remain silent or the right to an attorney. He confesses.

items.q: What happened when Clarence Earl Gideon was retried in 1963 with a lawyer representing him?
items.a: He was acquitted by the jury
items.ex: After the Supreme Court's ruling, Gideon was retried in Panama City, Florida, in August 1963; his appointed lawyer challenged the key witness, and the jury acquitted him after about an hour.
w: He was convicted a second time
With a lawyer, Gideon won; the jury found him not guilty.
He pleaded guilty for a lighter sentence
Gideon went to trial and was acquitted; he did not plead guilty.
The state dropped all charges first
Florida did retry him; the case ended in a jury verdict of not guilty.

alt.q: How did Gideon's case reach the U.S. Supreme Court?
alt.a: He mailed a handwritten petition from prison
alt.ex: Gideon wrote his petition in pencil from a Florida prison and filed it as a poor person (in forma pauperis); the Court agreed to hear it and appointed Abe Fortas to argue his side.
w: A civil rights group filed a class-action suit
Gideon filed on his own behalf; it was not a class action.
Florida's governor asked the Court for a ruling
The State of Florida opposed Gideon's claim.
Congress referred the case to the Court
Congress has no power to refer cases to the Supreme Court.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case contains this passage?
alt.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
alt.ex: Gideon (1963) held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to the states, so poor felony defendants must be given a lawyer.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Miranda concerns warnings before custodial police questioning, not lawyers at trial.
Mapp v. Ohio
Mapp concerns excluding illegally seized evidence.
Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
