Hazelwood concerns school-sponsored student newspapers.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“That government hires lawyers to prosecute and defendants who have the money hire lawyers to defend are the strongest indications of the widespread belief that lawyers in criminal courts are necessities, not luxuries.”
Source: United States Reports

items.q: A man charged in Florida with breaking and entering asked for a lawyer, but the judge refused because state law provided counsel only in capital cases. The defendant handled their own defense, was convicted, and appealed. Which case?
items.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
items.ex: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), 9–0, held that states must provide counsel to defendants who cannot afford one.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Concerned warnings before police questioning (1966).
Betts v. Brady
1942 case that Gideon overruled; it had denied a general right to appointed counsel.
Strickland v. Washington
1984 case setting the standard for ineffective assistance of counsel.

alt.q: Which case required states to provide lawyers to felony defendants who cannot afford them?
alt.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
alt.ex: Justice Hugo Black's unanimous opinion in Gideon (1963) incorporated the Sixth Amendment right to counsel.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Requires warnings about counsel during questioning, not trial counsel.
Betts v. Brady
Held the opposite in 1942 and was overruled by Gideon.
Strickland v. Washington
Concerned the quality, not the provision, of counsel.

alt.q: "...any person haled into court, who is too poor to hire a lawyer, cannot be assured a fair trial unless counsel is provided for him." Which case?
alt.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
alt.ex: Justice Black wrote this in Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Concerned custodial interrogation, not trial counsel.
Powell v. Alabama
1932 Scottsboro case requiring counsel in that capital case only.
Strickland v. Washington
Set the test for ineffective counsel in 1984.

items.q: Gideon v. Wainwright applied which right to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment?
items.a: Sixth Amendment right to the assistance of counsel
items.ex: Gideon (1963) held the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and binds the states.
w: Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination
The basis of Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches
The basis of Mapp v. Ohio (1961).
Eighth Amendment ban on excessive bail
Not involved in Gideon.

alt.q: A defendant charged with a felony in state court says they cannot afford a lawyer. Under Gideon, what must happen?
alt.a: The court must appoint counsel at public expense
alt.ex: Gideon (1963) requires appointed counsel for indigent felony defendants unless they knowingly waive the right.
w: The defendant must be read Miranda warnings first
Miranda governs police questioning, not court proceedings.
The defendant may be tried only if they waive a jury
Jury waiver is unrelated to the right to counsel.
The court may appoint counsel only in capital cases
That was Florida's pre-Gideon rule.

alt.q: Which development is a direct result of Gideon v. Wainwright?
alt.a: Expansion of public defender systems in the states
alt.ex: To meet Gideon's 1963 requirement, states built or expanded public defender offices.
w: Police reading suspects their rights before questioning
A result of Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
Exclusion of evidence from warrantless home searches
A result of Mapp v. Ohio (1961).
Bans on mandatory prayer in public classrooms
A result of Engel v. Vitale (1962).

items.q: Both Gideon v. Wainwright and Miranda v. Arizona involve a right to a lawyer. What is the key difference?
items.a: Gideon covers trial; Miranda covers police questioning
items.ex: Gideon (1963) guarantees counsel at trial; Miranda (1966) requires warnings, including the right to counsel, before custodial interrogation.
w: Gideon covers police questioning; Miranda covers trial
Reverses the two cases.
Gideon covers searches; Miranda covers jury selection
Searches are Mapp; neither case concerns jury selection.
Gideon covers federal courts; Miranda covers state courts
Gideon applied the right to state courts.

alt.q: Which situation would be governed by Gideon rather than Miranda?
alt.a: A poor defendant goes to trial without a lawyer
alt.ex: Gideon (1963) concerns appointed counsel at trial for those who cannot afford one.
w: A suspect in custody is questioned without warnings
Governed by Miranda (1966).
Police search a car without a warrant or consent
A Fourth Amendment search issue (Mapp).
A suspect confesses before being told they may stay silent
Governed by Miranda (1966).

alt.q: Which amendments are most associated with Gideon and Miranda, respectively?
alt.a: Sixth Amendment; Fifth Amendment
alt.ex: Gideon applied the Sixth Amendment right to counsel; Miranda rests mainly on the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
w: Fifth Amendment; Sixth Amendment
Reverses the amendments.
Fourth Amendment; Fifth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment is Mapp's, not Gideon's.
Sixth Amendment; Fourth Amendment
Miranda is not a search case.

items.q: The U.S. Supreme Court required which law enforcement practice in its ruling in Miranda v. Arizona?
items.a: warning suspects of their rights
items.ex: Miranda (1966) requires police to tell suspects in custody, before questioning, that they may remain silent, that statements can be used against them, and that they may have a lawyer.
w: getting a warrant before searching homes
Warrant and exclusionary rules for searches come from the Fourth Amendment and Mapp v. Ohio.
appointing lawyers for felony trials
Appointed trial counsel comes from Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
recording all interrogations on video
Miranda did not require recording; it required warnings.

alt.q: Based on the passage, in which situation would Miranda warnings be required?
alt.a: Police question a suspect held at the station
alt.ex: Miranda warnings are required for 'custodial interrogation': questioning by law enforcement after a person is in custody or otherwise significantly deprived of freedom.
w: An officer asks a bystander what they saw
A free bystander is not in custody, so no warnings are required.
A suspect walks into the station and confesses unprompted
A volunteered statement is not the product of interrogation.
A store guard questions a shoplifter
A private guard is not a law enforcement officer, so Miranda does not apply.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“By custodial interrogation, we mean questioning initiated by law enforcement officers after a person has been taken into custody or otherwise deprived of his freedom of action in any significant way.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that changed how police question suspects?
alt.a: Miranda v. Arizona
alt.ex: Miranda (1966) required warnings before custodial interrogation, changing police questioning practices nationwide.
w: Mapp v. Ohio
Mapp changed how police search for evidence, not how they question suspects.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Gideon concerns lawyers at trial, not police questioning.
Schenck v. United States
Schenck concerned wartime speech limits.

items.q: In Dickerson v. United States (2000), the Court refused to let a federal law replace the Miranda warnings. What does this show about Miranda?
items.a: It is a constitutional rule Congress cannot override
items.ex: Dickerson (7–2) held that 'Miranda announced a constitutional rule that Congress may not supersede legislatively,' so a 1968 federal statute (18 U.S.C. § 3501) could not replace it.
w: It is a police department policy that states may drop
Miranda binds all police, state and federal, as a constitutional requirement.
It was a statute passed by Congress in 1966
Miranda is a Supreme Court decision, not an act of Congress.
It applies only to federal law enforcement
Miranda itself involved Arizona state police; it binds state officers too.

alt.q: Based on Dickerson v. United States (2000), how would the Supreme Court most likely rule?
alt.a: The law cannot override Miranda's constitutional rule
alt.ex: Dickerson held that Miranda is a constitutional decision that 'may not be in effect overruled by an Act of Congress'; only the Court or a constitutional amendment could change it.
w: The law is valid because Congress sets evidence rules
Congress may set evidence rules only within constitutional limits; Dickerson rejected this exact argument.
The law is valid but only in federal courts
Dickerson involved a federal prosecution, and the Court still refused to apply the statute.
The law is valid if the states ratify it
Ordinary statutes do not go to the states; only amendments are ratified.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Congress passes a law stating that any voluntary confession may be used at trial, even if police never gave the suspect Miranda warnings. A defendant challenges the law.

alt.q: Miranda warnings are required by which source of law?
alt.a: the U.S. Constitution as interpreted by the Court
alt.ex: Miranda (1966) rests on the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination; Dickerson (2000) confirmed it is a constitutional rule, not a statute or policy.
w: a federal statute enacted by Congress and the President
No statute created Miranda; Congress's 1968 attempt to replace it was rejected in Dickerson.
an executive order of the President
Presidents did not create the warnings; the Supreme Court did.
regulations adopted by each state
States must follow Miranda; they did not create it and cannot drop it.

items.q: A suspect arrested in 1963 confessed after two hours of police questioning, but officers never said the suspect could remain silent or have a lawyer. The conviction was overturned. Which case?
items.a: Miranda v. Arizona
items.ex: Miranda v. Arizona (1966), 5–4, required warnings before custodial interrogation.
w: Mapp v. Ohio
1961 case on illegally seized evidence.
Gideon v. Wainwright
1963 case on appointed counsel at trial.
Escobedo v. Illinois
1964 case on a suspect denied access to a lawyer they had requested.

alt.q: Which case requires police to warn suspects in custody of their rights before interrogation?
alt.a: Miranda v. Arizona
alt.ex: Chief Justice Earl Warren's opinion in Miranda (1966) created the familiar warnings.
w: Mapp v. Ohio
Applied the exclusionary rule to searches.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Required counsel for poor defendants at trial.
Escobedo v. Illinois
A 1964 precursor that did not set out the full warnings.

alt.q: "He must be warned prior to any questioning that he has the right to remain silent, that anything he says can be used against him in a court of law..." Which case?
alt.a: Miranda v. Arizona
alt.ex: This is the core holding of Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
w: Mapp v. Ohio
Concerns searches and seizures, not warnings.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Concerns appointed counsel at trial.
Escobedo v. Illinois
Did not set out these warnings.

items.q: Miranda v. Arizona is based mainly on which constitutional protection?
items.a: Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination
items.ex: Miranda (1966) held that custodial interrogation without warnings violates the Fifth Amendment privilege.
w: Fourth Amendment protection from unreasonable searches
The basis of Mapp v. Ohio.
Sixth Amendment right to a speedy and public trial
Concerns trials, not interrogation.
Eighth Amendment ban on cruel and unusual punishment
Concerns punishment, not questioning.

alt.q: Police arrest a suspect, place them in an interrogation room, and question them without any warnings. The suspect confesses. Under Miranda, what is the usual result?
alt.a: The confession cannot be used to prove guilt at trial
alt.ex: Miranda (1966) bars the prosecution from using unwarned custodial statements as evidence of guilt.
w: The arrest is void and the suspect must be released
The arrest remains valid; only the statement is excluded.
The confession is allowed if a lawyer is appointed later
Later counsel does not cure the missing warnings.
The entire case must be dismissed with prejudice
Other lawfully obtained evidence can still be used.

alt.q: When do Miranda warnings apply?
alt.a: When a suspect is in custody and being interrogated
alt.ex: Miranda (1966) applies to custodial interrogation, not casual or voluntary conversations.
w: Whenever an officer speaks with any person on the street
Non-custodial questioning does not require warnings.
Only after formal charges are filed in court
Miranda applies before charges, during custody.
Only when a suspect asks for a lawyer by name
Warnings are required whether or not the suspect asks.

items.q: A student mixes up Mapp v. Ohio and Miranda v. Arizona. Which statement is correct?
items.a: Mapp excludes illegally seized items; Miranda, unwarned confessions
items.ex: Mapp (1961) is a Fourth Amendment search case; Miranda (1966) is a Fifth Amendment interrogation case.
w: Mapp excludes unwarned confessions; Miranda, illegally seized items
Reverses the two cases.
Both require a lawyer to be appointed for poor defendants
That is Gideon v. Wainwright.
Both apply only to federal agents, not state police
Both cases apply to state police.

alt.q: Three defendants: (A) evidence came from a warrantless home search; (B) no lawyer at a felony trial; (C) a confession without warnings. Which cases match A, B, C?
alt.a: Mapp; Gideon; Miranda
alt.ex: A = Mapp v. Ohio (1961); B = Gideon v. Wainwright (1963); C = Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
w: Miranda; Gideon; Mapp
Swaps A and C.
Mapp; Miranda; Gideon
Swaps B and C.
Gideon; Mapp; Miranda
Swaps A and B.

alt.q: Which protection did Miranda add that Gideon did not cover?
alt.a: A lawyer during custodial police questioning
alt.ex: Gideon (1963) guaranteed counsel at trial; Miranda (1966) extended the right to have counsel present during custodial interrogation.
w: A lawyer at trial for poor felony defendants
That is Gideon's own holding.
Exclusion of evidence from illegal searches
That is Mapp v. Ohio.
A jury trial for all serious state crimes
That is Duncan v. Louisiana (1968).

items.q: Why did the First Amendment protect the students against their school district in Tinker v. Des Moines?
items.a: Public school officials act for the government
items.ex: The First Amendment limits government, and through the 14th Amendment it binds the states and their 'creatures,' including public school boards.
w: The students were legal adults
The Tinker students were minors (ages 13 to 16).
The armbands were worn off school grounds
The armbands were worn at school; that is why the school acted.
Iowa's constitution copied the First Amendment
The ruling rested on the U.S. Constitution, not Iowa's.

alt.q: Why would Tinker v. Des Moines most likely NOT protect this student?
alt.a: The First Amendment limits only government
alt.ex: Tinker protected students against a public (government-run) school; the First Amendment does not restrict private organizations such as a privately funded school.
w: Tinker protects only written or spoken speech
Tinker protected armbands, which are symbolic, not written, speech.
Armbands are not a form of expression
Tinker held that armbands are protected symbolic speech.
Tinker was overruled by Hazelwood
Hazelwood narrowed Tinker for school-sponsored speech but did not overrule it.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A private religious school that receives no government funding suspends a student for wearing an armband to protest a war. The student's family cites Tinker v. Des Moines.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which conclusion did the Court draw in Tinker v. Des Moines?
alt.a: School boards must respect constitutional rights
alt.ex: Quoting West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), Tinker (1969) explained that the 14th Amendment protects citizens against the state 'and all of its creatures,' including boards of education.
w: School boards are exempt from constitutional limits
The passage says boards of education are 'not excepted.'
Only Congress may regulate public schools
States and local boards run schools; the passage limits them, it does not remove their authority.
Students have rights only outside of school
Tinker held that students keep their rights at school.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Fourteenth Amendment, as now applied to the States, protects the citizen against the State itself and all of its creatures — Boards of Education not excepted.”
Source: United States Reports

items.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that expanded the free speech rights of students?
items.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
items.ex: Tinker (1969, 7–2) held that public school students may express political views, such as wearing antiwar armbands, unless the expression would substantially disrupt school.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
Hazelwood narrowed student speech rights in school-sponsored publications.
Engel v. Vitale
Engel limited government-sponsored prayer; it was not about student speech.
Schenck v. United States
Schenck restricted an adult's wartime speech.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case contains this passage?
alt.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
alt.ex: Tinker (1969) rejected the idea that public schools hold unlimited power over students' expression, protecting students who wore antiwar armbands.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
Hazelwood gave schools more control over school-sponsored speech; it did not use this language.
Engel v. Vitale
Engel concerned a state-written school prayer.
Wisconsin v. Yoder
Yoder concerned Amish parents and compulsory attendance laws.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“In our system, state-operated schools may not be enclaves of totalitarianism. School officials do not possess absolute authority over their students.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: How did Tinker v. Des Moines change the rights of public school students?
alt.a: It recognized their right to political expression
alt.ex: Tinker held that students do not lose their First Amendment rights at school and may engage in political expression that does not substantially disrupt learning.
w: It let schools censor any student speech
Tinker limited schools' power to censor student expression.
It required public schools to allow organized prayer
Tinker concerned political armbands, not prayer.
It ended mandatory school attendance laws
Tinker said nothing about attendance; Yoder dealt with attendance for the Amish.

items.q: Several public school students wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War and were suspended under a policy adopted just before the protest. Which case?
items.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
items.ex: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), 7–2, held the suspensions violated the First Amendment.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
1988 case on a school-sponsored newspaper.
Texas v. Johnson
1989 case on flag burning at a protest.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
1986 case allowing discipline for a lewd assembly speech.

alt.q: Which case held that students keep free speech rights at school unless their expression would substantially disrupt the school?
alt.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
alt.ex: Justice Abe Fortas wrote the majority in Tinker (1969), setting the substantial-disruption test.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
Allowed censorship of school-sponsored speech.
Texas v. Johnson
Protected flag burning outside the school setting.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
Allowed punishment of lewd student speech.

alt.q: "It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." Which case?
alt.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
alt.ex: Justice Fortas wrote this in Tinker v. Des Moines (1969).
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
Limited student press rights in 1988.
Texas v. Johnson
Known for the 'bedrock principle' against banning offensive ideas.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
Upheld discipline for a lewd speech.

items.q: What standard did Tinker set for when a school may restrict student expression?
items.a: When it would materially and substantially disrupt school
items.ex: Tinker (1969) requires a showing of material and substantial interference with school operations, not mere fear.
w: When it poses a clear and present danger to the nation
The Schenck (1919) test for wartime speech.
When it appears in a school-sponsored student newspaper
The Hazelwood (1988) context.
When any teacher, parent, or classmate finds the message offensive
Tinker rejected suppression based on discomfort.

alt.q: A student wears a T-shirt with a political slogan; no classes are disrupted, but the principal fears future trouble and suspends the student. Under Tinker, the suspension is most likely
alt.a: unconstitutional, since fear of disruption is not enough
alt.ex: Tinker (1969) held that 'undifferentiated fear or apprehension of disturbance' does not justify suppressing student speech.
w: constitutional, since schools may ban all political messages
Tinker protected political speech in school.
constitutional, since the shirt is conduct, not speech
Tinker treated armbands as symbolic speech.
unconstitutional, since schools may never limit any speech
Too broad: schools may limit disruptive, lewd, or school-sponsored speech.

alt.q: The Tinker armbands were treated as symbolic speech. Which amendment protected them?
alt.a: The First Amendment, applied to states through the 14th
alt.ex: Tinker (1969) applied First Amendment free speech protection to a public school through the 14th Amendment.
w: The Fourth Amendment, applied to schools through the 14th
The Fourth concerns searches, not speech.
The Ninth Amendment's protection of unlisted rights
Free speech is listed in the First Amendment.
The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause alone
The Fifth binds the federal government; the ruling rested on the First.

items.q: Tinker v. Des Moines, Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier, and Texas v. Johnson all involve expression. Which pairing is correct?
items.a: Tinker–armbands; Hazelwood–school paper; Johnson–flag burning
items.ex: Tinker (1969): armbands; Hazelwood (1988): school-sponsored newspaper; Texas v. Johnson (1989): flag burning.
w: Tinker–school paper; Hazelwood–armbands; Johnson–flag burning
Swaps Tinker and Hazelwood.
Tinker–flag burning; Hazelwood–school paper; Johnson–armbands
Swaps Tinker and Johnson.
Tinker–armbands; Hazelwood–flag burning; Johnson–school paper
Swaps Hazelwood and Johnson.

alt.q: How does Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier limit Tinker v. Des Moines?
alt.a: Schools may edit school-sponsored papers for teaching goals
alt.ex: Hazelwood (1988) lets educators control school-sponsored speech when reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns.
w: Schools may ban any personal student speech they find offensive
Tinker still protects non-disruptive personal speech.
Schools may punish speech only if it causes violence
Neither case requires violence.
Schools may restrict personal speech without disruption
That would contradict Tinker, which still governs personal speech.

alt.q: A student wears an armband protesting a war (A), and another student's article is pulled from the school-run newspaper by the principal (B). Which cases apply to A and B?
alt.a: Tinker; Hazelwood
alt.ex: Personal symbolic speech falls under Tinker (1969); school-sponsored publications fall under Hazelwood (1988).
w: Hazelwood; Tinker
Reverses the matches.
Tinker; Texas v. Johnson
Johnson concerned flag burning at a public protest.
Texas v. Johnson; Hazelwood
The armband case is Tinker, not Johnson.

sections.name: New York Times v. United States (1971)

items.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that protected freedom of the press over the government's national security claims?
items.a: New York Times v. United States
items.ex: In the Pentagon Papers case (1971), the Court ruled 6–3 that the government had not met its heavy burden to justify stopping publication of a classified Vietnam War study.
w: Schenck v. United States
Schenck put national security ahead of speech, upholding a wartime conviction.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu put national security ahead of civil liberties.
Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier
Hazelwood upheld a principal's censorship of a school newspaper; it did not involve national security.

alt.q: In New York Times v. United States, which value did the Court place above the government's national security claims?
alt.a: freedom of the press
alt.ex: The Court refused to block publication of the Pentagon Papers, holding that the government had not justified a prior restraint on the press.
w: executive privilege
Executive privilege was the issue in United States v. Nixon (1974).
the right to privacy
Privacy was not at issue in the Pentagon Papers case.
the right to petition
The case involved newspapers publishing, not citizens petitioning government.

alt.q: Based on the passage, what role does the press play in the constitutional system?
alt.a: a check on government power
alt.ex: Justice Black's concurrence in New York Times v. United States (1971) described a free press as a watchdog that can 'censure the Government.'
w: a branch of the federal government
The press is private and independent; it is not one of the three branches.
a tool of national defense
The passage stresses freedom from government control, not service to defense.
a regulator of elections
The passage is about criticism of government, not running elections.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Justice Hugo Black's concurring opinion in New York Times v. United States (1971), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The Government's power to censor the press was abolished so that the press would remain forever free to censure the Government.”
Source: United States Reports

items.q: In New York Times v. United States, the Supreme Court acted as a check on which branch of government?
items.a: the executive branch
items.ex: The Nixon administration's Justice Department sought court orders to stop the Times and the Washington Post from printing the Pentagon Papers; the Court ruled against the executive.
w: the legislative branch
Congress did not bring the case; the executive branch sought the injunctions.
the state governments
The case involved the federal government, not the states.
the local governments
No city or county was a party; the federal executive was.

alt.q: Which pair of cases both involved Supreme Court rulings against President Nixon's administration?
alt.a: NYT v. United States and United States v. Nixon
alt.ex: In 1971 the Court refused to block the Pentagon Papers, and in 1974 it ordered Nixon to turn over the Watergate tapes; both rulings went against the Nixon administration.
w: NYT v. United States and Schenck v. United States
Schenck (1919) arose under President Wilson and upheld the government.
United States v. Nixon and Roe v. Wade
Roe involved a Texas law and a Dallas prosecutor, not the Nixon administration.
Tinker v. Des Moines and United States v. Nixon
Tinker involved an Iowa school district, not the federal executive.

alt.q: Which case limited the executive branch's power to stop the press from publishing?
alt.a: New York Times v. United States
alt.ex: The Court held that the executive branch had not justified a prior restraint on newspapers publishing the Pentagon Papers.
w: United States v. Nixon
This case limited executive privilege over Watergate tapes, not press restraints.
Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier
Hazelwood concerned a school principal, not the federal executive.
Citizens United v. FEC
Citizens United struck down limits set by an act of Congress.

items.q: In 1971 the Nixon administration went to court to stop two newspapers from publishing a classified Defense Department study of U.S. involvement in Vietnam. Which case?
items.a: New York Times v. United States
items.ex: In New York Times v. United States (1971), the 'Pentagon Papers' case, the Court ruled 6–3 against prior restraint.
w: New York Times v. Sullivan
1964 libel case requiring 'actual malice' for public officials.
United States v. Nixon
1974 case on the Watergate tapes.
Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier
1988 case allowing a principal to censor a school paper.

alt.q: Which case held that the government failed to justify blocking newspapers from printing a classified study on national security grounds?
alt.a: New York Times v. United States
alt.ex: The per curiam opinion in NYT v. United States (1971) found the government had not met its heavy burden for prior restraint.
w: New York Times v. Sullivan
Concerned libel suits by public officials.
United States v. Nixon
Concerned executive privilege and the Watergate tapes.
Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier
Upheld censorship of a school-sponsored paper.

alt.q: Justice Hugo Black wrote, "Only a free and unrestrained press can effectively expose deception in government." His concurrence supported which ruling?
alt.a: Newspapers could publish the Pentagon Papers
alt.ex: Black wrote this concurring in New York Times v. United States (1971).
w: A principal could censor a school newspaper
That was Hazelwood (1988), decided long after Black's death.
The President had to turn over the Watergate tapes
That was United States v. Nixon (1974).
Antiwar leaflets could be punished in wartime
That was Schenck (1919).

items.q: New York Times v. United States is a leading case on which First Amendment doctrine?
items.a: Limits on prior restraint of the press
items.ex: NYT v. U.S. (1971) held that prior restraint carries a heavy presumption against its constitutionality.
w: The clear and present danger test for speech
From Schenck v. United States (1919).
Protection of symbolic speech such as armbands
From Tinker (1969) and Texas v. Johnson (1989).
Actual malice in libel of public officials
From New York Times v. Sullivan (1964).

alt.q: A federal agency asks a judge to order a news website not to publish a leaked report, claiming harm to national security but offering no evidence of direct, immediate harm. Under NYT v. United States, the judge should most likely
alt.a: deny the order, since prior restraint is presumed invalid
alt.ex: NYT v. U.S. (1971) requires the government to overcome a heavy presumption against prior restraint.
w: grant the order, since national security concerns always prevail
The Court rejected a vague 'security' claim.
grant the order, since leaked documents lack protection
The Pentagon Papers were leaked, yet publication was allowed.
deny the order, since the press may never be restrained
Too broad: the Court left room for extreme, proven harms.

alt.q: "Any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity." What does this passage mean?
alt.a: Government must meet a very high bar to block publication
alt.ex: The NYT v. U.S. per curiam (1971) quoted this rule to reject blocking the Pentagon Papers.
w: Government may block publication if a court approves it first
Court approval does not remove the heavy presumption.
The press must get approval before printing secrets
That would be prior restraint, which the rule disfavors.
Publishers are liable for false statements about officials
That concerns libel (NYT v. Sullivan), not prior restraint.

items.q: New York Times v. United States (1971) and United States v. Nixon (1974) both involved the Nixon administration. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: NYT: press could publish; Nixon: President had to release tapes
items.ex: NYT v. U.S. rejected prior restraint of the Pentagon Papers; U.S. v. Nixon (8–0) rejected an absolute executive privilege.
w: NYT: President had to release tapes; Nixon: press could publish
Reverses the two cases.
Both upheld executive privilege over national security
Both ruled against the administration.
NYT: press was blocked; Nixon: tapes stayed confidential
Both outcomes are reversed.

alt.q: New York Times v. United States (1971) is often confused with New York Times v. Sullivan (1964). What did Sullivan decide?
alt.a: Public officials must prove actual malice to win libel suits
alt.ex: Sullivan (1964) required public officials to prove a falsehood was made knowingly or recklessly.
w: The government could not block the Pentagon Papers
That was NYT v. United States (1971).
Reporters must reveal their confidential sources to grand juries
That issue arose in Branzburg v. Hayes (1972).
Prior restraint is allowed in wartime emergencies
Sullivan did not address prior restraint.

alt.q: The government tried to stop a newspaper from printing leaked classified documents (A). Decades earlier, a man was jailed after distributing antidraft leaflets (B). How did the Court rule in A and B?
alt.a: A: publication allowed; B: conviction upheld
alt.ex: A is NYT v. U.S. (1971), which allowed publication; B is Schenck (1919), which upheld the conviction.
w: A: publication blocked; B: conviction upheld
The Court refused to block publication in A.
A: publication allowed; B: conviction reversed
Schenck's conviction was upheld 9–0.
A: publication blocked; B: conviction reversed
Both outcomes are reversed.

items.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that expanded religious liberty by exempting believers from a state law?
items.a: Wisconsin v. Yoder
items.ex: Yoder (1972) held that the Free Exercise Clause exempted Amish families from Wisconsin's requirement of school attendance beyond the eighth grade.
w: Engel v. Vitale
Engel limited government-sponsored prayer (Establishment Clause); it did not exempt anyone from a law.
Tinker v. Des Moines
Tinker protected political speech, not religious practice.
Texas v. Johnson
Johnson protected flag burning as symbolic political speech.

alt.q: In Wisconsin v. Yoder, the Court weighed the Free Exercise Clause against which state interest?
alt.a: universal education
alt.ex: The Court balanced Wisconsin's interest in compulsory education against the Amish parents' religious practice and found that the state's interest did not justify two more years of required schooling.
w: national security
National security was at stake in cases like Korematsu, not Yoder.
public health
The case concerned schooling, not health measures.
collecting tax revenue
Taxes were not at issue; the parents were fined for violating the attendance law.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which conclusion did the Court reach?
alt.a: State school laws can yield to religious liberty
alt.ex: Yoder held that a state's interest in education must be balanced against free exercise rights, and that for the Amish, religious liberty outweighed two extra years of compulsory schooling.
w: States must provide religious schooling
Yoder exempted the Amish from attendance; it did not require states to fund religion.
School laws override all religious claims
The passage says the state's interest is 'not totally free from a balancing process.'
Only Congress may set school attendance requirements
Attendance laws are state laws; Yoder limited a state law but did not move the power to Congress.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“...a State's interest in universal education, however highly we rank it, is not totally free from a balancing process when it impinges on fundamental rights and interests...”
Source: United States Reports

items.q: Which statement best describes the scope of Wisconsin v. Yoder?
items.a: It was limited to sincere religious objections
items.ex: Yoder stressed the Amish community's long-held religious way of life; the Court said a purely secular or philosophical objection would not qualify.
w: It let parents remove their children for any reason
The Court made clear that personal or philosophical reasons would not be protected.
It ended compulsory education laws nationwide
Compulsory attendance laws remain valid; Yoder created a narrow exemption.
It required states to fund religious schools
Yoder concerned an exemption from attendance, not public funding.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which kind of objection would the Court NOT protect?
alt.a: a personal philosophical objection
alt.ex: In Yoder (1972), the Court said that a rejection of secular values like Thoreau's, not grounded in religion, 'would not rest on a religious basis' and so would not receive Free Exercise protection.
w: a sincere religious objection
Sincere religious beliefs are what the Free Exercise Clause protects.
a long-established faith practice
The Amish's centuries-old practice was the basis for the ruling.
a belief shared by a religious community
The Court relied on the shared beliefs of the Amish community.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a landmark Supreme Court case opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Thus, if the Amish asserted their claims because of their subjective evaluation and rejection of the contemporary secular values accepted by the majority, much as Thoreau rejected the social values of his time and isolated himself at Walden Pond, their claims would not rest on a religious basis.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Under the reasoning in Wisconsin v. Yoder, the parent's claim would most likely
alt.a: fail, because it is not based on religion
alt.ex: Yoder protected the Amish because their objection was religious; the Court said philosophical or personal objections would not receive the same protection.
w: succeed, because all parents have this right
Yoder did not create a general parental right to end schooling.
succeed, because the teen is past eighth grade
Grade level alone was not the basis; the religious nature of the claim was.
fail, because Yoder was later overruled
Yoder has not been overruled.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A parent with no religious beliefs objects to modern schooling on philosophical grounds and withdraws a 15-year-old from public high school, citing Wisconsin v. Yoder.

items.q: Amish parents in a Midwestern state refused to send their children to school after eighth grade, saying high school conflicted with their religious way of life, and were fined under a compulsory-attendance law. Which case?
items.a: Wisconsin v. Yoder
items.ex: Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972), 7–0, held that the parents' free exercise rights outweighed the state's interest.
w: Engel v. Vitale
1962 Establishment Clause case on school prayer.
Employment Division v. Smith
1990 case denying a religious exemption from a drug law.
Pierce v. Society of Sisters
1925 case letting parents choose private schools.

alt.q: Which case held that a state could not force Amish children to attend school beyond the eighth grade?
alt.a: Wisconsin v. Yoder
alt.ex: Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote for the Court in Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972).
w: Engel v. Vitale
Struck down a state-written school prayer.
Employment Division v. Smith
Held neutral laws generally apply despite religious objections.
Pierce v. Society of Sisters
Struck down a law requiring public school attendance only.

alt.q: In which case did the Court rule that parents' free exercise of religion outweighed the state's interest in two more years of compulsory schooling?
alt.a: Wisconsin v. Yoder
alt.ex: Yoder (1972) found one or two more years of high school would gravely endanger Amish religious practice.
w: Engel v. Vitale
An Establishment Clause case, not free exercise.
Employment Division v. Smith
Ruled against the religious claimants in 1990.
Pierce v. Society of Sisters
Rested on parental liberty under due process, not free exercise.

items.q: Wisconsin v. Yoder was decided under which clause?
items.a: The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment
items.ex: Yoder (1972) protected the Amish families' free exercise of religion.
w: The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment
The basis of Engel v. Vitale (1962).
The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
Not the basis of the ruling.
The Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment
The case concerned religious practice, not speech.

alt.q: What principle does Wisconsin v. Yoder illustrate?
alt.a: Religious practice can outweigh some general state laws
alt.ex: Yoder (1972) balanced the state's interest in education against a sincere, long-established religious practice and sided with the parents.
w: Government may never require school attendance
Yoder allowed attendance laws through eighth grade.
States may write prayers if attendance is voluntary
Engel (1962) rejected this.
Religious groups must obey every neutral law without exception
Yoder granted an exception; compare Employment Division v. Smith.

alt.q: A state requires all teens to attend school until 16. A long-established religious community shows high school would undermine its faith and way of life. Under Yoder, the state should most likely
alt.a: exempt the community's children after eighth grade
alt.ex: Yoder (1972) held the state could not compel Amish children to attend school past eighth grade.
w: require attendance since the law applies to everyone
Yoder rejected applying the law to the Amish.
require the community to open its own public school
No such remedy was ordered.
exempt all children whose parents object for any reason
Yoder protected sincere religious practice, not any objection.

items.q: Which statement about Engel v. Vitale and Wisconsin v. Yoder is accurate?
items.a: Engel limited government religion; Yoder protected private religion
items.ex: Engel (1962) applied the Establishment Clause; Yoder (1972) applied the Free Exercise Clause.
w: Engel protected private religion; Yoder limited government religion
Reverses the two cases.
Both ruled that schools must allow prayer during class
Engel struck down school prayer.
Both ruled for the state against religious objectors
Both ruled against the state.

alt.q: A student says, 'Yoder is the school prayer case.' What is the best correction?
alt.a: Yoder concerned Amish schooling; Engel concerned prayer
alt.ex: Engel v. Vitale (1962) is the school prayer case; Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) concerned Amish compulsory education.
w: Yoder concerned Bible reading; Engel concerned Amish
Bible reading was Abington v. Schempp (1963).
Yoder concerned prayer at graduations; Engel at football games
Those are Lee v. Weisman (1992) and Santa Fe v. Doe (2000).
Yoder concerned a flag salute rule; Engel concerned prayer
The flag salute case was West Virginia v. Barnette (1943).

alt.q: In which pair of cases did the Court rule for the families challenging the state in both?
alt.a: Engel v. Vitale and Wisconsin v. Yoder
alt.ex: The families won in Engel (1962, prayer struck) and in Yoder (1972, Amish exemption granted).
w: Employment Division v. Smith and Wisconsin v. Yoder
The claimants lost in Smith (1990).
Engel v. Vitale and Employment Division v. Smith
The claimants lost in Smith.
Reynolds v. United States and Wisconsin v. Yoder
Reynolds (1879) upheld a ban on polygamy against a Mormon.

items.q: What was the immediate impact of Roe v. Wade (1973) on state abortion laws?
items.a: Many state bans became unenforceable
items.ex: Roe held that the right of privacy covers a woman's abortion decision, so laws in many states banning most abortions could no longer be enforced. (Roe was overruled by Dobbs v. Jackson in 2022.)
w: States gained new power to ban abortion
Roe limited state power; states regained broad power only after Dobbs (2022).
Congress had to pass a national abortion law
Roe was a constitutional ruling; it did not require Congress to act.
Only the Texas law was affected
As a constitutional ruling, Roe applied to similar laws in every state.

alt.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that expanded an individual right by limiting states' power to regulate a medical procedure?
alt.a: Roe v. Wade
alt.ex: Roe (1973) recognized a privacy-based right to choose abortion and limited state regulation through its trimester framework; it was overruled by Dobbs in 2022.
w: Wisconsin v. Yoder
Yoder limited a state's compulsory schooling law, not medical regulation.
Mapp v. Ohio
Mapp limited states' use of illegally seized evidence.
McDonald v. City of Chicago
McDonald limited state and local gun laws.

alt.q: Under Roe v. Wade, as the law stood in 1975, how would the courts most likely have ruled?
alt.a: unconstitutional, under the right to privacy
alt.ex: Under Roe's framework (1973), states could not ban abortion in the first trimester. Today the result would differ, since Dobbs (2022) overruled Roe.
w: constitutional, as a valid use of police power
Roe held that state police power could not justify a first-trimester ban.
constitutional, unless Congress objected
Constitutional rights do not depend on congressional objection.
unconstitutional, under the Commerce Clause
Roe rested on privacy under the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause, not commerce.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1975, a state legislature passes a law banning all abortions during the first trimester of pregnancy. A doctor challenges the law in federal court.

items.q: By what process was the constitutional right recognized in Roe v. Wade eliminated in 2022?
items.a: Supreme Court decision
items.ex: In Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022), the Court overruled Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey, returning abortion regulation to the states.
w: constitutional amendment
No amendment on abortion has been ratified.
act of Congress
Congress cannot overrule a constitutional ruling by statute; the Court itself overruled Roe.
executive order
A President cannot change the meaning of the Constitution by executive order.

alt.q: Based on the passage, who now decides abortion policy?
alt.a: the people and their elected lawmakers
alt.ex: Dobbs (2022) overruled Roe and returned the issue of abortion to 'the people's elected representatives,' mainly in the states.
w: federal judges in each district
Dobbs took the issue away from courts' constitutional review, not toward them.
the U.S. Supreme Court alone
The passage says the Court is returning the issue to elected representatives.
the President acting by executive order
The passage refers to elected representatives, meaning legislatures, not executive orders.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from the Supreme Court's opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“It is time to heed the Constitution and return the issue of abortion to the people's elected representatives.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: What do Plessy v. Ferguson and Roe v. Wade have in common?
alt.a: Both were later rejected by the Court itself
alt.ex: Brown v. Board (1954) rejected Plessy's 'separate but equal' doctrine, and Dobbs (2022) overruled Roe; both changes came from later Supreme Court decisions.
w: Both were overturned by constitutional amendments
No constitutional amendment overturned either case.
Both struck down state laws
Plessy upheld a Louisiana segregation law; only Roe struck down a state law.
Both were decided unanimously
Plessy was 7–1 and Roe was 7–2.

items.q: A pregnant Texas woman using a pseudonym challenged a state law banning abortion except to save the mother's life, and in 1973 the Court struck down the law. Which case?
items.a: Roe v. Wade
items.ex: Roe v. Wade (1973), 7–2, recognized an abortion right; it was overruled by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022).
w: Planned Parenthood v. Casey
1992 case that reaffirmed Roe's core and adopted the undue burden test.
Griswold v. Connecticut
1965 case recognizing privacy in contraceptive use.
Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health
2022 case that overruled Roe.

alt.q: Which 1973 case held that a constitutional right to privacy covered a woman's decision to have an abortion?
alt.a: Roe v. Wade
alt.ex: Justice Harry Blackmun wrote Roe v. Wade (1973); Dobbs (2022) overruled it.
w: Planned Parenthood v. Casey
Decided in 1992.
Griswold v. Connecticut
Concerned contraception in 1965.
Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health
Rejected any such constitutional right in 2022.

alt.q: A 1973 opinion said the right of privacy "is broad enough to encompass a woman's decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy." What later happened to this holding?
alt.a: It was overruled by Dobbs v. Jackson in 2022
alt.ex: Roe's holding was overruled on June 24, 2022, in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization.
w: It was reaffirmed by Dobbs v. Jackson in 2022
Dobbs overruled Roe and Casey.
It was overruled by Planned Parenthood v. Casey
Casey (1992) reaffirmed Roe's central holding while dropping the trimester framework.
It was made permanent by a constitutional amendment
No amendment on abortion has been adopted.

items.q: Roe v. Wade based the abortion right on which part of the Constitution?
items.a: The Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment
items.ex: Roe (1973) found a privacy right in the 14th Amendment's concept of liberty; Dobbs (2022) rejected that reading.
w: The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
Roe did not rest on equal protection.
The Fourth Amendment's search and seizure clause
Not the basis of Roe.
The Ninth Amendment standing alone
Roe noted the lower court's Ninth Amendment view but grounded the right in 14th Amendment liberty.

alt.q: What framework did Roe v. Wade use to balance a woman's right against state interests?
alt.a: A trimester system based on stages of pregnancy
alt.ex: Roe (1973) let states regulate more as pregnancy advanced, permitting bans after viability with life and health exceptions.
w: An undue burden test applied throughout pregnancy
Adopted by Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992).
Strict scrutiny with no state interest recognized
Roe recognized state interests in health and potential life.
A rule leaving all abortion law to the states
That is the result of Dobbs (2022).

alt.q: What is the current constitutional status of the abortion right recognized in Roe v. Wade?
alt.a: Overruled in 2022; states may now regulate or ban it
alt.ex: Dobbs (2022) held the Constitution confers no right to abortion and returned the issue to the people's elected representatives.
w: Still protected nationwide under Roe's trimester rule
Roe was overruled in 2022.
Protected under Casey's undue burden test since 1992
Casey was overruled along with Roe.
Banned nationwide by the Supreme Court in Dobbs
Dobbs did not ban abortion; it left the issue to states.

items.q: How did Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) change the law set by Roe v. Wade (1973)?
items.a: It overruled Roe and returned abortion law to the states
items.ex: Dobbs held 'Roe and Casey must be overruled' and returned the issue 'to the people's elected representatives.'
w: It upheld Roe but allowed a 15-week limit in Mississippi
That was roughly Chief Justice Roberts's concurrence, not the majority.
It banned abortion nationwide under the 14th Amendment
Dobbs did not ban abortion.
It replaced Roe's trimesters with an undue burden test
That was Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992).

alt.q: "The Constitution makes no reference to abortion, and no such right is implicitly protected by any constitutional provision..." Which case contains this statement?
alt.a: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health
alt.ex: Justice Samuel Alito wrote this in Dobbs (2022), which overruled Roe v. Wade (1973).
w: Roe v. Wade
Roe held the opposite in 1973.
Planned Parenthood v. Casey
Casey reaffirmed Roe's core holding in 1992.
Webster v. Reproductive Health Services
1989 case upholding some Missouri limits without overruling Roe.

alt.q: A state bans most abortions after 15 weeks, and the law reaches the Supreme Court in 2021–2022. What did the Court decide?
alt.a: Upheld the law and overruled Roe and Casey
alt.ex: In Dobbs (2022), the Court upheld Mississippi's 15-week law, 6–3 on the judgment, and overruled Roe and Casey 5–4.
w: Struck the law down under Roe's trimester rule
The law was upheld.
Upheld the law but kept Roe's core right
That was Chief Justice Roberts's separate view, not the Court's holding.
Struck the law down under Casey's undue burden test
Casey was overruled, and the law was upheld.

items.q: Which of the following reflects the most important consequence of the Watergate break-in?
items.a: resignation of the president of the United States
items.ex: The 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee offices led to a cover-up scandal. Facing likely impeachment and removal, Richard Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, the only U.S. president to do so.
w: legalization of capital punishment
Watergate had nothing to do with capital punishment, which the Supreme Court allowed again in Gregg v. Georgia (1976).
creation of levees around coastal cities
Levees are flood-control projects unrelated to Watergate.
integration of surveillance technology in society
Watergate involved illegal wiretapping, but its major consequence was the president’s resignation, not spreading surveillance technology.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court case arose from the Watergate scandal and required the president to turn over secret White House tape recordings?
alt.a: United States v. Nixon
alt.ex: In United States v. Nixon (1974), the Court unanimously ruled that executive privilege did not shield the tapes from a criminal subpoena. Nixon resigned about two weeks later.
w: New York Times v. United States
This 1971 case allowed newspapers to publish the Pentagon Papers.
Marbury v. Madison
This 1803 case established judicial review.
Miranda v. Arizona
This 1966 case required police to warn suspects of their rights.

alt.q: Which of the following was a long-term consequence of the Watergate scandal?
alt.a: new federal campaign finance limits
alt.ex: After Watergate, Congress amended the Federal Election Campaign Act in 1974, creating the Federal Election Commission and limiting campaign contributions, and later passed the Ethics in Government Act (1978).
w: a two-term limit for the president
The Twenty-Second Amendment, ratified in 1951, set the two-term limit.
abolition of the Electoral College
The Electoral College still exists; it was not abolished.
direct election of U.S. senators
The Seventeenth Amendment provided for direct election of senators in 1913.

items.q: A special prosecutor subpoenaed tape recordings of Oval Office conversations for a trial of the President's aides in the Watergate scandal. The President refused, claiming executive privilege. Which case?
items.a: United States v. Nixon
items.ex: United States v. Nixon (1974), 8–0, ordered President Nixon to turn over the tapes.
w: New York Times v. United States
1971 Pentagon Papers case on prior restraint.
Clinton v. Jones
1997 case allowing a civil suit against a sitting President for prior conduct.
Nixon v. Fitzgerald
1982 case giving Presidents immunity from civil damages for official acts.

alt.q: Which case unanimously held that executive privilege is not absolute and ordered the President to produce evidence for a criminal trial?
alt.a: United States v. Nixon
alt.ex: Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote the 8–0 opinion in United States v. Nixon (1974); Justice Rehnquist did not participate.
w: New York Times v. United States
Concerned newspapers, not presidential evidence.
Clinton v. Jones
Concerned a civil lawsuit, not a criminal subpoena.
Nixon v. Fitzgerald
Expanded presidential immunity in civil cases.

alt.q: "...neither the doctrine of separation of powers nor the need for confidentiality of high-level communications, without more, can sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege..." Which case?
alt.a: United States v. Nixon
alt.ex: This passage from United States v. Nixon (1974) rejected an absolute executive privilege against a criminal subpoena.
w: Nixon v. Fitzgerald
1982 case that expanded presidential immunity from civil damages.
Clinton v. Jones
1997 case on a civil suit over pre-office conduct.
New York Times v. United States
1971 case on prior restraint of the press.

items.q: United States v. Nixon is most closely tied to which constitutional principle?
items.a: Rule of law: even the President is subject to the courts
items.ex: U.S. v. Nixon (1974) held that a President must comply with a judicial subpoena in a criminal case.
w: Popular sovereignty: the people may recall a President
The Constitution has no recall; removal is by impeachment.
Federalism: states may prosecute federal officials
The case was a federal prosecution.
Executive privilege: the President decides what to share
The Court rejected an absolute privilege.

alt.q: What was the most immediate result of United States v. Nixon?
alt.a: Nixon released the tapes and resigned weeks later
alt.ex: The ruling came on July 24, 1974; Nixon released the tapes and resigned on August 9, 1974.
w: Nixon was impeached by the House and removed by the Senate
He resigned before the full House voted on impeachment.
Congress passed a law ending executive privilege
No such law was passed; a limited privilege still exists.
Nixon was pardoned by the Supreme Court itself
President Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon; courts do not pardon.

alt.q: A future President refuses to give a federal court evidence subpoenaed for a criminal trial, citing only a general need for confidential advice. Under United States v. Nixon, a court would most likely
alt.a: order the evidence produced, as privilege is not absolute
alt.ex: U.S. v. Nixon (1974) held a generalized interest in confidentiality must yield to a specific need for evidence in a criminal trial.
w: uphold the refusal, since privilege is absolute
The Court rejected an absolute privilege.
refuse to hear the case as a political question
The Court held the dispute was justiciable.
require a vote of Congress before any evidence is released
No congressional vote is required.

items.q: United States v. Nixon (1974) quoted Marbury v. Madison (1803). Which statement correctly links the two?
items.a: Both affirm courts' power to say what the law is
items.ex: Nixon relied on Marbury's statement that it is 'the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.'
w: Both struck down acts of Congress as unconstitutional
Nixon struck down no statute.
Both involved presidential appointments not delivered
Only Marbury involved an undelivered commission.
Both held the President immune from court orders
Nixon held the opposite.

alt.q: During the Watergate crisis, which branch did what?
alt.a: Courts ordered the tapes; the House pursued impeachment
alt.ex: The Supreme Court ordered the tapes released (1974), while the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment.
w: The House ordered the tapes; courts pursued impeachment
Courts do not impeach.
The Senate ordered the tapes; courts removed the President
Courts cannot remove a President.
Courts ordered the tapes; the Senate convicted Nixon
There was no Senate trial; Nixon resigned.

alt.q: United States v. Nixon (1974) is sometimes confused with Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982). What did Fitzgerald decide?
alt.a: Presidents are immune from civil damages for official acts
alt.ex: Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) granted absolute immunity from civil damages suits based on official presidential acts.
w: Presidents must turn over tapes for criminal trials
That was United States v. Nixon (1974).
Presidents may be sued over private acts taken before office
That was Clinton v. Jones (1997).
Presidents can be indicted while in office
Fitzgerald did not address indictment.

items.q: The Court wrote that "neither the doctrine of separation of powers, nor the need for confidentiality of high-level communications, without more, can sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances." Which case is this?
items.a: U.S. v. Nixon
items.ex: In U.S. v. Nixon (July 24, 1974), a unanimous 8-0 Court (Chief Justice Burger; Rehnquist recused) ordered Nixon to turn over White House tapes subpoenaed by the special prosecutor.
w: Marbury v. Madison
Marbury (1803) established judicial review.
Youngstown v. Sawyer
Youngstown (1952) struck down Truman's steel seizure.
Nixon v. Fitzgerald
Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) gave presidents absolute immunity from civil damages suits over official acts; it did not involve a criminal subpoena.

alt.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in United States v. Nixon (1974)?
alt.a: Privilege isn't absolute and gives way to a criminal subpoena
alt.ex: The Court recognized a presumptive privilege rooted in the separation of powers but held that it must yield to the specific need for evidence in a criminal trial.
w: Executive privilege does not exist anywhere in the Constitution
The Court recognized that the privilege has constitutional roots.
The President is immune from all court orders while in office
The Court ordered the President to comply with the subpoena.
Congress may not impeach a President for withholding evidence
The case did not limit impeachment.

alt.q: A special prosecutor subpoenas a President's recorded conversations for use in the criminal trial of the President's aides. The President refuses, citing executive privilege. Based on precedent, what is the most likely result?
alt.a: The President must produce evidence needed for the trial
alt.ex: Under U.S. v. Nixon (1974), a generalized claim of confidentiality must yield to a demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.
w: The President may withhold all of it as head of a branch
That claim of absolute privilege was rejected in 1974.
The Senate must vote on whether to release the tapes
The Senate has no role in enforcing court subpoenas.
The prosecutor must drop the case to protect secrecy
The Court put the needs of criminal justice ahead of general secrecy.

items.q: Which sequence best describes the end of the Watergate scandal in 1974?
items.a: Court ordered tapes released; Nixon resigned; Ford pardoned him
items.ex: After U.S. v. Nixon (July 24), the House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment; the 'smoking gun' tape was released August 5; Nixon resigned August 9, 1974; Ford pardoned him September 8, 1974.
w: Nixon was impeached; the Senate convicted him; Ford took office
The full House never voted, and there was no Senate trial.
Nixon was impeached; the Senate acquitted him; he finished his term
That pattern fits Andrew Johnson (1868) and Bill Clinton (1999).
Congress censured Nixon; he lost reelection; Ford pardoned him
Nixon won reelection in 1972 and resigned during his second term.

alt.q: Which statement about Richard Nixon's impeachment is accurate?
alt.a: A House committee approved articles, but he quit before a vote
alt.ex: The House Judiciary Committee approved articles for obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress in July 1974; Nixon resigned before the full House voted.
w: The full House impeached him, and then the Senate acquitted him
Nixon was never impeached by the full House.
The full House impeached him, and the Senate removed him
No President has been removed by the Senate.
The House committee rejected the articles, but he still resigned
The committee approved three articles.

alt.q: On taking the oath of office in August 1974, a new President declared, "Our long national nightmare is over." Who said this, and what had just happened?
alt.a: Gerald Ford, after Nixon resigned
alt.ex: Ford spoke at his swearing-in on August 9, 1974, the day Nixon's resignation took effect; a month later he pardoned Nixon.
w: Lyndon Johnson, after Kennedy was killed
Johnson took office in November 1963.
Jimmy Carter, after Vietnam ended
Carter took office in January 1977.
Richard Nixon, after his reelection
Nixon was the President who resigned.

items.q: Which reform was passed in response to the Watergate scandal?
items.a: The Ethics in Government Act, creating independent counsels
items.ex: Post-Watergate reforms included the 1974 Federal Election Campaign Act amendments (creating the FEC), the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 (independent counsel, financial disclosure) and the Presidential Records Act of 1978.
w: The Pendleton Act, creating a merit-based civil service
The Pendleton Act (1883) followed Garfield's assassination.
The 22nd Amendment, limiting presidents to two terms
The 22nd Amendment (1951) followed FDR's four elections.
The 25th Amendment, setting rules for presidential succession
The 25th Amendment was ratified in 1967, before Watergate, though it was used to make Ford Vice President.

alt.q: In the October 1973 "Saturday Night Massacre," what did President Nixon do?
alt.a: Had the Watergate special prosecutor fired
alt.ex: Nixon ordered Archibald Cox fired; Attorney General Elliot Richardson and his deputy William Ruckelshaus resigned rather than do it, and Robert Bork carried out the firing.
w: Fired the FBI director leading the inquiry
Nixon did not fire the FBI director.
Ordered arrests at the Watergate complex
The burglars were arrested by police on June 17, 1972.
Resigned rather than face a Senate trial
Nixon resigned in August 1974, ten months later.

alt.q: After Watergate, Congress amended federal campaign finance law in 1974. Which agency did this reform create?
alt.a: The Federal Election Commission
alt.ex: The 1974 FECA amendments set contribution limits and created the Federal Election Commission to enforce campaign finance law.
w: The Federal Communications Commission
The FCC was created in 1934 to regulate broadcasting.
The Civil Service Commission
The Civil Service Commission was created by the Pendleton Act (1883).
The Commission on Civil Rights
The Commission on Civil Rights was created in 1957.

sections.name: Regents of the Univ. of California v. Bakke (1978)

items.q: Based on the passage, which principle did Justice Powell apply in Bakke?
items.a: Equal protection covers people of every race
items.ex: Powell reasoned that the Equal Protection Clause protects every individual, so a white applicant could challenge a racial quota; government racial classifications receive strict scrutiny.
w: Equal protection covers only minority groups
Powell said the guarantee cannot mean one thing for one person and something else for another.
Equal protection applies only to federal laws
The 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause limits the states, including state universities.
Equal protection permits fixed racial quotas
Bakke struck down the medical school's fixed quota of 16 seats.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Justice Lewis Powell's opinion in Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The guarantee of equal protection cannot mean one thing when applied to one individual and something else when applied to a person of another color.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Which case applied the Equal Protection Clause to a claim brought by a white applicant denied admission under a racial quota?
alt.a: Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
alt.ex: Allan Bakke, a white applicant, challenged the UC Davis medical school's 16-seat set-aside; the Court (1978) struck down the quota.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Brown was brought on behalf of Black students challenging segregation.
Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy was brought by a man of mixed race challenging segregated rail cars.
Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education
Swann (1971) was brought by Black families seeking school desegregation through busing.

alt.q: Allan Bakke's claim against the University of California rested mainly on which argument?
alt.a: The quota treated him differently by race
alt.ex: Bakke argued that reserving 16 of 100 seats for minority applicants denied him equal protection and violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
w: The school charged him higher tuition
Tuition was not at issue; admission was.
The school rejected him for his religion
Bakke's claim concerned race, not religion.
The school denied him a fair hearing on appeal
His claim was about the racial set-aside, not a hearing.

items.q: Which goal did Justice Powell accept in Bakke as a valid reason for a university to consider race?
items.a: a diverse student body
items.ex: Powell called 'the attainment of a diverse student body' a 'constitutionally permissible goal for an institution of higher education,' though not through quotas. (SFFA v. Harvard, 2023, later ended race-conscious admissions.)
w: remedying discrimination in society at large
Powell held that helping victims of general 'societal discrimination' did not justify the classification.
filling a fixed number of reserved seats
Fixed set-asides were exactly what Bakke struck down.
raising average test scores of admitted students
This goal has nothing to do with race and was not the basis of Powell's opinion.

alt.q: Based on the passage, which admissions approach would Powell most likely accept?
alt.a: weighing race as one factor for diversity
alt.ex: Powell held that race could be a 'plus' factor in pursuit of diversity, citing Harvard College's program, but rejected quotas. Race-conscious admissions were later ended by SFFA v. Harvard (2023).
w: reserving seats for one racial group
Reserved seats were the quota Bakke struck down.
barring applicants of one racial group
Excluding an entire race plainly violates equal protection.
using separate admissions committees by race
UC Davis used a separate committee for its quota, which the Court rejected.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Justice Lewis Powell's opinion in Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978), to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“...the attainment of a diverse student body. This clearly is a constitutionally permissible goal for an institution of higher education.”
Source: United States Reports

alt.q: Under Justice Powell's opinion in Bakke, this justification is
alt.a: insufficient to support a racial classification
alt.ex: Powell wrote that helping groups perceived as victims of 'societal discrimination' does not justify a racial classification that burdens other applicants.
w: a compelling reason to use racial quotas
Powell rejected both the justification and the use of quotas.
valid as long as the state legislature approves it
Legislative approval cannot cure an equal protection violation.
valid because the school is public
Being public makes the school subject to the Equal Protection Clause, not exempt from it.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state medical school says it reserves seats for minority applicants to make up for discrimination in society at large, not for any discrimination by the school itself.

items.q: A white applicant was twice rejected by a public medical school that reserved 16 of 100 seats for minority applicants, though their scores exceeded those of admitted minority students. Which case?
items.a: Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
items.ex: In Bakke (1978), the Court struck down UC Davis's fixed quota and ordered Bakke admitted.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case ending school segregation.
Grutter v. Bollinger
2003 case upholding a law school's holistic use of race.
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
2023 case ending race-conscious admissions at Harvard and UNC.

alt.q: Which case struck down a fixed racial quota in admissions but allowed race to be considered as one factor among many?
alt.a: Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) produced split 5–4 holdings, with Justice Lewis Powell casting the deciding vote on both.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Concerned segregation, not admissions preferences.
Grutter v. Bollinger
Upheld holistic admissions in 2003, building on Bakke.
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
Ruled against race-conscious admissions in 2023.

alt.q: In which 1978 case did Justice Lewis Powell's controlling opinion reject reserved seats for minorities while allowing race as a 'plus' factor?
alt.a: Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
alt.ex: Powell's opinion in Bakke (1978) became the model for affirmative action in admissions for decades.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Decided in 1954 by Chief Justice Warren.
Grutter v. Bollinger
Decided in 2003, written by Justice O'Connor.
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
Decided in 2023, written by Chief Justice Roberts.

items.q: Along with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Bakke turned mainly on which constitutional clause?
items.a: The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
items.ex: Powell held the UC Davis quota violated the Equal Protection Clause (1978).
w: The Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment
UC Davis is a state school, so the 14th Amendment applied.
The Commerce Clause of Article I
Admissions quotas were not a commerce issue.
The Privileges or Immunities Clause of the 14th Amendment
Not the basis of Bakke.

alt.q: A state university gives applicants a modest boost for race as one of many factors, with no reserved seats. Under Bakke, this approach was
alt.a: permitted, as a flexible plus rather than a quota
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) allowed race as a 'plus' factor; Students for Fair Admissions (2023) later found such programs at Harvard and UNC unconstitutional.
w: forbidden, since any use of race was unconstitutional
Bakke allowed race as one factor.
required, since quotas were needed to fix past bias
Bakke struck down quotas.
permitted, only if seats were set aside by race
Set-aside seats were exactly what Bakke struck down.

alt.q: What was the main result of Bakke?
alt.a: Racial quotas were barred, but race could still be a factor
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) struck the 16-seat quota while allowing race as one consideration in admissions.
w: All affirmative action in admissions was banned
Bakke allowed race as one factor.
Affirmative action became mandatory in every public university
Bakke required no such programs.
Schools had to admit applicants by test scores only
The Court imposed no scores-only rule.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes Bakke (1978) from Brown v. Board of Education (1954)?
items.a: Bakke addressed affirmative action; Brown, segregation
items.ex: Both applied Equal Protection to race in education, but Brown ended segregation while Bakke limited affirmative action quotas.
w: Bakke addressed segregation; Brown, affirmative action
Reverses the two cases.
Bakke addressed school prayer; Brown, segregation
School prayer was Engel v. Vitale.
Bakke addressed voting districts; Brown, admissions
Neither description is correct.

alt.q: Bakke (1978) is often contrasted with Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023). What did the later case do?
alt.a: It found race-conscious admissions programs unlawful
alt.ex: SFFA (2023) held the Harvard and UNC programs violated equal protection, largely ending the race-as-a-factor approach Bakke allowed.
w: It reaffirmed Bakke's use of race as one plus factor
SFFA rejected those programs.
It required racial quotas to fix past discrimination
Quotas remain unconstitutional.
It required all public colleges to adopt racial quotas for admissions
SFFA did the opposite.

alt.q: A medical school (A) holds 16 seats only for minority applicants; a law school (B) considers race individually alongside many factors with no seats reserved. Under Bakke's reasoning, which is true?
alt.a: A is unconstitutional; B may be permissible
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) struck the fixed quota (like A) but allowed race as one factor (like B); Grutter (2003) later upheld a program like B.
w: A is permissible; B is unconstitutional
Reverses Bakke's reasoning.
Both are required by Brown v. Board
Brown required neither.
Both are unconstitutional under Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy concerned segregation and was overturned for schools by Brown.

items.q: Which of the following cases resulted in a decision that restricted student expression in favor of schools' educational goals?
items.a: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
items.ex: Hazelwood (1988) let educators control school-sponsored student speech when their actions are 'reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns.'
w: Tinker v. Des Moines School District
Tinker expanded student expression by protecting antiwar armbands.
Engel v. Vitale
Engel limited government-sponsored prayer; it did not restrict student expression.
Texas v. Johnson
Johnson expanded expression by protecting flag burning.

alt.q: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier expanded the authority of which officials?
alt.a: public school educators
alt.ex: Hazelwood (1988) gave educators editorial control over school-sponsored publications, such as a newspaper produced in a journalism class.
w: federal judges
The ruling told judges to defer to educators on school-sponsored speech.
state legislative leaders
The case concerned a principal's decision, not legislative power.
student editors
The ruling reduced student editors' control over school-sponsored papers.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the impact of Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier?
alt.a: Schools gained more control over school-sponsored media
alt.ex: Hazelwood allowed schools to edit or remove content from school-sponsored publications for legitimate teaching reasons, narrowing the protection students had under Tinker.
w: Students gained full press rights in class-produced papers
The ruling went the other way, favoring the school.
Schools lost the power to discipline students
Hazelwood increased school authority.
Private newspapers came under school review
The ruling applied only to school-sponsored expression.

items.q: After Hazelwood, a number of states passed laws giving student journalists more freedom than the ruling required. What does this show?
items.a: States may protect rights beyond the federal minimum
items.ex: Hazelwood sets a constitutional floor; states such as those with 'New Voices' laws may give student journalists greater protection by statute.
w: States may overrule Supreme Court decisions
States cannot overrule the Court; they can only add protections the Constitution does not forbid.
Hazelwood was later declared unconstitutional by the Court
Hazelwood remains the law; state statutes simply go further.
Congress must approve state education laws
States make their own education laws without congressional approval.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the principal's position?
alt.a: The state law's stronger protection still applies
alt.ex: Hazelwood says the Constitution allows censorship of school-sponsored papers, but it does not stop a state from granting students more protection by statute; the principal must follow the state law.
w: Hazelwood overrides any state law on student newspapers
Hazelwood permits schools to censor; it does not require them to, so a state can limit censorship.
The state law is void under the Supremacy Clause
No federal law conflicts with the state law, so the Supremacy Clause does not apply.
Only a federal court may enforce school rules
State law can be enforced in state courts and by state officials.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A state law says public school principals may not censor student newspapers unless content is libelous, obscene, or likely to cause a substantial disruption. A principal removes an article on a controversial topic and cites Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier.
