alt.ex: Rep. David Wilmot's 1846 proviso passed the House repeatedly but failed in the Senate, sharpening the sectional fight over the Mexican Cession.
w: The Missouri Compromise
The 1820 compromise drew the 36°30' line in the Louisiana Purchase and did pass Congress.
The Ostend Manifesto
The 1854 Ostend Manifesto urged acquiring Cuba from Spain.
The Freeport Doctrine
Douglas's 1858 Freeport Doctrine said territories could block slavery by refusing to protect it.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854?
items.a: It let settlers vote on slavery, voiding the 36°30' line
items.ex: Written by Sen. Stephen Douglas and signed by Franklin Pierce, it organized Kansas and Nebraska under popular sovereignty, effectively repealing the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery north of 36°30'.
w: It admitted Kansas as a free state and Nebraska as a slave state
Neither became a state in 1854; Kansas entered as a free state in 1861.
It banned slavery in all lands acquired in the war with Mexico
That was the goal of the Wilmot Proviso, which never passed.
It freed enslaved people taken into free territory by owners
No law did this; Dred Scott (1857) held the opposite.

alt.q: Which earlier agreement did the Kansas-Nebraska Act effectively repeal?
alt.a: The Missouri Compromise of 1820
alt.ex: By letting settlers north of 36°30' decide on slavery, the 1854 act overturned the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery in that part of the Louisiana Purchase.
w: The Compromise of 1850
Supporters cited the 1850 compromise's popular sovereignty as a precedent; it was not repealed.
The Northwest Ordinance of 1787
The Northwest Ordinance banned slavery north of the Ohio River; the 1854 act did not touch it.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
That 1848 treaty ended the Mexican-American War.

alt.q: Which Illinois senator wrote the Kansas-Nebraska Act, partly to organize land for a transcontinental railroad route?
alt.a: Stephen Douglas
alt.ex: Douglas, chair of the Senate Committee on Territories, pushed the 1854 act; his popular sovereignty approach angered antislavery Northerners.
w: Abraham Lincoln
Lincoln was not a senator; his opposition to the act revived his political career.
Henry Clay
Clay died in 1852, two years before the act.
Charles Sumner
Sumner, of Massachusetts, opposed the act; he was beaten in the Senate in 1856 after his 'Crime Against Kansas' speech.

items.q: A law stated that its "true intent and meaning" was "not to legislate slavery into any Territory or State, nor to exclude it therefrom, but to leave the people thereof perfectly free to form and regulate their domestic institutions in their own way." Which law is this?
items.a: The Kansas-Nebraska Act
items.ex: This is Section 14 of the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), the clearest statement of popular sovereignty; it replaced the Missouri Compromise's geographic ban.
w: The Missouri Compromise
The Missouri Compromise excluded slavery north of 36°30'; it did not leave the choice to settlers.
The Northwest Ordinance
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) prohibited slavery in the Northwest Territory.
The Fugitive Slave Act
The Fugitive Slave Act (1850) dealt with capturing escapees, not slavery in territories.

alt.q: A law said it meant "not to legislate slavery into any Territory or State, nor to exclude it therefrom, but to leave the people thereof perfectly free to form and regulate their domestic institutions in their own way." Which principle does this express?
alt.a: Popular sovereignty in the territories
alt.ex: Leaving slavery to 'the people thereof' is popular sovereignty, the principle of the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854).
w: Congress's power to ban slavery in territories
The excerpt rejects Congress excluding slavery, which was the Republican position.
Federal protection of slavery in all territories
That was the Southern position later backed by Dred Scott; the excerpt also refuses to 'legislate slavery into' territories.
Gradual emancipation with payment to owners
Compensated emancipation (e.g., D.C. in 1862) is unrelated to this territorial principle.

alt.q: A historian argues that the 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act backfired by turning a territory into a battleground. Which event best supports that claim?
alt.a: Armed clashes between rival settlers in the new territory
alt.ex: 'Bleeding Kansas' (1854-1859) saw rival governments, fraudulent votes and raids such as the sack of Lawrence and the Pottawatomie killings.
w: Nat Turner's revolt among enslaved people in Virginia
Turner's rebellion was in 1831, long before the act.
The Lincoln-Douglas debates over a Senate seat in Illinois
The 1858 debates were political speeches, not territorial violence.
The secession of South Carolina after Lincoln's election
South Carolina seceded in December 1860 because of Lincoln's victory.

items.q: Which was a major political result of the Kansas-Nebraska Act?
items.a: Foes of slavery's spread formed the Republican Party
items.ex: Anger over repeal of the Missouri Compromise led antislavery Whigs, Free-Soilers and Democrats to found the Republican Party in 1854, while the Whig Party collapsed.
w: Southern Democrats left the Union and formed the Confederacy
Secession came in 1860-61 after Lincoln's election.
The Whig Party grew into the strongest party in the North
The Whigs collapsed in the mid-1850s, partly over this act.
Congress passed the Wilmot Proviso to ban slavery in the West
The Wilmot Proviso never passed the Senate.

alt.q: In 1855 thousands of Missourians cross the border to vote illegally for a proslavery legislature, while antislavery settlers form a rival government. Which 1854 law set the stage for this conflict?
alt.a: The Kansas-Nebraska Act
alt.ex: By leaving slavery to a vote of settlers, the Kansas-Nebraska Act invited both sides to rush in, producing 'Bleeding Kansas.'
w: The Compromise of 1850
The 1850 compromise organized Utah and New Mexico, not Kansas.
The Homestead Act
The Homestead Act was passed in 1862.
The Missouri Compromise
The Missouri Compromise had banned slavery in Kansas; its repeal caused the conflict.

alt.q: Which party collapsed in the 1850s as many of its Northern members joined the new Republican Party after the Kansas-Nebraska Act?
alt.a: The Whig Party
alt.ex: The Whigs split over slavery; after 1854 Northern 'Conscience Whigs' moved to the Republicans and the party disappeared.
w: The Federalist Party
The Federalists faded after the War of 1812, decades earlier.
The Democratic Party
The Democrats survived, though they split in 1860.
The Populist Party
The Populists were an 1890s farmers' party.

items.q: Which legislation reflects federal efforts to regulate transportation?
items.a: Interstate Commerce Act
items.ex: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 regulated railroads, requiring their rates to be reasonable and just, and created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first federal regulatory agency.
w: Sherman Anti-Trust Act
The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) targeted monopolies and trusts in general, not transportation specifically.
Bland-Allison Act
The Bland-Allison Act (1878) required the government to buy silver and coin it into dollars.
Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act (1883) created a merit-based civil service.

alt.q: Which federal agency was created by the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 to oversee railroad rates?
alt.a: Interstate Commerce Commission
alt.ex: The Interstate Commerce Act created the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) to oversee railroads, making it the first federal regulatory agency.
w: Federal Trade Commission
The FTC was created in 1914 to police unfair business practices.
Securities and Exchange Commission
The SEC was created in 1934 to regulate stock markets.
Federal Reserve Board
The Federal Reserve was created in 1913 to oversee banking and money.

alt.q: Which legislation reflects federal efforts to break up monopolies and trusts that restrained trade?
alt.a: Sherman Anti-Trust Act
alt.ex: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 outlawed contracts and combinations in restraint of trade and attempts to monopolize, the first federal antitrust law.
w: Interstate Commerce Act
This 1887 law regulated railroads rather than breaking up trusts.
Pendleton Act
This 1883 law created a merit-based civil service.
Homestead Act
This 1862 law gave settlers public land in the West.

items.q: In order to attract investment and business and reduce expenses, a state legislature proposes passing a law that removes the need for certain federal regulatory features relating to office and factory environments. Which legislative action would most likely cause the U.S. Supreme Court to decide that this violated the Supremacy Clause?
items.a: Occupational Safety and Health Act
items.ex: The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 sets federal workplace safety and health standards. A state law trying to excuse employers from those federal standards would conflict with federal law and be invalid under the Supremacy Clause.
w: Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act (1883) created a merit-based federal civil service, not workplace safety rules.
Fair Housing Act
The Fair Housing Act (1968) bans discrimination in housing, not workplace conditions.
Social Security Act
The Social Security Act (1935) created pensions and unemployment insurance, not workplace safety standards.

alt.q: Which federal law created national standards for workplace safety and health?
alt.a: Occupational Safety and Health Act
alt.ex: The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 created the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) to set and enforce workplace safety standards.
w: Fair Labor Standards Act
The Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) set a minimum wage, overtime pay, and child labor limits.
Labor Management Relations Act of 1947
This law, known as the Taft-Hartley Act, restricted the activities of labor unions.
Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act (1883) created a merit-based civil service.

alt.q: Which federal law would most likely lead the courts to strike down this state law under the Supremacy Clause?
alt.a: Fair Housing Act
alt.ex: The Fair Housing Act (1968) bans discrimination in the sale or rental of housing based on race, religion, national origin, and other traits. A conflicting state law would be invalid under the Supremacy Clause.
w: Occupational Safety and Health Act
OSHA covers workplace safety, not rental housing.
Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act concerns hiring in the federal civil service.
Social Security Act
The Social Security Act concerns pensions and unemployment insurance.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: To attract new residents of its choosing, a state legislature passes a law allowing landlords to refuse to rent apartments to people because of their religion or national origin.

items.q: Which law contains this provision?
items.a: Sherman Anti-Trust Act
items.ex: Section 1 of the Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890) outlawed trusts and other combinations that restrain interstate or foreign trade; Section 2 outlawed monopolizing.
w: Interstate Commerce Act
The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) regulated railroad rates and created the Interstate Commerce Commission.
Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act (1883) set up merit exams for federal jobs.
Bland-Allison Act
The Bland-Allison Act (1878) required the Treasury to buy and coin silver.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from an 1890 act of Congress, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is hereby declared to be illegal.”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which legislation reflects federal efforts to break up monopolies and trusts?
alt.a: Sherman Anti-Trust Act
alt.ex: The Sherman Anti-Trust Act of 1890 made business combinations that restrain trade illegal; Theodore Roosevelt and William Howard Taft later used it to break up trusts such as Northern Securities and Standard Oil.
w: Morrill Land-Grant Act
The Morrill Act (1862) gave states land to fund colleges.
Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act (1883) created the federal civil service merit system.
Pure Food and Drug Act
The Pure Food and Drug Act (1906) dealt with food and drug safety, not monopolies.

alt.q: Which law did the federal government rely on?
alt.a: The Sherman Anti-Trust Act
alt.ex: In Northern Securities Co. v. United States (1904), the Supreme Court used the Sherman Anti-Trust Act to break up a railroad holding company, a key victory in Theodore Roosevelt's trust-busting.
w: The Interstate Commerce Act
Although the case involved railroads, it was about an illegal combination, which the Sherman Act covers; the 1887 act regulated rates.
The Clayton Antitrust Act
The Clayton Act was not passed until 1914, a decade after this case.
The Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act deals with hiring federal employees, not business combinations.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1902 the federal government sues a holding company formed to control two competing railroads in the Northwest. The government argues that the combination illegally restrains trade among the states. In 1904 the Supreme Court agrees and orders the company dissolved.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970?
items.a: It created an agency to set workplace safety rules
items.ex: Signed by President Nixon on December 29, 1970, the act created the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in the Labor Department to set and enforce workplace safety and health standards.
w: It set national limits on air pollution from factories
That describes the Clean Air Act, also passed in 1970.
It required railroads to charge reasonable and just rates
That describes the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887.
It created a merit system for hiring federal workers
That describes the Pendleton Act of 1883.

alt.q: Which law states this purpose?
alt.a: Occupational Safety and Health Act
alt.ex: Congress declared the purpose of the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 was “to assure so far as possible every working man and woman in the Nation safe and healthful working conditions.”
w: National Environmental Policy Act
NEPA (1970) requires federal agencies to study environmental effects of their projects.
Fair Labor Standards Act
The Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) set a minimum wage and limited child labor.
National Labor Relations Act
The National Labor Relations Act (1935) protected workers' right to form unions.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1970 act of Congress, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“. . . to assure so far as possible every working man and woman in the Nation safe and healthful working conditions . . .”
Source: U.S. Department of Labor

alt.q: Which law gives the federal government this authority?
alt.a: Occupational Safety and Health Act
alt.ex: The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 lets OSHA inspect workplaces, set safety standards and fine employers who violate them.
w: National Environmental Policy Act
NEPA concerns environmental reviews of federal projects, not inspections of private workplaces.
Fair Labor Standards Act
The Fair Labor Standards Act covers wages and hours, not safety hazards.
National Labor Relations Act
The National Labor Relations Act protects union organizing, not workplace safety.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A factory worker notices that machines lack safety guards and that toxic fumes fill the work floor. The worker files a complaint with a federal agency. An inspector visits the plant, finds violations of national workplace standards and fines the employer.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Homestead Act of 1862?
items.a: It gave settlers 160 acres of public land for farming it five years
items.ex: Signed by Lincoln on May 20, 1862, it let a citizen or intending citizen (head of a family or age 21+) claim up to 160 acres by living on and improving it for five years and paying a small fee.
w: It gave states public land to fund colleges of agriculture and engineering
That was the Morrill Land-Grant Act, also signed in 1862.
It granted land and bonds to companies building a transcontinental railroad
That was the Pacific Railway Act, also of 1862.
It broke up reservation lands into allotments for individual Native Americans
That was the Dawes Act of 1887.

alt.q: A 23-year-old immigrant who has filed papers to become a citizen moves west in 1870, builds a cabin on 160 acres of federal land and farms it for five years. Which law lets them gain title to the land?
alt.a: The Homestead Act
alt.ex: The Homestead Act gave title to 160 acres to a person 21+ (or head of family) who was a citizen or had declared intent to become one, after five years of residence and improvement.
w: The Morrill Act
The Morrill Act granted land to states to fund colleges, not to individual farmers.
The Dawes Act
The Dawes Act (1887) divided Native American reservation land into allotments.
The Land Ordinance
The Land Ordinance of 1785 surveyed western land into townships for sale, not free homesteads.

alt.q: Why was Congress able to pass the Homestead Act in 1862 after similar bills had been blocked in the 1850s?
alt.a: Southern members had left Congress after secession
alt.ex: Southern lawmakers feared free homesteads would fill the West with free-soil farmers; President Buchanan vetoed an 1860 bill. Secession removed that opposition.
w: The Supreme Court had ruled such land grants were required
No court ruling required homesteads; the change was political.
The states had ratified an amendment allowing land grants
No amendment was needed; Congress has power over federal territory (Article IV).
Lincoln issued it as an executive order without a vote
The Homestead Act was passed by Congress and signed by Lincoln.

items.q: A law provided that "any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States, or who shall have filed his declaration of intention to become such," could claim public land. Which goal does this reflect?
items.a: Settling the West with small farms
items.ex: This is Section 1 of the Homestead Act (1862), which offered up to 160 acres to settlers who lived on and improved the land for five years.
w: Funding public universities in each state
That was the goal of the Morrill Land-Grant Act of 1862.
Paying pensions to Union army veterans
Pensions were handled by separate laws; this excerpt sets eligibility for land claims.
Paying railroad companies to lay track
That was the purpose of the Pacific Railway Acts.

alt.q: Which law contained this eligibility rule: "any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States"?
alt.a: The Homestead Act
alt.ex: Section 1 of the Homestead Act (May 20, 1862) set these eligibility rules for claiming up to 160 acres of public land.
w: The Morrill Land-Grant Act
The Morrill Act gave land to states for colleges, not to individuals.
The Land Ordinance of 1785
The Land Ordinance set up the survey and sale of western lands.
The Dawes Severalty Act
The Dawes Act (1887) allotted reservation land to Native American households.

alt.q: Under the 1862 law that let "any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years" claim land, which person would have been eligible to file?
alt.a: A 30-year-old unmarried woman who was a citizen
alt.ex: Because eligibility turned on being 21+ or a head of family (plus citizenship or declared intent), single and widowed women could and did file homestead claims.
w: A 19-year-old single man who still lived with his parents
He was under 21 and not a head of family.
A Confederate officer still in arms against the Union
The act barred anyone who had borne arms against the United States.
A foreign visitor with no intent to become a citizen
A claimant had to be a citizen or have filed a declaration of intent.

items.q: Which statement best describes the primary purpose of the Pendleton Act of 1883?
items.a: To fill some federal jobs by merit exams, not party loyalty
items.ex: Passed after a disappointed office-seeker assassinated President Garfield, the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act (signed by Chester Arthur) created the Civil Service Commission and competitive exams, weakening the spoils system.
w: To break up business trusts that restrained interstate trade
That was the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890).
To regulate railroad rates through a new federal commission
That was the Interstate Commerce Act (1887).
To limit how many terms a single President could serve
Term limits came with the 22nd Amendment (1951).

alt.q: Which event built public support for the Pendleton Act?
alt.a: Garfield's murder by a frustrated office-seeker
alt.ex: Charles Guiteau, angry at being denied a patronage job, shot President James Garfield in 1881; outrage fueled civil service reform.
w: Lincoln's murder by a Confederate sympathizer
Lincoln's 1865 assassination was unrelated to patronage reform.
McKinley's murder by an anarchist in Buffalo
McKinley was killed in 1901, after the Pendleton Act.
Andrew Johnson's impeachment by the House in 1868
Johnson's 1868 impeachment involved the Tenure of Office Act.

alt.q: Which practice was the Pendleton Act designed to weaken?
alt.a: The spoils system
alt.ex: The spoils system handed government jobs to party loyalists; the Pendleton Act began a merit-based civil service.
w: The seniority system
Seniority governs congressional committee posts; the act concerned federal hiring.
Gerrymandering
Gerrymandering is drawing district lines for partisan advantage.
The pocket veto
A pocket veto is a President's unsigned bill dying after Congress adjourns.

items.q: In 1885 a federal customs clerk who got the job by passing a competitive exam is told to donate part of their salary to the governing party or be fired. Which law protects the clerk?
items.a: The Pendleton Act
items.ex: The Pendleton Act provides that no person in the public service is "under any obligations to contribute to any political fund" and cannot be removed for refusing.
w: The Sherman Antitrust Act
The Sherman Act (1890) targets monopolies and trusts.
The Interstate Commerce Act
The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) regulated railroads.
The Tenure of Office Act
That 1867 law limited the President's power to remove Senate-confirmed officials; it was repealed in 1887.

alt.q: An 1883 law called for "open, competitive examinations for testing the fitness of applicants for the public service." Which reform does this excerpt reflect?
alt.a: Replacing patronage with a merit system
alt.ex: The Pendleton Act (January 16, 1883) required competitive exams for classified federal jobs, replacing appointments based on party service.
w: Expanding the President's power to hire allies
Merit exams reduced, not expanded, presidential patronage.
Giving the Senate a veto over federal hiring
Senate confirmation applies to high officers, not exam-based clerks.
Letting voters directly elect federal clerks
Civil service jobs are filled by examination, not election.

alt.q: Which President signed the Pendleton Act, despite once having held a patronage post at the New York Custom House?
alt.a: Chester A. Arthur
alt.ex: Arthur, a former machine politician whom Hayes removed as Collector of the Port of New York, surprised critics by signing the act in 1883.
w: James A. Garfield
Garfield's assassination in 1881 inspired the act; he did not sign it.
Rutherford B. Hayes
Hayes pushed reform and removed Arthur, but left office in 1881.
Grover Cleveland
Cleveland took office in 1885 and later expanded the classified service.

items.q: Which statement best describes the primary purpose of the Sedition Act of 1798?
items.a: To punish false, malicious writings that attacked the federal government
items.ex: The Sedition Act (signed by John Adams, July 14, 1798) made it a crime to publish "false, scandalous and malicious" writings against the government, Congress or the President; it was used mostly against Democratic-Republican editors.
w: To let the President deport any noncitizen he judged dangerous to the nation
That was the Alien Act, a separate 1798 law aimed at noncitizens, not at critics' writings.
To lengthen the residency period required before immigrants could naturalize
That was the Naturalization Act of 1798 (raised the residency requirement to 14 years).
To allow the detention of citizens of an enemy nation once war was declared
That was the Alien Enemies Act of 1798, which applies to nationals of a hostile nation in wartime.

alt.q: In 1798 a Democratic-Republican newspaper editor is fined and jailed for printing that President John Adams is a power-hungry tyrant. Under which law were they most likely prosecuted?
alt.a: The Sedition Act
alt.ex: The Sedition Act of 1798 punished "false, scandalous and malicious" writings against the President, Congress or the government; editors such as James Callender were jailed under it.
w: The Alien Enemies Act
It allowed detention or removal of enemy-nation nationals in wartime; it did not punish citizens' speech.
The Espionage Act
That was a 1917 World War I law (the law at issue in Schenck v. United States), not a 1798 law.
The Naturalization Act
It only lengthened the residency needed for citizenship to 14 years.

alt.q: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison secretly drafted resolutions for two state legislatures in 1798, arguing that states could judge federal laws unconstitutional. Which federal laws were they protesting?
alt.a: The Alien and Sedition Acts passed by the Federalists
alt.ex: The Kentucky (Jefferson) and Virginia (Madison) Resolutions of 1798 attacked the Alien and Sedition Acts as violating the First Amendment and exceeding Congress's delegated powers.
w: The tariff that South Carolina called the Tariff of Abominations
That 1828 tariff triggered John C. Calhoun's nullification arguments in 1828-1832, three decades later.
The whiskey excise tax that sparked a rebellion in Pennsylvania
The 1791 whiskey tax led to the Whiskey Rebellion (1794), which Washington put down; it was not the target of the 1798 resolutions.
The Judiciary Act that created the lower federal court system
The Judiciary Act of 1789 organized the federal courts; it was not the subject of the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.

items.q: A 1798 federal law punished anyone who published "any false, scandalous and malicious writing or writings against the government of the United States." Which constitutional protection did critics say this law violated?
items.a: The First Amendment's freedoms of speech and of the press
items.ex: Jefferson, Madison and other critics argued the Sedition Act abridged the speech and press freedoms of the First Amendment (1791); the act expired on March 3, 1801, and Jefferson pardoned those convicted.
w: The Fourth Amendment's ban on unreasonable searches and seizures
The Fourth Amendment governs searches and seizures, not punishment for what someone publishes.
The Fifth Amendment's privilege against being forced to testify
The self-incrimination privilege concerns compelled testimony, not criticism of officials.
The Sixth Amendment's guarantee of a trial by an impartial jury
Sedition Act defendants did get jury trials, and truth was allowed as a defense; the complaint was about punishing speech itself.

alt.q: Which 1798 law contained this language: "any false, scandalous and malicious writing or writings against the government of the United States, or either house of the Congress of the United States, or the President of the United States"?
alt.a: The Sedition Act
alt.ex: This is Section 2 of the Sedition Act (July 14, 1798), which made such writings, published "with intent to defame," a federal crime.
w: The Alien Act
The Alien Act let the President order out aliens he judged "dangerous to the peace and safety of the United States"; it did not punish writings.
The Espionage Act
The Espionage Act was passed in 1917 during World War I.
The Judiciary Act
Judiciary Acts (1789, 1801) organized the federal courts; they did not define speech crimes.

alt.q: Which question about government power did the Sedition Act of 1798 most directly raise?
alt.a: Whether officials may punish citizens for criticizing them
alt.ex: The Sedition Act tested whether the government could jail critics for 'false' and 'malicious' writings, a core First Amendment question about political speech.
w: Whether states may tax a national bank chartered by Congress
That was the question in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Whether Congress may ban slavery in the federal territories
That was the question in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).
Whether federal courts may strike down acts of Congress
That was settled in Marbury v. Madison (1803); the Supreme Court never ruled on the Sedition Act.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions of 1798?
items.a: State protests claiming states could judge federal laws void
items.ex: Drafted secretly by Madison (Virginia) and Jefferson (Kentucky), they argued the Alien and Sedition Acts were unconstitutional and that states could judge and resist (interpose against) such laws, an early states'-rights argument.
w: Federal laws that widened the President's power to deport aliens
That describes the Alien Acts themselves, which the resolutions protested.
Supreme Court rulings that struck down the Sedition Act as invalid
The Supreme Court never ruled on the Sedition Act; it expired in 1801.
Constitutional amendments approved by Virginia and Kentucky voters
They were legislative resolutions, not amendments; no amendment resulted from them.

alt.q: A 1798 law authorized the President to order out of the country "all such aliens as he shall judge dangerous to the peace and safety of the United States." Which law was this?
alt.a: The Alien Act
alt.ex: The Alien Act ("An Act Concerning Aliens," June 1798) gave the President power to deport noncitizens he judged dangerous, even in peacetime; it expired in 1800.
w: The Sedition Act
The Sedition Act punished false, scandalous and malicious writings against the government, not noncitizens as such.
The Naturalization Act
The Naturalization Act lengthened the residency required for citizenship to 14 years.
The Chinese Exclusion Act
That 1882 law barred Chinese laborers from immigrating, almost a century later.

alt.q: Who secretly drafted the Kentucky Resolutions of 1798 opposing the Alien and Sedition Acts?
alt.a: Thomas Jefferson
alt.ex: Vice President Thomas Jefferson secretly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions; James Madison wrote the Virginia Resolutions.
w: James Madison
Madison wrote the companion Virginia Resolutions, not Kentucky's.
John C. Calhoun
Calhoun developed nullification in the 1828 South Carolina Exposition and Protest, decades later.
Alexander Hamilton
Hamilton was a leading Federalist who generally supported the Adams administration's measures.

items.q: Which law first declared that "all persons born in the United States and not subject to any foreign power, excluding Indians not taxed, are hereby declared to be citizens of the United States"?
items.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1866
items.ex: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 defined national citizenship and guaranteed equal rights to make contracts, sue and hold property; the 14th Amendment (1868) later put birthright citizenship in the Constitution with different wording.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1875
The 1875 act banned discrimination in inns, theaters and public transport; the Court struck it down in 1883.
The Fourteenth Amendment
The 14th Amendment's wording is different: persons born or naturalized here and "subject to the jurisdiction thereof."
The Emancipation Proclamation
The 1863 proclamation freed enslaved people in rebel areas; it said nothing about citizenship.

alt.q: What was the main purpose of the Civil Rights Act of 1866?
alt.a: To give freedpeople citizenship and equal legal rights
alt.ex: It made those born in the U.S. citizens and guaranteed all citizens the same rights as white citizens to make contracts, sue, and own property.
w: To desegregate inns, theaters and public transportation
That was the Civil Rights Act of 1875.
To guarantee Black men the right to vote in all states
That was the Fifteenth Amendment (1870).
To create the Freedmen's Bureau to aid formerly enslaved people
The Freedmen's Bureau was created by a separate 1865 law.

alt.q: How did the Civil Rights Act of 1866 become law?
alt.a: Congress overrode President Andrew Johnson's veto
alt.ex: Johnson vetoed the bill in March 1866; Congress overrode him in April, the first major law passed over a presidential veto.
w: President Lincoln signed it shortly before his death
Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865, a year before the act.
Three-fourths of the state legislatures approved it
That is how amendments are ratified, not how statutes pass.
President Grant signed it soon after taking office
Grant took office in 1869; he signed the 1875 act.

items.q: Southern states passed Black Codes in 1865-66 that limited where freedpeople could work, travel and own property. Which federal measure most directly targeted these codes?
items.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1866
items.ex: The 1866 act guaranteed all citizens the same rights as white citizens to make contracts, sue, and buy, hold and sell property, directly attacking the Black Codes.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment
The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery but did not spell out rights such as making contracts or owning property, which the Black Codes restricted.
The Compromise of 1877
The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction by withdrawing federal troops from the South.
The Civil Rights Act of 1957
The 1957 act focused on voting rights, nearly a century later.

alt.q: Why did Congress propose the Fourteenth Amendment soon after passing the Civil Rights Act of 1866?
alt.a: To shield the act's rights from repeal or challenge
alt.ex: Doubts about Congress's power to pass the 1866 act, and fear a later Congress might repeal it, led to writing citizenship and equal protection into the Constitution.
w: To repeal the act after President Johnson had vetoed it
Congress overrode Johnson's veto; it did not repeal the act.
To give the President sole power to enforce the act
Section 5 of the 14th Amendment gives enforcement power to Congress.
To extend the act's protections to women's suffrage
Women's suffrage came with the 19th Amendment in 1920.

alt.q: Which later amendment wrote the core idea of the Civil Rights Act of 1866, birthright citizenship, into the Constitution?
alt.a: The Fourteenth Amendment
alt.ex: The 14th Amendment (1868) declares that all persons born or naturalized in the U.S. and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment
The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery.
The Fifteenth Amendment
The 15th Amendment (1870) barred denying the vote because of race.
The Nineteenth Amendment
The 19th Amendment (1920) barred denying the vote because of sex.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Civil Rights Act of 1957?
items.a: The first such federal law since Reconstruction, aimed at voting
items.ex: Signed by Eisenhower, it created the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights and a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department, and let federal prosecutors seek court orders to protect voting rights; enforcement was weak.
w: The law that banned segregation in hotels, restaurants and theaters
That was Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
The law that suspended literacy tests in Southern counties
That was the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
The law that outlawed racial discrimination in home sales
That was the Fair Housing Act (Civil Rights Act of 1968).

alt.q: Which two bodies did the Civil Rights Act of 1957 create?
alt.a: The Civil Rights Commission and DOJ Civil Rights Division
alt.ex: The 1957 act set up a bipartisan Commission on Civil Rights to investigate and a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department to litigate.
w: The EEOC and the Office of Federal Contract Compliance
The EEOC came from the Civil Rights Act of 1964; the contract compliance office from Johnson's EO 11246.
The Freedmen's Bureau and the U.S. Civil Service Commission
These were created in 1865 and 1883.
The Federal Election Commission and Election Assistance Commission
The FEC was created in 1974 after Watergate; the Election Assistance Commission was created by the Help America Vote Act of 2002.

alt.q: Senator Strom Thurmond spoke for over 24 hours in 1957, a record-setting one-person filibuster, trying to block which measure?
alt.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1957
alt.ex: Thurmond's 24-hour-18-minute filibuster in August 1957 failed; the bill passed and Eisenhower signed it.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
The 1964 bill faced a group filibuster of about two months, ended by cloture.
The Voting Rights Act of 1965
The VRA passed in 1965, eight years later.
The Fair Housing Act of 1968
The Fair Housing Act passed in 1968.

items.q: Which law states: "All persons shall be entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the goods, services, facilities, privileges, advantages, and accommodations of any place of public accommodation... without discrimination or segregation on the ground of race, color, religion, or national origin"?
items.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
items.ex: This is Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (signed by Lyndon Johnson on July 2, 1964), which banned discrimination in hotels, restaurants, theaters and similar places.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1875
The 1875 act covered inns, conveyances and theaters but was struck down in the Civil Rights Cases (1883); its wording differs.
The Civil Rights Act of 1968
The 1968 act's main title (Fair Housing) covers housing, not public accommodations.
The Voting Rights Act of 1965
The VRA protects voting, not access to businesses.

alt.q: In 1964 a motel near an interstate highway refuses to rent rooms to Black travelers. Which law and constitutional power did the Supreme Court rely on to require the motel to serve them?
alt.a: Civil Rights Act of 1964, under the Commerce Clause
alt.ex: In Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964), the Court upheld Title II because discrimination against interstate travelers burdens interstate commerce.
w: Civil Rights Act of 1964, under the 14th Amendment alone
Right law, wrong basis: the Court relied on the Commerce Clause, since the 14th Amendment was read to reach only state action.
Civil Rights Act of 1875, under the 13th Amendment
The 1875 act was struck down in 1883 and was no longer law.
Fair Housing Act of 1968, under the Commerce Clause
The Fair Housing Act concerns housing and passed in 1968.

alt.q: Why did Congress base the public accommodations section of the 1964 act mainly on the Commerce Clause?
alt.a: Prior rulings limited the 14th Amendment to state action
alt.ex: The Civil Rights Cases (1883) held the 14th Amendment did not reach private businesses' discrimination, so Congress relied on its power to regulate interstate commerce.
w: The Commerce Clause lets Congress overrule any Court decision
No clause lets Congress overrule constitutional rulings by statute.
Hotels and restaurants were owned by the federal government
They were private businesses, which is why the commerce power was needed.
The Fourteenth Amendment had not yet been fully ratified
The 14th Amendment was ratified in 1868.

items.q: A company with 50 employees refuses to promote a qualified worker solely because of the worker's sex. Which law most directly makes this illegal?
items.a: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
items.ex: Title VII bars employers with 15 or more employees from discriminating based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin, and created the EEOC to enforce it.
w: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972
Title IX bans sex discrimination in federally funded education programs, not private employment.
The Nineteenth Amendment to the Constitution
The 19th Amendment (1920) protects the right to vote regardless of sex.
The Equal Rights Amendment to the Constitution
The ERA was proposed in 1972 but was not ratified by the 1982 deadline.

alt.q: Which agency did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 create to enforce its ban on job discrimination?
alt.a: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
alt.ex: Title VII of the 1964 act created the EEOC, which began work in 1965.
w: The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights
The Civil Rights Commission was created by the 1957 act and investigates rather than enforces.
The National Labor Relations Board
The NLRB was created by the Wagner Act (1935) to oversee union matters.
The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs
That Labor Department office oversees federal contractors; it enforced Executive Order 11246 until that order was revoked in January 2025.

alt.q: A federal law makes it unlawful for an employer "to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual... because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin." Which law is this?
alt.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
alt.ex: This is Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; 'sex' was added during House debate.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1957
The 1957 act dealt with voting rights and created the Civil Rights Commission.
The Fair Labor Standards Act
The FLSA (1938) sets minimum wages and maximum hours.
The Americans with Disabilities Act
The ADA (1990) bans disability discrimination.

items.q: A public school district that receives federal money still runs separate schools for Black and white students in 1966. Which part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 lets federal agencies cut off its funds?
items.a: Title VI, banning bias in federally funded programs
items.ex: Title VI bars discrimination by race, color or national origin in any program receiving federal financial assistance; the threat of losing funds sped school desegregation after Brown.
w: Title II, banning bias in places of public accommodation
Title II covers hotels, restaurants and theaters, not schools' funding.
Title VII, banning bias by employers against workers
Title VII covers employment.
Title I, setting uniform rules for voter registration
Title I of the 1964 act dealt with voting procedures.

alt.q: "No person in the United States shall, on the ground of race, color, or national origin, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance." Where is this found?
alt.a: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
alt.ex: This is the core sentence of Title VI (1964); Title IX (1972) later copied its structure to ban sex discrimination in federally funded education.
w: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972
Title IX uses similar wording but covers sex in education programs.
Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
Section 2 bars voting practices that deny or abridge the vote on account of race or color.
Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968
Title VIII (the Fair Housing Act) covers housing.

alt.q: What protection did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 add for people in programs that receive federal grants?
alt.a: A ban on race-based exclusion from those programs
alt.ex: Title VI bars exclusion or discrimination by race, color or national origin in federally funded programs and allows agencies to cut off funds.
w: A ban on poll taxes in state and local elections
Poll taxes in federal elections were banned by the 24th Amendment; in state elections by Harper v. Virginia (1966).
A requirement of racial hiring quotas for recipients
The 1964 act does not require quotas; Title VII expressly does not require preferential treatment.
A ban on discrimination in the sale of houses
Housing discrimination was banned by the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

items.q: Which law provides: "No voting qualification or prerequisite to voting, or standard, practice, or procedure shall be imposed or applied by any State or political subdivision to deny or abridge the right of any citizen of the United States to vote on account of race or color"?
items.a: The Voting Rights Act
items.ex: This is Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, signed by Lyndon Johnson on August 6, 1965, to enforce the Fifteenth Amendment.
w: The Fifteenth Amendment
The 15th Amendment (1870) says the vote shall not be denied 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude'; the excerpt is statutory language enforcing it.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The 24th Amendment (1964) bans poll taxes in federal elections.
The Civil Rights Act of 1957
The 1957 act let the Justice Department sue to protect voting but did not contain this section.

alt.q: Which constitutional amendment was the Voting Rights Act of 1965 primarily designed to enforce?
alt.a: The Fifteenth Amendment
alt.ex: The 15th Amendment (1870) bars denying the vote on account of race; Section 2 of that amendment gave Congress enforcement power, which the VRA used.
w: The Nineteenth Amendment
The 19th Amendment (1920) protects voting regardless of sex.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment
The 26th Amendment (1971) set the voting age at 18.
The Seventeenth Amendment
The 17th Amendment (1913) provided for direct election of senators.

alt.q: Which event in March 1965, when state troopers beat marchers on a bridge in Alabama, pushed Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act?
alt.a: Bloody Sunday in Selma
alt.ex: On March 7, 1965, troopers attacked voting-rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma; televised images built support for the VRA.
w: The March on Washington
The 1963 March on Washington supported the civil rights bill that became the 1964 act.
The Montgomery bus boycott
The 1955-56 boycott challenged bus segregation.
The Greensboro sit-ins
The 1960 Greensboro sit-ins challenged lunch-counter segregation.

items.q: In 1970 a Mississippi county covered by a 1965 federal law wants to move its polling places. Before doing so it must get approval from the U.S. Attorney General or a federal court in D.C. What is this requirement called?
items.a: Preclearance
items.ex: Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act required jurisdictions identified by the Section 4(b) coverage formula to 'preclear' any change in voting rules with federal authorities.
w: Judicial review
Judicial review is a court's power to strike down unconstitutional laws (Marbury v. Madison).
Redistricting
Redistricting is redrawing district lines; it was one kind of change that needed preclearance.
Incorporation
Incorporation applies Bill of Rights protections to the states through the 14th Amendment.

alt.q: In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), what did the Supreme Court decide about the Voting Rights Act?
alt.a: Its formula for picking covered places was outdated
alt.ex: The Court struck down Section 4(b)'s coverage formula as based on decades-old data, leaving Section 5 preclearance with no jurisdictions to apply to; Section 2 remains in force.
w: Its ban on racial discrimination in voting was void
Section 2's nationwide ban was not struck down.
Its preclearance rule had to cover every state
The Court did not extend preclearance; it disabled it.
Its protections applied to federal elections only
The VRA applies to state and local elections too.

alt.q: Which tool of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 most directly removed a common barrier used to keep Black citizens from registering?
alt.a: Suspending literacy tests in covered areas
alt.ex: The VRA suspended literacy tests in covered jurisdictions and sent federal examiners to register voters; later amendments banned such tests nationwide.
w: Banning poll taxes in all federal elections
That was the 24th Amendment (1964), not the VRA.
Lowering the voting age to eighteen
That was the 26th Amendment (1971).
Creating the Commission on Civil Rights
That was the Civil Rights Act of 1957.

items.q: Which statement best describes the effect of the Voting Rights Act of 1965?
items.a: Black registration in the South rose sharply within a few years
items.ex: With literacy tests suspended and federal examiners on site, Black registration soared; in Mississippi it rose from about 7% in 1964 to about 60% by 1967.
w: Black voter registration fell as states switched to poll taxes
The 24th Amendment and court rulings blocked poll taxes; registration rose.
It had little effect until the Supreme Court enforced it in 2013
The 2013 Shelby County ruling limited the act; its effects came in the 1960s.
It extended the right to vote to women in the Southern states
Women's suffrage was secured by the 19th Amendment (1920).

alt.q: In Mississippi about 7% of eligible Black adults were registered to vote in 1964, and about 60% in 1967. Which measure best explains this change?
alt.a: The Voting Rights Act
alt.ex: The VRA suspended literacy tests and sent federal registrars into covered states such as Mississippi, causing the sharp rise.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1957
The 1957 act relied on slow lawsuits and produced little change.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The 24th Amendment ended poll taxes only in federal elections and did not address literacy tests.
The Fair Housing Act of 1968
The Fair Housing Act concerns housing and came after 1967.

alt.q: Which President signed the Voting Rights Act after urging Congress in a televised March 1965 speech to pass it?
alt.a: Lyndon B. Johnson
alt.ex: Johnson addressed Congress on March 15, 1965, after Selma, and signed the VRA on August 6, 1965.
w: John F. Kennedy
Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963.
Dwight D. Eisenhower
Eisenhower signed the Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960.
Richard M. Nixon
Nixon signed a 1970 extension of the VRA, not the original act.

items.q: In 1970 a landlord refuses to rent an apartment to a family because the family is Jewish. Which law most directly prohibits this?
items.a: The Fair Housing Act of 1968
items.ex: Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 bans discrimination in selling, renting and financing housing based on race, color, religion or national origin (sex added 1974; disability and familial status 1988).
w: Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title II covers public accommodations such as hotels and restaurants, not apartment rentals.
Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title VII covers employment.
Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
Section 2 covers voting.

alt.q: Which event in April 1968 helped push Congress to pass the Fair Housing Act within a week?
alt.a: The assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.
alt.ex: King was killed on April 4, 1968; Johnson urged quick passage and signed the Civil Rights Act of 1968 on April 11.
w: The assassination of Senator Robert F. Kennedy
RFK was shot in June 1968, after the act passed.
The Tet Offensive launched in South Vietnam
The Tet Offensive (January 1968) affected war policy, not housing law.
The Watts uprising in Los Angeles
The Watts riots occurred in 1965.

alt.q: A 1968 law's housing title begins: "It is the policy of the United States to provide, within constitutional limitations, for fair housing throughout the United States." Which practice was this law mainly aimed at?
alt.a: Refusing to sell or rent homes due to race
alt.ex: This opens Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (Fair Housing Act), which outlawed discrimination in sales, rentals and financing of housing.
w: Refusing to serve diners at lunch counters
Lunch-counter segregation was addressed by Title II of the 1964 act.
Using literacy tests to block registration
Literacy tests were addressed by the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Paying women less than men for the same work
Unequal pay by sex was addressed by the Equal Pay Act of 1963.

items.q: In 1975 a bank refuses to make home loans in any neighborhood where most residents are Black. Which law makes this practice, known as redlining, illegal?
items.a: The Fair Housing Act of 1968
items.ex: The Fair Housing Act (1968) bans discrimination in the financing of housing as well as in sales and rentals, which covers redlining.
w: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title VII covers employment discrimination.
Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title II covers public accommodations.
The Civil Rights Act of 1875
The 1875 act was struck down in 1883 and covered inns and transport.

alt.q: Which activities are covered by the Fair Housing Act of 1968?
alt.a: Selling, renting and financing homes
alt.ex: Title VIII of the 1968 act bans discrimination in the sale, rental and financing of dwellings.
w: Hiring, promoting and firing workers
That is Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Serving guests in hotels and diners
That is Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Registering voters and running polls
That is the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

alt.q: Which category was not protected when the Fair Housing Act was first passed in 1968 but was added by Congress in 1974?
alt.a: Sex
alt.ex: The original act covered race, color, religion and national origin; sex was added in 1974, and disability and familial status in 1988.
w: Race
Race was protected from the start in 1968.
Religion
Religion was protected from the start in 1968.
Color
Color was protected from the start in 1968.

items.q: Which statement best describes the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001?
items.a: It expanded surveillance powers to fight terrorism
items.ex: Signed by George W. Bush on October 26, 2001, it expanded wiretap and records-search powers (roving wiretaps, delayed-notice searches, Section 215 business records), raising Fourth Amendment privacy concerns.
w: It created a new cabinet department for homeland security
That was the Homeland Security Act of 2002.
It authorized military force against those behind 9/11
That was the Authorization for Use of Military Force (September 18, 2001).
It banned cruel treatment of detainees in U.S. custody
That was the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005.

alt.q: After 2001 federal agents get a court order to tap any phone a terrorism suspect uses, rather than one line, and delay telling a person their home was searched. Critics argue these tools strain which amendment?
alt.a: The Fourth Amendment
alt.ex: The PATRIOT Act's roving wiretaps and 'sneak and peek' delayed-notice warrants raised concerns under the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures.
w: The Fifth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment covers self-incrimination, double jeopardy and due process.
The Sixth Amendment
The Sixth Amendment covers rights at criminal trial, such as counsel and jury.
The Eighth Amendment
The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishment.

alt.q: Which law, passed weeks after the September 11 attacks, authorized "roving" wiretaps and expanded access to business records in terrorism investigations?
alt.a: The USA PATRIOT Act
alt.ex: The USA PATRIOT Act (October 26, 2001) expanded surveillance tools, including roving wiretaps and Section 215 orders for business records.
w: The Homeland Security Act
The Homeland Security Act (2002) created the Department of Homeland Security.
The USA FREEDOM Act
The USA FREEDOM Act (2015) narrowed, rather than created, these surveillance powers.
The Intelligence Reform Act
The 2004 Intelligence Reform Act created the Director of National Intelligence; it came three years later.

items.q: Supporters and critics of the USA PATRIOT Act mainly debated which tension in American government?
items.a: National security versus personal privacy
items.ex: Supporters said expanded surveillance was needed to prevent terrorism; critics said it weakened Fourth Amendment privacy and due process protections.
w: States' rights versus national supremacy
The PATRIOT Act debate was not mainly about state versus federal power.
Free trade versus protective tariffs on imports
Trade policy was not the issue.
Majority rule versus voting rights
The act did not deal with elections or voting.

alt.q: In 2015 Congress ended the PATRIOT Act's bulk collection of Americans' phone records and replaced it with a narrower system. Which law did this?
alt.a: The USA FREEDOM Act
alt.ex: After Edward Snowden's 2013 disclosures, the USA FREEDOM Act (2015) ended NSA bulk collection under Section 215.
w: The Homeland Security Act
The Homeland Security Act (2002) created DHS.
The Intelligence Reform Act
The 2004 Intelligence Reform Act created the Director of National Intelligence.
The Privacy Act
The Privacy Act (1974) regulates how federal agencies handle personal records.

alt.q: A city council member argues that letting the FBI obtain library records without telling patrons sacrifices too much privacy for too little safety. Which law is the member criticizing?
alt.a: The USA PATRIOT Act
alt.ex: Section 215 of the PATRIOT Act let investigators obtain 'tangible things,' including library records, drawing protests from librarians and civil liberties groups.
w: The Freedom of Information Act
FOIA (1966) gives the public access to government records.
The Privacy Act of 1974
The Privacy Act limits, rather than expands, government use of personal records.
The War Powers Resolution
The War Powers Resolution limits military deployments.

items.q: Based on the passage, which government program would the speaker support?
items.a: New Deal
items.ex: The passage is from Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1932 speech accepting the Democratic nomination, in which he also pledged “a new deal for the American people.” The New Deal created jobs programs and economic security measures such as Social Security.
w: Great Society
The Great Society was Lyndon B. Johnson’s program of the 1960s.
Fair Deal
The Fair Deal was Harry Truman’s program after World War II.
Brain Trust
The Brain Trust was a group of FDR’s advisers, not a government program.

sc.title: Use the passage below, taken from a presidential nomination speech, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“What do the people of America want more than anything else? To my mind, they want two things: work, . . . and with work, a reasonable measure of security . . .”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which set of government programs is most closely associated with the speaker’s goal?
alt.a: Great Society
alt.ex: President Lyndon B. Johnson declared the War on Poverty in his January 8, 1964 State of the Union address; it became a central part of his Great Society programs, such as Head Start and Medicaid.
w: New Deal
The New Deal was Franklin D. Roosevelt’s response to the Great Depression in the 1930s.
Square Deal
The Square Deal was Theodore Roosevelt’s program in the early 1900s.
Fair Deal
The Fair Deal was Harry Truman’s program in the late 1940s.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1964 presidential address to Congress, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“This administration today, here and now, declares unconditional war on poverty in America.”
Source: The American Presidency Project, Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union, January 8, 1964

alt.q: Which New Deal law best reflects Franklin D. Roosevelt’s goal of giving Americans economic security in old age and unemployment?
alt.a: Social Security Act
alt.ex: The Social Security Act of 1935 created old-age pensions and a federal-state unemployment insurance system.
w: Civilian Conservation Corps
The CCC gave young men jobs on conservation projects; it did not create pensions.
Tennessee Valley Authority
The TVA built dams to bring electricity and flood control to the Tennessee Valley.
Works Progress Administration
The WPA provided work-relief jobs, not pensions or unemployment insurance.

items.q: A 1935 law is titled "An act to provide for the general welfare by establishing a system of Federal old-age benefits, and by enabling the several States to make more adequate provision for aged persons, blind persons, dependent and crippled children..." Which law is it?
items.a: The Social Security Act
items.ex: Signed by FDR on August 14, 1935, the Social Security Act created federal old-age insurance funded by payroll taxes, plus federal-state unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children and the blind.
w: The Fair Labor Standards Act
The FLSA (1938) set a minimum wage and maximum hours and limited child labor.
The National Labor Relations Act
The Wagner Act (1935) protected workers' right to unionize.
The Railroad Retirement Act
The Railroad Retirement Acts (1934-1937) created pensions only for railroad workers, not a general old-age and child-welfare system.

alt.q: How were old-age benefits funded under the Social Security Act of 1935?
alt.a: Payroll taxes paid by workers and employers
alt.ex: The act levied matching taxes on wages paid by employees and employers; FDR wanted workers to feel they had earned a right to benefits.
w: Special income taxes on the wealthiest households
Social Security was built on a payroll tax, not a special income tax on the rich.
Tariffs on imported manufactured goods
Tariffs were not the funding source.
Voluntary deposits into private savings accounts
Participation was mandatory for covered workers, not voluntary private accounts.

alt.q: In 1940 a retired factory worker receives a monthly federal check based on taxed wages, and an unemployed neighbor gets state jobless benefits backed by federal law. Which single New Deal law created both programs?
alt.a: The Social Security Act
alt.ex: The Social Security Act (1935) created both old-age insurance (monthly payments began in January 1940) and the federal-state unemployment insurance system.
w: The National Labor Relations Act
The Wagner Act (1935) protected union organizing and collective bargaining.
The Fair Labor Standards Act
The FLSA (1938) set minimum wages and maximum hours.
The Agricultural Adjustment Act
The AAA (1933) paid farmers to reduce crop production.

items.q: In 1936 workers at a steel plant want their employer to recognize their union and bargain with it. Which New Deal law guaranteed that right?
items.a: The National Labor Relations Act
items.ex: The Wagner Act (July 1935) guaranteed private-sector workers the right to organize and bargain collectively and created the NLRB; it replaced NIRA's Section 7(a) after Schechter Poultry (1935).
w: The Social Security Act
The Social Security Act created old-age and unemployment insurance.
The Fair Labor Standards Act
The FLSA (1938) set wages and hours and did not exist in 1936.
The National Industrial Recovery Act
NIRA's Section 7(a) had protected bargaining, but the Court struck NIRA down in 1935.

alt.q: Which New Deal law set the first federal minimum wage and banned most child labor?
alt.a: The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938
alt.ex: The FLSA (1938) set a 25-cent minimum wage, a maximum workweek with overtime pay, and limits on child labor.
w: The National Labor Relations Act of 1935
The Wagner Act protected unions and collective bargaining.
The Social Security Act of 1935
The Social Security Act created old-age and unemployment insurance.
The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933
The AAA paid farmers to cut production to raise crop prices.

alt.q: During the 1933 banking crisis, Americans feared losing their savings if their bank failed. Which New Deal measure addressed this fear most directly?
alt.a: Federal insurance of deposits via the FDIC
alt.ex: The Banking Act of 1933 (Glass-Steagall) created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure bank deposits.
w: Old-age pensions paid through Social Security
Social Security (1935) provided retirement income, not deposit protection.
Public works jobs created through the WPA
The Works Progress Administration (1935) created jobs.
Crop subsidies paid to farmers through the AAA
The Agricultural Adjustment Act supported farm prices.

items.q: Which statement best describes the New Deal's lasting effect on American government?
items.a: It made economic security a federal responsibility
items.ex: FDR's New Deal (1933-1939) created a federal safety net and regulation (Social Security, FDIC, labor law), changing expectations of what Washington should do in hard times.
w: It returned most economic regulation to state governments
The New Deal moved regulation toward the federal level, not away from it.
It stopped federal taxes from funding social programs
Social Security itself is funded by a federal payroll tax.
It limited presidents to two terms to curb executive power
The 22nd Amendment (1951) reacted to FDR's four elections; it was not a New Deal program.

alt.q: In Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935), the Supreme Court struck down a major New Deal law. Which one?
alt.a: The National Industrial Recovery Act
alt.ex: In Schechter (1935) the Court unanimously held that NIRA's industry codes exceeded the commerce power and improperly delegated legislative power.
w: The Agricultural Adjustment Act
The first AAA was struck down in a different case, United States v. Butler (1936).
The National Labor Relations (Wagner) Act
The Court upheld the Wagner Act in NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel (1937).
The Tennessee Valley Authority Act
The Court upheld TVA activities in Ashwander v. TVA (1936).

alt.q: Which group of laws best illustrates the New Deal's expansion of the federal role in the economy?
alt.a: Social Security, the Wagner Act and the FDIC
alt.ex: These 1933-1935 measures put Washington in charge of retirement insurance, labor relations and bank deposit insurance.
w: The Sherman Act, ICC and Pendleton Act
These are Gilded Age laws from 1883-1890.
Medicare, Medicaid and the Head Start program
These are 1960s Great Society programs under Lyndon Johnson.
The Clean Air Act, OSHA and the EPA
These are 1970s environmental and safety measures under Nixon.

items.q: Which statement best describes the difference between Medicare and Medicaid, both created in 1965?
items.a: Medicare covers older Americans; Medicaid covers low-income people
items.ex: The Social Security Amendments of 1965 (signed July 30, 1965) created Medicare, federal health insurance for people 65+, and Medicaid, a joint federal-state program for people with low incomes.
w: Medicare covers low-income people; Medicaid covers older Americans
This reverses the two programs.
Medicare covers veterans; Medicaid covers federal civil servants
Veterans' care is through the VA; federal workers have their own plans.
Medicare covers children; Medicaid covers only the disabled
Medicare is mainly for those 65+; Medicaid covers many low-income groups, including children.

alt.q: A 70-year-old retiree is hospitalized for surgery in 1967, and the federal government pays most of the hospital bill through a program funded by payroll taxes. Which program is this?
alt.a: Medicare
alt.ex: Medicare (1965) is federal health insurance for people 65 and older; its hospital coverage (Part A) is funded by payroll taxes.
w: Medicaid
Medicaid is for low-income people and is run jointly by states and the federal government.
Head Start
Head Start is a preschool program for low-income children.
Job Corps
Job Corps (1964) is a job-training program for young people; it does not pay hospital bills.

alt.q: A low-income family with two young children gets health coverage through a program their state runs and the federal government helps pay for. Which program is this?
alt.a: Medicaid
alt.ex: Medicaid (1965) is a joint federal-state program covering eligible low-income people; states administer it with federal matching funds.
w: Medicare
Medicare is a federal program mainly for people 65 and older.
Social Security
Social Security pays retirement, survivor and disability cash benefits.
Job Corps
Job Corps is a job-training program for young people.

items.q: Which statement best describes the primary goal of Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs?
items.a: To end poverty and racial injustice using federal power
items.ex: Johnson's Great Society (1964-1966) included the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, and civil rights laws.
w: To end the Depression through relief, recovery and reform
Relief, recovery and reform were FDR's New Deal goals in the 1930s.
To shrink federal spending and return programs to states
That describes Reagan-era 'New Federalism,' not the Great Society.
To break up monopolies and make food and drugs safer
Trust-busting and food safety laws belong to the Progressive Era.

alt.q: Which group of laws belongs to Lyndon Johnson's Great Society?
alt.a: Medicare, Head Start and school aid (ESEA)
alt.ex: Medicare (1965), Head Start (1965) and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965) were core Great Society programs.
w: Social Security, the Wagner Act and the FLSA
These are FDR's New Deal laws (1935-1938).
The Meat Inspection, Pure Food and Hepburn Acts
These are Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal laws (1906).
The PATRIOT Act, No Child Left Behind, Part D
These are George W. Bush-era laws (2001-2003).

alt.q: Lyndon Johnson declared an "unconditional war on poverty" in 1964. Which law launched programs such as the Job Corps and VISTA as part of that effort?
alt.a: The Economic Opportunity Act
alt.ex: The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 created the Office of Economic Opportunity, Job Corps, VISTA and Community Action programs.
w: The Social Security Act
The Social Security Act was a 1935 New Deal law.
The Fair Labor Standards Act
The FLSA (1938) set minimum wage and hours.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964
The Civil Rights Act banned discrimination; it did not create anti-poverty job programs.

items.q: Which set of provisions best describes the Affordable Care Act of 2010?
items.a: No denials for preexisting conditions; dependents covered to 26
items.ex: Signed by Barack Obama on March 23, 2010, the ACA barred denial for preexisting conditions, let young adults stay on parents' plans to 26, created marketplaces with subsidies, expanded Medicaid, and included an individual mandate.
w: Health insurance for everyone 65 and older, funded by payroll taxes
That describes Medicare (1965).
A single government-run insurer that replaces all private health plans
The ACA kept private insurance; a single-payer system was not enacted.
Prescription drug coverage added to Medicare for older Americans
That was Medicare Part D, created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003.

alt.q: In 2014 a 24-year-old graduate stays on a parent's health plan, and a neighbor with diabetes buys a policy on a state marketplace without being denied for that condition. Which law made both possible?
alt.a: The Affordable Care Act of 2010
alt.ex: The ACA (2010) extended dependent coverage to age 26 and barred insurers from denying coverage for preexisting conditions starting in 2014.
w: The Social Security Amendments of 1965
Those created Medicare and Medicaid.
The Medicare Modernization Act
That 2003 law created Medicare Part D drug coverage.
The Health Insurance Portability Act
HIPAA (1996) limited some preexisting-condition exclusions in group plans but did not create marketplaces or age-26 coverage.

alt.q: Which ACA feature was most controversial because it required most Americans to obtain health insurance or pay a penalty?
alt.a: The individual mandate
alt.ex: The individual mandate required most people to have coverage or pay a penalty; Congress reduced the penalty to $0 starting in 2019.
w: The employer mandate
The employer mandate applied to large employers, not individuals.
The public option
A government-run 'public option' was dropped from the final bill.
The Medicaid expansion
The expansion widened eligibility for low-income adults; it did not require anyone to buy insurance.

items.q: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), how did the Supreme Court rule on the Affordable Care Act?
items.a: It upheld the mandate as a tax but made Medicaid expansion optional
items.ex: Chief Justice Roberts found the mandate exceeded the Commerce Clause but was valid under the taxing power; threatening states' existing Medicaid funds was unconstitutionally coercive, so expansion became optional.
w: It upheld the mandate under the Commerce Clause and full expansion
The Court rejected the Commerce Clause basis and limited the Medicaid expansion.
It struck down the mandate but kept the rest of the law in force
The mandate was upheld as a tax.
It struck down the entire law as beyond Congress's enumerated powers
Most of the law survived; only the Medicaid penalty was limited.

alt.q: After 2012 some states decline to expand Medicaid under the ACA, and the federal government cannot take away their existing Medicaid funds. Which ruling and principle explain this?
alt.a: NFIB v. Sebelius; Congress can't coerce states with funds
alt.ex: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), the Court held that threatening all of a state's Medicaid money to force expansion was unconstitutionally coercive.
w: U.S. v. Lopez; Congress may not ban guns near local schools
Lopez (1995) limited the Commerce Clause; it did not involve Medicaid.
McCulloch v. Maryland; states may not tax federal banks
McCulloch (1819) concerned implied powers and state taxation of the national bank.
King v. Burwell; ACA tax credits apply in every state
King (2015) upheld subsidies on federal exchanges, not Medicaid funding.

alt.q: Under which power did the Supreme Court uphold the ACA's individual mandate in 2012?
alt.a: The power to lay and collect taxes
alt.ex: Roberts's majority treated the mandate's penalty as a tax within Congress's Article I taxing power.
w: The power to regulate interstate commerce
The Court said the Commerce Clause cannot compel people to buy a product.
The Necessary and Proper Clause alone
The Court held the Necessary and Proper Clause could not support the mandate by itself.
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme; it is not a source of power to create a mandate.

items.q: How was the Environmental Protection Agency created in 1970?
items.a: By a presidential reorganization plan Congress let stand
items.ex: President Nixon sent Reorganization Plan No. 3 to Congress on July 9, 1970. Congress did not block it, and the EPA began on December 2, 1970, combining pollution programs from several departments.
w: By a constitutional amendment ratified by the states
No amendment was involved; agencies are created by law or reorganization plans.
By a Supreme Court order enforcing the Clean Air Act
Courts do not create executive agencies.
By a section of the 1969 National Environmental Policy Act
NEPA created the Council on Environmental Quality, not the EPA.

alt.q: What did President Nixon's Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1970 accomplish?
alt.a: It merged pollution programs into the new EPA
alt.ex: Reorganization Plan No. 3 consolidated federal air, water, pesticide and other pollution programs into a new independent Environmental Protection Agency, which opened in December 1970.
w: It created a new cabinet Department of Energy
The Department of Energy was created by law in 1977.
It placed OSHA inside the Department of Labor
OSHA was created by the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, not this plan.
It moved the national parks into a new department
The National Park Service has been in the Interior Department since 1916.

alt.q: Which agency resulted?
alt.a: The Environmental Protection Agency
alt.ex: Nixon's Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1970 merged scattered pollution programs into the Environmental Protection Agency, which began work on December 2, 1970.
w: The Council on Environmental Quality
The CEQ is a White House advisory body created by NEPA, not by merging programs.
The Department of the Interior
The Interior Department was created in 1849.
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
OSHA deals with workplace safety and was created by a 1970 law.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1970 federal pollution programs are scattered: air pollution is handled in one department, water pollution in another and pesticide rules in a third. The President sends Congress a plan to merge them into one independent agency, and Congress does not block it.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Clean Water Act of 1972?
items.a: It required permits to discharge pollutants into U.S. waters
items.ex: The Clean Water Act created a permit system for anyone discharging pollutants into covered waters and set national wastewater treatment standards, with the goal of restoring the nation's waters.
w: It set national limits on smog from cars and factories
That describes the Clean Air Act of 1970.
It required studies of environmental effects of federal projects
That describes the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.
It protected endangered fish and their river habitats
That describes the Endangered Species Act of 1973.

alt.q: Which law contains this statement of purpose?
alt.a: Clean Water Act
alt.ex: The Clean Water Act of 1972 opens by stating that its objective is to restore and maintain the integrity of the nation's waters.
w: Clean Air Act
The Clean Air Act concerns air quality, not the nation's waters.
Endangered Species Act
The Endangered Species Act protects listed plants and animals.
Safe Drinking Water Act
The Safe Drinking Water Act (1974) sets standards for public drinking water systems; this text is from the Clean Water Act.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1972 federal law, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The objective of this chapter is to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation's waters.”
Source: United States Code, Title 33, Section 1251

alt.q: Which law imposed these requirements?
alt.a: The Clean Water Act
alt.ex: The Clean Water Act of 1972 required permits for discharging pollutants into waterways and set minimum wastewater treatment standards for communities.
w: The Clean Air Act
The Clean Air Act regulates air pollution, not discharges into rivers.
The National Environmental Policy Act
NEPA requires federal agencies to study environmental effects; it does not issue discharge permits.
The Endangered Species Act
The Endangered Species Act protects listed species, not general water quality.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1969 Ohio's polluted Cuyahoga River catches fire. A few years later, a new federal law requires a city on the river to treat its sewage and requires a paper mill to obtain a permit before releasing wastewater into the river.

items.q: Which statement about how the Clean Water Act of 1972 became law is accurate?
items.a: Congress passed it over President Nixon's veto
items.ex: Nixon vetoed the bill on October 17, 1972, calling its $24 billion cost too high. The Senate voted 52–12 to override that same day and the House voted 247–23 the next day, and the act became law.
w: President Nixon signed it on the first Earth Day
The first Earth Day was April 22, 1970; Nixon vetoed this bill in 1972.
The Supreme Court ordered Congress to pass it
Courts cannot order Congress to pass laws.
The states ratified it as a constitutional amendment
It is an ordinary statute, not an amendment.

alt.q: President Nixon vetoed the Clean Water Act in 1972, calling it too costly, but it became law anyway. Which action made this possible?
alt.a: A two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress
alt.ex: Under Article I, Section 7, Congress can override a veto by a two-thirds vote in each house; in October 1972 the Senate voted 52–12 and the House 247–23.
w: A majority vote of the Senate alone
An override requires two-thirds of both houses, not just the Senate.
Ratification by three-fourths of the state legislatures
