Federalized Guard units helped protect the students at the school.

items.q: Which statement best describes an executive order?
items.a: A President's written directive to federal agencies
items.ex: An executive order is a written directive by which a President manages the executive branch and shapes policy. It has the force of law only if based on the Constitution or a law passed by Congress.
w: A law passed by Congress at the President's request
Executive orders are issued by the President alone; laws require Congress.
A ruling by the Supreme Court on presidential power
Court rulings are opinions, not executive orders.
A constitutional amendment proposed by the President
Presidents have no formal role in proposing amendments.

alt.q: Which statement about executive orders is accurate?
alt.a: They have the force of law if based on valid authority
alt.ex: An executive order resting on the Constitution or on power Congress delegated has the force of law, but courts can strike down orders that lack such authority, as in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952).
w: They must be approved by the Senate within 60 days
Executive orders need no Senate approval.
They cannot be changed by any later President
Later Presidents can revoke or change them.
They are listed by name in Article II of the Constitution
The Constitution never mentions executive orders.

alt.q: Which presidential tool is being used?
alt.a: An executive order
alt.ex: Directing how federal agencies operate through a signed, published written directive is a classic use of an executive order.
w: A pocket veto
A pocket veto kills a bill; it does not direct agencies.
An executive agreement
Executive agreements are made with foreign governments.
A joint resolution
A joint resolution is passed by Congress, not issued by the President.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A President wants federal agencies to buy only energy-efficient vehicles. Instead of waiting for Congress to pass a bill, the President signs a written directive telling agencies how to manage their purchasing. The directive is published in the Federal Register and takes effect.

items.q: In January 2025, President Trump revoked Executive Order 11246, which had required affirmative action by federal contractors since 1965. What does this show about executive orders?
items.a: A later President can cancel them without Congress
items.ex: Trump's Executive Order 14173 of January 21, 2025 revoked Lyndon Johnson's EO 11246. Orders that Congress has not written into law can be revoked or changed by a later President.
w: They expire automatically sixty years after being issued
Executive orders have no automatic expiration date.
They can be revoked only by the Supreme Court
Presidents can revoke them; courts can strike down invalid ones.
They need Senate approval to be changed
No Senate approval is needed to issue or revoke an order.

alt.q: Which statement best explains why the new President could do this?
alt.a: Orders not written into statute can be revoked by a successor
alt.ex: Because an executive order is a presidential directive rather than a law passed by Congress, a later President can generally revoke or modify it by issuing a new order.
w: Orders expire automatically when the signing President leaves
Orders stay in effect after a President leaves unless revoked.
Every order needs approval by Congress each term
Congress does not reapprove executive orders.
The Supreme Court must first declare the order void
No court ruling is needed for a President to revoke an order.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: A President issues an executive order setting new hiring rules for companies with federal contracts. Four years later, a new President from the other party takes office and, on the second day, signs an order canceling the earlier one.

alt.q: Which executive order, issued by Lyndon Johnson in 1965, was revoked by President Trump on January 21, 2025?
alt.a: Executive Order 11246
alt.ex: EO 11246 (1965) required federal contractors to take affirmative action and not discriminate; Trump's EO 14173 revoked it on January 21, 2025.
w: Executive Order 9981
EO 9981 (1948) was Truman's order to desegregate the armed forces.
Executive Order 9066
EO 9066 (1942) authorized Japanese American internment; President Ford formally ended it in 1976.
Executive Order 10730
EO 10730 (1957) was Eisenhower's order sending troops to Little Rock.

items.q: Which part of the Constitution provides the main basis for a President's executive orders?
items.a: Article II, which grants the executive power
items.ex: The Constitution never mentions executive orders. They rest on Article II, which vests the executive power in the President, requires him to take care that the laws are faithfully executed and makes him commander in chief, or on powers Congress grants by law.
w: Article I, which lists Congress's powers
Article I gives lawmaking power to Congress, not the President.
Article III, which creates the federal courts
Article III deals with the judicial branch.
Article V, which sets the amendment process
Article V concerns amending the Constitution.

alt.q: Based on the passage, when may a court strike down an executive order?
alt.a: When neither a law nor the Constitution supports it
alt.ex: In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952), the Court struck down Truman's order seizing the steel mills because neither an act of Congress nor the Constitution authorized it.
w: When most voters say they oppose the order in polls
Public opinion is not a legal test for an order's validity.
When the President issued it during a foreign war
Wartime orders can be valid; the test is legal authority.
When the order was not first approved by the Senate
Executive orders do not need Senate approval.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1952 Supreme Court opinion, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The President's power, if any, to issue the order must stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself.”
Source: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952)

alt.q: Which of the following is a valid source of authority for an executive order?
alt.a: A power Congress gave the President by law
alt.ex: An executive order must rest on the Constitution or on authority Congress delegated by statute, such as the Defense Production Act.
w: A resolution passed by a state legislature
States cannot give the President power.
A request from a federal agency head
Agency requests do not create presidential authority.
A majority vote of the President's cabinet
The cabinet advises the President but cannot grant legal authority.

items.q: Which pressure helped lead President Truman to issue Executive Order 9981 in 1948?
items.a: A. Philip Randolph's threat of draft resistance by Black men
items.ex: A. Philip Randolph and Grant Reynolds led a campaign against military segregation and threatened a nationwide draft-resistance campaign. After Congress rejected his civil rights proposals, Truman signed EO 9981 on July 26, 1948.
w: A Supreme Court ruling that military segregation was illegal
No such ruling existed; Truman acted by executive order.
A new law from Congress ordering the military to integrate
Congress did not pass such a law, which is why Truman used an executive order.
A demand by Southern governors to end segregated units
Southern leaders generally opposed integrating the military.

alt.q: Which action did the President take?
alt.a: Ordered equal treatment in the armed forces
alt.ex: Truman's Executive Order 9981 (July 26, 1948) declared a policy of equal treatment and opportunity in the armed services and set up a committee (the Fahy Committee) to carry it out.
w: Signed the Civil Rights Act banning segregation
The Civil Rights Act was signed by Johnson in 1964.
Sent troops to integrate a high school
Eisenhower sent troops to Little Rock in 1957.
Ended the peacetime draft by executive order
The draft continued; Truman did not end it.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1948 Congress debates a new peacetime draft. A civil rights and labor leader warns that he will urge young Black men to resist the draft unless segregation in the armed forces ends. Congress has refused the President's civil rights proposals. In July, the President acts on his own.

alt.q: Which civil rights leader's 1948 campaign against a segregated military helped push President Truman toward Executive Order 9981?
alt.a: A. Philip Randolph
alt.ex: Labor leader A. Philip Randolph co-led the Committee Against Jim Crow in Military Service and Training, which pressed Truman with rallies, letters and a threatened draft-resistance campaign.
w: Martin Luther King Jr.
King was a college student in 1948; his national leadership began in 1955.
Booker T. Washington
Washington died in 1915.
Malcolm X
Malcolm X did not become a public figure until the 1950s.

items.q: Which civil rights advance was achieved through an executive order rather than an act of Congress?
items.a: Ending segregation in the armed forces
items.ex: Truman desegregated the military with Executive Order 9981 in 1948; the other changes came through acts of Congress.
w: Banning segregation in hotels and restaurants
This came from the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Banning literacy tests for voting
This came from the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Banning housing discrimination nationwide
This came from the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

alt.q: Which of the following was created by executive order?
alt.a: Affirmative action for contractors
alt.ex: Federal contractor affirmative action began with Kennedy's EO 10925 (1961) and was expanded by Johnson's EO 11246 (1965), which was revoked in January 2025.
w: The Medicare program
Medicare was created by the Social Security Amendments of 1965.
Social Security retirement benefits
These were created by the Social Security Act of 1935.
The federal minimum wage
This was created by the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938.

alt.q: Why could a President desegregate the military by executive order but not ban segregation in private restaurants the same way?
alt.a: He directs the armed forces but cannot legislate for businesses
alt.ex: As commander in chief, the President controls military policy, but banning discrimination by private businesses required a law from Congress, the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
w: Restaurants were run by state governments at the time
Most restaurants were private businesses, not state-run.
The Supreme Court had forbidden Congress to regulate restaurants
No such ruling existed, and Congress banned such segregation in 1964.
The military is not covered by the Constitution
The military is subject to the Constitution and civilian control.

items.q: "It is hereby declared to be the policy of the President that there shall be equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services without regard to race, color, religion or national origin." Which action does this begin?
items.a: Truman's 1948 order to desegregate the military
items.ex: Executive Order 9981 (July 26, 1948) created the Fahy Committee to carry out the policy; the last all-Black Army units were abolished by 1954.
w: Roosevelt's 1941 order banning bias in defense plants
That was EO 8802, which covered defense industries, not the armed services.
Eisenhower's 1957 order sending troops to Little Rock
That was EO 10730.
Kennedy's 1961 order on affirmative action in hiring
That was EO 10925, which covered federal contractors.

alt.q: Why did Truman desegregate the military by executive order rather than through legislation?
alt.a: Southern senators could block civil rights bills
alt.ex: Southern Democrats could filibuster civil rights bills, so Truman used his authority as Commander in Chief to act alone.
w: The Supreme Court ordered him to act alone
No court ordered military desegregation.
The Constitution bars Congress from military rules
Article I gives Congress power to make rules for the armed forces.
Military rules can only be changed by treaty
Treaties govern relations with other nations.

alt.q: A Black soldier who enlisted in 1951 serves in an integrated unit in Korea, though their father served in an all-Black unit in World War II. Which executive action best explains the difference?
alt.a: Executive Order 9981
alt.ex: Truman's EO 9981 (1948) began military desegregation, which accelerated during the Korean War.
w: Executive Order 9066
EO 9066 (1942) led to the incarceration of Japanese Americans.
Executive Order 8802
EO 8802 (1941) covered defense industries, not the armed forces.
Executive Order 11246
EO 11246 (1965) covered federal contractors.

items.q: Which statement best describes Executive Order 10925, issued by John F. Kennedy in 1961?
items.a: It required federal contractors to take affirmative action
items.ex: EO 10925 (March 6, 1961) was the first to use the phrase 'affirmative action,' requiring government contractors to hire and treat workers without regard to race, creed, color or national origin; it created the President's Committee on Equal Employment Opportunity.
w: It ordered the armed services to end racial segregation in units
That was Truman's EO 9981 (1948).
It banned discrimination by hotels, restaurants and theaters
That was Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
It required racial quotas in admissions at public universities
It concerned contractor employment; quotas in admissions were struck down in Bakke (1978).

alt.q: A 1961 executive order required that "the contractor will take affirmative action to ensure that applicants are employed, and that employees are treated during employment, without regard to their race, creed, color, or national origin." Which President issued it?
alt.a: John F. Kennedy
alt.ex: This is from Kennedy's Executive Order 10925 (March 6, 1961), the first use of 'affirmative action' in this sense.
w: Lyndon B. Johnson
Johnson issued EO 11246 in 1965; as Vice President he chaired Kennedy's committee.
Dwight D. Eisenhower
Eisenhower left office in January 1961.
Harry S. Truman
Truman issued EO 9981 in 1948 on the military.

alt.q: Which group was most directly required to act under Kennedy's Executive Order 10925?
alt.a: Firms holding federal contracts
alt.ex: EO 10925 applied to businesses doing work under government contracts, using federal purchasing power to fight discrimination.
w: All private firms with 15 workers
That is Title VII's coverage (15+ employees since a 1972 amendment; 25 in the original 1964 act).
Public schools getting federal aid
That is Title VI's coverage under the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
State officials running elections
That is the Voting Rights Act's focus.

items.q: How did Lyndon Johnson's Executive Order 11246 (1965) build on earlier affirmative action orders?
items.a: It gave the Labor Department power to enforce contractor rules
items.ex: EO 11246 (September 24, 1965) required federal contractors to take affirmative action and made the Secretary of Labor responsible for enforcement (later the OFCCP); EO 11375 (1967) added sex. It was revoked in January 2025 by EO 14173.
w: It extended affirmative action to all private employers nationwide
It covered only federal contractors and subcontractors.
It ended affirmative action requirements for federal contractors
It strengthened them; revocation came only in 2025.
It applied affirmative action to voter registration in the South
Voting was handled by the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

alt.q: Which category did Johnson add to federal contractor nondiscrimination rules in 1967 by amending his 1965 order?
alt.a: Sex
alt.ex: Executive Order 11375 (1967) amended EO 11246 to bar sex discrimination by federal contractors.
w: Age
Age discrimination was addressed by the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967, a statute.
Disability
Contractor disability rules came from the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.
Veteran status
Protections for veterans at federal contractors came from the Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974.

alt.q: A construction firm with a large federal highway contract in 1970 is told it must set goals for hiring minority workers or risk losing the contract. Which executive action is being enforced?
alt.a: Executive Order 11246
alt.ex: The Labor Department enforced EO 11246 through plans such as Nixon's 1969 Philadelphia Plan, which set minority hiring goals for federal construction contractors.
w: Executive Order 9981
EO 9981 desegregated the military.
Executive Order 9066
EO 9066 led to Japanese American incarceration.
Executive Order 10730
EO 10730 sent troops to Little Rock.

items.q: Based on the passage, which policy would the speaker support?
items.a: Setting aside public lands as national forests
items.ex: Theodore Roosevelt argued resources should be handed to the next generation in better condition, and he protected about 230 million acres of public land, including national forests and monuments.
w: Selling federal forests to private timber firms
Selling forests for logging conflicts with protecting resources for future generations.
Opening national parks to mining and drilling
This would use up resources rather than conserve them.
Giving all federal lands to the western states
Roosevelt expanded federal protection of land rather than giving it away.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1910 speech by Theodore Roosevelt, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“The nation behaves well if it treats the natural resources as assets which it must turn over to the next generation . . .”
Source: Address to the Colorado Live Stock Association, Denver, August 29, 1910

alt.q: Theodore Roosevelt used the bully pulpit and his executive power to protect about 230 million acres of public land. Which cause did he champion?
alt.a: Conservation
alt.ex: Conservation, the careful protection and wise use of natural resources, was one of the “three Cs” of Roosevelt's Square Deal.
w: Prohibition
Prohibition of alcohol was a separate reform adopted in 1919.
Isolationism
Isolationism is a foreign policy of avoiding foreign entanglements.
Laissez-faire
Laissez-faire means limited government action, the opposite of federal land protection.

alt.q: Which action by Theodore Roosevelt best reflects his promotion of conservation?
alt.a: Using the Antiquities Act to create national monuments
alt.ex: Roosevelt used the 1906 Antiquities Act to proclaim 18 national monuments, starting with Devils Tower, as part of protecting about 230 million acres.
w: Pressuring coal owners to settle a miners' strike
The 1902 coal strike settlement concerned labor, not conservation.
Breaking up the Northern Securities railroad trust
That was trust-busting under the Sherman Act.
Sending the Great White Fleet on a voyage around the world
That was a display of naval power in foreign policy.

items.q: After Upton Sinclair's 1906 novel The Jungle exposed filthy conditions in meatpacking plants, President Theodore Roosevelt used public outrage to push which law through Congress?
items.a: The Meat Inspection Act
items.ex: Roosevelt used the novel and his own investigators' report on the stockyards to press Congress, which passed the Meat Inspection Act on June 30, 1906, along with the Pure Food and Drug Act.
w: The Sherman Anti-Trust Act
The Sherman Act was passed in 1890 and targets monopolies.
The Interstate Commerce Act
The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) regulated railroads.
The Pendleton Act
The Pendleton Act (1883) reformed the federal civil service.

alt.q: Which presidential tool does this best illustrate?
alt.a: Using the bully pulpit to win support for reform
alt.ex: Theodore Roosevelt used publicity about the Neill-Reynolds report on the stockyards to build public pressure, and Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act in 1906.
w: Using the pocket veto to block a bill
A pocket veto kills a bill; here the President pushed for one.
Using the pardon power to end a dispute
Pardons apply to federal crimes, not reform campaigns.
Using executive privilege to withhold government records
The President released findings rather than withholding them.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1906 a President sends investigators into Chicago's stockyards after a popular novel describes filthy meatpacking plants. He releases part of their shocking report to build pressure on Congress. Within weeks he signs a law requiring federal inspection of meat sold across state lines.

alt.q: Which consumer protection laws of 1906 did Theodore Roosevelt promote as part of his Square Deal?
alt.a: Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act
alt.ex: Consumer protection was one of the Square Deal's “three Cs”; both laws were passed in June 1906 after public outrage over food safety.
w: Interstate Commerce Act and Sherman Anti-Trust Act
These were passed in 1887 and 1890, before Roosevelt's presidency.
Social Security Act and National Labor Relations Act
These were New Deal laws of 1935.
Federal Reserve Act and Clayton Antitrust Act
These were passed under Woodrow Wilson in 1913 and 1914.

items.q: Based on the passage, which policy was the speaker building support for?
items.a: Lend-Lease Act
items.ex: In his December 29, 1940 radio address, Franklin Roosevelt urged Americans to supply nations fighting the Axis; Congress passed the Lend-Lease Act on March 11, 1941.
w: Neutrality Acts
The Neutrality Acts of the 1930s tried to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars, the opposite of the speech's aim.
Marshall Plan
The Marshall Plan (1948) rebuilt Europe after World War II.
Social Security Act
The Social Security Act (1935) was a New Deal domestic program.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a December 1940 radio address by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“We must be the great arsenal of democracy. For us this is an emergency as serious as war itself.”
Source: Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum

alt.q: In a December 1940 fireside chat, Franklin Roosevelt urged Americans to make the United States “the great arsenal of democracy.” How did this speech use the bully pulpit?
alt.a: It rallied support for arming Britain against the Axis
alt.ex: Speaking directly to the public by radio, Roosevelt argued that supplying Britain was safer than isolation, building support for the Lend-Lease Act of March 1941.
w: It asked Congress to declare war on Germany right away
Roosevelt said it was not a talk on war; the U.S. entered the war after Pearl Harbor.
It announced the end of the New Deal's work programs
The speech was about national security, not ending domestic programs.
It urged Americans to avoid all ties to Europe's war
Roosevelt argued for helping Britain, rejecting full isolation.

alt.q: Which law resulted?
alt.a: The Lend-Lease Act
alt.ex: After Roosevelt's “arsenal of democracy” radio address, Congress passed the Lend-Lease Act on March 11, 1941, letting the U.S. supply weapons to Britain and other Allies.
w: The Neutrality Act
The Neutrality Acts restricted aid to warring nations and came before this speech.
The Selective Service Act
The peacetime draft law was passed in September 1940, before the speech.
The National Security Act
The National Security Act (1947) reorganized the military after the war.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In late 1940 Britain is fighting Nazi Germany and running out of money to buy weapons. Many Americans want to stay out of the war entirely. The President goes on national radio to argue that supplying Britain is the best way to keep war away from America. In March 1941 Congress passes his aid plan.

items.q: Based on the passage, which program was the speaker promoting?
items.a: The Apollo space program
items.ex: In his September 12, 1962 speech at Rice University, Kennedy rallied public support for the costly effort to land astronauts on the Moon, which became the Apollo program.
w: The Peace Corps
The Peace Corps sent volunteers abroad; it was not about the Moon.
The interstate highway system
The interstate highways were begun under Eisenhower in 1956.
The Strategic Defense Initiative
The Strategic Defense Initiative was Reagan's 1980s missile defense plan.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from a 1962 speech by President John F. Kennedy at Rice University, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.”
Source: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum

alt.q: How did President Kennedy's 1962 “We choose to go to the Moon” speech at Rice University use the bully pulpit?
alt.a: It built public support for a costly space program
alt.ex: Kennedy used a nationally covered speech to persuade Americans that the expense of reaching the Moon was worth it, strengthening support for funding the space effort.
w: It asked Congress to declare war on the Soviet Union
The Cold War space race involved no declaration of war.
It announced the end of the space race with the Soviets
The speech pushed to win the race, not end it.
It urged states to fund their own rocket programs
The space program was a federal effort run by NASA.

alt.q: Which President used speeches to rally public support for landing astronauts on the Moon before the end of the 1960s?
alt.a: John F. Kennedy
alt.ex: Kennedy set the goal of a Moon landing within the decade and promoted it in speeches such as his 1962 address at Rice University.
w: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Eisenhower created NASA in 1958 but did not set a Moon-landing goal.
Harry S. Truman
Truman left office in 1953, before the space race.
Gerald Ford
Ford became President in 1974, after the Moon landings.

items.q: Based on the passage, which government program would the speaker support?
items.a: Reaganomics
items.ex: Reagan's statement reflects his program of tax cuts, reduced federal spending and deregulation, known as Reaganomics, which shrank government's role rather than expanding it.
w: Great Society
Johnson's Great Society expanded federal programs, the opposite of Reagan's view.
New Deal
Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal greatly expanded the federal government's role.
Fair Deal
Truman's Fair Deal sought to extend New Deal programs.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from President Ronald Reagan's 1981 inaugural address, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.”
Source: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum

alt.q: In his first inaugural address in 1981, Ronald Reagan said it was his intention “to curb the size and influence of the Federal establishment.” Which policies did he then use the bully pulpit to promote?
alt.a: Tax cuts and reduced federal regulation
alt.ex: Reagan used speeches and television addresses to win support for cutting income tax rates and reducing regulation, passing the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981.
w: New federal health insurance for all
Universal federal health insurance would expand government, against Reagan's goals.
Higher taxes to expand welfare programs
Reagan sought lower taxes and less federal spending.
Government ownership of major industries
Reagan favored private enterprise and less government control.

alt.q: Which presidential tool does this best illustrate?
alt.a: The bully pulpit
alt.ex: Reagan's July 1981 televised appeal urged Americans to contact Congress, and the House approved his tax plan days later, a clear use of the bully pulpit.
w: The line-item veto
A line-item veto strikes parts of spending bills; the Court struck down the 1996 version in 1998.
Executive privilege
Executive privilege is withholding information, not rallying the public.
The pocket veto
A pocket veto kills a bill; here the President pushed for one to pass.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1981 a newly elected President goes on national television and urges viewers to call and write their members of Congress in support of his plan to cut income tax rates. Within days, the House approves the plan.

items.q: Which statement best describes the "bully pulpit," a phrase coined by Theodore Roosevelt?
items.a: The President's use of the office to rally public opinion
items.ex: TR called the White House a 'bully pulpit' ('bully' meaning excellent) and used speeches and publicity to build support for his Square Deal.
w: The President's power to veto bills that Congress has passed
The veto is a formal Article I, Section 7 power, not persuasion.
The President's power to remove cabinet officers at will
Removal power is a formal executive power.
The President's duty to report on the state of the Union
Article II, Section 3 requires the report; the bully pulpit is the broader use of the office to persuade.

alt.q: In 1902 Theodore Roosevelt publicly pressured coal mine owners and striking miners into arbitration, winning public support. Which presidential tool does this best illustrate?
alt.a: The bully pulpit
alt.ex: With no law requiring arbitration, Roosevelt used public pressure and the prestige of his office to settle the anthracite coal strike.
w: The pocket veto
A pocket veto lets a bill die after Congress adjourns.
Executive privilege
Executive privilege shields internal communications from disclosure.
The pardon power
The pardon power forgives federal crimes.

alt.q: Theodore Roosevelt promoted conservation, consumer protection and control of corporations. What was this domestic program called?
alt.a: The Square Deal
alt.ex: TR's Square Deal centered on the 'three Cs': conservation, control of corporations and consumer protection.
w: The New Deal
The New Deal was Franklin Roosevelt's 1930s program.
The Fair Deal
The Fair Deal was Truman's postwar program.
The New Freedom
The New Freedom was Woodrow Wilson's 1912 program.

items.q: In a 1933 radio talk, a President told listeners: "I can assure you that it is safer to keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress." What was the main purpose of such talks?
items.a: To explain policy directly to the public and build trust
items.ex: FDR's first fireside chat (March 12, 1933) explained the bank holiday; he gave about 30 such radio talks through 1944.
w: To announce declarations of war after Congress voted
Declarations are made by Congress; the chats were about explaining policy.
To deliver the annual State of the Union message to Congress
The State of the Union is a formal report to Congress.
To campaign for reelection against a rival candidate
The chats were policy talks, not campaign speeches.

alt.q: What were Franklin Roosevelt's informal radio talks to the nation called?
alt.a: Fireside chats
alt.ex: FDR's fireside chats (1933-1944) used radio to speak directly to Americans in their homes.
w: Front-porch speeches
McKinley ran a 'front-porch campaign' in 1896.
Kitchen debates
The 'Kitchen Debate' was Nixon versus Khrushchev in 1959.
Hundred Days talks
The Hundred Days was FDR's first burst of legislation in 1933.

alt.q: In March 1933, after a nationwide bank holiday, a family listens as the President calmly explains on the radio how banks will reopen; within weeks deposits exceed withdrawals. Which practice does this illustrate?
alt.a: FDR's use of fireside chats
alt.ex: FDR's first fireside chat (March 12, 1933) helped restore confidence; when banks reopened, deposits outpaced withdrawals.
w: TR's use of antitrust lawsuits
TR's trust-busting was in the 1900s and used courts, not radio.
Hoover's voluntary business pledges
Hoover relied on voluntary cooperation from business, 1929-1933.
LBJ's televised addresses to Congress
LBJ's addresses came in the 1960s, on television.

items.q: In a 1964 commencement speech, a President said, "The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all." How did this speech use the bully pulpit?
items.a: It rallied public support for a broad antipoverty agenda
items.ex: Lyndon Johnson's May 22, 1964 University of Michigan speech named the Great Society; he later used a March 15, 1965 address to Congress to push the Voting Rights Act.
w: It announced a declaration of war against North Vietnam
Congress never declared war on North Vietnam.
It explained a veto of a civil rights bill from Congress
Johnson signed civil rights bills; he did not veto them.
It ordered troops to desegregate a Southern university
Kennedy sent troops to Ole Miss (1962); this speech gave no orders.

alt.q: Which President called his domestic program the "Great Society" and used speeches to the public and Congress to push Medicare and voting rights?
alt.a: Lyndon B. Johnson
alt.ex: LBJ named the Great Society in 1964 and used televised addresses to win passage of laws such as Medicare and the Voting Rights Act (1965).
w: John F. Kennedy
Kennedy's program was called the New Frontier.
Franklin D. Roosevelt
FDR's program was the New Deal.
Harry S. Truman
Truman's program was the Fair Deal.

alt.q: Days after the violence at Selma in 1965, Lyndon Johnson told Congress on national television, "Their cause must be our cause too." Which law was he urging Congress to pass?
alt.a: The Voting Rights Act
alt.ex: In his March 15, 1965 'We Shall Overcome' address, Johnson called for a voting rights bill; it became law on August 6, 1965.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
The 1964 act had already passed the year before.
The Fair Housing Act
Fair housing was enacted in 1968.
The Economic Opportunity Act
The antipoverty law passed in 1964.

items.q: Which war power does the Constitution give to Congress rather than to the President?
items.a: Raising and funding the armed forces
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress power to declare war, raise and support armies, and provide and maintain a navy, while Article II makes the President commander in chief.
w: Commanding troops in the field
The President, as commander in chief, directs military operations.
Appointing generals without Senate consent
No one may do this; the President nominates officers with Senate consent.
Negotiating peace treaties with enemies
The President negotiates treaties; the Senate approves them.

alt.q: Based on the passage, how can Congress check a President's conduct of a war?
alt.a: By refusing to renew funding for the military
alt.ex: Because Article I, Section 8 limits army appropriations to two years, Congress controls the money for the military and can cut off funds for a war it opposes.
w: By ordering the Supreme Court to end the war
Congress cannot order the Court to act.
By appointing its own commander for the army
The Constitution makes the President commander in chief.
By voting to extend the President's term two years
The passage limits funding, and Congress cannot extend a President's term.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from Article I, Section 8 of the U.S. Constitution, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“To raise and support Armies, but no Appropriation of Money to that Use shall be for a longer Term than two Years;”
Source: National Archives and Records Administration

alt.q: Which congressional power does this illustrate?
alt.a: The power of the purse
alt.ex: In 1973 Congress used appropriations laws to bar funds for combat in Indochina after August 15, 1973, showing how control of spending can end military action.
w: The power to impeach
No impeachment took place.
The power to ratify treaties
Treaty approval belongs to the Senate and was not involved.
The power to override vetoes
The measure became law through appropriations bills the President signed.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In June 1973, with U.S. ground troops already out of Vietnam, Congress passes spending bills that bar the use of any funds for combat in Indochina after August 15, 1973. The President signs them, and U.S. bombing in Cambodia stops on that date.

items.q: Which principle about presidential war powers did the Court accept?
items.a: A President may resist an attack before Congress acts
items.ex: In the Prize Cases (1863), the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that while only Congress can declare war, the President must meet an insurrection or attack with force without waiting for Congress.
w: A President may declare war when Congress is not in session
The Court said only Congress can declare war.
Only Congress may order any use of military force at all
The Court upheld the President's use of force before Congress acted.
The Supreme Court must approve blockades in advance
Courts do not approve military actions in advance.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In April 1861, after Confederate forces fire on Fort Sumter, President Lincoln orders a naval blockade of Southern ports while Congress is out of session. Navy ships seize merchant vessels before Congress recognizes a state of war in July. In 1863 the Supreme Court upholds the seizures by a 5–4 vote.

alt.q: In the Prize Cases (1863), the Supreme Court upheld President Lincoln's blockade of Southern ports, ordered before Congress acted. What did the ruling suggest about presidential power?
alt.a: The President may meet an insurrection with force
alt.ex: The Court held that only Congress can declare war, but the President has a duty to resist an insurrection or invasion with force without waiting for Congress.
w: The President may declare war on foreign nations
The Court said declaring war belongs to Congress.
Congress may not fund a war it did not declare
The case did not limit Congress's spending power.
States may block federal warships from entering their ports
The case upheld federal power against the rebelling states.

alt.q: Which Supreme Court decision upheld President Lincoln's 1861 blockade of Confederate ports, ordered before Congress recognized a state of war?
alt.a: The Prize Cases
alt.ex: The Prize Cases (1863) upheld Lincoln's blockade 5–4, recognizing the President's power to respond to an insurrection.
w: Ex parte Milligan
Ex parte Milligan (1866) limited military trials of civilians.
Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
Youngstown (1952) struck down Truman's seizure of the steel mills.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu (1944) upheld Japanese American internment.

items.q: What does this episode best show about presidential war powers?
items.a: A President's troop moves can lead Congress into war
items.ex: Polk sent troops under Zachary Taylor to the Rio Grande in 1846. After a clash, he told Congress Mexico had shed American blood, and Congress declared war on May 13, 1846, showing how a commander in chief can create conditions for war.
w: Congress can declare war only after a court approves
Courts play no role in declaring war.
The President needs Senate consent to move troops
As commander in chief, the President can move troops without Senate consent.
A President may declare war if troops are attacked
Polk asked Congress, which declared war; Presidents cannot.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: In 1846 President Polk orders U.S. troops into land claimed by both Texas and Mexico, between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande. After a clash in which American soldiers are killed, he tells Congress that Mexico has shed American blood on American soil. Congress declares war within days.

alt.q: Congressman Abraham Lincoln's 1847 “spot resolutions” asked President Polk to identify the exact spot where American blood was first shed in the war with Mexico. What did Lincoln suspect?
alt.a: Polk provoked the war on land that was disputed
alt.ex: Lincoln questioned whether the clash happened on U.S. soil at all, suggesting Polk had used his command of the army to start a war in territory claimed by Mexico.
w: Polk had declared war without asking Congress
Congress declared the war in May 1846.
Mexico had attacked deep inside Louisiana
The clash took place near the Rio Grande, far from Louisiana.
Britain had secretly armed and trained the Mexican army
The resolutions asked about the location of the clash, not Britain.

alt.q: Which war did Congress formally declare in 1846 after President Polk sent troops into territory disputed with Mexico?
alt.a: The Mexican-American War
alt.ex: Congress declared war on Mexico on May 13, 1846, after Polk reported that Mexican troops had attacked U.S. soldiers near the Rio Grande.
w: The War of 1812
Congress declared that war against Britain in 1812.
The Spanish-American War
That war was declared in 1898.
The Texas Revolution
The Texas Revolution (1835–1836) was fought by Texans, not declared by Congress.

items.q: Before launching Operation Desert Storm against Iraq in January 1991, how did President George H. W. Bush handle Congress?
items.a: He sought and narrowly won a vote authorizing force
items.ex: Bush asked Congress for a joint resolution; on January 12, 1991 the Senate approved it 52–47 and the House 250–183. It authorized force but did not declare war.
w: He asked for and received a formal declaration of war
Congress authorized force but did not declare war.
He ignored Congress and relied on a UN vote alone
Bush asked Congress for authorization, which it granted.
He waited for Congress to pass a constitutional amendment
No amendment was involved.

alt.q: What does this episode best illustrate?
alt.a: Shared war powers between Congress and the President
alt.ex: The President deployed troops as commander in chief, but sought Congress's approval before attacking, as in the 1991 Persian Gulf War authorization.
w: A formal declaration of war under Article I
The joint resolution authorized force but did not declare war.
Judicial review of the President's military decisions
No court was involved.
State control over National Guard deployments
States did not decide on the deployment.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: Over five months, a President sends more than 500,000 troops to the Persian Gulf. Before ordering an attack, he asks Congress for a joint resolution authorizing force. The Senate approves it 52–47 and the House 250–183.

alt.q: Which statement about the 1991 Persian Gulf War is accurate?
alt.a: Congress authorized force but did not declare war
alt.ex: Congress passed a joint resolution authorizing force against Iraq on January 12, 1991. It was not a declaration of war; Congress has not declared war since World War II.
w: Congress formally declared war on Iraq by a narrow margin
The narrow votes were on an authorization, not a declaration of war.
Congress refused to vote on any use of force
Congress voted and approved force in January 1991.
The Supreme Court approved the use of force
The Court played no role in authorizing the war.

items.q: In April 1951 President Truman removed General Douglas MacArthur from command after the general publicly challenged Truman's Korean War policy. Which principle does this best illustrate?
items.a: Civilian control of the military
items.ex: As commander in chief, Truman relieved MacArthur on April 11, 1951, saying the general could not wholeheartedly support U.S. policy; military commanders answer to elected civilian leaders.
w: Judicial review
Judicial review is a court's power to strike down laws.
Federal supremacy over the states
National supremacy over state law has nothing to do with removing a general.
Separation of church and state
This principle concerns religion and government, not military command.

alt.q: Which constitutional role gave Truman the authority to take this action?
alt.a: Commander in chief of the armed forces
alt.ex: Article II makes the President commander in chief, which allowed Truman to relieve MacArthur in April 1951.
w: Head of the President's political party
Party leadership is not a constitutional power.
Chief diplomat who negotiates treaties
Treaty power does not include removing generals.
Chief legislator who proposes bills
Proposing laws has nothing to do with military command.

sc.title: Use the passage below, from President Truman's April 1951 statement relieving General Douglas MacArthur of his commands, to answer the question that follows.
sc.text:
“With deep regret I have concluded that General of the Army Douglas MacArthur is unable to give his wholehearted support to the policies of the United States Government . . .”
Source: Harry S. Truman Presidential Library and Museum

alt.q: Which constitutional principle supports the President's action?
alt.a: Civilian control of the military
alt.ex: Under the Constitution an elected civilian President, not a general, sets military policy, which is why Truman could remove MacArthur in 1951.
w: Judicial review
No court decision is involved.
Federal supremacy over the states
The scenario concerns the President and the military, not state laws.
Separation of church and state
The scenario has nothing to do with religion.

sc.title: Use the scenario below to answer the question that follows.
sc.text: During a war, a popular general publicly calls for expanding the fighting into another country, contradicting the President's strategy. The President removes the general from command, despite angry protests from many members of Congress and the public.

items.q: Which statement best describes how the Constitution divides war powers?
items.a: Congress declares war; the President commands the armed forces
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress power to declare war and raise and support armies; Article II, Section 2 makes the President Commander in Chief. Congress has formally declared war in only five conflicts, the last being World War II.
w: The President declares war; Congress commands the armed forces
This reverses the two roles.
The Senate declares war; the House pays for the armed forces
Both houses must pass a declaration of war.
Congress declares war; the Supreme Court approves deployments
The courts have no role in approving deployments.

alt.q: Since 1945 U.S. forces have fought in Korea, Vietnam, the Persian Gulf and Iraq. Which statement about these conflicts is accurate?
alt.a: None began with a formal declaration of war
alt.ex: Congress has not declared war since 1942; later conflicts relied on UN resolutions, presidential action, or congressional authorizations such as the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and AUMFs.
w: Each began with a formal declaration of war
No declaration was made for any of them.
Each rested only on a United Nations treaty
Vietnam and the 2003 Iraq War did not rest on UN authorization alone.
None ever received any vote from Congress
Congress passed the Tonkin Resolution (1964) and authorizations for Iraq (1991, 2002).

alt.q: At the Constitutional Convention, Madison and Elbridge Gerry moved to change Congress's power to "make" war to "declare" war, "leaving to the Executive the power to repel sudden attacks." What does this change suggest?
alt.a: The President could defend the nation in an emergency
alt.ex: Madison's notes (August 17, 1787) show the framers kept the decision to start war with Congress while letting the President defend against sudden attack.
w: The President alone could decide to start any war abroad
The change kept the power to begin war with Congress.
Congress would command troops after a declaration
Command belongs to the President as Commander in Chief.
States would defend themselves without federal help
The change concerned the federal branches, not the states.

items.q: During the Korean War, President Truman ordered the government to seize the nation's steel mills to prevent a strike. In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952), what did the Supreme Court rule?
items.a: The seizure was invalid because Congress had not authorized it
items.ex: In a 6-3 decision, the Court held that neither the Commander in Chief power nor executive power allowed the seizure without a law; Justice Jackson's concurrence said presidential power is weakest when acting against Congress's will.
w: The seizure was valid under the President's Commander in Chief power
The Court rejected that argument; the mills were not a theater of war.
The seizure was valid because Congress had declared war on Korea
Congress never declared war in Korea.
The case was dismissed as a political question for the branches
The Court decided the case on the merits.

alt.q: Which principle does Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) best illustrate?
alt.a: Limits on presidential power, even in war
alt.ex: Youngstown held that the President cannot make law on his own, even during a war, without authority from Congress or the Constitution.
w: Federal supremacy over state labor laws
The case was about the President versus Congress, not states.
Freedom of the press during times of war
Press freedom was the issue in New York Times v. U.S. (1971).
Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce
The case turned on executive power, not the Commerce Clause.

alt.q: A President, citing a foreign war, orders federal officials to take over a private industry without any law from Congress allowing it. Which case would the owners most likely cite?
alt.a: Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer
alt.ex: Youngstown (1952) struck down Truman's seizure of the steel mills as beyond his powers without congressional authorization.
w: U.S. v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.
Curtiss-Wright (1936) described broad presidential power in foreign affairs, which would hurt the owners' case.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu (1944) deferred to wartime military orders, which would not help the owners.
New York Times Co. v. United States
That 1971 case concerned prior restraint of the press.

items.q: In 1950 Truman sent U.S. troops to Korea under a UN Security Council resolution, without asking Congress for a declaration of war. What does this illustrate?
items.a: Presidents starting conflicts as commander in chief
items.ex: Korea set a precedent for major wars fought without a declaration; Truman agreed with a reporter's description of it as a 'police action.'
w: Congress using its power to declare war on a new enemy
Congress did not declare war in Korea.
The Senate using its power to ratify a peace treaty
The Korean War ended with an armistice (1953), not a ratified treaty.
The courts using judicial review to approve a war
No court approved the war.

alt.q: What term did Truman accept for the U.S. intervention in Korea in 1950, avoiding the word "war"?
alt.a: A police action
alt.ex: Truman agreed with a reporter's phrase 'police action,' reflecting that Congress never declared war.
w: A quarantine
Kennedy called the 1962 naval blockade of Cuba a 'quarantine.'
A peacekeeping mission
'Peacekeeping' describes later UN operations; Truman's own phrase for Korea was 'police action.'
A containment
Containment was the broader Cold War strategy, not a name for the Korean intervention.

alt.q: After the September 11 attacks, how did Congress authorize military action against those responsible?
alt.a: By passing an Authorization for Use of Military Force
alt.ex: The AUMF of September 18, 2001 authorized force against those who planned or aided the attacks; Congress did not declare war.
w: By formally declaring war on Afghanistan's Taliban government
No declaration of war was made.
By ratifying a new mutual defense treaty with NATO allies
NATO invoked its existing Article 5; Congress ratified no new treaty.
By amending the War Powers Resolution of 1973
The War Powers Resolution was not amended; the AUMF satisfied its terms.
